Over 200 US rabbis demand US Senate candidate El-Sayed make Jewish safety commitments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
17:02:14 UTC
02:02:14 KST

More than 220 liberal and progressive rabbis from 34 states signed an open letter to Democratic US Senate nominee Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, endorsing the campaign demands of Nonnegotiable Michigan.
This initiative was launched in September by rabbis, cantors, and lay leaders representing congregations serving an estimated 40,000 Jewish Michiganders.
The signatories allege that a disconnect exists between El-Sayed’s public assurances regarding Jewish safety and rhetoric that they argue undermines it.
The letter was released on Friday ahead of a Saturday Get Out the Vote rally at Cass Technical High School in Detroit, where former president Barack Obama made his first public campaign appearance alongside El-Sayed.
Addressing thousands of rally attendees, Obama praised El-Sayed’s candidacy, compared the Senate nominee’s political path to his own, and urged voters to back Democratic candidates as a crucial check on the Trump administration.
However, Obama avoided mention of the ongoing primary disputes over Jewish inclusion and foreign policy.
Throwing their support behind Nonnegotiable Michigan, the new signatories called on El-Sayed to align his campaign with Obama’s legacy of Jewish inclusion within the Democratic Party and requested that Obama reaffirm that Zionist Jews remain full members of the political coalition.
Disconnect between Obama, El-Sayed's inclusion of Jewish voters in Democratic Party
The letter points to what the rabbis describe as a contrast between Obama’s political record and El-Sayed’s campaign statements.
While Obama “welcomed Zionist Jews as full partners in his coalition, and never asked [them] to leave [their] love of Israel at the door,” the rabbis claimed that El-Sayed has repeatedly dismissed concerns raised by Jewish voters.
Further, they said that El-Sayed has been using language that they allege echoes antisemitic stereotypes.
“You have described your campaign as picking up the baton [Obama] carried,” the rabbis wrote. “We urge you to honor the part of his legacy that made Jewish Americans feel safe in our communities and at home in the Democratic Party.”
The signatories stated that while El-Sayed has expressed a commitment to Jewish safety when speaking to Jewish audiences, his broader public rhetoric presents a different narrative.
“Asked about our safety here at home, you offer warm words about Jews and Judaism, but immediately pivot to Israel and foreign wars,” the signatories wrote. “Where [US] President [Donald] Trump blames immigrants for our country’s woes, your rhetoric casts Israel and American supporters of Israel, which includes most of mainstream Jewry, as the source of our neighbors’ pain.”
Specific concerns raised by the rabbis cited past instances where they allege El-Sayed called Israelis “bloodthirsty,” characterized American financial and diplomatic support for Israel as “legalized bribery” and “purchased loyalty,” and described a Jewish state as inherently illiberal.
They also say he told a national audience that Israel uses American funds to push the US into foreign wars. “When El-Sayed’s words reach a national audience, Jews across America feel the consequences – in our inboxes, on our campuses and, even, painfully, within our sanctuaries,” the letter stated.
National impact of El-Sayed's platform
Addressing the national scope of the Senate race, the signatories argued that El-Sayed’s platform extends beyond local Michigan politics.
“Until now, this has been a conversation between you and Michigan’s Jewish community,” the letter noted. “But you are asking to serve in the United States Senate. There, the laws you write, the votes you cast, and the words you speak would shape the safety and belonging of Jews throughout America. A senator from Michigan legislates for all of us.”
The letter even urged Obama directly to use his platform during Saturday’s Detroit rally to address the coalition.
“Please use your voice in Detroit to remind the coalition you built that Jews belong in it fully, safely, and proudly,” the rabbis wrote. “That includes the many of us deeply and inextricably connected to Israel.”
The open letter follows a renewed appeal issued Wednesday by Nonnegotiable Michigan, which said it documented six weeks of unanswered requests for dialogue with El-Sayed before expanding its campaign to include elected officials, Democratic leaders, and college students.
In the letter, the signatories endorsed five core commitments and urged El-Sayed to adopt them publicly.
The five fundamental points are: Affirming that Jewish safety is nonnegotiable; supporting Jewish statehood and self-determination in Israel; asserting that Jews alone define Jewish identity; ensuring Zionist Jews are welcomed in the Democratic Party; and pursuing Palestinian aspirations for safety, dignity, and freedom alongside Israel rather than in place of it.
“When you stand beside president Obama in Detroit, say these five things publicly, in your own words,” the rabbis wrote.
“Then, demonstrate through your words and actions that you mean them. Jewish safety cannot be something you invoke when speaking to Jews, but undermine when speaking to everyone else.”
Neither El-Sayed nor Obama responded to The Jerusalem Post’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Don't waste your vote: What Israelis should consider before election day - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
17:01:23 UTC
02:01:23 KST

Despite my two academic degrees in political science, 12 years working in the Knesset for three different MKs, as well as a few more years there as a lobbyist, and a lifelong interest in Jewish politics in the Diaspora and in Israel, what follows, while reasonable in my opinion, is only a recommended guideline for voters in this week’s elections for the Knesset.
In a democracy, every citizen is free to choose which party’s slip he or she will place in the envelope on election day. Following that principle, I think the best way of assisting voters to make their choice is to concentrate on the factors and elements that should be considered when voting for a candidate and the party one is thinking of supporting.
In other words, I hope to offer an outline of warnings or alerts that should give one a chance to rethink a possible choice one is contemplating. In a sense, my guide highlights who not to vote for. My suggestions that follow are not listed in order of importance, but they are an essential whole.
Polls: Anyone following the polls, and there are at least half a dozen, knows the differences between them.
Differences? I would think there are surprising gaps. The average voter is not privy to the methodology the pollsters are using, the phrasing of the questions, nor the demographics serving as the poll pool.
Even Shimon Peres once said that public opinion surveys, while useful to an extent, “are like perfume: nice to smell, dangerous to swallow.” In fact, in the past few decades, the overwhelming number of polls for the elections have not been accurate, to put it mildly.
I am inclined to remind the voters that our polls have often failed to predict the final distribution of Knesset seats accurately. Moreover, they have overlooked major surprises. Mina Zemach, a famous pollster, had to admit major errors in her reports in the 2003, 2006, and 2019 campaigns.
Threshold clearance: Estimating the vote at 70% of the eligible population in order to cross the threshold for the distribution of the 120 mandates would require a party to gain 166,000 votes. At 65%, the amount would be 154,000, and at 75%, it would total 177,500 votes. Think hard about whether you will be wasting your vote, even for principled reasons, or you have a second-best choice.
Protest vote: Following my previous point, if you are determined to vote for a party hovering around the threshold cut-off, or considering not paying attention to that aspect, are you aware of the ramifications of losing a vote for the camp you belong to? Think how many mandates could be lost to a parallel party.
More questions to consider when deciding whom to vote for
Plans and proposals: Are clear, actual plans being presented? Is the party or the candidates presenting actual plans, or are we being told either platitudes or slogans? Admittedly, very few party platform booklets appear nowadays, but there are party websites where proposals can be fleshed out and read carefully.
Furthermore, do those proposals have a chance of being either legislated or put into practice? Is what the voter is looking for truly achievable?
For example, can all funds be withheld from those who do not serve in the army, including women and children, or at least from the basic civic service they benefit from? Would Israel’s Arab population be included in that plan? Would the courts uphold it?
Another aspect is whether your candidates have enough experience and background to put those plans into action. Has he a proven record of sorts? Political maneuvering is not a battlefield exercise or a laboratory experiment procedure. Are you aware of his previous performance in a critical field of endeavor?
Vote for, not against: It is much better to use your voting slip for someone, on behalf of a program and a political agenda, that you wish to advance. To vote against is a negative action that may help you but may not help the country.
Ability to represent: The reality of Israel’s position and status in world affairs has grown exponentially. Whether engaging with world leaders, speaking at the UN, and confronting foreign ministers or CNN interviewers, a voter would want that; in addition to all the other qualities and ideas a candidate brings, his rhetorical skills will serve him and the country as best as possible.
Ideological stability: Has your candidate made a complete reversal of positions recently? Politicians can change their minds, of course, or even experience an epiphany of sorts. On the one hand, they could feel slighted, insulted, or even threatened. Or the candidate could simply be seeking to continue to receive a salary and an eventual pension.
Candidate lists: Are the rest of the list’s candidates for show and display? Or do they also have some sort of public engagement record? Perhaps there are politicians with previous multiple party affiliations who are just seeking to maintain their public persona or looking for a home? Rethink your choice constantly.
Multiple information sources: Watch as many television channels as you can tolerate, such as 11, 12, and 14. After all, they’re all on your cell phone. Also, if possible, read items from at least two opposing newspapers, like Haaretz and Makor Rishon.
Remember that a media setting of agendas is at play to fix a dominant memory in your minds. Also, when scanning social media platforms, don’t forget the bots trying to play you.
Above all, even though it is your personal vote, think of the country at all times.
The writer is a researcher, analyst, and commentator on political, cultural, and media issues.

Saudi Arabia turns to US AI system as Yemeni pressure mounts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
17:00:37 UTC
02:00:37 KST

Saudi Arabia turns to US AI system as Yemeni pressure mounts
TEHRAN – Failing to protect itself and its proxies in southern Yemen, Saudi Arbia has turned to an American-AI generated system to unsuccessfully counter Yemeni Armed Forces (YAF), also known as Ansarallah.
The war between Ansarallah and Saudi Arabia was resumed after Saudi Arabia on July 13 prevented a passenger plane carrying Ansarallah officials from landing in Sanaa by bombarding the airport, forcing the plane to land at Hodeidah International Airport.
After this reckless move, Ansarallah declared an eye-for-eye reprisal and started to target Saudi facilities, including airports and oil infrastructure. It also began targeting Saudi vessels in the Red Sea in response to the blockade of Yemen which has been in force for more than a decade.
Feeling helpless, Saudi Arabia has asked numerous allies for help. That includes the United States, even though media report that Donald Trump refused when Saudi ruler Mohammed bin Salman asked him to take direct military action against Ansarallah.
Ansarallah’s latest military campaign, which primarily began in September, has taken further control of Yemen's coast. So far, though, military campaigns against Ansarallah by Saudi Arabia, the United States and others have all failed.
Wary of Ansarallah, the U.S. is providing Saudi Arabia with intelligence, which includes a targeting tool that uses AI. A September report by U.S. broadcaster CNN, quoting several unnamed American officials, said that between 100 and 200 U.S. soldiers were in Saudi Arabia as part of new joint force command to facilitate this.
The U.S. personnel were helping the Saudis "use a targeting tool that allows military officers to see in real-time what is happening on the battlefield," CNN reported.
Officials said the system in Saudi Arabia was similar to that known as the Maven Smart System, or MSS for short, which the U.S. military has also used as it sought targets in Iran, Iraq and Syria.
MSS came out of what's known as Project Maven, the U.S. flagship artificial intelligence program for the military, first launched in 2017. MSS itself is an AI-enabled digital platform that "aggregates, organizes and visualizes vast streams of intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance data," analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington explained in a June text.
The software system identifies patterns in data coming from, for example, live satellite feeds or drone cameras and then labels potential targets such as possible rocket launchers, tanks or suspicious vehicle convoys.
Using the MSS dramatically speeds up what is known as "the kill chain" — that is, the time it takes to detect a target, decide if it's dangerous and then order a strike.
Up until recently, the long-simmering war in Yemen had been comparatively calm following an informal ceasefire negotiated in 2022.
Yemen’s Ansarallah has held large parts of northern and western Yemen since 2015. The pro-Saudi government and other groups held territory across the south and east.
There are certain technical issues users have noted with the MSS in the past that could also prove problematic in Yemen.
Ansarallah tends to be highly mobile, using truck-mounted ballistic missiles and small drone swarms as they operate from hills and canyons in rugged countryside. It's possible that fighters might be long gone before they can be attacked even with the help of AI-assisted targeting.
Though MSS is known to work best in relatively unpopulated areas, factors such as changes in desert terrain, dust storms, high wind, snowfall and dense foliage — and even deliberately planted decoys — can reduce its success rate.
There is also a worrying ethical aspect to shortening the kill chain. A human is always supposed to verify the target that the AI-assisted tool has identified and decide how to react.
But it doesn't always work that way. For example, among the sites MSS targeted in Iran on the first day of the war was a school. An American missile killed almost 200 people at a primary school in southern Iran, most of them children aged between seven and 12.
In its military campaign in Gaza, Israel has also used AI-assisted targeting. An Israeli system known as the Gospel, or Habsora, is the closest to MSS in the way it works.
But, as has been documented elsewhere, including by Israeli and British journalists and in the recent documentary Naza, the use of such AI targeting tools have also been highly problematic because of the numbers of civilian casualties that can result.
"On the one hand [in Gaza], AI has enhanced commanders' situational awareness, lessened the human costs of tunnel mapping, improved the speed of military strikes, and boosted the survivability of troops," analysts Frederic Wehrey and Andrew Bonney wrote for War on the Rocks, a specialist media outlet. "Yet the benefits afforded by such functions have been overshadowed by mounting civilian deaths reportedly resulting from this technology's safeguards being loosened or eliminated."
All of which is why Antony Loewenstein, an independent journalist based in Australia who has researched the impact of Israel's AI-assisted technology, doesn't believe similar technology will lead to the defeat of Ansarallah.
"I don't think there's much evidence at all that using an AI tool is going to make much difference on the ground, except for causing huge amounts of civilian casualties," Loewenstein, who authored the book, "The Palestine Laboratory: How Israel Exports The Technology of Occupation Around the World," told DW. "And I think what the US and the Saudis will find is that the Houthis (Ansarallah) have an incredibly high tolerance level for destruction."

The Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado has announced she has returned to Venezuela almost a year after she left the country to receive the Nobel peace prize.

Her close ally Edmundo González, who is in exile, confirmed her arrival. “Venezuela! I am thrilled to announce to you that our leader, my dear María Corina, is on Venezuelan soil,” he posted on social media.

Israel seizes civilian houses in al-Khalil, establishes frontline military posts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Israel seizes civilian houses in al-Khalil, establishes frontline military posts
TEHRAN — Israeli forces have sealed every major entry point into al-Khalil (Hebron), driving more than 2,200 Palestinians out of their homes and transforming entire residential quarters into military barracks.
The punitive siege, ordered directly by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu following a resistance operation on Friday that killed two Israeli soldiers at a nearby checkpoint, has paralyzed the governorate of nearly 800,000 residents.
Municipal leadership in al-Khalil declared the city a disaster zone after troops moved systematically through neighborhoods including al-Jalda, Ein Deir Baha, Khallat Manna, and Dahiyat al-Zaytoun, forcing families out at gunpoint.
The mechanics of this latest aggression follow a pattern perfected by the Israeli army across the northern West Bank.
Soldiers give residents minutes to gather basic belongings before bulldozing storefronts, knocking down outer walls, and stringing razor wire across residential streets.
Over 490 housing units spanning roughly 350 dunams have been commandeered or targeted for clearing, with municipal officials warning that expulsion orders could soon reach 2,500 additional residents.
Concurrently, Israeli forces shut down the historic Ibrahimi Mosque, barring Muslim custodians and worshippers while suspending the call to prayer across the Old City.
Mass arrests have swept through more than 400 sites in a single 24-hour period, according to local prisoner groups, leaving schools closed and municipal services unable to clear accumulating waste beyond the military perimeter.
The timing of this campaign coincides with intense domestic political maneuvering ahead of Israel’s upcoming parliamentary vote.
Far-right ministers such as Itamar Ben-Gvir and Israel Katz have openly touted the displacement of al-Khalil’s population as proof of military resolve.
Local Palestinian officials and experts point out Netanyahu’s cabinet’s use of collective punishment and the desecration of holy sites as a brutal campaign stunt to secure nationalist votes.
Meanwhile, on the agricultural front across the West Bank, regime-backed Israeli settler rampages have damaged nearly 300,000 olive trees since last year, turning the traditional harvest season into another front of land theft and displacement.

France meets second weekend of mass protests with 70,000 police, arrests 1,314
TEHRAN — French police arrested 1,314 people and sealed off city centers on Saturday as hundreds of thousands marched for a second consecutive weekend. Rather than addressing the root causes of the nationwide unrest, the government focused entirely on silencing the demonstrators through state repression.
The Interior Ministry initially said nearly 1,000 people had been detained, then raised the figure to 1,314, along with 75 fires and 24 looted shops.
It counted 410,000 marchers nationwide, 110,000 of them in Paris. Unions and activists say the real turnout was close to double. Whichever number is right, the crowds held steady against a deployment of 70,000 police officers and gendarmes, 20 percent more than a week earlier, backed by SWAT units, helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannon. Shopkeepers boarded up. Museums closed.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez defended the state’s security lockdown by noting that demonstrators had been successfully barred from staging unauthorized marches or entering city centers. For an official representing a self-proclaimed republic, the remarks offered a striking public confirmation of a strategy that kept citizens out of their own urban cores.
The government had already banned non-union demonstrations it labeled “illegitimate.”
The Paris march was mostly calm. Brass bands played, and grandparents walked beside students.
Trouble came at Porte de Vincennes, where the route ended. Masked groups threw bottles and stones, and police replied with tear gas, water cannon and stun grenades, then charged a wider crowd with batons.
Tear gas also kept demonstrators from the centers of Lyon, Lille, Montpellier, Nantes and Toulouse. Two people were seriously hurt in Clermont-Ferrand and Toulouse, one reportedly losing fingers.
French authorities claimed that investigations are already under way into children and other protesters maimed by explosive police weapons.
A plan to switch off the platforms
Two days before the march, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu wrote to Orange, SFR, Free and Bouygues Telecom, according to French outlet Blast.
He asked them to be ready to block TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat and X in the event of “urban violence,” and said he wanted the power to suspend access outright.
The operators answered that they lacked the capacity to do it quickly and that VPNs would defeat the block.
Paris has done this before. It cut off TikTok during the 2024 unrest in New Caledonia and lifted the ban only after several days. The pattern is familiar to anyone who has watched Western governments hypocritically denounce internet shutdowns in Iran and elsewhere, then reach for the same switch at home.
Whose violence gets attention
The destruction on the margins of Saturday’s marches was real, and shopkeepers are counting losses. Yet the official story leaves out who else showed up.
In Nice, prosecutors said 59 people were taken into custody, 11 of them suspected of extreme-right affiliation. Some were stopped in two vehicles carrying masks, gloves, gas sprays, and truncheons. Local media reported these groups going after peaceful demonstrators.
Others found a use for the chaos. Facing elections, Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu seized on the riots to attack immigration, with Netanyahu blaming “Islamic extremists.”
Observers of the unrest describe the wreckers as mostly apolitical young men, many of immigrant origin but born in France. In Orléans, thousands marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen’s National Rally, the party that polls and analysts currently position as the frontrunner for next year’s presidency.
A president with little left to offer
The revolt began in mid-September, when students aged 15 to 18 protested teacher shortages, leaking roofs and classrooms without enough chairs.
Teachers, parents and unions joined, and the grievances grew to cover the cost of living. On October 17, more than half a million people marched.
At least 2,700 were arrested, and Paris City Hall said 450 shops were damaged, 228 of them looted. Police later conceded they had misjudged the scale of the trouble.
Emmanuel Macron meets this with an approval rating of 15 percent, according to Ipsos BVA. He has struggled to pass budgets since losing his parliamentary majority in 2024, and Lecornu has called himself “the weakest prime minister of the Fifth Republic.”
Public debt is near 120 percent of GDP, and Macron’s one signature reform, a higher pension age, had to be frozen.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who marched in Paris, warned that protests will recur every week unless Macron gives in, and he pointed to possible industrial action on November 5.
The anger is not French alone. Tens of thousands marched in Madrid to defend pensions. Portuguese police cleared housing encampments in Lisbon and Porto. Catalan police arrested 128 people in Barcelona, and Italy sent hundreds of troops to Milan. Brussels police used a water cannon on students.
Jérôme Rodrigues, a leading voice of the yellow vests, summed up the standoff. “It’s not police shields that will provide an answer to French people struggling and unable to make ends meet,” he said, according to The Guardian’s Sunday report.

Israeli elections: What can Palestinians expect?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:58:30 UTC
01:58:30 KST

Israeli elections: What can Palestinians expect?
TEHRAN — Israeli elections, scheduled for October 27, are about more than who becomes the next prime minister or whether Netanyahu stays in power.
For Palestinians, the more pressing question is whether the vote could shift Israeli policy on Palestinian statehood and rights. This includes the future of the Gaza Strip and the genocidal war that has devastated it, as well as the regime's approach to the occupied West Bank and the Palestinian Authority.
The positions of the occupation regime's main political candidates show that opposition to Palestinian statehood extends beyond Benjamin Netanyahu.
Palestinian statehood: limits of change
Netanyahu has made blocking Palestinian statehood an explicit policy goal. Naftali Bennett, who is running in an alliance with Yair Lapid, also opposes an independent Palestinian state and any territorial concessions to establish one.
Gadi Eisenkot, a leading challenger to Netanyahu, considers a Palestinian state unrealistic at this stage and has offered no concrete plan to establish one. While his positions on settlements and annexation differ somewhat, his openness to a path toward statehood does not imply support for an independent, sovereign Palestine.
Yair Golan is arguably the only opposition figure to claim that “responsible disengagement” from the Palestinians is a potential path toward some kind of statehood. Yet his plan would still sharply limit Palestinian sovereignty through demilitarization and continued Zionist control over strategic areas.
Avigdor Lieberman goes further, proposing to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, cancel the Oslo Accords, separate Gaza from the West Bank, impose Zionist sovereignty over Area C, and establish an Israeli-Jordanian arrangement to manage other parts of the West Bank.
The main divide is not whether Palestinians should have a sovereign state, which all of these candidates oppose, but how the territories should be governed. Rejecting annexation does not mean ending the occupation. Parties may oppose annexation for demographic and political reasons while still rejecting Palestinian statehood and maintaining Israeli control. This changes the management and nature of the occupation over Palestinians, not its reality.
The West Bank: Annexation, not rights
The parties’ differences are clearer in their positions on the West Bank and illegal settlements.
Lieberman proposes extending sovereignty over Area C, roughly 60 percent of the West Bank, while transferring responsibility for other areas to Jordan. His plan offers no path to Palestinian statehood.
Eisenkot has criticized the E1 settlement project, opposed certain forms of annexation, and condemned settler violence. But opposing specific measures does not mean supporting a withdrawal from settlements or committing to dismantle them.
Bennett rejects territorial concessions for a Palestinian state. Golan, meanwhile, proposes “responsible disengagement” and a halt to annexation, but under broad regime restrictions.
The Palestinian Authority
The dispute over the Palestinian Authority (PA) is another key aspect as it remains the only Palestinian body with a level of administrative power in the West Bank. The PA’s future will shape the relationship between Gaza and the West Bank, the prospects for unified Palestinian leadership, and the path to self-determination.
Israeli parties differ sharply on this issue. Lieberman calls for dismantling the PA and canceling the Oslo Accords. The Democrat party, by contrast, support strengthening the PA and maintaining security coordination, viewing it as a partner in governing West Bank areas and confronting Palestinian resistance forces.
But preserving the PA does not necessarily offer a path to self-determination. Dismantling it could lead to more direct regime control, while maintaining it without a political horizon would leave it administering Palestinian areas without sovereignty over land or borders.
The main parties largely frame the PA in terms of security and administration, rather than the Palestinians’ right to establish an independent political system that reflects their national aspirations.
Gaza: Disarmament without withdrawal
In Gaza, the parties broadly agree on preventing Hamas from returning to power, disarming it, and establishing new governing arrangements. But this consensus does not resolve Gaza’s future or establish whether the occupying regime is prepared to end its military presence and control. Nobody had managed to explain how Hamas will be disarmed considering that a genocidal war failed to achieve this.
Netanyahu and Bennett both condition withdrawal of the Israeli Occupation Forces (IOF) on Hamas’s disarmament. Eisenkot also calls for ending Hamas rule and dismantling its military capabilities. Golan proposes civilian administration, disarmament, and reconstruction under an Arab and international framework, with continued Israeli control of borders and crossings. Lieberman calls for eliminating Hamas and transferring Gaza’s administration to an external body.
The main differences concern who will govern Gaza, the role of Arab and international actors, the terms of reconstruction, and the extent of the IOF withdrawal. Agreement on disarmament and new governing arrangements does not necessarily imply support for Palestinian statehood or a unified Gaza and West Bank.
If the IOF withdrawal remains conditional on open-ended security demands, those conditions could become a means of prolonging Israeli control rather than a path to ending it.
Palestinians: How to read the elections?
Palestinians should assess the elections against three key considerations.
First, the contest is not simply between individual parties but between political blocs. A bloc that secures 61 Knesset seats can form a government, whose policies will be shaped by coalition agreements and commitments among its members.
Second, the main differences between Netanyahu’s camp and its rivals have less to do with Palestinian national aspirations or Gaza’s future than with domestic issues, including the Israeli regime's political direction, ultra-Orthodox military conscription, Zionism, and judicial reform.
Third, although the Palestinian issue remains a security concern for the regime, other priorities have gained prominence following the genocidal war and destruction in Gaza. For instance, developments and worsening conditions in West Bank refugee camps is one. Others include Iran, Lebanon, regional competition with Turkey, expanding the Abraham Accords, and relations with the West.
A key dividing line is Netanyahu’s handling of security. His opponents argue that he has failed to translate military gains into lasting security.
Palestinians should not pin their hopes on who becomes prime minister, but on their ability to rebuild a unified national project, restore political and geographic unity, and mobilize Arab and international support to confront occupation, annexation, and displacement. Only a coherent strategy grounded in their right to freedom and self-determination can turn divisions within Israel’s political system into leverage to challenge and end the occupation.

Venezuela opposition leader María Corina Machado returns to country after 10-month exile
Venezuelan opposition leader and Nobel laureate María Corina Machado is back in her home country after nearly a year in exile, her team confirmed to CBS News on Sunday.
"I am here. With you," Machado posted in Spanish on X.
She did not disclose more details about her current location or how she returned.
Machado's senior adviser David Smoalnsky said in a statement to CBS that her return is "a major step toward a democratic transition and free, fair, and verifiable presidential elections in the near future."
"Machado returns to stand with Venezuelans in their pursuit of freedom, democracy, and justice, and to help advance a peaceful, inclusive, and sustainable transition leading to free, fair, and verifiable presidential elections, with guarantees for all," he said, thanking President Trump, the U.S. government and others for "their continued leadership and support."
Machado covertly snuck out of the South American country in December with a private U.S. rescue team to accept the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize in Norway, her first public appearance in 11 months. The event was a month before the U.S. military deposed the country's then-President Nicolás Maduro.
Machado, who was barred by Maduro's government from exiting Venezuela, is considered a fugitive by the Venezuelan government, which accuses her of calling for military intervention against the country.
Edmundo Gonzalez, a former presidential candidate for Machado's movement who has been living in Spain, confirmed her return in his own social media post and said he would be next to her "very soon."

"María! María!" someone cried out, as another shouted, "Welcome to Venezuela!"
"Long live freedom, damn it!" a man yelled.
One woman wiped away tears and called it "a miracle" while another woman's hands flew to her face as she saw Machado enter the church.
Asked by reporters Sunday about Machado's return to Venezuela, President Trump said, "I don't know anything about it, but I think she's a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel Prize. So how can I say anything else? And I hope she's safe. She's a very nice woman. But we're doing really well in Venezuela."
Machado made several failed attempts to return to her home country, including during the aftermath of the devastating June 24 double earthquakes.
In September, the opposition leader was denied entry into Venezuela three times over 24 hours, Smoalnsky said in a statement shared with CBS News' Margaret Brennan and other journalists.
"She has attempted to enter the country by air and sea but has been turned away each time," he said at the time.
Machado's homecoming comes as doubts over Venezuela's democratic future — and the U.S.'s role in it — deepen.
Since Maduro's ouster, Venezuela has been run by acting President Delcy Rodríguez, a longtime Maduro ally who received the Trump administration's blessing to succeed him.
Rodríguez has exceeded the time she was authorized to serve as acting president following Maduro's capture and no election is scheduled.
Machado and her allies have been demanding a date for a presidential election in Venezuela, but U.S. officials have emphasized economic stabilization first.

Rhino Titan: RAF Delivers Airborne Combat Power at Scale
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:57:17 GMT
01:57:17 KST

The roar of four Atlas C1 A400M aircraft breaks the silence over the German countryside. Inside, hundreds of paratroopers sit shoulder to shoulder beneath the red glow of aircraft lighting, carrying everything they need for the mission ahead. As the aircraft approach the drop zone, final checks are completed, equipment is secured and Parachute Jump Instructors move through the cabin. When the green light illuminates, soldiers dispatch into the sky below.
It is a moment measured in seconds.
Exercise Rhino Titan marks a significant milestone for UK Defence, demonstrating the ability of the Royal Air Force and British Army to generate and deliver a large-scale airborne force at range. At its heart is the Joint Airborne Task Force, bringing together the RAF Air Mobility Force and 16 Air Assault Brigade Combat Team to prove that combat power can be inserted rapidly, precisely and at scale.
For the RAF, the exercise represents the return of battlegroup-level airborne insertion using the Atlas, combining personnel, equipment and supplies in a way not previously achieved with the aircraft.
"Rhino Titan demonstrates the return of large-scale airborne insertion as a capability. The Atlas allows us to deploy combat forces further, faster and more efficiently than previous generations of aircraft, giving Defence the ability to project force rapidly wherever it is required."
Squadron Leader Luke,
Flight Commander on 30 Squadron
Airborne Mission Commander
The exercise sees approximately 700 paratroopers delivered across multiple waves of aircraft onto a German drop zone. While airborne operations have long formed part of British military capability, what makes Rhino Titan different is the scale of the operation and the integration of troops and stores within the same aircraft.
More Than Just Paratroopers
Modern airborne operations are no longer simply about delivering personnel.
Alongside the soldiers will come all the equipment necessary for successful mission execution. These capabilities arrive with the force, enabling troops to become operational almost immediately on landing.
The result is a significant increase in capability.
Previously, stores often required separate aircraft. Now, personnel and equipment can arrive together, generating greater combat power from the same number of aircraft.
The Capability Behind the Jump
What the public sees is a parachutist descending beneath a canopy.
What they rarely see is the extensive planning, training and coordination required before a single soldier boards an aircraft.
"By the time soldiers board the aircraft, a significant amount of planning and preparation has already taken place. Parachute Jump Instructors will have delivered specialist ground training, while detailed planning between aircrew, dispatchers and ground forces coordinates every aspect of the mission."
Squadron Leader Nick,
Officer Commanding Parachute Training Squadron
RAF Brize Norton
Paratroopers often board carrying substantial loads, including parachute equipment, weapons, communications systems and bergen loads weighing up to 50 kilograms. Air Loadmasters and Parachute Jump Instructors supervise the process to ensure soldiers are correctly equipped and positioned before departure.
As the aircraft approaches the drop zone, activity intensifies.
Equipment is checked one final time. Static lines are connected. Soldiers move into position.
Every action follows a precise sequence coordinated with the aircrew. When the green light is given, personnel exit in carefully controlled intervals designed to ensure safety and separation in the air.
Over the last 18 months, the Air Mobility Force and Parachute Training Squadron have increased activity between RAF Brize Norton, Weston-on-the-Green and Salisbury Plain. Training has progressed from basic parachuting serials to formation flying, simulated mass drops and integrated personnel-and-stores delivery.
Force generation has required aircraft, crews and specialist instructors to be dedicated to training despite ongoing global operational commitments.
"The harder we train in exercises, the easier it is to deliver the capability when it's needed."
Squadron Leader Luke
Rhino Titan is now the most significant test of that work, proving the UK's ability to rapidly generate and deploy an airborne force capable of responding to evolving threats and crises.
A NATO Capability
The exercise is also a demonstration of interoperability.
The United Kingdom routinely trains alongside NATO allies through activities such as Exercise Falcon Leap, working with Atlas operators and other tactical airlift nations to develop common tactics, procedures and operating methods.
Exercise Rhino Titan builds on that foundation, bringing together British, French and German partners to demonstrate NATO's ability to deploy combat power collectively and at pace.
The exercise reinforces the importance of strategic air mobility in modern warfare.
The ability to insert personnel by parachute enables forces to deploy beyond established infrastructure, providing commanders with more options while increasing unpredictability for potential adversaries.
Ready to Respond
At the heart of the operation is the Joint Airborne Task Force.
Pathfinders deploy ahead of the main force, validating the drop zone and providing reconnaissance and surveillance capabilities before the larger airborne force arrives. The main force then follows, delivered by RAF aircraft and supported by specialist personnel from across the Air Mobility Force.
While a descending parachute may appear to represent a single-service capability, Squadron Leader Nick is clear that airborne operations depend on a truly joint effort.
"It takes RAF aircrew, engineers, Air Loadmasters, Parachute Jump Instructors and support personnel working alongside the Army to deliver that capability safely and effectively."
Squadron Leader Nick
Rhino Titan is ultimately about demonstrating readiness:
Readiness to deploy.
Readiness to reinforce allies.
Readiness to deliver combat power wherever required.

Europe’s next crisis is already hiding behind the riots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:54:49 UTC
01:54:49 KST

Europe’s next crisis is already hiding behind the riots
These days, European headlines resemble reports from a war zone: from stormed city halls in Marseille and Lille, to looted boutiques along the French Riviera, burned tourist offices in Lyon, and clouds of tear gas enveloping the Élysée Palace. The ‘day of rage’ in France drew over 800,000 protesters onto the streets – an event that was dismissed by Paris and the European mainstream as merely the “spontaneous revolt of the outskirts” or a “raid by migrants.” However, a closer look at the ‘rebels’ reveals respectable, bourgeois-looking students and well-off citizens engaging in destruction and violence.
None of these people know what to expect from the future of mainstream European politics. In this shifting landscape, old institutions are losing their legitimacy, while right-wing political forces – whose ideas are increasingly seen as rational amid the chaos – are emerging on the broader European stage.
Portrait of the protesters: what happened?
French President Emmanuel Macron arrogantly advised the people to express their political will in six months during the forthcoming presidential elections; however, the streets responded to Macron’s proposal with looting and arson targeting government buildings. This reaction serves as a precise diagnosis of the French political system. The country’s civic framework can no longer hold society together and there is no confidence in a stable future.
Many believe that the current riots in France are a “spontaneous revolt of the outskirts.” However, as Fyodor Lukyanov, Research Director at the Valdai International Discussion Club writes, we are witnessing an inverted version of May 1968. Nearly 60 years ago, the nationwide wave of protests led by students and leftist intellectuals shaped the liberal framework that has dominated global and European politics ever since.
Today, it has reached the point of aggressive absurdity. The old narratives of ‘liberation’ have been successfully adopted by the bourgeois youth, whose behavior is more violent that of an uncivilized tribe, as HSE professor Alexander Filippov notes. But then, one may remember that, centuries ago, the Bastille wasn’t stormed by migrants either.
How did this happen? The liberal establishment in Paris and Brussels has become totally detached from ordinary citizens. Its agenda is completely irrelevant to society. Having imposed a rigid “confrontation with Russia” at the expense of the prosperity and development of its own people, the EU offers its citizens no viable ideas for survival.
President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen suggested at a Paris business forum in August that Europeans should tighten their belts and become a continent that “produces, invests, and protects” by tapping into “idle” domestic savings. Her logic implies using household savings to fund the real economy through the Capital Markets Union. Clearly, the proposal to dip into citizens’ savings while shifting the risks of factory bankruptcies onto them can only be met with outrage by the decent bourgeoisie brought up on ‘European ideals’.
The system has set a trap for itself: in order to retain its waning power, the left-liberal establishment is forced to close its eyes to the riots of anarchists and radical leftists. The authorities fear street protests far less than the rise of their right-wing opponents. The liberal mainstream would rather burn cities than allow rational thinkers with worldviews grounded in national interests to come to power.
Despite their passion for destruction, the rioters have no idea how to reconstruct the future of united Europe. Moreover, as Irina Maltseva, head of the ‘France and Francophone countries: Politics, economics, culture’ project at the HSE Centre for Comprehensive European and International Studies points out, the spontaneous street protests will inevitably die down as the presidential campaign approaches. Protests will wane, leaving us to wonder – what comes next?
The fight between left-wing and right-wing forces in Europe
The escalating competition between right and left-wing factions in Europe has transcended mere philosophical debate. It would be a mistake to view each new crisis as an isolated anomaly within the EU. Incidents like the riots in Paris, the brief unrest in Milan, the migration chaos in Ceuta, or the victory of the far-right in Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt state are all interconnected threads in the same narrative, best described as the collapse of the prevailing model.
Beneath the ideological clash between the right and left lies a harsh economic reality – the struggle over who will bear the costs of the sanctions crisis orchestrated by the European Commission. The establishment has attempted to persuade the world that a post-industrial economy – characterized by AI integration, cryptocurrency transactions, a shift toward green energy, Capital Markets Union speculations, and “normative” values – is more important than factories, raw materials, ports, and affordable energy. However, this is a path to economic self-destruction. The street protests in France and Italy vividly illustrate that Europe can no longer afford to uphold its previous social contract. Budget deficits are spiraling out of control and are becoming the EU’s economic curse.
Budapest serves as a prime example of this systemic failure. The Hungarian Parliament is currently reviewing the national budget proposal. Prime Minister Peter Magyar acknowledged that the country is grappling with a record-breaking, suffocating budget deficit of 7.5% to 8.3% of GDP. The economic strategies of past years, reliant on uninterrupted cheap energy from Russia and long-term loans from China, have collapsed under the pressure of the REPowerEU plan.
The Hungarian government’s only remaining support mechanism is the so-called ‘solidarity contribution’ tax imposed on excessive profits in opposition-led cities, but local governments can no longer afford to pay it amid the current crisis. To prevent Hungary from experiencing large-scale social upheavals similar to those in France, Magyar is urgently implementing a progressive tax system, cutting government contracts, imposing a wealth tax on billionaires, and escalating tensions with EU leadership by demanding the immediate unfreezing of €16 billion in EU grants, while threatening Orban with lifetime imprisonment if he pushes the opposition onto the streets.
The analysis of the internal dynamics of economic issues in the EU, however, should not boil down to a simplistic equation of ‘budget deficit = street protests’. For example, we may wonder why there are no protests in Poland and Romania, despite similar or even more severe budget deficits (7.3% and 7.9%, respectively), while Albania (a rather financially stable country and non-EU member) is engulfed in turmoil and the Flamingo Revolution.
The answer seems to lie in the differing nature of the deficit and the resilience of national institutions. In Poland and Romania, budget shortfalls are currently masked by rampant electoral populism and ‘social bribes’ – like Romania’s subsidies for farmers or Poland’s price caps at gas stations.
The government manages to mitigate discontent with funds extracted from big business. However, in France, the government has completely exhausted this option. The budget deficit has led to direct cuts in essential social commitments – from school funding to suburban support – quickly eroding its legitimacy.
For many Europeans, the right-wing agenda and national self-interest have become the only rational option. Right-wing pragmatists propose a clear audit and financial protection, while Brussels’ liberal framework advocates for insolvency for the sake of rather dubious dogmas.
The tactics of growing competition, or how to succeed in the ‘darkroom’
Contemporary global politics resembles a sort of ‘darkroom’ where old rules no longer apply, and new ones are still taking shape. The key revelation is that the ‘new right’ has learned to navigate this darkness by playing by Brussels’ own rules. There’s a growing understanding that to save the industrial base from stifling deficits, ideological romanticism must be abandoned.
A good example is Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni. Her approach has shown that it’s possible to dutifully follow external Euro-Atlantic rituals while negotiating exceptions from Brussels on crucial issues vital to the national economy – such as energy or migration.
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico follows a similar path, cleverly blending leftist social principles with hardline national populism. Bratislava is demanding official transitional periods and exemptions from the European Commission to continue receiving Russian gas, citing the need to protect the wallets of its voters.
A comparable maneuver is being executed by Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis; while his policies can’t be called pro-Russian, pragmatism dictates a simple truth: if Czech factories want to survive amid America’s selfish diesel policy, they’ll need to negotiate with Moscow. Even Hungary has adeptly shifted the discussion to a language of tough bargaining. Budapest has formally agreed to comply with REPowerEU requirements and phase out Russian energy supplies by October 2027, but insists that the EU must provide compensation, or else Hungarian companies will face bankruptcy.
Poland’s stance is particularly notable. Rhetorically, Warsaw demands a complete sanctioning of Eurasian projects, presenting itself as Europe’s “primary eastern shield.” Yet this is merely an attempt to maintain appearances during a losing game. Internal realities compel Warsaw to negotiate with Beijing to preserve transit through the Malaszewicze hub and to impose a 60% windfall tax on its state-owned company Orlen to temporarily quell public dissatisfaction at gas stations ahead of elections.
Remarkably, this ‘trial by rage’ is unfolding not only within the EU, and it doesn't only affect Western capitalist giants. The trend is taking on a global scale.
In Albania, the ‘Flamingo Revolution’ is brewing. The social upheaval was sparked by the allocation of resort zones for a mega project spearheaded by Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and undermined the decade-long stability of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama’s left-liberal government. In a desperate attempt to cling to his dwindling legitimacy, Rama resorted to his usual tactics, accusing street protesters of links to the American Antifa political movement and “Moscow’s influence.”
The pendulum has swung even further in India, where a massive youth uprising led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and Rahul Gandhi’s opposition alliance has paralyzed major cities from New Delhi to Mumbai. Although the immediate trigger was the Special Intensive Revision of electoral polls, the underlying issue is similar to the problem in France: the pro-American digital outsourcing model and liberal dogmas can no longer sustain the younger generation amidst a global crisis.
The issue isn’t capitalism per se, but rather the collapse of its specific, degenerate form: liberal globalization. In its place arises a rigid, sovereign capitalism rooted in national self-interest. The new right-wing pragmatists are not ‘Moscow’s friends’. They merely advocate for their own wallets in times of scarcity.
For Russia, this is an important signal: the West’s ‘unified’ sanctions policy has turned into an uncomfortable, but purely decorative facade; and behind it, we glimpse scenes of impressive but ultimately meaningless discontent. In this light, a critical question arises – will the political mainstream acknowledge its defeat and negotiate with its opponents, or will it continue to operate under the “apres nous, le deluge” (after us, the flood) principle? A key indicator will be the formation of a coalition between the ruling government and right-wing forces in Saxony-Anhalt, and their ability to govern effectively and maintain power in the long term.

Israeli-founded app Waze 'mapped sensitive areas of Malaysia': official
Israeli-founded navigation app Waze has mapped out sensitive locations not registered on public maps in Malaysia, the head of the country's National Cyber Security Agency (NACSA) has said.
The app, which is now owned by Google's parent company, has come under scrutiny from the Malaysian government in recent weeks over concerns about data being accessible to the state of Israel.
"We do not deny that the data is with them, including locations that may not have been placed on the map, sensitive areas," said NACSA head Megat Zuhairy Megat Tajuddin in a Malay-language statement carried by local media.
"If you remember, in the early stages of Waze's development, if we wanted to go back to our hometown, the directions given were not correct. However, after years of use, we Malaysians have provided the information the application needs."
He also said Malaysia had around 6.9 million Waze users in 2019, making it the app’s fifth-largest national user base at the time.
"Because of the input provided by us, Waze has a huge amount of information on locations and mapping in Malaysia," Megat said.
Earlier this week, Malaysia's government barred civil servants from using the app while on official duties, citing the need to "protect government information and users' personal data from the threat of misuse by the Israeli regime".
Several Malaysian officials have raised concerns over Waze’s terms of service, which state that the agreement is governed by Israeli law and disputes fall under the exclusive jurisdiction of courts in Israel’s Tel Aviv district.
Waze has rejected Malaysia’s claims, saying allegations that the platform collected sensitive information or allowed any entity to exploit users’ personal data were entirely false.
Earlier this month, Iraq banned the navigation app citing similar concerns.
Israel, which has no diplomatic ties with Malaysia, has previously been accused of conducting operations within Malaysia targeting Palestinians. This includes the 2018 assassination of engineer Fadi al-Batsh in Kuala Lumpur, and a failed attempt to kidnap a Palestinian computer engineer in 2022.

Thousands of sheep take over Madrid's streets for Transhumance Festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:52:23 UTC
01:52:23 KST

The flock of 1,250 sheep and 160 goats set off from Casa de Campo before crossing the Puente del Rey and making its way through the historic centre. Bells chimed and animals bleated as crowds of residents and tourists lined the streets to watch, take photographs and follow the procession.
Several shepherds wore traditional dress, while others carried young lambs or offered treats to their animals. Folk musicians added to the festive atmosphere as the flocks filled streets and squares normally dominated by traffic.
The event marks transhumance, the centuries-old practice of moving livestock between summer and winter pastures along vías pecuarias (drovers’ routes). At Plaza de la Villa, officials staged the traditional payment of 50 maravedís per thousand animals, a symbolic ceremony dating from 1418.
This year’s route was altered to avoid Puerta del Sol, where housing campaigners have set up a protest camp following the eviction and subsequent death of an 87-year-old local resident.
Beyond celebrating rural heritage, the festival highlights the environmental value of traditional grazing: by consuming vegetation, the animals help reduce flammable undergrowth and lower wildfire risks.

Algeria senate approves sending troops to Niger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:50:07 UTC
01:50:07 KST

Breadcrumb
Algeria senate approves sending troops to Niger
Algeria's upper house of parliament on Sunday approved a proposal to deploy troops to neighbouring Niger to "protect energy facilities", a senator speaking on condition of anonymity told AFP.
Any overseas deployment would mark a first since Algiers sent troops to support Egypt during the 1973 Arab-Israeli war.
The legislator said 148 senators in the 174-seat body voted in favour of the move. The parliament's lower house is set to vote on the proposal later in the day, likely to approve it as well.
The rare measure from Algeria comes as Algiers and Niamey strengthen security ties after moving earlier this year to repair strained relations and following a thwarted mutiny in Niger in August.
Niger faces persistent attacks by armed groups, including in areas near the border with Algeria.
The neighbours, who share a 960-kilometre (600-mile) desert border, have agreed to deepen cooperation against jihadist violence, cross-border crime and trafficking.
"This decision marks a historic break with Algeria's doctrine of non-intervention in military conflicts beyond its borders," said Abdellah Akir, an international relations researcher.
"It's driven by the need to protect Algeria's strategic depth in the Sahel and to secure the future trans-Saharan gas pipeline," Akir told AFP.
The two countries have been working to build the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline (TSGP), a vast project to export natural gas to Europe from Nigeria via Niger.
'Strong signal'
Akir said the measure also sought to "send a strong signal to competing actors, including Morocco and the United Arab Emirates" - two countries with which Algiers no longer has diplomatic ties.
Geoff Porter, an analyst with the North Africa Risk Consulting group, said the move was "illustrative of a shift in Algerian policy".
Algeria "had tried to maintain its national interests and exert its regional influence through its customary means - dialogue, international law, multilateral forums," Porter told AFP.
"But in a multipolar and transactional world, those don't work anymore. Instead, Algeria moved toward more tangible means - actual physical presence."
"Algeria is still committed to its foreign policy principles," he added. "It's just demonstrating them in a new way."
Earlier this month, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune signalled the possibility of military involvement in the Sahel country.
"We will protect Niger no matter what," he said in a televised address on 3 October. "There are countries, which I will not name, that have conspired against (Niger). We stand by its side."
"Today, we have interests," Tebboune then said. "We have reached agreements (with Niger) in the oil, mining and other sectors, and some are seeking to destroy all of this overnight."
Algeria's highly unusual measure to deploy troops outside its territory requires the approval of two-thirds of its parliament, according to a constitutional amendment from 2020.
Gifted warplanes
The vote followed a visit last Wednesday by Niger's Defence Minister Salifou Modi to Algeria, where he met with Tebboune and army chief Said Chengriha.
A military cooperation protocol was signed by the two sides, according to Algerian reports, but no details were given at the time.
The move also comes months after Algiers gifted four military helicopters to Niamey.
The warplanes were deployed at the request of Nigerien authorities, the Algerian defence ministry said.
Additionally, Algeria inaugurated a 40-megawatt power plant in June intended to supply electricity to Niamey and surrounding areas.
Algeria and Niger's relations had been strained for months following Algeria's downing last year of a drone from Mali.
The incident triggered a diplomatic row, with Niger joining fellow junta-led allies Mali and Burkina Faso in recalling its ambassador from Algiers.
Algeria and Mali have since resumed diplomatic ties.
Niger has been run by General Tiani since a coup in July 2023 that toppled the elected president Mohamed Bazoum, who has been detained ever since.

While Trump’s DoJ has claimed there might be “voter confusion” on Alaskan ballots, potentially propelling Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola to victory, election experts maintain that this position is legally weak.
“The legal claim is so absurdly thin, there’s essentially no likelihood of success,” said Derek Mueller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, in a blogpost.
Another expert, David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research, said this suit marked “an unprecedented intervention by the federal government” and noted that Alaska’s courts had “fully litigated” this issue.
The lawsuit, Becker said, “raises serious concerns about political interference” and that he could not remember “ever attempting to stop the certification of an election – and certainly not 11 days before polls close”.
Richard H Pildes, a law professor at New York University who focuses on elections, told the New York Times: “It is one of the weakest election lawsuits I’ve ever seen.”
“It should have no realistic chance of success in the courts,” Pildes said.

Google-backed Clear Sky honors teen suicide prevention app amid Israel's trauma crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:52 UTC
01:46:52 KST

In collaboration with Clear Sky
The mental health crisis that followed the October 7 attacks has exposed a major challenge for Israel: How can a healthcare system meet soaring demand for psychological treatment when the number of people seeking help far exceeds the available resources? One Israeli organization believes technology can help bridge that gap, not by replacing therapists, but by giving professionals and patients additional tools to cope with trauma and emotional distress.
Clear Sky, a nonprofit established in response to the October 7 attacks, marked a significant milestone this week with a technological innovation awards ceremony at Google's offices in Tel Aviv. The event highlighted initiatives designed to improve mental health care, including a digital tool intended to support teenagers at risk of suicide.
"We established Clear Sky right after October 7, with the idea and vision of bringing technology into the mental health field and trying to narrow the gap between supply and demand through the Israeli innovation we've trusted for so many years," said Adi Yoffe, a business futurist and co-founder of the organization.
According to Yoffe, the goal is to harness Israel's technological capabilities to address the country's growing emotional and psychological needs.
One of the main obstacles the organization's founders identified was the relatively conservative approach that has characterized medicine and mental health treatment for decades.
"Mental health is one of the most conservative fields in medicine," said Prof. Ehud Davidson, chairman of Clear Sky and former CEO of Clalit Health Services, Israel's largest health maintenance organization, who has also headed hospitals.
"We saw a field of medicine with almost no technologies capable of advancing or accelerating treatment, or allowing us to move beyond the traditional one-on-one model toward an entirely different approach."
The organization stresses that technology should not come at the expense of the human relationship between therapists and patients. Instead, it aims to strengthen that relationship by making practical, accessible tools available to more people.
"Technology and therapy can work wonderfully together if technology is introduced in the right places," said Clear Sky CEO Yael Aberman. "The human being is always part of the process. We're not removing people or the human connection. Quite the opposite. We want to empower people and give them tools."
An app designed to help teenagers at risk of suicide
The annual innovation awards ceremony brought together organizations involved in mental health care and technology, including the Defense Ministry, pharmaceutical company Teva and its Caring for the Mind initiative, Joint Israel and Google.
The event showcased technological projects aimed at strengthening mental resilience and improving access to mental health support.
Among the winners was Dr. Amit Shalev, a psychiatrist and head of child and adolescent psychiatry at Hadassah Medical Center in Jerusalem, who presented a digital tool already being used at the hospital.
"The app we submitted to the competition is a safety-planning program designed for teenagers with suicidal tendencies," Shalev explained.
"The app was developed in the United States and translated into Hebrew by our team. It helps identify triggers, cope with moments of intense impulses, regulate emotions and deal with distress. It also addresses the question: Who can I turn to when things get difficult?"
The application is intended to provide structured support during periods of emotional distress. Its recognition at the awards reflects the effort to incorporate digital tools into existing mental health services, rather than rely exclusively on traditional treatment methods.
"It's encouraging to have an organization that supports these processes, provides encouragement and accompanies them," Shalev said.
For Yoffe, the awards ceremony represented an opportunity to recognize organizations already bringing technology into mental health care. "We want to celebrate organizations in Israel that are implementing technologies in mental health and helping large numbers of people through technological innovation," she said.
Google's involvement is a central part of Clear Sky's effort to bring together the technology sector and mental health professionals. The awards initiative was supported by Google.org, the company's philanthropic arm, and the ceremony took place at Google's Tel Aviv offices.
Noa Elefant-Loffler, Google's director of public policy and government affairs in Israel, described the collaboration as an opportunity to address a pressing social challenge. "We see technology as an important tool for solving social problems, certainly in mental health, where there is so much need and so few solutions," she said.
"The collaboration between Google and Clear Sky gives us an opportunity to bring the power of technology together with entrepreneurs and people working on the ground to create positive change. From our perspective, this is an excellent model, and it's important that it continues."
The partnership reflects the organization's broader ambition to connect Israeli technological expertise with the people and institutions providing mental health care. Looking ahead, Aberman believes Israel's experience of turning urgent national challenges into technological innovation could offer a model for the mental health sector.
"When I look at Israel today, I see that we're leaders in technology, agriculture and cybersecurity because we faced existential needs," she said. "The same is true today of our need in mental health. We have to find ways to harness technology to serve that need."
In collaboration with Clear Sky

HK agents risk losing Taiwan status
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:50 UTC
01:46:50 KST

Any Hong Kongers who collaborate with China to carry out transnational repression in Taiwan would have their Taiwanese citizenship or residency revoked, an official familiar with the matter said yesterday.
The comment came after the Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office on Oct. 7 issued arrest warrants for two Hong Kongers, who allegedly in 2024 hired a Taiwanese private investigation agency to surveil Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋).
Two Taiwanese private investigators, Cheng Yung-chin (鄭永津) and Hsieh Yi-chen (謝乙辰), were indicted on charges of illegally collecting and using personal data under the Personal Data Protection Act (個人資料保護法), alongside two employees, Chiang Wen-hsin (江文鑫) and Hou Kai-han (侯凱瀚), over the surveillance of Shen, the DPP’s Taipei mayoral candidate in next month’s local elections.
Photo: Reuters
Cheng was allegedly hired by Hong Kongers Kuk Kok-yin (鞠覺賢) and Lam Hing (林慶) on Sept. 5, 2024.
The suspects allegedly recorded Shen’s and his family’s movements from Oct. 1 to Nov. 8, 2024, and sent the footage via Telegram to Cheng, who forwarded it to Kuk, prosecutors said.
The suspects ran into difficulties tailing Shen because of his bodyguards, investigators found, adding that Kuk and Lam, flew to Taiwan to allegedly oversee the operation, and discuss surveillance tactics with the investigators.
Kuk and Lam entered Taiwan multiple times starting in September 2024, but are not currently in the country, prosecutors added.
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the two Hong Kongers were not residing in Taiwan, but they allegedly committed a crime in the nation, which appeared to have been directed as part of a systematic campaign of transnational repression.
While arrest warrants have been issued for the two suspects, judicial cooperation between Taiwan and Hong Kong has almost frozen, making the case difficult to prosecute, they said, adding that the Hong Kong government is unlikely to extradite the suspects.
The priority is to quickly apprehend the suspects, they said, adding that securing arrests was crucial in cases of Chinese transnational repression.
The government aims to establish a system that would ensure swift arrest and severe sentences as a countermeasure, they said.
That would require rapid communication and coordination among government agencies to ensure a timely response to transnational repression, they said.
Close cooperation among police, prosecutors and judicial authorities is also required to quickly investigate crimes, track suspects and arrest them before they leave Taiwan, they added.
The Ministry of Justice is considering amendments to the Anti-Infiltration Act (反滲透法) to increase penalties, they said.
If acts of transnational repression orchestrated by the Chinese Communist Party continued to be prosecuted under ordinary laws, the penalties would be too lenient, the official said.
Citing the attack on Japanese political commentator Akio Yaita in July as an example, the official said the assailant, who allegedly punched Yaita in the face, was also a Hong Konger.
Prosecutors on Oct. 6 indicted Liao Gangfa (廖港發), 33, on charges of assault, public insult and participation in a criminal organization, seeking a five-year prison sentence.
The official also cited a case in which China allegedly dispatched a female real-estate agent to follow and collect information about President William Lai’s (賴清德) family members in the US.
While such offenses carry severe penalties in the US, Taiwan lacks a dedicated law targeting transnational repression, making legislative amendments necessary to deter such acts, the official said.
Transnational repression crimes should no longer be treated solely as contraventions of individual rights, but as offenses against national interests that warrant heavy sentences, they said.
Otherwise, suspects would face relatively minor charges, such as violations of the Personal Data Protection Act, they said.

χ A number of countries have lost their independence as a result of foreign “economical aid.”
Photo: AdobeStock 照片：AdobeStock
註：economical 是「節儉的」、「節約的」、「合算的」。economic 是「有關經濟方面的」，如 economic policies, economic history 等。
2. 他的實驗雖然失敗了，可是他的努力卻值得稱讚。
ˇ Though his experiment failed, his efforts are worthy of praise.
Photo: Adobe Stock 照片：Adobe Stock
ˇ Though his experiment failed, his efforts are worth praising.
χ Though his experiment failed, his efforts are worth praise.
註：to be worth 作「價值」解時，後面接金額；作「值得」解時，後面接動名詞。例如：
The pen is worth 8 dollars.
The book is well worth reading.
to be worthy of 作「值得」解，後面接名詞。
3. 這本書值得你看。
ˇ It is worth your while to read this book.
ˇ This book is worth reading.
χ It is worth to read this book.
註：worth 作「值得」解時，不能單獨在句中作補語形容詞用，在以先行詞 it 引導的句型中，應與 while 連用。例如：
It is worth while to see this film twice.
It is not worth while to bother about such trifles.
4. 首先，你們都必須用功讀書。
ˇ First, you all must study hard.
χ At first, you all must study hard.
註：at first 是「起初」、「當初」或「開始時」，等於 in the beginning，而不是「首先」或「第一」。例如：
At first I found French difficult, but I liked it from the start.
「首先」、「第一」是 first, in the first place 或 first of all。例如：
First, I will explain my topic. Next, I will give you some background material.。
5. 他努力學習日語。
ˇ He studies Japanese hard.
χ He studies Japanese hardly.
註：hard 和 hardly 都是副詞，但 hardly 作「幾乎不」解。例如：I could hardly understand him.（我幾乎不懂他的話）。hard 指「努力」、「用功」，兩者絕不可混淆。
Exercises
A. 起初我不喜歡英文，但現在卻喜歡。
__________ I didn’t like English but now I do.
1. Firstly 2. At first 3. First 4. In first
B. 這博物館很值得參觀。
This museum is well __________ visiting.
1. worthy 2. worth of 3. worth 4. worthy for
Answers: A. 2 B. 3

OpenAI resumes training AI, but without Internet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:45 UTC
01:46:45 KST

OpenAI has begun cutting off Internet access for its most capable artificial intelligence (AI) models during the training process in response to prior incidents in which its systems breached other companies.
The company said in a blog post on Friday that, after a pause last month, it had resumed training its most advanced models, but intends to block Internet access until it feels it has adequate safeguards in place to mitigate the risk of unreleased models being able to take unapproved actions online during training.
“Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems and the security of Internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no Internet access,” the company said.
Photo: Reuters
Late last month, the company said it would pause training its most advanced AI models after it discovered that one of its AI agent systems that was being trained in what was supposed to be a secured, Internet-free environment was able to gain access to the Web to reach an external, third-party chatbot.
At the time, OpenAI described the breakout as the first security incident of its kind since a combination of models gained Internet access during internal testing and inadvertently breached the system of the AI platform Hugging Face in July.
OpenAI said that after the Hugging Face incident, it reduced the connections through which its models might be able to reach the Internet during training and testing, but kept some for the purpose of metrics, logging and authentication. It also spent a vast amount of computing power on tasking agentic AI systems with identifying vulnerabilities in its training environments as part of a red-teaming effort, a phrase typically used to describe deliberate attempts to break into systems to uncover vulnerabilities before real attackers can.
“Our red-teaming agents found vulnerabilities in almost every one of these services that gave them limited forms of Internet access,” the firm said.
The company said it has since deployed software patches, imposed tighter network restrictions and disclosed the findings to vendors.
There have been a series of disclosures in the past few months from OpenAI and rivals including Anthropic PBC about incidents in which their models carried out self-directed attacks or unsanctioned actions on third-party Web sites and systems.
These cases, and a series of stark warnings from within the industry, have vaulted the safety debate into the mainstream. AI developers have warned that their systems could become too sophisticated for people to control, adding to concerns the technology could be used by malicious human actors.

“Limited visibility has resulted in the cancellation of the Australian MotoGP,” organizers said.
Photo: AFP

While a blow for Ducati’s Marquez, it was an escape for Aprilia’s Martin, who had been ruled out of the race with a fractured forearm sustained when he crashed during the sprint on Saturday, won by his fellow Spaniard.

His team said in a statement the break was not as bad as initially thought.
“The only confirmed injury is a non-displaced fracture of the distal radius,” Aprilia said, meaning the bone remains aligned. “Consequently the rider will not be returning to Spain and will undergo the necessary treatment over the coming days.”
The picturesque and often windswept Phillip Island track has been a staple on the calendar since 1997, but its contract expires this year.
Promoter MotoGP Sports Entertainment wanted to broaden its appeal and shift it to Melbourne’s Albert Park, which hosts the Australian Formula One.
The Victoria state government was adamant it should remain at Phillip Island.
With negotiations breaking down, South Australia stepped in and secured the race for six years from next year in Adelaide — the first MotoGP to be held in a city center location.
