128 arrested in Barcelona riots as Italy detains activist who praised Hamas' October 7 massacre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:51:08 UTC
00:51:08 KST

Spanish police arrested 128 people during a night of looting, vandalism and violent unrest in Barcelona, authorities announced Sunday, as a wave of youth-led protests continued to sweep across European cities. Meanwhile, Italian police detained a 30-year-old pro-Palestinian activist suspected of encouraging further unrest through social media, with local reports revealing his history of praising Hamas' October 7 attack on Israel.
The disturbances in Barcelona began Saturday evening, when hundreds of young people gathered around Plaça de Catalunya, one of the city's busiest central squares, following calls circulated on social media. The gathering had not been authorized by local authorities and quickly descended into violence.
Video footage shared online showed groups of young people, many dressed entirely in black and wearing masks, running through the streets, smashing store windows and carrying away stolen merchandise. Clothing, footwear and electronics stores were among the businesses targeted.
According to the Catalan regional police, known as the Mossos d'Esquadra, 23 businesses were vandalized or looted, while firefighters responded to 33 fires involving street furniture, garbage containers and other property.
More than half of those arrested were minors, according to authorities. Catalan police chief Sílvia Catà said 73 detainees were under 18, while other police summaries put the figure at 72. Only two of those arrested had previous records for public disorder offenses. Fifteen police officers were injured during the disturbances, four of them seriously.
Some of the most alarming scenes unfolded inside shopping establishments. Videos showed customers trapped inside stores, including the El Corte Inglés department store, after security shutters were lowered to prevent looters from entering.
Other footage showed masked rioters kicking through shop windows before fleeing with merchandise. In several cases, participants broadcast their actions live on social media, where viewers could be seen encouraging them.
Barcelona Mayor Jaume Collboni condemned the violence and warned that those responsible would face legal consequences, including potential action against the guardians of minors involved.
Catà described the disturbances as violence for its own sake, saying investigators were working to establish the backgrounds of those detained and determine how the unrest had been organized.
Although the participants did not appear to belong to a single organization, police said they had coordinated their activities through social media. Online posts encouraged young people to join an anti-establishment movement, sometimes using the slogan Instituts Indignats, a reference to the French Lycéens Indignés, or "Angry High School Students," movement that has mobilized demonstrators in France in recent weeks.
The incidents come amid a broader wave of demonstrations across Europe, although the protests have varied significantly in their demands and levels of violence.
Soldiers deployed in Milan, protesters enter Rome's Colosseum
Italy has become another focal point of the unrest, particularly Milan, where violent clashes and looting the previous weekend involved approximately 2,000 young demonstrators, according to police. Many were teenagers from working-class suburbs, including children of immigrant families.
Italian authorities responded to fears of renewed violence Saturday by deploying large numbers of police officers and soldiers to major cities.
In Milan, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government sent an additional 500 soldiers to reinforce the security presence, alongside thousands of police and other law enforcement personnel. Authorities also conducted preventive checks and tightened security around transport hubs and shopping districts.
Businesses prepared for the worst. Luxury retailers in Milan's famous fashion district, including Omega, Tiffany and Gucci, covered their windows with wooden boards to protect them from potential attacks.
Thousands of demonstrators nevertheless gathered in the city, chanting slogans against Meloni and displaying banners reading "No to the lies of the state." One group dumped waste outside the offices of Italy's energy regulator and burned a symbolic oversized electricity bill in protest against rising costs.
Despite fears of another violent outbreak, the main demonstration in Milan ended largely peacefully, in contrast to the previous weekend's destruction. A separate group of about 30 far-right activists, described as soccer hooligans associated with Inter Milan, appeared briefly and shouted anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim slogans before being isolated by police.
Rome also saw heightened security, with authorities restricting access to luxury shopping streets and major landmarks. A small group of protesters attempted to force its way into the Colosseum, and some entered the ancient amphitheater before being escorted out by security personnel.
Elsewhere in the capital, an anti-war march turned tense despite organizers' efforts to prevent violence. Participants had been urged to keep their faces uncovered and their hands visible to demonstrate that they had no intention of attacking police.
Nevertheless, brief confrontations broke out near Piazza della Repubblica, where officers used batons, tear gas and water cannons to disperse demonstrators. Similar tensions were reported in other Italian cities, including Turin, as protests continued over economic hardship, government policies and international conflicts.
The Moroccan-origin activist suspected of inciting unrest
As Italian authorities investigated the violence in Milan, attention turned to Youssef Siher, a 30-year-old Italian citizen of Moroccan descent who had become prominent in pro-Palestinian activist circles.
Police detained Siher on Saturday following an investigation into a social media movement called Movimento 17 ottobre, or "October 17 Movement," which promoted demonstrations across several Italian cities.
According to Italian reports, Siher created an Instagram page and Telegram group after the initial outbreak of violence in Milan, using the platforms to encourage further demonstrations and urge followers to take control of public squares.
Investigators suspect that the online campaign sought to capitalize on anger among young Italians, particularly those from immigrant backgrounds, toward the authorities.
Following searches of properties associated with Siher, investigators reportedly recovered electronic files containing proposed gathering points and organizational details for demonstrations planned for Saturday. At least one of those locations was subsequently used by pro-Palestinian protesters.
Siher was detained on orders from Milan prosecutors and is under investigation for alleged criminal incitement, organized violence at public demonstrations and terrorism-related offenses. He has not been convicted. Italian authorities also placed his wife under investigation in connection with the same alleged offenses, although she remained free.
There is an important distinction between the allegations against Siher and his possible responsibility for the earlier unrest. His online movement emerged after the initial disturbances in Milan, and Italian reporting has cautioned that investigators have not established whether he exercised actual command over the original rioters.
The investigation has nevertheless brought renewed scrutiny to Siher's background and his previous activities.
Siher, who grew up in the Brescia area in northern Italy, pursued higher education in communications and political science at the University of Milan. He also studied political Islam, Middle Eastern politics and geopolitical affairs.
His academic background included research experience at the Italian Institute for International Political Studies, known as ISPI. He also worked as a freelance journalist, contributing to Italian publications including Il Fatto Quotidiano and Il Foglio. Although he had no previous criminal record, Siher had become increasingly active in pro-Palestinian organizations and demonstrations in Italy.
According to Corriere della Sera, Italian intelligence agencies had taken an interest in him in 2024 after he established an organization called Alba Nascente, or "Rising Dawn." The group reportedly promoted demonstrations against Israel and disseminated material sympathetic to Hamas and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine.
Italian media also reported that Siher had collaborated with a satellite television channel described as close to Hezbollah. The nature and extent of that alleged relationship have not been independently established.
His past statements about the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel have attracted particular attention. On the day of the attack, Siher responded to a social media message by Italian Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini expressing solidarity with Israel by writing "Allahu Akbar," meaning "God is greatest."
In a subsequent article published by the online magazine Miccia, Siher argued that few people in the West had understood the true meaning of Hamas' October 7 operation, known by the organization as Al-Aqsa Flood.
He described it as "a revolutionary act of decolonization," portraying the assault through an ideological framework of resistance to colonialism. The statement has since resurfaced in Italian media coverage of his detention.
Siher continued publishing criticism of Israel and the Italian government in recent months. In some writings, he sought to connect separate incidents involving the deaths of young men from immigrant backgrounds during encounters with law enforcement, presenting them as examples of wider institutional discrimination.
Investigators are now examining whether his online activity went beyond political advocacy and crossed the legal threshold into criminal incitement or the organization of violence.
The case comes as European authorities confront the growing role of social media in mobilizing demonstrations, including gatherings that begin with political demands but escalate into coordinated attacks on property and confrontations with police.

The dollar has hit an all-time record in Ukraine: what is happening with the exchange rate
Kyiv • UNN
The NBU set the dollar exchange rate for October 26 at UAH 45.2021 — a new all-time record. Cash exchange rates may differ.
The National Bank of Ukraine set the official exchange rate of the dollar for Monday, October 26, at UAH 45.2021. The U.S. currency reached a new all-time high against the hryvnia. UNN reports this, citing NBU data.
Details
The previous record was recorded on October 14, when the official dollar exchange rate stood at UAH 45.0802. Thus, the new figure exceeded the previous high by approximately 12 kopecks.
At the same time, the euro also remains near record levels. However, the exact exchange rate of the European currency for October 26 is not provided in the data cited.
What the new dollar record means
The NBU’s official exchange rate is used for accounting and other calculations stipulated by law. At the same time, cash exchange rates at banks and exchange offices may differ from the rate set by the regulator.
The new dollar high indicates a further nominal weakening of the hryvnia against the U.S. currency. At the same time, the official exchange-rate record alone does not mean a sharp jump in the dollar’s value on the cash market.

BEIJING (Reuters) -- The Chinese commerce ministry urged the United States on Saturday to stop expanding restrictions on American investments in China, saying a proposed rule on sensitive technologies would disrupt trade ties.
The U.S. Treasury Department issued proposals on Thursday to update its outbound-investment security program, adding biotechnology to restricted sectors and expanding coverage of high-performance computing and hypersonic systems.
Beijing's commerce ministry said in a statement that the proposal "discriminatorily" widened China-related investment restrictions and intensified curbs.

The U.S. program had already restricted certain U.S. investments involving China in semiconductors, quantum technologies and artificial intelligence.

Netanyahu rebuked for plan to use crypto to bypass economic sanctions
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces re-election this week, is drawing criticism from economists and political rivals after suggesting Israel could use cryptocurrency to help shield its economy from potential international sanctions.
In an interview with Israel's Channel 10 on Friday, Netanyahu said he was preparing for a scenario in which broader sanctions were imposed on Israel.
Last month, Britain, France and Canada said they would block imports from Israeli settlements in the West Bank in what was the latest in a series of actions targeting Israel's settlement policy, underscoring its growing diplomatic isolation among some of its traditional allies.
"There could be sanctions, and sanctions on banks so you need to set up a bypass economy," Netanyahu said. "You know, there are currencies that can bypass (sanctions). We are also working on that."
Asked whether he was referring to cryptocurrency, Netanyahu replied: "Very true, very true," adding that blockchain technology was another possibility.
The comments drew a rare rebuke by the Bank of Israel, which said cryptocurrencies cannot serve as a route to bypass sanctions and that political leaders should focus on policy that would render such measures unnecessary.
"The right course for Israel's economy is to preserve our economic relations with our main trading partners, and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy," it said.
Netanyahu on Sunday continued to defend his record, urging voters to back him and saying he and US President Donald Trump had two years left to work together to topple Iran's rulers.
Plan draws criticism
On Sunday, more than 100 economists, including former Bank of Israel officials, ex-central bank governor Jacob Frenkel and several Nobel laureates, signed a letter expressing alarm over Netanyahu's proposal. They said it would lead to higher unemployment, a fall in foreign investment and the collapse of Israel's economic standing in the world.
"As we have seen in countries that have suffered similar sanctions, such as South Africa, Iran, and Russia, the living standards of Israeli citizens would plummet dramatically, and the state's ability to finance its security and defend itself against its enemies would be severely damaged," the letter read.
"Netanyahu is knowingly leading the State of Israel toward boycott and international economic isolation, and all he has to offer the Israeli economy is a puzzling solution, one accepted in criminal organisations, that will not help in the slightest."
Netanyahu's main rival in Tuesday's election, Gadi Eisenkot, called the crypto plan "madness" and said he feared that the "BibiCoin policy" would drive companies abroad and undermine national security.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid said: "Netanyahu has gone off the rails ... He promises the citizens of Israel before these elections that they'll be standing in line for an hour and a half for bread, like in Russia and Iran."
Opinion polls point to a potential stalemate in the election with neither Netanyahu's ruling coalition nor an opposition alliance securing a governing majority in parliament.

Russia failed to create its own strategic silicon: the multimillion-ruble contract was terminated
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
17:41:05 EET
00:41:05 KST

Russia failed to create its own strategic silicon: the multimillion-ruble contract was terminated
Kyiv • UNN
Russia terminated a 400 million ruble contract due to the failure to carry out work on producing silicon for power electronics. The launch may be postponed until 2028.
The Ministry of Industry and Trade of the Russian Federation terminated a RUB 400 million contract with a Rosatom enterprise that was supposed to develop technology for producing special silicon for power electronics. UNN reports this, citing the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine.
Details
Due to the failure to fulfill its obligations, the launch of domestic production of the strategically important material in Russia may be postponed until at least 2028.
The contract was with JSC Research Institute of Instruments, which is part of the Rosatom structure. The enterprise was supposed to develop technology for manufacturing 150 mm-diameter silicon wafers needed to produce high-power electronic components.
The agreement was concluded in December 2024, and the work was scheduled to be completed by the end of 2026. However, the contractor was unable to fulfill its obligations even under the first stage of the project, which involved manufacturing pilot batches of the material and conducting preliminary tests. The deadline for completing the first stage expired on May 15, 2026. At the same time, the institute failed to provide the required reporting documentation and documents for accepting the work. Due to the breach of the contract terms, the Russian ministry imposed a fine of RUB 1.5 million on the enterprise, which remained unpaid at the time the agreement was terminated.
The project envisaged mastering the production of ingots and polished wafers of neutron-transmutation-doped single-crystal silicon. This material is used to manufacture power thyristors, IGBT transistors, and high-speed diodes, which are used in electric transport, power equipment, as well as the defense and space industries. However, Russia currently has no domestic production of this type of silicon, while the procurement of foreign counterparts is complicated by the material's strategic purpose. That is why the development was supposed to become one of the elements of Russia's import-substitution program in the field of high-tech electronics.
The enterprise was expected to prepare the technological foundation for creating production with a capacity of at least 100,000 silicon wafers per year. The transition to mass production was planned for 2027. However, following the termination of the contract, these deadlines have been called into question. According to Oleksandr Tymoshenko, head of Troichni Technologies, the development of production of the strategic material in Russia may now be postponed until 2028 or later.
Recall
In March 2026, the Armed Forces of Ukraine attacked the Kremniy El Group plant in the Russian Federation, which manufactures chips for missile systems and unmanned aerial vehicles. The plant produces components for Iskanders and S-400s.

The Abraham Accords are the 2020 agreement, mediated by President Donald Trump's first administration, that saw Israel establish relations with the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. It later reestablished official ties with Morocco.
Representatives for Ben-Gvir and Smotrich did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
As ministers in Netanyahu's religious-nationalist coalition, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have overseen policies widely perceived as discriminatory against Israel's minority Arab population and Palestinians living in the occupied West Bank.
Several countries, including Britain, Canada and Australia, have imposed sanctions on the two ministers over accusations that they have incited violence against Palestinians in the West Bank.
Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power party is projected to win around 10 parliamentary seats at Tuesday's election, up from 6, while Smotrich's Religious Zionism is projected to win 8, up from 7.
Ackman, who was visiting Israel last week, and who along with his wife Neri Oxman owns 5% of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, supported Donald Trump's candidacy for president in 2024. Trump last week publicly endorsed Netanyahu for prime minister.

Algeria moves to send troops to Niger to protect energy assets in historic policy shift
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:32:23 UTC
00:32:23 KST

Algeria’s upper house of parliament on Sunday approved a proposal to deploy troops to neighbouring Niger to protect energy facilities, marking a potential turning point in the country’s long-standing policy of military non-intervention beyond its borders.
A senator, speaking to AFP on condition of anonymity, said 148 members of the 174-seat Council of the Nation voted in favour of the measure. The lower house was expected to vote on the proposal later on Sunday.
Any overseas deployment would mark Algeria’s first such military operation since it sent troops to support Egypt during the 1973 Arab-Israeli war.
The move comes as Algeria and Niger strengthen security cooperation following efforts to repair strained relations earlier this year, amid persistent attacks by armed groups in Niger and concerns over regional stability.
Energy security at the heart of the deployment
Algeria and Niger share a 960-kilometre (600-mile) desert border and have pledged to deepen cooperation against jihadist violence, cross-border crime and trafficking.
The proposed deployment is also linked to strategic economic interests, particularly the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline (TSGP), a major project designed to transport natural gas from Nigeria through Niger and Algeria towards European markets.
International relations researcher Abdellah Akir described the proposal as a historic departure from Algeria’s traditional reluctance to intervene militarily beyond its borders.
He told AFP that the move reflected a desire to protect Algeria’s strategic interests in the Sahel and secure the future of the planned pipeline.
Akir also said the decision was intended to send a strong signal to regional competitors, including Morocco and the United Arab Emirates, with which Algeria has severed diplomatic relations.
Algiers adopts a more direct regional role
Geoff Porter, an analyst with North Africa Risk Consulting, said the proposal illustrated a shift in Algerian foreign policy towards a more direct physical presence in the region.
Algeria had traditionally pursued its interests through dialogue, international law and multilateral institutions, Porter told AFP, but was increasingly turning to more tangible measures to protect its regional influence.
He added that Algeria remained committed to its foreign policy principles while demonstrating them in a different way.
Earlier this month, Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune signalled his country’s willingness to support Niger during a televised address.
“We will protect Niger no matter what,” Tebboune said on October 3, accusing unnamed countries of conspiring against the West African nation.
He also pointed to agreements between the two countries covering oil, mining and other sectors, warning that Algeria’s interests were at stake.
Under a constitutional amendment adopted in 2020, deploying Algerian troops abroad requires approval from two-thirds of parliament.
Military and economic ties gather pace
The parliamentary vote followed a visit to Algeria last Wednesday by Nigerien Defence Minister Salifou Modi, who met Tebboune and Algerian army chief Said Chengriha.
Algerian reports said the two sides signed a military cooperation protocol, although details were not disclosed.
The latest move follows other forms of support from Algiers. Algeria previously supplied Niger with four military helicopters at the request of Nigerien authorities, according to the Algerian Defence Ministry.
In June, Algeria also inaugurated a 40-megawatt power plant intended to provide electricity to Niger’s capital, Niamey, and surrounding areas.
Relations between the neighbours had deteriorated after Algeria shot down a drone from Mali last year, triggering a diplomatic dispute. Niger joined Mali and Burkina Faso in recalling its ambassador from Algiers. Algeria and Mali have since restored diplomatic relations.

2026-10-25
15:32:20 UTC
00:32:20 KST

Police in Portugal have dismantled housing protest camps in Lisbon and Porto, baton-charging campaigners in the early hours of Sunday and arresting more than 30 people.
The raids were the latest incident in days of clashes between police and campaigners who – inspired by similar camps in Spain – had sought to pitch tents in central squares to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis.
Dozens of officers, some with dogs, moved shortly after 2am on Sunday to clear out the more than 100 tents that had sprung up in Lisbon’s Rossio Square. Police said they had also taken down a smaller camp of about 50 tents in Porto’s Dom João I Square.
The camp in the heart of Lisbon had been set up after thousands of people marched along one of the Portuguese capital’s main thoroughfares to rail against housing prices that have soared past average incomes in the country.
Police described their actions on Sunday as proportionate and said they had earlier urged people to leave the camps of their own accord. The operations in the two cities led to the arrests of 31 people for disobedience and 171 structures were removed, police said on social media. Eleven people were injured, including three police officers.
Reuters reported that 25 people detained in Lisbon had been released with orders to appear in court on Monday.
The group Casa Para Viver (A Home to Live In) contested the police figures, saying the raids had left more than 20 people injured as police moved into the camps with batons, dogs and rubber bullets.
“Choosing the early morning to deploy police dogs and fire rubber bullets at people who were sleeping or peacefully protesting is a political decision,” the group said in a statement as it called for further protests on Wednesday. “It shows that this government would rather crack down on those who speak out against the housing crisis than solve the crisis itself.”
Fabian Figueiredo, an MP with the Left Bloc, described the police action as a “wound that had been inflicted” on the country’s democracy. “Fighting for a home is a right. So is peaceful protest. The constitution guarantees both,” he said on social media. “Let’s keep going – for the sake of our future.”
The housing protest camps in Portugal trace back to early October when campaigners began pitching tents in Porto, prompting police to clear them out. Similar actions soon began sprouting up in Lisbon, leading to dozens of arrests and reports of injuries as police repeatedly clashed with campaigners.
As European cities grapple with a wave of discontent, much of the focus in Spain and Portugal has been on housing costs that have priced many local people out of the market.
House prices in Portugal have more than doubled since 2017, while those seeking to rent have struggled with prices that have nearly doubled, fuelling one of Europe’s most acute home affordability crises.
Residents have long told of bearing the brunt of a market that has surged as a result of liberalisation, the issuing of so-called golden visas, digital nomad schemes and the proliferation of short-term rentals.
Campaigners have called on the centre-right government to scrap proposed legislation that would make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases. The legislation recently passed a first parliamentary reading.
In Spain, the sprawling housing camp in the centre of Madrid marked its fourth week on Saturday, becoming one of the most tangible symbols of a widespread protest movement that has led to early general elections on 29 November.

Moscow will host the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships, the International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) announced on Sunday.
No world championships in an Olympic sport, summer or winter, have been held in Russia since the start of the war in Ukraine. The 2025 World Aquatics Championships, originally awarded to the Russian city of Kazan, were later moved to Singapore.
“Concerning the IWF Senior World Championships, Ahmedabad (India) will host the 2029 edition and Moscow (Russia) will host the 2030 edition,” the IWF said in a statement.
It will be the first time since 1983 that Moscow has hosted the World Weightlifting Championships.
“All the bids we received were excellent and we are sure that the Championships in your respective countries will be a huge success,” said IWF General Secretary Jose Quinones.
Russian and Belarusian weightlifters have been eligible to compete in IWF events since the International Olympic Committee provisionally lifted its suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee in July, a step seen as advancing Russia's gradual return to international sport.
The IOC Executive Board, when it lifted the suspension, said athletes should not be held responsible for the actions of their governments. No decision has yet been taken on whether Russian athletes will compete under their national flag, colors and anthem at the Olympic Games.
The National Olympic Committee of Ukraine has appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport against the IOC's decision.
The ROC was suspended in October 2023 after recognizing regional Olympic councils in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories of Luhansk, Donetsk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Russia's return to international competition also comes against the backdrop of one of the biggest doping scandals in Olympic sport.
The country has been under scrutiny since a 2015 World Anti-Doping Agency-commissioned report found evidence of systematic doping in Russian athletics, while subsequent investigations uncovered a state-backed cover-up linked to the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics.
The IOC said all Russian athletes now returning to international competition would have to meet relevant anti-doping requirements.

Netanyahu's final campaign strategy: Fear - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:30:39 UTC
00:30:39 KST

Benjamin Netanyahu has entered the scorched-earth phase of his election campaign. It is a familiar ritual for Israelis, one that almost always comes in the final days before an election. And the message is always the same: I am the only person who can protect Israel. Without me, the country will fall apart. Without me, Israel will be destroyed. You need me.
The talk last week about a possible new military operation against Iran was just the preview. The real campaign began on Friday.
In an interview on Channel 10, Netanyahu warned that Israel could soon face unprecedented international banking sanctions and that he was already working on ways to circumvent them using blockchain technology and cryptocurrency.
The comments sent shock waves through Israel’s financial establishment. Even the Bank of Israel issued an unusually harsh statement, rejecting the idea that cryptocurrency could provide a way around sanctions. The central bank made an obvious point: The best way to deal with sanctions is to prevent them in the first place, not to look for ways to bypass them.
But Netanyahu was just getting started.
On Saturday night, he released a video warning that Iran had resumed its nuclear program, wanted to destroy Israel, and that the country’s very survival was at stake in Tuesday’s election. If Israelis wanted to stop Iran, he said, they needed to listen to US President Donald Trump and vote for Netanyahu.
Netanyahu's message: If you want Israel to survive, vote Bibi
Then came Sunday afternoon. Netanyahu shared an AI-generated image of a mushroom cloud rising over Tel Aviv after a nuclear explosion, accompanied by a warning that if Iran obtains a nuclear weapon, nothing else will matter.
The message could not be clearer. If you want Israel to survive, vote Netanyahu. If you are willing to risk the country’s destruction, whether through financial collapse brought on by international sanctions or a nuclear explosion over Tel Aviv, then go ahead and vote for someone else.
This is Netanyahu’s election strategy in its most naked form: Fear.
Let’s be clear. Iran poses a genuine and serious threat to Israel. The danger of international sanctions is also real. These are challenges that any Israeli government will have to confront. But there is a difference between confronting threats and exploiting them, between preparing the public for difficult decisions and deliberately frightening people into believing that the survival of their country depends on one man.
And that is precisely what Netanyahu is doing.
This is electioneering at its worst. It is fear-mongering dressed up as national security. It is the familiar Netanyahu playbook of trying to scare Israelis into submission, convincing them to vote not out of confidence in his leadership or support for his policies, but out of fear of what might happen without him.
The tragedy is that this strategy has worked before. Netanyahu knows it, which is why he keeps returning to it.
But Israelis should know better by now. After October 7, after everything this country has endured, the idea that any one politician has a monopoly on protecting Israel should be dismissed.
Israel existed before this prime minister, and it will exist after him. Its survival does not depend on one politician, one party, or one election.

"We have explored ways to speed up work at the sites, including alternative connection points to gas networks, carrying out construction and gas-related work in parallel, reinforcing crews and working multiple shifts. It is important to complete every stage through to commissioning, so that the equipment can reliably supply heat," Kalashnyk said.
The team also inspected a facility transferred from state to municipal ownership. It is expected to become an additional source of power for part of the city in the near future.
"Protecting infrastructure and creating backup capacity are key components of Kyiv's resilience plan. A difficult winter lies ahead, and the capital needs these solutions now. Responsibility for this work is shared, and the outcome is tangible: equipment that operates and provides people with heat and electricity," Kalashnyk said.

Libya exports natural gas to Europe through pipelines and relies on it domestically to generate electricity and meet the needs of industrial sectors.

Instead of earning money—war against Ukraine: three countries demand that the Russian Federation return their citizens
Kyiv • UNN
Citizens of Kazakhstan, Kenya, and Kyrgyzstan were recruited into the Russian army through deception or coercion. The countries' governments are seeking their return and investigating cases of human trafficking.
Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Kenya report cases of their citizens being recruited into the Russian army through deception or coercion. The authorities of these countries are seeking to secure the return of their fellow citizens home, while the issue of recruiting foreigners to participate in the war against Ukraine is increasingly becoming a subject of diplomatic negotiations. The Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine reported this, according to UNN.
Details
Kyrgyzstan’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Jeenbek Kulubayev confirmed that the diplomatic service is receiving information about cases of the country’s citizens being forced to sign contracts with Russia’s Ministry of Defense. According to him, such cases are being recorded, in particular, at Russian military enlistment offices and pretrial detention centers. If information about forced recruitment is received in a timely manner, Kyrgyz diplomats attempt to intervene and prevent their citizens from being sent to the front.
Kazakhstan is also negotiating with the Russian side over the return of citizens who ended up in the combat zone in Ukraine. According to Kazakh diplomats, the ministry responds to appeals from fellow citizens seeking to return home. Some of these cases involve men who initially traveled to Russia for work but later ended up serving in the Russian military. In particular, relatives of one Kazakh citizen said that after he complained about working conditions, he and other men were taken to a military enlistment office, where they were forced to sign military contracts.
Kenya has also reported a similar problem. The authorities of the African country are seeking the return of its citizens who fought on Russia’s side and were captured by Ukraine. Kenya’s Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi said that the recruited men had been promised civilian employment in Russia. In particular, the jobs involved working as drivers, security guards or cooks. Instead, after arriving, they ended up serving in the Russian occupying army.
Cases of foreigners being drawn into the war against Ukraine through deception or coercion are causing growing concern among the governments of other countries. Some countries are considering such situations as possible cases of human trafficking.
Previously mentioned
Earlier, UNN reported that Russia had begun recruiting residents of Thailand into its army, promising "safe" service far from Ukraine.

‘He had so many dreams’: Israel mourns soldier killed in West Bank shooting attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:23:42 UTC
00:23:42 KST

Hundreds of mourners gathered Sunday at the Neve Hadar military cemetery in Hod Hasharon, central Israel, to bid farewell to Sgt. Yuval Shai Svilem, 20, who was killed Friday in a shooting attack near the West Bank city of Hebron.
Svilem, a soldier in the 755th Battalion of the Home Front Command Search and Rescue Brigade, was killed alongside Staff Sgt. Ron Yonatan Roytman, 23, of Ashkelon, a squad commander in the same battalion. Roytman was laid to rest earlier Sunday.
Svilem was the eldest of three children born to Amnon and Sivan Svilem and the older brother of Shira and Itamar. Family members and friends described him as a quiet, kindhearted and beloved young man who was always willing to help others.
Capt. Or, commander of the battalion's Eitan Company, praised Svilem's actions during the attack, saying he had helped prevent a much larger assault.
"Terrorists arrived at the scene, and the force thwarted the attack," Or said in his eulogy. "Yuval was an outstanding and energetic soldier. He fought the terrorists, returned fire and prevented a major and significant attack. He fell in heroic combat."
"Yuval was someone you could always turn to," he added.
'We thought he would have so much more time'
Svilem's parents, Amnon and Sivan, delivered emotional eulogies, recalling their son's ambitions and the future they had imagined for him.
"Our boy was only 20 years old," his father said, thanking those who had come to accompany his son on his final journey.
"He had so many dreams. We thought he would have so much more time. We wanted to see him build a life, and now we are left with longing and pain, with everything we will never get to experience."
Amnon referred to the weekly Torah portion, Lech Lecha, which recounts God's command to Abraham to leave his homeland.
"He died during the week of Lech Lecha, and he went to a high and good place, a place everyone would want to reach, just as you did. You reached the very highest heights," he said.
But his grief also turned to anger as he demanded answers from the military and the government about the circumstances of his son's death.
"Our home has fallen apart. We are not living. They took our souls," he said.
"Yuval wanted to save his friend. He was hit, and his weapon jammed. We will not give up. We want to know how we reached this situation."
Amnon called for the families of the Palestinian terrorists to be expelled from Israel before the end of the seven-day Jewish mourning period, known as shiva.
"We will not forget, and we will not remain silent. We hope the government and the judiciary will take this into account," he said. "The terrorists shattered several families and took everything from us."
"Just as they destroyed our families, I demand that the state expel them from the country before the end of the shiva," he continued.
"If the state does not do its job, we will take matters into our own hands. The military should have been prepared, and if the state does not act, we will take the law into our own hands. That is my final pledge to Yuval."
His sister, Shira, spoke of the private bond they had shared.
"Only you and I know the secret language we had between us," she said. "Don't worry. The terrorists will not tarnish what you were to me."
Svilem's cousin Linoy recalled the milestones he would never experience.
"You were only 20. You hadn't had the chance to do anything — not to travel, not to get married," she said.
"You were brutally murdered by a criminal. You were clearing a jam in your weapon, and in an instant, a bullet struck you. Now you're no longer here."
Linoy described her cousin as generous, sensitive and funny, a devoted older brother who always looked out for his siblings.
"Yuval was a child who gave to others, a sensitive and funny person, a good brother who always protected his siblings," she said.
"A wonderful young man was murdered in cold blood, and he will never return. Nothing will ever fill the hole left here."
"We hope you weren't afraid or in pain. Send us strength, and rest in peace, our hero."
Another cousin, Ben, said he had always imagined speaking about Svilem at his wedding, never at his funeral.
"I imagined I would speak about you only at your wedding, not under these circumstances," he said.
"He took command and prevented civilians from being harmed. He went beyond his capabilities and did everything to protect the people of Israel."
Ben recalled a conversation before Svilem enlisted in the military.
"Before he joined the army, he told me he wanted to go as far as possible in the military because he knew there was nobody else to protect us," he said.
"It seems you reached the place you wanted, the unit that goes deep into enemy territory. Yuval Shai was the pillar of our family."
'You were a hero who saved lives'
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir attended the funeral and delivered a eulogy.
Hod Hasharon Mayor Amir Kochavi was the final speaker, recalling Svilem's devotion to his family and the small gestures that had defined his character.
"I looked into your eyes, the eyes of a good soul," Kochavi said.
"Since Friday, I have been hearing about you, about the wonderful boy you were. The boy who looked after his mother and grandmother, whether near or far, who performed Havdalah with his father, Amnon, and who kept in touch with his childhood caregiver."
Havdalah is the Jewish ceremony marking the end of the Sabbath.
"You were not just a boy, not just a soldier. You were a hero who saved lives," Kochavi said.
"In recent years, we have known far too much pain. May we find a way to end this cycle of bereavement and suffering."
Deadly gunbattle near Hebron
The attack occurred Friday at approximately 7:10 a.m. at the Yehuda Junction near Hebron, a major Palestinian city in the southern West Bank.
According to the IDF, two Palestinian gunmen arrived at the junction in a vehicle, got out and opened fire on Israeli troops stationed in the area.
Svilem and Roytman were killed in the ensuing exchange of fire, while three other soldiers sustained minor injuries.
The gunbattle lasted more than 20 minutes before additional Israeli forces arrived, maneuvered around the attackers and shot them dead.
Security forces subsequently discovered a large quantity of ammunition inside the attackers' vehicle.
Security officials believe the two terrorists had been preparing to carry out a larger attack against civilians and that the soldiers' response prevented potentially more extensive casualties.
Following the shooting, the IDF launched a large-scale counterterrorism operation in the Hebron area.
Svilem and Roytman were the first two soldiers from the 755th Battalion to be killed in action since the unit was established within the past year.
The battalion is part of the Home Front Command's Search and Rescue Brigade, whose soldiers are trained for rescue operations and combat missions.
Military seals attackers' homes ahead of demolition
Overnight Saturday into Sunday, Israeli forces operating under the Yehuda Brigade sealed the homes of the two Palestinian terrorists in preparation for their demolition.
The military said the measures followed the shooting that killed Svilem and Roytman and wounded three other soldiers.
Israel has long used punitive home demolitions against Palestinians who carried out deadly attacks, describing the policy as a deterrent against future violence.
The two attackers were killed in the gunbattle with Israeli security forces.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian drone manufacturer Fire Point on October 24, its FP-1 drones traveled more than 2,500 kilometers before striking the Omsky Kauchuk chemical plant and an Ozon logistics complex.
Omsky Kauchuk, part of Russia’s Titan Group, is one of the country’s largest producers of synthetic rubber. The facility accounted for approximately 25% of Russia’s production of butadiene-methylstyrene rubber during the first nine months of 2024.

Khotsenko subsequently acknowledged that an Ozon logistics facility had also been struck. According to the regional authorities, personnel were evacuated from the warehouse, while emergency crews continued working at the site.
Ozon operates one of Russia’s largest online marketplaces, with logistics centers responsible for receiving, storing, processing, and distributing goods across the country.
The Omsk attack followed another Ukrainian drone strike earlier on October 24 against the Tolyattikauchuk petrochemical plant in Tolyatti, Russia’s Samara region. Both facilities manufacture chemical products used in industrial production, including materials associated with fuel manufacturing.

Thousands mourn victims of deadly Jordan church attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:21:26 UTC
00:21:26 KST

Thousands mourn victims of deadly Jordan church attack
Jordan’s prime minister represents king at funeral for eight of the church attack victims as hunt for gunmen continues.
Thousands of mourners have gathered for the funerals of eight of the victims of a deadly attack on a church in southern Jordan, with Prime Minister Jafar Hassan also in attendance.
The burials on Sunday were beside St George’s Greek Orthodox Church in the village of Hamoud, southwest of the capital, Amman, two days after attackers opened fire during another funeral there.
Nine people were killed and dozens wounded in a rare attack on Jordan’s Christian minority, prompting three days of national mourning.
The ninth victim, Mohammed al-Qasous, is due to be buried on Monday, his family told the AFP news agency.
Coffins wrapped in Jordanian flags were carried through crowds gathered around the church in Karak province, as priests led prayers and security personnel stood guard.
Prime Minister Hassan attended the service alongside government ministers and senior military and civilian officials, according to Jordan’s state news agency, Petra.
Thousands of citizens also participated in the funeral procession, Petra said.
Among those caught in Friday’s shooting was Sahar al-Halsa, who told the Reuters news agency from her nearby home that she sheltered behind a pillar as gunfire erupted and people screamed.
When she rushed outside, she found her cousin Assem lying wounded.
“Assem, Assem, my darling, answer me,” she recalled calling to him. He briefly opened his eyes before dying, she said.
Father Yohanna Hamati told AFP that about 170 to 200 people were at the church for Friday’s funeral when firing began outside.
The mourners initially struggled to understand what was happening, he said, before people began rushing into the church to escape.
By Saturday, bullet holes remained in the walls and wooden pews, and windows had been shattered.
Church workers were cleaning away blood as villagers prepared to bury the dead. Jordanian authorities have described the attack as “extremist terrorism”.
King Abdullah, who visited some of the wounded in hospital on Friday, has promised a forceful response and the assailants are still being sought.
Officials say they have not established whether the attackers were connected to an armed group and no organisation has claimed responsibility.
The violence has also drawn expressions of solidarity across religious lines. Christians account for about 3 percent of Jordan’s largely Muslim population and AFP reported that Muslims were among those wounded.
Young volunteers visited a hospital in Karak with flowers and a message reading, “Our loss is one”.
The mourning reached Washington, DC, on Sunday, where members of the Jordanian community lit candles outside their country’s embassy.
Jordan’s ambassador to the US, Dina Kawar, told those gathered that efforts to stir religious division were “bound to fail”. Back in Hamoud, Father Hamati appealed for unity, stressing that Muslims had also suffered in the attack.
“We make no distinction between Muslim and Christian,” he told AFP.

Transcript: Texas Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 25, 2026

Transcript: Texas Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 25, 2026
The following is the transcript of the interview with Texas Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 25, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We turn now to the Texas governor's race and Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa. She joins us from Austin. Good to have you here.
TEXAS STATE REPRESENTATIVE GINA HINOJOSA: It's great to be with you.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, if you win, you would be the first Democratic governor and the first female governor in over 30 years. You're running in a state, though, that has more Republicans than Democrats. So, what is your message to get Republicans to cross over and vote for you?
HINOJOSA: Well, right now, nobody wants politics as usual. Most of us see that it is broken, and so what we are seeing in Texas is because there is deep disappointment in both political parties, people are forging a new way for- forward. One that is postpartisan in some ways. The data centers are a physical manifestation of a governor, Governor Abbott, and a government that's working for the moneyed interests and leaving the people of Texas to fend for themselves. Public schools are another issue where there has been a bipartisan coming together in support of our public schools. And so, listen, this creates an opportunity for Texans to evaluate the candidate. I believe that's why we have now six or seven polls out of the last six weeks that show us winning. All polls show us within the margin of error. Turnout is high. Enthusiasm is high on our side, so we feel really good about where we are.
MARGARET BRENNAN: You mentioned schools. I was surprised to see that 181 school districts in Texas are operating just four days a week. Some schools have shut down. How much of this is people just moving to more populated areas out of the rural ones, and how much of it is funding?
HINOJOSA: A lot of it is funding. Greg Abbott in 2023 withheld funding our schools needed because we didn't pass vouchers. He said he would withhold it if we didn't pass it, and we did it. We fought it. Myself- myself and James Talarico led that fight to stop school vouchers. He passed it last year. That took a billion dollars from our neighborhood public schools to take and put into unaccountable private schools. And so, school districts are really struggling. Our schools are shutting down. Teachers have left. And you should know that public schools are part of our identity as Texans. They are enshrined in our Texas Constitution, as being essential to our liberties, they are the largest employer in most or many of our counties. They are Friday Night Lights, and so there is bipartisan anger about what Greg Abbott has done to our public schools. And listen, I'm running my broad agendas to secure the American Dream, and public schools are essential- are an essential part of the American dream because they provide the gateway and the opportunity to the American dream. So saving Texas public schools is a key part of my agenda, and that's why this campaign has resonated amongst Texans.
MARGARET BRENNAN: You've been campaigning on the issue of Texas having the highest uninsured rate and the highest number of uninsured children in this country. If you win, you're still going to have a Republican-controlled legislature. You're likely to have a Republican lieutenant governor. How do you work with them to improve health care?
HINOJOSA: Well, I'll tell you that my agenda is not a Democratic agenda, it is a popular, populist agenda, one that delivers for the people of Texas. So my healthcare policy and platform and plan is to ensure every Texas child has quality healthcare because we have the most uninsured children of any state in America. We're one of the few states that hasn't expanded Medicaid. Expanding Medicaid is one way to get there. HINOJOSA: Yes, but we're not running on that. That is just the process. It's kind of a geeky way to talk about insuring people. thinking with animals in the sicilian village of santo pietro explores the human-animal divide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:15:23 UTC
00:15:23 KST

thinking with animals in the sicilian village of santo pietro explores the human-animal divide
co-director marco navarra discusses the ecological regeneration project connecting community life, the post-anthropocene, and design.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
bosco colto campus co-director marco navarra
In and around the forests of Santo Pietro, near Caltagirone in southeastern Sicily, is Bosco Colto, the ecological regeneration project established in 2022 by Makramè APS. Through interdisciplinary programming, the organization explores the Bosco di Santo Pietro area and develops new ways of inhabiting and caring for the territory. In the summer of 2026, it invited guests and community members to participate in its annual Bosco Colto Campus, a summer session of workshops and activations that takes place across the village of Santo Pietro.
Titled Thinking with Animals, this year’s edition welcomed the likes of Yoshiharu Tsukamoto of Atelier Bow-Wow, Food Hack Lab, and other practitioners in academia, design, and architecture. Through experiments in architecture, agroecology, ceramics, sound, and spatial practices, the program explored environmental justice through a nonhuman lens. In conversation with designboom, Marco Navarra, who co-directs the program with Dario Felice, Beatrice Fontana, and Antonio Scarponi, talks about the organization’s growth and what was cultivated—both literally and philosophically—during Thinking with Animals.
Thinking with Animals and a New Approach to Architecture
From the end of July through the first week of August, Bosco Colto Campus featured Fabio Ciaravella’s workshop Order of the Oaks of Santo Pietro, which focused on the study of the ancient relationship between the forest and the city. It also brought to life a hybrid train kiln, a wood-fired kiln for experimental ceramics. Additionally, the program engaged with audio, digital, and culinary modalities for interacting with the world around Santo Pietro.
Navarra comments on how the framework of Thinking with Animals unified these activities by ‘[providing] an opportunity to experiment in practice with a shift in perspective away from the anthropocentric framework that has characterized traditional approaches to architecture.’ He remarks that the Campus, a nearly ten-day event, ‘became a living research tool, where design was transformed from a mere formal exercise into a situated practice, capable of embracing the unexpected, other presences and the logics of the non-human world as an integral part of the process.’
on designing spaces shared with other species
The name of its governing organization, Bosco Colto, plays on the Italian words bosco (woodland or forest) and colto (cultivated or cultured). These fundamental principles were further manifested in Thinking with Animals, with Navarra emphasizing that ‘Designing spaces shared with other species means, on the one hand, recognizing one’s own limits—the limits of humankind—and establishing them as the starting point for the design; on the other hand, it means simultaneously exercising a great capacity for listening and imagination.’
Sicilian Satoyama with Yoshiharu Tsukamoto
A standout workshop during the late-summer program was Yoshiharu Tsukamoto’s Sicilian Satoyama, in which the group participated in the collective construction of the Zucca Gazebo and Mulberry Canopy, two permanent installations on the site. Navarra explains the concept: ‘Satoyama is the traditional Japanese agricultural landscape, where different forms of land use coexist, within a mosaic-like structure that brings together woodland and rice paddies. This balance is made possible by a social system that ensures its care and management over time.’ Reflecting on the workshop, he adds that ‘Tsukamoto’s team experimented with a different way of applying these materials in construction, to create more opportunities for utilizing local resources and to build something within this network of elements that make up a Sicilian Satoyama.’
Navarra remarks on the success of adapting this concept to the Sicilian landscape, saying that ‘the Satoyama model can be replicated and adapted to the Boschi di Santo Pietro area, which also features a mosaic structure composed of agricultural landscapes and edges of an ancient forest…. Of course, Sicily has historically developed certain agricultural practices similar to Satoyama, but it has been particularly valuable to link Bosco Colto’s activities to the Satoyama revitalization actions that Tsukamoto is carrying out in Japan.’
A Space to Practice at Casa Bosco Colto
Alongside the Campus, Casa Bosco Colto is the project’s developing permanent infrastructure, conceived as a network of buildings and outdoor spaces in Santo Pietro. In summer 2026, the Campus inaugurated a wood-fired ceramic kiln in the village, a permanent addition to the Casa project. The broader plan to redevelop four public buildings into a connected cultural infrastructure is underway. Navarra describes the space as ‘an independent research center that will serve as a facility (with laboratories and guest accommodation) dedicated to field research in architecture, art and nature, with the local community involved in all daily activities.’
On the importance of continually engaging with the Sicilian region through Bosco Colto’s program and spaces, Navarra remarks: ‘Foundations bloom seeds buried in the past like a regenerating fire that brings them back to light and makes them blossom again. The actions and small architecture of Bosco Colto work with time to build the future through a self-regeneration of places.’
project info:
name: Bosco Colto, a project by Makramè APS
program: Bosco Colto Campus 2026, Thinking with Animals
dates: July 30 – August 9, 2026
location: Caltagirone, southeastern Sicily
directors: Marco Navarra, Dario Felice, Beatrice Fontana, and Antonio Scarponi

Iran's Araghchi doubles down on national positions amid war threat
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that a potential resumption of war with Israel and the United States would not change his country's positions.
The remarks come amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, as President Donald Trump said on Friday that Washington "may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the US-Israeli campaign on Iran that began on 28 February.
"Recently, there has been talk of a new war, but I am already thinking about the post-war period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same," said Araghchi during a televised event in Tehran.
"They have already done so twice and have seen the results. If they want to try again, they know they will achieve no different outcome from those of the past."
An April 8 ceasefire between Iran and the United States put an end to the most intense fighting, apart from sporadic exchanges of fire in and around the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies.
These military flare-ups have lulled in recent weeks.
Iran has claimed control over the strait since the outbreak of the war and has regularly targeted vessels that attempt crossing without its authorisation - moves strongly opposed by Washington and countries in the region.
In response, the US has been maintaining a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.
In June, Iran agreed with the United States to a memorandum of understanding laying out a pathway to a permanent settlement of the conflict, only for the deal to later unravel as each side accused the other of violating it.
Tehran has since called for a return to the accord to end the conflict.
"The current war has changed everything. We must accept that new realities are taking hold. Shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz will no longer be the same, and the management of the strait will no longer be the same," said Araghchi.
"To achieve peace and stability, our region must move towards the complete absence of foreign forces."

Early reports suggest record high turnout in Serbia elections
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:07:00 GMT
00:07:00 KST

Early reports suggest record high turnout in Serbia elections
- Published
Early reports suggest Serbian voters have turned out in large numbers for its parliamentary election, as a student protest movement attempts to end the rule of the country's right-wing populist leader.
Preliminary reports suggest a record high turnout, with 46% having cast their vote by 14:00 local time (13:00 GMT), nearly a million more than the comparable figure for the previous election in December 2023.
The apparent high turnout is fuelling the hopes of opposition party Student List that they can oust Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), who have been in power since 2012.
The snap elections called by Vučić follow two years of student protests triggered by the 2024 collapse of a train station canopy, which killed 16 and was seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence in Serbia.
Anti-corruption movement Student List are running on a manifesto including purging officials who broke rules cracking down on protesters, stopping party loyalists heading public enterprises, and freeing the public broadcaster of political control.
Vučić and the SNS party deny corruption and seeking to influence the media.
- What you need to know about Serbia's pivotal election 
  - Published2 days ago
Most commentators suggest that a high final turnout, 65% or above, would favour the students.
Voting ends at 20:00, with first indications of results expected two hours later.
Long queues formed outside polling stations in larger cities and smaller towns alike in Serbia, and at polling stations abroad - including Slovenia's capital Ljubljana, Munich, Los Angeles and Chicago. In Paris, Serbian voters waited in line in heavy rain.
Tensions are high across Serbia. In Belgrade, police have closed streets around the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK).
In the street nearby, cars at the traffic lights lowered their windows to blast one of the students' anthems from loudspeakers, 'I want three kisses' - a folk song favoured because the Students' List is number three on the ballot paper. Young people on the pavement nearby started dancing.
Vučić and his SNS party are number one on the ballot paper. He has spent two terms as president and cannot seek a third term, so he is now leading his party with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.
He retains strong support among a significant section of Serbia's population. They view him as a strong leader who stands up for the country's interests. He can also point to significant economic growth over the past decade and numerous improvements in infrastructure.
Vučić, who backs Serbia's candidacy for the European Union while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia over its war in Ukraine, has pledged higher pensions and public sector salaries, and investment in state healthcare.
SNS posters plastered around cities show two hands clasped together in solidarity: the hands of doctors and nurses, farmers, construction workers, teachers and parents.
"These are the hands that hold Serbia in their palms," says Vučić in his campaign video. "And with these hands, calmly and with dignity, we shall finish what we started."
That is question of this election, continuity or change.
Amid fears of electoral fraud by the SNS, the students have delegated at least two observers to each of Serbia's 8,210 voting stations.
Videos circulating on social media on Sunday morning show a cafe in the southern city of Nis, where ballot papers were allegedly filled out in advance in a practice known as 'chain voting'. Signs in the window read "private party". When they realise that they are being filmed, the papers are quickly hidden.
There have also been reports of attacks on election monitors and journalists at several polling stations.
"We are witnessing a unique experiment in European contemporary history," Žarko Korać, a former deputy prime minister and long-term opponent of nationalist parties in Serbia including the SNS, told the BBC.
Instead of running for office themselves, student-led assemblies at the country's university faculties have chosen 250 candidates to stand in the parliamentary election, with Ilija Srdanović, professor at Novi Sad University, heading the list.
The Student List of candidates for parliament also includes doctors, actors, academics and sports personalities
"These are people that don't know each other, you have no idea what their political beliefs are, and we now expect them to create a functioning government. So it's anybody's guess what happens after they win," Korać says.
"On the other hand, if Vučić declares victory this evening, probably late in the evening, I don't think the students will accept that."
Korać suggests that many former Vučić loyalists in high office could change sides at the last moment, if the students win. A close result, however, with both sides claiming victory, could result in weeks or months of political instability.
The electorate is 6.45 million in a population of 6.53 million, raising concerns about the reliability of the electoral register. Serbs from Kosovo, and dual Serbian citizens from neighbouring Bosnia also have the right to vote.
Katarina, 29, told the BBC she had travelled from the Netherlands back home to Serbia to vote for Student List, even though she could have cast her ballot remotely.
"I wanted to be a part of this, and I wanted to be part of a movement," she told the BBC outside a polling station in the capital's Zvezdara district.
"I think they have a chance of winning," she said, but expressed doubt about whether such a result would be respected by Vučić.
Asked whether the party's selection of candidates from different walks of life might hinder its ability to govern, she responded: "Just because they're politically inexperienced, they are experts in their own fields, which we have not seen thus far."

Gugging Museum: How Art Changes Our View of Humanity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:04:00 UTC
00:04:00 KST

Near Vienna, in Lower Austria, there is a museum whose history challenges conventional ideas about art, mental health, and human dignity. Here, works by people long regarded primarily as psychiatric patients, have become part of the international art scene.
The Gugging Museum, located in Maria Gugging near Klosterneuburg, is dedicated to artists associated with a former psychiatric institution. Their drawings, paintings, and distinctive visual worlds have attracted the attention of curators, collectors, and researchers, becoming an important part of the history of art beyond academic traditions.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
                                                                                                                                                                         Gugging Museum (Photo by Myroslava Makarevych)                             
In 2026, the museum marks its 20th anniversary. The jubilee exhibition “museum gugging.! 20 jahre kUNSt” runs from March 15, 2026, to January 17, 2027. It presents the work of artists from different generations. Yet Gugging’s history encompasses more than artistic recognition: it also includes Nazi crimes against the hospital’s patients. This combination makes the museum an important setting for conversations about culture, human rights, and historical responsibility.
From psychiatric hospital to international art center
Gugging’s history began in 1885, when a psychiatric hospital was established in Maria Gugging. A turning point came in the 1950s, when psychiatrist Leo Navratil began using drawing as part of his diagnostic work. He noticed the unusual expressiveness and originality of works produced by some of his patients.
Zoom Versus The Hague: Anatomy of a Russian Sleight of Hand
                                                                                                                                                                         Gugging Museum (Photo by Myroslava Makarevych)                             
In 1965, Navratil published “Schizophrenia and Art.” He later corresponded with French artist Jean Dubuffet, who developed the concept of “Art Brut” – art created outside established academic conventions and traditional systems of artistic education.
Dubuffet was interested in creative expression that did not conform to the expectations of the art establishment. The work produced by Gugging’s artists reflected this vision. During the 1970s, they began attracting recognition beyond the walls of the psychiatric institution.
In 1981, Navratil founded the Center for Art and Psychotherapy, providing 18 patients with a dedicated place to live and work. In 1983, psychiatrist and sculptor Johann Feilacher joined the project, encouraging the artists to transform not only sheets of paper but also their surroundings into works of art.
In 1986, the center became “Haus der Künstler” – the House of Artists. The focus gradually shifted from residents’ diagnoses to their creative work and identities as artists.
In September 1994, British rock singer and songwriter David Bowie and music producer Brian Eno visited the artists at Gugging. The encounter inspired Bowie while he was working on his album 1. Outside (1995) and later became the subject of special exhibitions, including “gugging inspires.! from bowie to roth.”
                                                                                                                                                                         Gugging Museum (Photo by Myroslava Makarevych)                             
Transformations
A broader cultural infrastructure subsequently emerged, including a gallery, studios, and a museum that opened in 2006. The psychiatric hospital closed in 2007, but the site continued to develop as a center for art, research, and cultural dialogue.
                                                                                                                                                                         Gugging Museum (Photo by Myroslava Makarevych)                             
Gugging’s history shows how perceptions of people can change when they are no longer defined exclusively by a medical diagnosis. At the same time, artistic recognition alone does not resolve every issue involving human rights, personal autonomy, and the quality of medical care. These are distinct, though interconnected, aspects of human dignity.
Among Gugging’s best-known artists are Johann Hauser, August Walla, and Oswald Tschirtner. Their works demonstrate the diversity of artistic languages that emerged beyond academic traditions.
                                                                                                                                                                         Gugging Museum (Photo by Myroslava Makarevych)                             
Works by Gugging artists are held in international art collections, including specialized Art Brut collections. Their creativity has attracted attention beyond Austria, and Gugging has become an important reference point in discussions about art that develops outside conventional systems of professional training, establishing criteria of artistic skill, with its own imagery, symbols, and ways of seeing the world.
Nazi crimes – history that must not be silenced
Gugging’s history also contains a tragic chapter. Under the Nazi regime, the psychiatric hospital became a site associated with the systematic persecution and killing of people with mental health conditions.
According to a historical study commissioned by the Institute of Science and Technology Austria, 675 people were deported from the hospital to the killing center at Hartheim Castle between November 1940 and May 1941. They were murdered. Among the victims were 116 children and adolescents aged four to 17. In the following years, patients also fell victim to violence, deprivation of adequate care, and denial of necessary treatment.
These events formed part of Nazi policy, which classified people according to supposedly measurable social worth and declared certain lives unworthy of existence. Dehumanization became a justification for state violence, while institutions intended to protect people were turned into instruments of persecution.
This context is essential to understanding Gugging. The history of a place where the creative abilities of people often overlooked by society were later recognized also preserves the memory of those who were denied the right to live.
Honoring the art, therefore, cannot be separated from remembering the victims. Without that memory, the story of Gugging would remain incomplete. The museum is located at Am Campus 2 in Maria Gugging, near Vienna. A memorial to the victims of Nazi medical crimes stands near the campus of the Institute of Science and Technology Austria. Their proximity is a reminder that cultural heritage cannot be separated from historical memory.
The museum’s anniversary and the significance of its history
The jubilee exhibition “museum gugging.! 20 jahre kUNSt” presents the work of 20 artists from different generations, bringing historical and contemporary works together.
                                                                                                                                                                         In the museum’s anniversary exhibition. (Photo by Myroslava Makarevych)                             
Gugging offers an important lesson: human dignity does not depend on a diagnosis, social status, or conformity to generally accepted norms. Ensuring that people whose voices are often pushed to the margins are heard requires more than good intentions. It requires institutions, professional support, and access to culture.
                                                                                                                                                                         Gugging Museum (Photo by Myroslava Makarevych)                             
Today, as far-right movements gain strength in various countries and intolerance and exclusionary rhetoric spread, Gugging’s history takes on particular relevance. Cruelty does not emerge overnight. It is preceded by a habit of failing to recognize another person as an equal human being.
That is why such museums, memorials, and cultural institutions also remind us what can happen when a society forgets the lessons of history.
