‘They paved paradise’: fighting back over the loss of green spaces in Cameroon’s capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:00:05 UTC
00:00:05 KST

A little piece of paradise is buried under the asphalt that is now lined with parked cars. The romantic spot where Sosthène Hugues Ngono used to bring his first dates had been green and beautiful. “It wasn’t just a park,” he says, standing at the edge of what is now a private car park in Cameroon’s capital, Yaoundé.
“It was where I came to clear my head when things felt confused,” he says. “Where I met people; where I fell in love, more than once.”
Ngono, 36, a mathematics teacher, watched in dismay as the public park in Essos, a densely populated neighbourhood of Yaoundé, was razed in February last year, but his loss was only a small, personal version of a larger one playing out across the city.
Green space in Yaoundé is under mounting pressure from unregulated urban expansion. Yaoundé covered nearly 33 sq miles (85 sq km) in 1984. By 2024 it had spread to cover 181 sq miles, according to a study by the University of Yaoundé.
Over the same period, the share of wooded areas in the city’s land cover dropped from 28.6% to just 5.4%.
Yaoundé’s rapid development reflects growing demand for housing and infrastructure as its population expands. The UN put the capital’s population at 5.1 million in 2025. Cameroon’s housing ministry estimated a national housing deficit of 2.5m units in 2020, most acutely felt in the city.
With formal housing supply falling far short of demand, much of Yaoundé’s growth has taken the form of informal settlements and slums, often built without permits over the valleys, wetlands and hillsides of its green belt.
However, its disappearance has given rise to a quiet counter-movement. Jean-Baptiste Tchengang, a 34-year-old self-taught gardener, grows mostly ornamental plants, decorative foliage and small shrubs suited to Yaoundé’s climate, chosen because they multiply easily and fit into small yards.
“Their value is as much practical as it is beautiful,” he says. “They bring colour and coolness, but they also give people a simple way to rebuild small green spaces where the big gardens are disappearing.”
Since 2022, Tchengang has run community workshops on composting and preserving local plant species from his own plot in Nkolbisson, a district on Yaoundé’s outskirts that researchers identify as one of the city’s historic areas of urban expansion, dating from 1984.
“I have trained or helped about 300 people since I started,” he says. Ten of his trainees have gone on to build their own gardens on abandoned plots, providing vegetables, medicinal plants and social spaces.
“Getting access to land is the hardest part,” Tchengang says. “There’s no funding, plants get stolen, and the ones you can buy are scarce and expensive. But somehow, I make it work.”
When funds allow, Yaoundé city council buys shrubs and gets him to plant and maintain them, but it is not regular work. In July, Tchengang brought together about 50 young nature conservation volunteers who wanted to learn his methods to make their own case to the authorities. Trees especially have been suffering, disappearing from the urban landscape.
“Trees are not there simply to make Yaoundé more beautiful,” says Jean-Marie Essoh, a climate specialist in the city. “They absorb rainwater, slow runoff and help hold the soil together.
“They also cool a city where concrete keeps spreading,” he says. “When they disappear, it weakens far more than the landscape.”
As trees are carbon sinks, absorbing CO2, their disappearance makes climate adaptation harder in a city regularly hit by heavy rains and flooding; when they are felled, that carbon is released back into the atmosphere.
A 2023 report on urban forests by the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) found that trees and green spaces play a vital role in climate resilience and warned that their benefits are increasingly under threat as cities expand.
Knowing where those benefits are being lost is the starting point for Mireille Nonga’s work. A 33-year-old urban-planning student at the University of Yaoundé I, she has mapped the city’s green spaces with 20 classmates since 2023, identifying 10 potential sites for reforestation.
“There are several criteria,” says Nonga. “First, the position of the plot in relation to urban development in the area, its availability and its land status, whether it belongs to the state.
Other points to consider, she says, are “accessibility, access to water and the flow of people around it”.
Today, the Sainte-Anastasie wood and the nearby garden at Place Charles Atangana are among the few green spaces remaining in Yaoundé. According to Nonga, even these central spaces are inconsistently maintained.
Yaoundé’s authorities do recognise the problem. The MoVe Yaoundé project, launched in January 2024, includes a four-year urban renewal plan for the city centre, with about 1,000 sq metres (10,800 sq ft) of green space planned, including tree-lined avenues.
In September, the council published a call for tenders that included landscaping works, new parks, tree-lined avenues and permeable paving.
But until the green spaces promised under MoVe Yaoundé take shape, the work of preserving what is left falls to people such as Nonga. “If we don’t know what we’re losing, we can’t defend it,” she says.
The Guardian contacted the Yaoundé urban council about the loss of Essos park and the authorisation of the private car park. The council referred the questions to the official in charge of the MoVe Yaoundé project, who did not respond to requests for comment.

Israel will close all crossings into the West Bank on election day — BBC
Kyiv • UNN
Israel will close all land crossings with the West Bank on October 27 due to the parliamentary elections and escalating tensions in Hebron. More than 2,600 Palestinians have left their homes.
Israel announced the closure of all land checkpoints between its territory and the occupied West Bank on October 27, the day of the parliamentary elections. The decision was made amid an escalation of the situation in Hebron, where a large-scale military operation is underway following the deaths of two Israeli servicemen. This is reported by the BBC, according to UNN.
Details
According to the Israeli military, the restrictions will be introduced in stages. On October 25–26, Palestinian workers will be prohibited from entering Israeli settlements in the West Bank and the Jordan Valley, with the exception of certain industrial zones.
On Tuesday, October 27, when parliamentary elections will be held in Israel, all land crossings between the country and the West Bank will be closed. The restrictions will also apply to industrial zones.
The Israeli authorities explain the decision as necessary to strengthen security measures during the vote. The restrictions are expected to be lifted after the elections. The decision was made following an attack near Hebron on October 23, in which two Israeli servicemen were killed and three others were wounded. According to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF), two attackers were killed by return fire.
Following the incident, Israeli forces launched a large-scale operation in the West Bank. According to the military, from October 23–24, security forces conducted raids in approximately 40 areas, searched about 400 sites, and detained around 40 suspects. The main operations are taking place in Hebron and nearby communities. The military blocked roads, restricted residents' movement, and began demolishing a number of buildings that the Israeli side considers illegal or a security threat.
According to local authorities, as cited by the Associated Press, more than 2,600 Palestinians were forced to leave their homes because of the military operation. The restrictions also disrupted the work of educational institutions and businesses and made it more difficult for residents to access medical care.
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said that residents of certain areas would not be able to return to their homes until the operation against Hamas infrastructure was completed.
Context
At the same time, the Palestinian authorities condemned the actions of the Israeli military, accusing them of forcibly displacing civilians and destroying residential buildings. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu promised a tough response after the attack in Hebron and emphasized the need to prevent further attacks.
The escalation is taking place ahead of the parliamentary elections scheduled for October 27. Security issues and the Palestinian-Israeli conflict remain among the key topics of the election campaign.
It is currently unknown how long the military operation in Hebron will last and when all displaced residents will be able to return to their homes.

Ex-Mossad chief Barnea intended for Iran to see Israel's operations to overwhelm IRGC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
14:58:01 UTC
23:58:01 KST

When the Mossad took the stunning move of publishing multiple videos in real time of its agents acting against the regime within Iran in June 2025, one of the main reasons was to overwhelm and confuse the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), former Mossad chief David Barnea has revealed.
Leaked on Sunday from comments he made to a closed audience at the Priority Summit this past Thursday.
On June 13, 2025, the Mossad released sensational and rare video footage of its co-lead role with the air force in Israel’s preemptive strike on Iran’s ballistic missiles and air defenses.
Three videos showed the Mossad targeting ballistic missile targets, air defense targets, and general preparations for the attacks (with the agents’ faces covered up).
From the perspective of the videos, it appeared that the Mossad used drones from inside Iran to attack various targets.
Iran had previously accused the Mossad of using drones to attack the Karaj facility in June 2021 as well as other operations.
Mossad's warehouse of drones used to sabotage Iran
It was later confirmed that the Mossad used an entire warehouse of drones to attack and sabotage Iran, along with helping with a large number of remote-controlled vehicles attacking regime targets, and a significant number of human agents on the ground also assisting in assassinations.
Although far more information was quickly publicized about the IDF’s actions, these videos gave readers a rare front-row and real-time seat into what normally were entirely clandestine operations which the Mossad would not even admit to.
Barnea said at the Priority Summit that the video was deliberately published to trigger mass arrests and make it more difficult for the IRGC to identify actual Israeli agents.
“One of the reasons we immediately released an official video on the morning of Operation Rising Lion, with the Mossad logo, was to protect the agents who were there,” Barnea said in a video which Yediot Ahronot shared, and regarding which the Jerusalem Post confirmed the authenticity. “We wanted to make sure they arrested so many people in Iran that they wouldn’t be able to distinguish the wheat from the chaff and would eventually release everyone,” adding that Iran did release all of the detainees.
IRGC arrested over 20,000 people on second day of war
The former Mossad chief said that the IRGC arrested 21,000 people on the second day of the fighting.
“You have to imagine that when you arrest 21,000 people, even if you’ve caught an agent or two, eventually you have to release them because everyone’s story will be the same: I was walking down the street, I was driving a car, they arrested me,” he said, emphasizing that the IRGC would have no way of knowing who was a real agent with such a vast number of detainees,
Barnea added that many of those arrested or executed by the IRGC as “Mossad agents” had nothing to do with the agency.
In addition, he said that nearly all of the Mossad agents were never caught, and at the end of the June 2025 operation, he even publicly taunted the IRGC, issuing a statement, “We will [continue to] be there, like we have been there.”
His explanation may close the book on the unexplained mystery of why the Mossad would have risked broadcasting some of its agents’ actions in real time during the June 2025 operation.
In September 2025, the Post reported exclusively that dozens of Mossad women penetrated Iran and were on the ground performing a variety of kinds of operations during Israel’s attacks on Tehran’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs in June 2025.
While the Mossad does not want to bring too much attention to any one sub-group of potential spies, the Post’s impression was that the Mossad women of 2025 were doing more of every kind of spy role as compared to their sisters of yesterday.
In that same September report, the Post noted that Barnea sent hundreds of Mossad agents, or individuals being run by agents, into operations in Iran simultaneously. All of the varying groups of staff were highly coordinated.
The spy chief directed a project leading to a diverse spectrum of all of the different kinds of agents and backgrounds of those agents one could imagine.
On top of actual Israeli Mossad agents, the spy service has reached new levels in recruiting and training local dissident Iranian agents to act against the ayatollahs’ regime, the Post reported at the time.
While the early 2026 war with Iran is viewed by many as a mixed bag, the June 2025 war was viewed as the most successful Israeli operation of the last three years, along with the exploding beepers used against Hezbollah.

Democrats aim to flip key Senate seats as Trump's popularity sinks to historic low - CNN

Ahead of the US midterms in nine days, Democrats are hopeful for a blue wave to flip several Senate seats, as US President Donald Trump’s approval ratings hit an all-time low of 31%, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll from last week.
According to CNN, the most likely Senate seats to flip include several Republican strongholds, including states that Trump won by double digits in the 2024 election.
In order, CNN analysts believe that the most likely seats to flip are: North Carolina, Ohio, Alaska, Maine, Texas, Michigan, Iowa, Kansas, New Hampshire, and Georgia.
Democrats would need to win seven of these 10 seats to gain a 51-seat majority in the Senate. However, it is rare for a party to take control of the House and the Senate in one singular election.
Of the Senate seats listed, Georgia is the only state where the seat could flip from blue back to red. However, a recent Atlanta Journal-Constitution found that Sen. John Ossoff (D-Georgia) has an eight-point lead over his challenger, Republican Rep. Mike Collins.
Will Democrats be able to take the House?
Cook Political Report found that the Democrats would only need to take one or two seats out of 435 in the House of Representatives to regain a majority. Cook labeled 21 seats in races across the US as “toss-ups”; 16 of them are held by Republicans, and five are held by Democrats.
Ten Republican-held seats could flip blue, while eight Democratic seats could flip red, Cook reported.
A separate Reuters/Ipsos poll earlier this month showed Democrats leading Republicans by 7 points, 44% to 37%.
Much of the drop in support for Republican congressional candidates was due to a larger share of women saying they would pick Democrats. Some 50% of female voters said they would vote Democratic, compared to 32% eyeing Republican candidates. Men also favored Democrats, but by a smaller margin.
While the data collected shows potential for a series of wins for the Democrats, CNN noted that the House and the Senate rarely change control in the same year. The last time the Democrats took control of both chambers was in 2006 as part of the Blue Wave against the war in Iraq.
What have Republicans done to strengthen their chances of winning?
The president’s party historically loses House seats in the midterms. The Trump administration and Republicans have stressed to their base for months the importance of voting, and have resorted to unorthodox ways of trying to boost turnout.
At the beginning of October, Trump promised voters that if Republicans win big in the midterms, he will send US adults $5,000.
It is unclear how the president will get the money to Americans, and where the money would come from.
NBC reported that the endeavor would cost at least $1.3 trillion.
Trump told Republicans earlier this month that he will be blamed if the GOP loses several seats in the midterms.
“If we don’t win the midterms, they’re going to blame me,” Trump told crowds in Tennessee earlier this month. “You know that. And if we do win them, I will get no credit whatsoever. It’s true. I won’t get any.”
“But I’m working my ass off. You better get out there and vote,” he added.
Sources close to Trump told NBC that he is in “grind it out mode” ahead of the midterms and is prepared for the worst-case scenario.
How many Americans have voted so far?
Notably, at least 26 million Americans have already cast their ballots in early voting ahead of November 3 midterms, according to data from NBC News updated on Sunday.
Of them, 47% are registered Democrats, 35% are registered Republicans, and 18% are registered as other, according to NBC.
According to data from NBC, 14.3 million voters have sent in mail-in ballots, while at least another 12.6 million have voted in person at early in-person voting locations.

News from occupied Ukraine: Former Oleshky resident warns people 'won't survive this winter'
This weekly update from the Kyiv Independent aims to shed light on the situation facing Ukrainians living under Russian occupation and the ever-tightening control of information imposed by the Kremlin.
Key news as of Oct. 25:
- Oleshky native warns residents may not survive winter as evacuation hopes rise
- Russian-occupied Crimea imposes power and water restrictions after drone attack
- Russia sentences 77-year-old Crimean activist to 18 years over alleged plot against Moscow's proxy
- At least 34 Ukrainians were brought back from occupied territories, including over 20 children
- Russia intensifies pressure on occupied Ukrainians without Russian passports, military intelligence says
- Data center in occupied Donetsk destroyed following Ukraine's strikes
A woman who fled Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast has warned that residents remaining in the town may not survive the winter, as hopes grow for a possible evacuation mission.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity, while mined roads and constant drone attacks make safe evacuation virtually impossible.
"If the evacuation goes ahead, it will be a lifeline for those who remain. People won't survive the winter," a woman who left Oleshky in recent months told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 24. She declined to reveal her name for security reasons.
The woman pointed to severe food shortages and a lack of fuel for heating and cooking. She said residents had already burned much of the available wood during the previous winter, leaving few options to keep their homes warm as temperatures fall.
"There is almost no chance of survival," she added.
U.S. First Lady Melania Trump mediated a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in and around Oleshky to allow the safe evacuation of civilians and delivery of humanitarian aid, Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets confirmed on Oct. 23.
Under the agreement, a ceasefire will be implemented, humanitarian cargo will be delivered to Oleshky, and civilians will be allowed to leave the city freely, according to Lubinets.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 24 that Ukraine will fulfill its part of the "extremely difficult" humanitarian operation in Oleshky.
The move came amid increased attention to the worsening humanitarian crisis in the city, which over the past weeks has gained international attention, including from Pope Leo XIV.
Despite hoping the evacuation would proceed, the woman expressed concern that Russian authorities could prevent it from going ahead.
"I'd like to believe that this mission will go ahead, but you can expect anything from the Russian Federation," she said, adding that she believed civilians were being kept in the area as human shields.
Stefan Vorontsov, a volunteer coordinator with the NGO Humanity, which helps evacuate civilians from occupied territories, told the Kyiv Independent that while he hoped that people would be saved, he expects Russian provocations, blackmail, and propaganda surrounding those who manage to get out.
"God willing, we will be able to set a precedent where Russia admits what they did in the occupied territories, and we will be able to organize the first official evacuation from there, then maybe the rest of us will be able to do it too. But again, I have little faith," Vorontsov said.
In spring 2026, evacuation volunteers still managed to help Oleshky residents leave for other occupied settlements in Kherson Oblast or Ukraine-controlled areas in exhausting multi-day trips through Russia and Belarus. Now, they said, the risk of Russian attacks and mines has made organized evacuation impossible.
In recent months, some residents have started walking out of Oleshky to the neighboring village of Radensk alone or in pairs, on roads mined by Russian forces. At the end of September, four people were attempting to leave the town when they stepped on a mine and were injured, while a man collecting nuts was killed by another mine.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said that around 2,000 people, including nearly 50 children, remained in the occupied town with severely limited access to food, drinking water, electricity, and other basic services.

Russian-occupied Crimea imposes power and water restrictions after drone attack
Russian-installed authorities in occupied Crimea introduced electricity and water restrictions on Oct. 24 following a reported Ukrainian drone attack on energy infrastructure outside the peninsula, the Russian proxy governor of occupied Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said.
The restrictions came after Ukrainian strikes on energy infrastructure in southern Russia on Oct. 23-24, including damage to the Taman substation in Krasnodar Krai, which supplies electricity to occupied Crimea.
Major cities, including Sevastopol and Yalta, were left without electricity following the hit on the key power station.
Aksyonov said repairs were underway while rolling power cuts were implemented.
In Sevastopol, Russian-installed governor Mikhail Razvozhaev said on Oct. 25 that renewed strain on the power grid had prompted rolling blackouts on a "three hours on, three hours off" schedule.
Razvozhaev added that electricity supply to industrial sites and shopping centers will be restricted "as much as possible" to reduce the load on the grid.
"The capacity freed up must be channeled first and foremost to residential properties. This is our top priority," Razvozhaev said.
Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ reported on the evening of Oct. 23 that "the entire peninsula" was without electricity.
Crimea, which was occupied and illegally annexed by Russian forces in 2014, has been hit with widespread power outages before. This summer, Ukrainian forces reportedly hit 16 power stations across Crimea in 48 hours, in an effort to hinder Moscow in its war effort.

A Russian court in Rostov-on-Don said on Oct. 22 it had sentenced 77-year-old Crimean political prisoner Volodymyr Ananiev to 18 years in prison over an alleged plot to assassinate Sergey Aksyonov, the Russian proxy governor.
"Volodymyr Ananiev is the oldest Crimean political prisoner. He suffers from vision problems and issues with his spine, muscles, kidneys, and legs, and walks with a cane," The NGO Crimean Tatar Resource Center said.

At least 34 Ukrainians brought back from occupied territories, including over 20 children
Over the past week, Ukraine brought back at least 34 citizens who were forced to stay in Russian-occupied territories, including 23 children, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and the presidential initiative Bring Kids Back UA said.
On Oct. 22, Lubinets said that 11 Ukrainian citizens returned to government-controlled territory. Some of those who returned faced additional challenges due to health conditions, the need for medical care, and difficulties arranging a safe way back.
Among them was a married couple whose return journey involved two attempts. The woman had previously managed to leave occupied territory, but returned after her husband became seriously ill and was admitted to intensive care. After his condition improved, she arranged for them to leave together.
Separately, Bring Kids Back UA announced on Oct. 19 that it brought home 23 more children from Russian-occupied territory.
Among the children returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory was 9-year-old Stefan, who was forced to undergo military training at a school under Russian occupation, including instruction in handling grenades and firearms, the statement said.
The Ukrainian ombudsman's office coordinates returns through the humanitarian route connecting Mokrany in Belarus with Domanove in Ukraine's northwestern Volyn Oblast. Lubinets said the office is effectively the only Ukrainian state institution systematically organizing returns from occupied territories through this route, assisting people who cannot leave independently.
The Volyn humanitarian corridor is the main working checkpoint between Ukraine and Belarus. There are currently no functioning checkpoints between Ukraine and Russia.
According to Lubinets, 24,953 people, including 2,054 children, returned to Ukraine through this humanitarian corridor between May 24, 2024, and Oct. 15, 2026. Of these, 11,815 people, including 802 children, returned in 2026 alone.

Russia intensifies pressure on occupied Ukrainians without Russian passports, military intelligence says
Russian security forces carried out a new round of raids across occupied Ukrainian territories in early October, targeting residents who have refused to obtain Russian passports, Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) said on Oct. 22.
The raids were conducted jointly by the Russian police and the Federal Security Service (FSB) during the first 10 days of October as part of an operation dubbed "Illegal-2026," according to HUR.
Ukrainians without Russian passports are classified by occupation authorities as "foreign citizens" and subjected to Russian migration law.
According to the agency, residents can face pressure to obtain Russian citizenship, expulsion from occupied territory, dismissal from work, and property seizure.
Russia has pressured residents of occupied Ukrainian territories to take Russian passports since 2014, tying access to employment, social services, property rights, and other aspects of daily life to possession of Russian documents.
This is part of Moscow's long-running campaign of forced passportization. Russian President Vladimir Putin, on March 4, signed a decree that indefinitely extended the simplified process of obtaining Russian citizenship in the occupied territories.
"The goal of the decree is to passportize as many people as possible, pressuring them," Nataliia Yurlova, lawyer for the NGO Donbas SOS, told the Kyiv Independent.

How is the US-Israeli war on Iran causing havoc in Europe?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
14:47:55 UTC
23:47:55 KST

How is the US-Israeli war on Iran causing havoc in Europe?
Rising energy costs and protests are sharpening European opposition to renewed US-Israeli attacks on Iran.
Several Western European nations have expressed their opposition to the potential resumption of the Iran war, as spiralling global oil prices have worsened the cost of living crisis across Europe.
Countries such as Germany and the UK, among other major powers, which initially remained silent on the US-Israeli bombardment of Iran, have aired their views, calling for diplomacy to end the war which has disrupted global oil supplies.
Continued disruption to energy supplies is pushing up household costs as winter in Europe approaches, adding fuel to protests over living standards that have engulfed European capitals in recent weeks.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei on Sunday drew attention to what he described as a shift in Germany’s position on attacks against Iran.
In a post on X, Baghaei recalled German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s remarks during Israel’s June 2025 military campaign: “This is the dirty work Israel is doing for all of us.”
He contrasted those words with German officials’ recent warnings against renewed attacks and calls to prevent further escalation, before citing Friedrich Schiller’s The Maid of Orleans, quoting a passage that portrays reason being helplessly dragged towards an abyss by the forces of madness.
Experts say Baghaei’s remarks reflect a broader shift across Europe, where leaders are increasingly questioning their support for the US-Israeli war on Iran.
With Washington reportedly preparing options for renewed attacks, what would further escalation mean for Europe and could the war further strain already frayed relations with the United States?
Here is what we know.
How has Europe’s position changed?
When the US and Israel launched their attacks on February 28 , the leaders of Britain, France and Germany issued a joint statement condemning Iran’s retaliatory strikes on countries across the region. “We condemn Iranian attacks on countries in the region in the strongest terms,” British Prime Minister Keir Starmer, French President Emmanuel Macron and Merz said.
Their statement did not condemn the opening US-Israeli attacks. However, it called for negotiations to follow. Nearly eight months into the war, European governments are now explicitly warning against another military campaign.
On Friday, the foreign ministers of Britain, France, Germany and Italy met their counterparts from Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt in Istanbul to discuss the conflict and the Strait of Hormuz. Further escalation between Iran and the US “would create nothing but losers and would undoubtedly have very serious consequences for hydrocarbon prices”, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said.
“And so the first thing this group of eight countries … will do is call on both sides to exercise the utmost restraint, because we cannot afford another escalation in the region,” he added.
The warnings against new attacks do not necessarily mean European governments have abandoned their positions on Iran’s nuclear programme or regional activities, but they do show a change of position and have revealed that European governments are not united in their approach to the Iran war.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has consistently opposed the US-Israeli campaign. At this month’s European summit, he again described the war as “illegal, unjust and unjustified”, linking it to Europe’s mounting economic costs.
Western countries have opposed Iran’s nuclear programme, which Tehran says is for civilian purposes only. European countries were part of the landmark 2015 nuclear deal with Iran that limited Tehran’s nuclear programme in exchange for sanctions relief. But during his first term in 2018, United States President Donald Trump withdrew from the deal. Both the US and Israel invoked Iran’s nuclear programme to launch their attack in February.
Have European bases been used?
Europe’s divisions have been particularly visible over access to military bases and airspace. “We did not participate in these strikes, but are in close contact with our international partners, including the United States, Israel and partners in the region,” said the February 28 statement from Britain, France and Germany.
But non-participation in the opening attacks did not mean European countries would uniformly refuse support for subsequent operations. Germany said early in the war that it would not restrict US use of its bases, including Ramstein, a major American military hub.
Britain initially withheld permission for the opening attacks. However, it authorised US use of British bases for what London described as specific, limited defensive strikes against Iranian facilities involved in attacks on regional allies. Then, after initial reluctance, Britain expanded that permission to include operations against missile sites and capabilities being used to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
France allowed US support aircraft at Istres, while saying they would support the defence of regional partners rather than participate in attacks on Iran. It later blocked a weapons flight to Israel connected to the campaign. Spain went further. After refusing permission for attacks from the jointly operated Rota and Moron bases, Madrid closed its airspace to US aircraft involved in the war.
Those were different restrictions with different purposes, rather than a single European refusal to cooperate, but they provoked Trump. Calling Spain “terrible”, he threatened to cut off trade and said Washington wanted “nothing to do with Spain”.
The dispute has therefore exposed a widening argument over whether alliance commitments require European governments to facilitate a war they did not choose.
Mark Hilborne, a senior lecturer at the School of Security Studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera: “As to whether the war might push European leaders to openly challenge Trump, and limit support, it is certainly possible. What was initially a diplomatic disagreement is turning into something that has much more direct … and we could see increased resistance to any support from European countries.”
High prices and protest
After Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in the opening strikes, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said there was “renewed hope for the people of Iran”. She also warned then that instability could push the region into a spiral of violence. But by October 16, the costs to Europe had become central to her message. “Households and industry are paying the price for a war far beyond our borders,” she said after an EU summit.
According to von der Leyen, Europe’s bill for imported fossil fuels had increased by 106 billion euros, while gas prices had risen about 140 percent since late February and diesel prices had doubled.
Disruption to Gulf supplies and restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have also caused energy prices to spike. Brent crude settled at $72.48 a barrel on February 27, before the war began. It reached $126.41 at the end of April and remains well above $100 a barrel, with no sign of falling any time soon.
“For Europe, there is the economic interest as well, knowing it would further take a toll on energy markets, pushing up prices at a time when European countries are going into winter and the pushback to that,” Julie Norman, an associate fellow at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera.
Hilborne added that “there is an impact as well on food and fertiliser … The Persian Gulf is a hub for nitrogen-based fertilisers and disruptions have sent prices of urea up by something like 70 percent. Also, supply chains are feeling the impact as well, as shipping companies are facing large increases in their insurance premiums and/or need to reroute to longer journeys”.
“I would say that the Iranian war has had a direct, measurable and quite a rapid impact on European prices,” he added.
The search for relief from the energy crisis has created further friction, with Washington pressing European governments to release emergency diesel stocks, while Trump eased restrictions on Russian diesel in an effort to lower prices. That move provoked criticism from Ukraine and its supporters, who warned that renewed energy revenues would strengthen Moscow’s war effort.
But some of the sharpest political consequences are unfolding closer to home. Protests over living costs, housing, wages and public services have been seen across France, Belgium, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Greece and Albania. Their causes vary, and they do not constitute a single coordinated movement, but experts say the cost of living crisis, compounded by price rises caused by the Iran war, is a common thread that unites the protesters across the continent.
Donatella della Porta, a sociologist and political scientist, told Al Jazeera that opposition to war was central to recent protests by young people across Europe, alongside anger over military spending at the expense of welfare.
She pointed to opposition to military recruitment in schools, weapons-related university research and the use of ports to transport arms, linking those concerns to wider fears about the future.
“Especially the young protesters are afraid that their future will be stolen not only by global warming but also by wars in which they will be sent to die on the battlefield,” she said.
“Young people also connect wars with genocide, having often been socialised into politics during the large protests against the Israeli genocide of the Palestinians.”

Netanyahu’s pitch: Can Israel use crypto to evade economic sanctions?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
14:46:38 UTC
23:46:38 KST

Netanyahu’s pitch: Can Israel use crypto to evade economic sanctions?
PM Netanyahu mulls cryptocurrency as the answer to economic sanctions and Israel’s growing international isolation. But there are few buyers.
Two days before the general elections, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said that Israel should prepare to use cryptocurrency to circumvent potential sanctions on the country amid growing global isolation over its genocidal war on Gaza and settlement expansions in the occupied West Bank.
Netanyahu on Friday said that blockchain-based cryptocurrency is the solution to bypass the mounting economic sanctions that would keep the country out of the international financial system.
The Bank of Israel, the country’s central bank, rejected Netanyahu’s plan, and opposition parties said the incumbent prime minister’s vision is a recipe for disaster and increasing isolation.
So, can Israel really circumvent sanctions by dealing in crypto?
What’s behind Netanyahu’s crypto pitch?
“We need to prepare ways to evade banking sanctions through an alternative economic system,” Netanyahu said in an interview with Israel’s Channel 10 last Friday.
“You know what that means – the currencies that can bypass them,” he said, adding that he was referring to blockchain-based crypto.
Netanyahu’s crypto pitch comes as Israel has been facing international isolation over its extreme policies against Palestinians: a surge in settler violence, anti-Palestinian rhetoric and the acceleration of illegal settlements in the occupied territories of the West Bank and East Jerusalem.
Israel has killed more than 74,500 Palestinians since launching its genocidal war on Gaza three years ago. It has also been accused of committing war crimes in southern Lebanon, which has been hit almost daily by Israeli attacks despite a “ceasefire” now in place.
Israel has also carried out attacks on regional countries, including Iran, as part of its expansionist Greater Israel project, which is rooted in the biblical claim that Israel is entitled to the land between the Nile (in present-day Egypt) and the Euphrates (present-day Iraq).
Netanyahu has vowed to expand settlements, which are considered illegal under international laws, and has reiterated that he would not allow the formation of a Palestinian state, drawing condemnation from his European allies.
Last month, at least 12 major economies, including the United Kingdom, pledged coordinated measures against Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The European Union has also sanctioned settlement-linked individuals and groups. Spain and the Republic of Ireland have introduced restrictions on settlement goods, while the Netherlands brought a broader ban on their import, purchase and sale into force in September.
Israel’s banking system has not yet been targeted by sanctions.
Moreover, Netanyahu also warned that Israel needs to look out for financing its own military, in the face of less support from Washington in bankrolling its wars – because “America has changed”.
“It [financing] will end. It is only a matter of time,” Netanyahu said, adding that after US President Donald Trump’s tenure ends in two years, Israel should prepare for a less favorable White House.
The United States funnels billions of dollars to the Israeli military annually, but the genocidal war on Gaza has changed unrestricted military support for Israel, which a growing number of Americans have started to question.
Netanyahu also faces an arrest warrant by the International Criminal Court (ICC) for war crimes, while the International Court of Justice (ICJ) is hearing the case of genocide against Israel brought by South Africa.
If the ICJ verdict goes against Israel, it would further intensify calls for sanctions against the country, including restrictions on arms exports, trade and financial ties, as governments around the world face mounting pressure to hold Israeli officials accountable.
Can crypto help evade sanctions?
If Israeli banks are restricted from international transfers, then businesses could attempt to pay overseas suppliers using cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin, stablecoins, or other digital assets.
Cryptocurrency is digital money, transferred between people or businesses over the internet, where transactions are recorded on a digital ledger called a blockchain. Public blockchains can transfer assets directly between digital wallets without a bank processing every transaction.
Sanctioned actors have used cryptocurrencies for cross-border payments, including transactions connected to oil sales and procurement. Russia, which has been slapped with sanctions for its invasion of Ukraine, has reportedly used cryptocurrencies to make some payments to evade sanctions.
But crypto cannot replace conventional banking at the scale of today’s economy. It can be a parallel medium, but cannot replace the traditional banking system, experts note.
Moreover, crypto does not solve a fundamental problem that Israel faces from sanctions: financial isolation, which by design also demoralises investors and businesses. It also restricts access to financial institutions or penalises third parties that deal with designated entities. Therefore, even if a business uses crypto for payments, the transaction would still be illegal.
Israel’s economy also depends on international trade and technology supply chains, wherein its defence and tech industry need foreign components and specialist equipment.
More than 100 experts and former Israeli officials, in a statement issued on Sunday, expressed “grave concern and anxiety” over Netanyahu’s crypto plan.
They accused the Israeli prime minister of failing to grasp the seriousness of the threat, and criticised his proposal as a solution more commonly associated with criminal organisations.
Sanctions would cause “enormous and irreversible damage” to the Israeli economy, they said.
Who opposes Netanyahu’s plan in Israel?
The Bank of Israel rejected Netanyahu’s plan, arguing that cryptocurrencies “cannot be used as a route for bypassing sanctions”.
“The right thing for Israel’s economy is preserving the economic relationships with our principal trade partners and focusing on preventing sanctions and their negative influence on the economy,” the central bank said in a statement. “This issue is within the responsibilities of the political echelon, and it should act to advance it.”
However, Netanyahu responded by saying that he is grateful for the bank’s advice, “But I do what I think [is best].”
Netanyahu’s main opponent, Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, said that the PM’s vision “is a threat to national security”.
“After he finished dismantling Israeli society and weakening the [Israeli military], Netanyahu has marked the next target: the dismantling of the Israeli economy for generations ahead,” he said.
Eisenkot further said that the prime minister has “lost touch with reality” — referring to the crypto-based solution “to the nadir in international [relations] that he himself brought upon us — to disconnect Israel from the global economy.”
Taking a dig at the gaps in the approach, Eisenkot said he wondered, “How will Google buy an Israeli company on the condition that it bypass an international bank and pay in crypto?”

He also suggested that Abdullah’s comments were directed at what he described as discrimination against minorities across the country and the policies pursued by BJP governments in various states.“The remarks reflected resentment against a pattern of oppression and discrimination,” the Congress leader said.Sharma further said Jammu and Kashmir continued to face resentment over the delay in restoring statehood, despite repeated assurances by the Centre before the Supreme Court, Parliament and the public.Meanwhile, some Kashmiri Pandit groups have filed a police complaint seeking an FIR against the former chief minister over his comments.His remarks drew criticism from some Kashmiri Pandit groups, which lodged a police complaint seeking the registration of an FIR against the former chief minister.Meanwhile, Kashmiri Pandit groups Panun Kashmir and the Jammu State People's Movement (JSPM) have lodged a police complaint at the Channi police station in Jammu, seeking the registration of an FIR against Abdullah over his remarks.The complaint, submitted by Panun Kashmir chairman Tito Ganju and JSPM chairman Col Ajay Raina (retd), sought an investigation into statements attributed to Abdullah concerning the constitutional status of Jammu and Kashmir and alleged religious polarisation.It cited his reported remarks questioning the prospects of justice from the Union government and warning that the people of J&K risked losing their identity if they failed to confront the prevailing political circumstances.The complainants also referred to remarks attributed to Abdullah about the demolition of mosques, homes and shops, as well as his assertion that Hindus and Muslims were being pitted against each other. They urged the police to examine the statements in their entirety, taking into account their context, the audience addressed and their potential implications.The complaint sought an FIR under Sections 152, 196 and 197 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), along with any other provisions that may apply based on the investigation.The provisions cited concern acts endangering India's sovereignty, unity and integrity, promoting enmity between groups, and certain imputations or assertions prejudicial to national integration, a Panun Kashmir spokesperson said.BJP leader Jahanzaib Sirwal also criticised Abdullah, accusing him of double standards for invoking Pakistan to question India's intentions while overlooking the suffering of people across the Line of Control.“It was deeply unfortunate that a leader who has dominated J&K’s political landscape for decades continues to rely on the Pakistan narrative rather than account for the consequences of his own politics.“Farooq Sahib has spent decades building a political narrative around Pakistan, but has he ever honestly answered what this politics has delivered to the people of J&K?“His party does not have to seek votes in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir, but that cannot be an excuse to remain silent on the atrocities and sufferings of the people living there. Human rights cannot be selective, and political morality cannot change with electoral convenience,” Sirwal said.He added that the NC leadership must stop treating Pakistan as a convenient political instrument to invoke whenever it suited its narrative.
What Farooq Abdullah saidAddressing a party event in Baramulla on Saturday, Abdullah questioned whether people in Jammu and Kashmir could expect justice from the Centre.“What hope will you (people of J&K) have from them (Delhi)? Will you expect that they will do justice for you?" he said.Urging Kashmiris to remain courageous in confronting Delhi, Abdullah warned that their identity could disappear if they failed to do so.“If not, you will be erased. Even our trace and identity will disappear. They are silent today because there is noise in the world, and our neighbour is constantly behind this. Everywhere they say, 'the decision regarding Kashmir has not been made'. That is what is saving us. Otherwise, their intentions are not good,” he said.

Over 268,000 displaced in Yemen, thousands flee to Djibouti: UN migration agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
14:44:18 UTC
23:44:18 KST

Rania Abushamala
25 October 2026•Update: 25 October 2026
More than 268,000 people have been displaced inside Yemen since July amid escalating conflict between government forces and the Houthi group, while thousands have fled by sea to Djibouti, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said.
The UN agency said in a statement published Sunday that the figure was recorded as of Oct. 23, with almost all those affected were displaced since the beginning of September.
Escalating conflict in western Yemen has also driven people beyond the country’s borders. As of Oct. 17, at least 3,836 Yemenis had arrived in Djibouti, half of them children, including 282 under five.
Most reported fleeing worsening insecurity, with several boats reportedly coming ashore short of their destination after running out of fuel, the IOM said.
Separately, the organization recorded 1,327 migrants crossing by sea from Yemen to Djibouti as they returned toward their countries of residence.
Inside Yemen, families are increasingly seeking safety farther south. The number of displaced people in Aden has more than doubled since Oct. 7 to over 42,000, while Lahj hosts around 67,000.
The IOM said displaced families have taken shelter in 62 districts across 10 governorates, as far east as Al Maharah.
“The scale and speed of this displacement is leaving families in desperate need of help, and our response is struggling to keep pace,” said Abdusattor Esoev, IOM’s chief of mission in Yemen.
“Our teams are reaching people every day, but funding is falling far short. Without urgent support, more families will go without assistance that could save their lives.”
Many face difficulties accessing clean water, health care and basic services amid severe fuel shortages and soaring food and medicine prices.
Families are sheltering in overcrowded public buildings or sleeping outdoors, often without adequate sanitation, IOM said.
Women, children, older people and people with disabilities face heightened protection risks, while humanitarian access restrictions in Taiz continue to delay aid delivery.
“Many families have had to flee more than once, each time facing the struggle to find somewhere safe to stay and access the support they need,” Esoev said.
“Support must reach both displaced families and the communities hosting them now, before more lives are put at risk.”
IOM urged donors to increase support and called on all parties to protect civilians and humanitarian workers and ensure safe, unimpeded access to those in need.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several other provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.
The Houthis control much of northern and western Yemen, while government forces and their allies hold Aden and large parts of the country’s southern and eastern provinces.

Ramzi Mahmud, Hosni Nedim and Rania Abushamala

At least six Palestinians were killed and 10 others injured, including five university students, in Israeli attacks across the Gaza Strip on Sunday, in further violations of last year’s ceasefire agreement, medical sources said.
Three Palestinians lost their lives and others were injured in an Israeli strike on the Islamic University campus in Gaza City, one of the sources told Anadolu.
The attack came shortly after five students were injured, some critically, when an Israeli drone strike targeted a gathering of students on campus, the university said in a statement.
The university suspended administrative and academic activities at its Gaza City premises following the attack, which caused panic among students and displaced Palestinians sheltering on campus after their homes were destroyed during Israel’s genocidal war.
In northern Gaza, an Israeli strike on a gathering of civilians along Al-Rashid coastal road in the northwest of the enclave wounded several Palestinians, medical sources said, without specifying their number.
A Palestinian was also hospitalized with a gunshot wound to the foot after Israeli forces opened fire in the Al-Faluja area west of Jabalia refugee camp.
In southern Gaza, two Palestinians were killed and three others injured in an Israeli strike in al-Mawasi, west of Khan Younis, according to medical sources.
The sources also reported that a woman sustained moderate injuries from Israeli gunfire in Khan Younis.
Israeli artillery also shelled areas east and south of the city, while gunboats fired bullets and shells toward its coast, witnesses told Anadolu.
In central Gaza, a 33-year-old man was killed in an Israeli strike east of Deir al-Balah.
At dawn Sunday, Israeli forces carried out two demolitions of homes and buildings in areas under their control in the Al-Tuffah neighborhood of eastern Gaza City, causing two large explosions, local sources said.
Despite a ceasefire that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, the Israeli army has killed 1,551 Palestinians and injured 5,573 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Since October 2023, Israel's war in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded over 175,000, while causing widespread destruction to about 90% of the territory's civilian infrastructure.

October 7 victims' families to hold 'Remember them at the voting booth' rallies on Election Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
14:40:56 UTC
23:40:56 KST

Families of the victims of the October 7 massacre will hold a series of rallies outside of voting sites across the country on Tuesday, Election Day, under the banner "Remember them at the voting booth."
The victims and families emphasized that the initiative was not tied to any specific political party, but was intended only to remind Israeli citizens of the horrors that the nation endured on October 7, 2023, and ensure that the victims' memories were not forgotten.
The participants will be pushing the campaign across social media up until the day of the election, using signs reminding the Israeli public of those killed and taken hostage on October 7.
Among those taking part in the initiative are Yocheved Lifshitz, a former hostage whose husband, Oded, was abducted alive and murdered in captivity; Yona Adam, mother of Mapal, who was murdered at the Nova music festival; Hadas Calderon, daughter of Carmela Dan and aunt of Noya, both of whom were murdered on October 7, and mother of former hostages Sahar and Erez; Dvora Shani, mother of soldier Ido Shani, who was killed while defending communities near the Gaza border; Danny Elgart, brother of Itzik, who was abducted alive and murdered in captivity; Gil Dickmann, cousin of Carmel Gat, who was abducted alive and murdered in captivity; Noam Alon, sister of soldier Dor Sadeh, who was killed in battle in Kfar Aza; Noam Perry, daughter of Haim Perry, who was abducted alive and murdered in captivity; and Michel Iluz, father of Guy, who was abducted alive and murdered in captivity.
The planned election-day protests follow a rally organized by the October Council on Saturday evening in Hostage Square in Tel Aviv, three days before the Knesset elections.
Likud calls for networks to not broadcast rally speeches live
The Likud Party, on Thursday morning, called on television networks not to broadcast live the speeches at the rally.
In an urgent letter sent by attorney Ilan Bombach on behalf of the party, Likud argued that the event could be used for prohibited election campaigning, given the participation of opposition party leaders and the political messages surrounding the rally.
The letter was addressed to the legal advisers of KAN News, N12 news site, Channel 13, and Channel 14, as well as the Second Authority for Television and Radio and the attorney-general.
Likud is not demanding that the event's coverage be prohibited. Instead, the party is calling for speeches to be broadcast with a delay of at least 10 minutes, allowing news editors to review their content and prevent the airing of messages that constitute election propaganda.
The rally was held under the slogan, "In three days, we vote for a state commission of inquiry."
Naftali Bennett, Gadi Eisenkot, and Avigdor Liberman attended, alongside bereaved families, families of hostages, former hostages, and residents of communities near the Gaza border.
Rally organizers demand October 7 commission of inquiry
The rally's organizers sought to place the demand for a state commission of inquiry into the failures surrounding October 7 at the center of the public agenda.
Their promotional materials state: "This is what we are all going to vote on October 27."
Likud argued that explicitly linking the public demand for an inquiry to voting in the elections, combined with the participation of opposition leaders, raised concerns that the broadcast could become a platform for one-sided political campaigning.
Bombach cited a March 2019 ruling by former Central Elections Committee chairman Justice Hanan Melcer. At the time, following a petition by the Labor Party, it was determined that a Likud conference could not be broadcast live and must instead be aired with a delay of at least 10 minutes to allow broadcasters to distinguish between legitimate news coverage and election propaganda.
The letter also included guidelines issued by the Second Authority's legal adviser, attorney Ofir Bitan, emphasizing the prohibition on election propaganda in news broadcasts and the responsibility of editors to exercise independent judgment.
The legal distinction rests on whether the broadcast's primary purpose is to inform the public or to persuade viewers politically.
The appeal came a day after the attorney-general instructed broadcasters not to air Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's speech live at the IDF officer training course graduation ceremony at Bahad 1, citing concerns over prohibited election propaganda.
October Council accuses Netanyahu of trying to silence bereaved families
"Netanyahu is once again trying to silence the bereaved families," the October Council said in response. "Are Roni Eshel, Kfir and Ariel Bibas, Ido Edri, Neta Baram, Ori Danino, and 2,200 murdered victims election propaganda? Who is afraid of hearing from the bereaved families, the former hostages, and the survivors of the October 7 massacre?
"Three years have passed since the largest massacre of the Jewish people since the Holocaust. Three years during which Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister responsible for the failure, refused to meet with us, look us in the eye, and give us answers. Three years during which the coalition responsible for the failure did everything in its power to silence the bereaved families and prevent the public from learning the truth. And now, once again, Israel's prime minister is trying to silence the bereaved families!
"He does not want Israelis to hear the stories of former hostages, of those who were murdered and killed, or of residents of the communities near Gaza and in the North. He does not want Israelis to hear, alongside the pain, a message of hope for the establishment of a state commission of inquiry, which he has continued to evade to this day. Anyone who repeatedly seeks to silence bereaved families is afraid of the truth.
"The hundreds of thousands of Israelis who will come to Hostages Square this coming Saturday night will prove that the truth is stronger than anything. We call on all Israelis: Come to Hostages Square this Saturday night, stand alongside us, and demand a state commission of inquiry. Together, we will prove that the truth will prevail and that no one will silence it."

====================================================================================================

How One Danish Entrepreneur Is Bringing Ukrainian Art to the World
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
14:37:00 UTC
23:37:00 KST

For many international audiences, Ukraine remains synonymous with war. But beyond the headlines, artists continue to paint landscapes, portraits, and scenes of everyday life, preserving the country’s identity and documenting what Ukrainians are fighting to protect.
Danish entrepreneur Caspar Ejsing founded artfromukraine, an online gallery selling works by Ukrainian artists to international buyers. The platform allocates 70% of each sale to the artist, 25% to operating costs, and 5% to the Hospitallers Medical Battalion, whose volunteer medics evacuate wounded soldiers from the front.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Recently featured by UNITED24 Media and Spend With Ukraine, the project aims to expand the international market for Ukrainian art and introduce audiences to a side of the country that often goes unseen.
In an interview with Kyiv Post, Ejsing explains how his experience in Ukraine shaped the initiative, why art can change perceptions of a country at war, and how he plans to build a sustainable platform for Ukrainian artists.
Kyiv Post: What do international audiences still fail to understand about Ukrainian society?
Caspar Ejsing: I find this question hard to answer on behalf of others, because my own view of Ukraine is very different from that of most people in Denmark. I have seen the side of Ukraine that rarely makes the news: the warmth of its people, its culture, and the way life goes on in cities like Kyiv. That is why I fell in love with the country.
Peskov Says Kremlin Open to EU Envoy if Focused on Genuine Peace
For many people abroad, Ukraine has become synonymous with war. When they think of Ukrainians, they often picture soldiers on the front line or elderly women in damaged villages. Those images are real and important, but they are only part of the picture.
What is often missing is a modern, creative, and highly educated society, with artists, musicians, young professionals, and entrepreneurs who continue to build their lives and their country under attack.
In Denmark, I think understanding is better than in many places. We have a strong Ukrainian community in Copenhagen, including around Ukraine House, and many Danes now have Ukrainian colleagues, neighbors, and friends – myself included.
On the wider international stage, especially in the US, I think the picture is still much narrower. That is exactly where art can make a difference.
How did your time in Ukraine shape your understanding of Ukrainian art, and why did you decide to build a business around it?
I spent most of my time in Kyiv, a city full of culture – not only visual art, but also music and countless grassroots initiatives. What struck me was how Ukrainians use art and culture to express themselves, including their feelings about the war.
Art has always been a personal interest of mine. I have spent a lot of time drawing myself and attended art schools here in Denmark, so the connection came naturally.
Artfromukraine had already started when the real turning point came. I was invited by Professor Leonid Pavlenko to visit the National Academy of Fine Arts and Architecture in Kyiv. Seeing the studios and the quality of the work, I realized that it deserved a much bigger international audience. That was the moment I decided to take the project seriously.
The gallery is possible because of cspaar, a Danish IT company, which develops and operates the platform. Without cspaar, artfromukraine would not exist.
What do these works reveal about Ukraine that war reporting cannot capture?
War reporting naturally focuses on the front line: which towns are taken, which are lost, and how the lines move back and forth. That is necessary, but it reduces Ukraine to a battlefield.
The paintings show what Ukrainians are fighting for. a landscape, a street in Kyiv, a portrait of a friend – these are the places, the people, and the everyday life the war is trying to destroy.
They show a country with its own identity, traditions, and beauty, making it much harder to see Ukraine as just a headline.
At the same time, we do not avoid the war. On our channels, we regularly remind our audiences in Denmark, the UK, and the US that the war is ongoing and devastating, and that Ukraine still needs support.
Art opens the door. Once people care about the culture, they also care about the country.
How do you balance the commercial side of the gallery with supporting Ukraine, and what impact has the initiative made so far?
The model is built in from the start: 70% of every sale goes directly to the artist, 25% covers operating costs such as shipping and export documentation, and 5% goes to the Hospitallers Medical Battalion. The donation is not decided case by case. It is part of every sale.
Our costs are low because the platform is developed and operated by cspaar. This means the gallery does not need large margins to survive, and the artist always receives the majority of the price.
Artfromukraine is still at an early stage. So far, the biggest impact has been visibility: we have onboarded Ukrainian artists, and the project has been covered by UNITED24 Media and Spend With Ukraine.
That matters because it puts Ukrainian artists in front of international buyers who would otherwise never have seen their work.
How do you plan to grow artfromukraine and strengthen the international market for Ukrainian art?
We plan to grow slowly and steadily. In the short term, the focus is on onboarding more artists and building a stronger network in Ukraine. We are also working on establishing a Ukrainian company, which will make payments and cooperation with Ukrainian partners much easier.
In the longer term, I want to run the project together with Ukrainian partners, whether they are co-investors, development partners, or marketing companies.
The goal is for artfromukraine to become a trusted place for international buyers to discover Ukrainian art, and a reliable source of income for the artists we work with.

Zimbabwean president calls for unconditional lifting of sanctions
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
22:32:39 CST
23:32:39 KST

HARARE, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa on Sunday called for the unconditional lifting of sanctions imposed by Western countries on Zimbabwe, saying the measures constrain economic development.
In a speech marking the Southern African Development Community (SADC) Anti-Sanctions Day held annually on Oct. 25, Mnangagwa said Zimbabwe was making progress in its development aspirations despite the sanctions, stressing that regional integration was crucial to achieving the country's development goals.
The SADC Anti-Sanctions Day was established by the 16-member regional organization in 2019 as a collective initiative to denounce the sanctions, which were imposed on Zimbabwe following the country's land reform program that redistributed land from minority white farmers to indigenous black Zimbabweans.
"Sanctions not only punish our country, but the entire SADC family and infringe Zimbabwe's role in advancing an integrated Africa," said Mnangagwa, who also expressed appreciation to SADC member states for supporting the call to remove the unilateral sanctions.
"This reflects our shared commitment to a just and fair global order, where the principles of sovereign equality, non-interference in the internal affairs and the sovereign right of every country to chart its own destiny are respected," said Mnangagwa.
He called for increased regional integration, saying SADC and the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa offered opportunities to improve regional connectivity and strengthen cooperation in trade, industry, agriculture, energy and infrastructure.
Mnangagwa said Zimbabwe would broaden international partnerships and deepen regional integration to drive economic transformation, while pursuing diplomatic and domestic measures to lift sanctions and boost industrial competitiveness.
He also reaffirmed Zimbabwe's commitment to multilateralism, international cooperation, and the peaceful resolution of conflicts.
The United States enacted the Zimbabwe Democracy and Economic Recovery Act in December 2001, restricting its support for multilateral financial assistance to Zimbabwe.
In March 2024, former U.S. President Joe Biden signed an executive order terminating a Zimbabwe sanctions program that had been in force since 2003 but immediately imposed sanctions on 11 individuals, including Mnangagwa and Vice President Constantino Chiwenga, over alleged human rights abuses and corruption under the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act. ■

Economic Watch: European firms put Chinese technology to work
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
22:32:36 CST
23:32:36 KST

CHENGDU, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- At a machinery factory in Vicenza, Italy, Chinese-made robots weld components and move materials. The machines come from Chengdu CRP Robot Technology Co., Ltd., which now has more than 20 partners across 13 European countries.
Thirty years ago, German entrepreneur Harald Kumpfert relied largely on European technology for his energy-saving projects in China. Today, he buys Chinese heat pumps, thermal storage equipment and heat exchangers, and is trying to introduce Chinese technology to Europe.
"Now most technology is actually from China," Kumpfert said at a business fair in Chengdu, capital of southwest China's Sichuan Province.
The 19th Europe-China Business and Technology Cooperation Fair, which concluded Friday, brought together about 200 Chinese and European companies for nearly 400 one-on-one business meetings.
Kumpfert's experience shows the importance European businesses place on Chinese suppliers.
In a 2026 survey by the European Union Chamber of Commerce in China, 94 percent of respondents said sourcing from China was important or very important to their supply chains and business success, while 75 percent said that their production lines in China were more efficient than those elsewhere.
The automotive industry shows how competition and cooperation can develop side by side.
China's rapid advances in new energy vehicles have intensified competition for established European automakers. Yet European carmakers remain interested in investing in China and are working with Chinese companies to explore opportunities in European markets, according to Adam Dunnett, secretary-general of the chamber.
Dunnett described China's electric vehicle development as "nothing short of amazing" and said there was considerable scope for further cooperation.
"I think there is a much bigger upside to what can happen in the future than perhaps the focus on all the challenges that we are facing right now," he said.
Some European businesses are also expanding their research and development operations in China.
Swiss specialty chemicals maker Sika Group has 33 factories and four of its nine global R&D centers in China. Zhang Yejiong, President of Sika China, said the company was expanding local R&D while incorporating low-carbon requirements into product development.
Chinese components are also attracting European researchers. Juha Röning, a professor at Finland's University of Oulu and euRobotics' Vice President of Research, said the availability of Chinese-made sensors, motors and gears allowed researchers to concentrate on developing new applications rather than building every component themselves.
For equipment manufacturers, selling to Europe increasingly involves more than shipping machines.
CRP Robot is working with European local partners to improve technical support and after-sales services, its deputy general manager Deng Shihai said. Luigi Gambardella, president of the international digital association ChinaEU, said Chinese robots entering European factories could also generate business for local engineers, software developers and service providers.
European producers, meanwhile, are pursuing opportunities in China's consumer market.
Hervé Grangeon, founder of Ergaster Distillery in France, came to Chengdu seeking distributors for his gin and whisky, while Spanish ham producer Garcia Lizana is preparing the documents needed to enter China.
Smaller European businesses, however, often struggle to find local partners and navigate market-entry requirements, Zhang said. He suggested that local governments and business associations could help them identify opportunities by providing policy guidance and connecting them with potential Chinese partners.
Among the technologies on display was a Chinese elevator energy-saving system that caught Kumpfert's attention. Having spent much of his career bringing European technology to China, he now plans to explore cooperation with its Chinese developer. ■

Organized by UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) and hosted by Qatar, the three-day forum, themed "Investing in the Future," is attended by the prime ministers of Qatar, Lesotho, Libya and Madagascar, four deputy prime ministers and nearly 50 government ministers.
More than 80 sessions featuring over 400 speakers will cover investment policies, artificial intelligence, entrepreneurship, sustainable finance, climate change, tourism and emerging industries.
The forum opened as new UNCTAD data showed continued weakness in global investment activity.
Its latest Global Investment Trends Monitor, released Sunday, said the value of international investment rose in the first half of 2026, supported by major transactions in strategic sectors, while new investment projects and cross-border transactions continued to decline worldwide.
Investment in sectors critical to development, including infrastructure, energy, healthcare and food systems, fell by more than 25 percent in developing countries, the report showed.
UNCTAD's World Investment Report 2026 also found that more than 80 percent of global foreign direct investment was concentrated in just 20 economies in 2025, highlighting persistent disparities in international capital flows.
The forum's agenda includes two ministerial meetings on investment and entrepreneurship, as well as discussions on investment opportunities in the Gulf region and other emerging markets.
For the first time, the event features a dedicated track on artificial intelligence (AI), focusing on investment in AI infrastructure and opportunities for developing economies.
Other new topics include investment in post-conflict reconstruction and recovery, the space industry and cultural sectors.
Launched in 2008, the World Investment Forum is held every two years to discuss international investment policies and promote investment in sustainable development. ■

China Focus: Health work, emergency facilities back post-quake resettlement in China's Xizang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
22:32:30 CST
23:32:30 KST

BAQEN, Xizang, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Rescue and relief efforts continue after a 7.0-magnitude earthquake struck southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, with public health and epidemic prevention work underway in affected areas, according to local authorities.
The earthquake, which struck Baqen County in the city of Nagqu at 10:33 p.m. on Thursday, has left 16 people dead and 76 others injured so far. More than 12,000 residents were evacuated after the quake.
To prevent public health risks after the quake, disease control teams in Baqen County have carried out comprehensive epidemic prevention work. The work includes infectious disease monitoring of more than 3,600 residents across 35 resettlement sites, disinfection of public areas and high-risk contamination spots, and drinking water safety testing, the earthquake relief headquarters of Nagqu said on Sunday.
In the immediate aftermath of the earthquake, hospitals near the disaster zone swiftly dispatched medical workers for rescue efforts.
On Saturday, a female villager from an affected area with an abrasion on her left ankle told Xinhua, "The doctor arrived before dawn on Friday and promptly applied ointment and bandaged it for me." A 23-year-old woman, 28 weeks pregnant, also received basic health checks, including vital-sign measurements.
Multiple resettlement sites have set up mobile medical stations, each staffed with health workers ready to treat common illnesses and minor injuries, with regular checkups, medicine supplies, disinfection, and basic psychological counseling.
The epicenter in Baqen County sits at an average altitude of nearly 4,800 meters, where temperatures are already low in late October. Yet inside the tents set up for displaced residents, stoves keep the shelters warm.
On Saturday, the first batch of new-generation emergency relief facilities, including a mobile food vehicle, a water purification station, and an eco-friendly toilet, was put into use in the affected area in Baqen County.
The mobile food vehicle allows four people to work inside the truck-sized box and eight outside at the same time. Meals for 300 to 500 people can be fully prepared in just two hours.
At 6:30 p.m., the first meal off the stove was braised beef with potatoes and stir-fried greens, drawing many residents over to try it.
"The truck is really cool, and the food tastes great too," said Norbu Tsering, a villager from Maru Township.
"The truck is equipped with a high-pressure rice steamer which can cook 18 trays of rice at once. The stainless steel tableware is washed after use, then sterilized in a disinfection cabinet for the next round," said Ma Hua, deputy director of the 999 emergency rescue center in Xizang.
Access to clean water is crucial but challenging in the quake-hit plateau, especially in winter.
In Maru Township, a mobile water purification station can purify two tonnes of well water per hour. Equipped with solar power generation, insulation materials and an energy storage system, it is designed to operate in temperatures as low as minus 30 degrees Celsius, said Ji Tao, head of the Baqen branch of the company that provided the purification facilities.
Five administrative villages in Maru Township had already received the water purification facilities, Ji said, adding that coverage would be expanded.
Near the purification station, an eco-friendly toilet with rooftop solar panels and a waterless, flush-free system has been put up. Solar power provides lighting and drives fermentation, while enzymes break down waste in a sealed tank, which can be used as fertilizer, according to Tsewang Ngodrup, an official with the Nagqu municipal science and technology bureau.
More than 5,000 rescue personnel have been deployed at all levels. Relief supplies from central and local governments are arriving in the disaster zone in succession. ■

China
