The Black Sea has become the most dangerous route for merchant vessels - FT
Kyiv • UNN
Since the beginning of 2026, more than 570 vessels have been hit in the Black Sea and more than 40 sailors have been killed. NATO and the EU are strengthening shipping security.
The Black Sea has become the world’s most dangerous route for commercial shipping due to a sharp increase in attacks on civilian vessels amid Russia’s war against Ukraine. Since the beginning of 2026, more than 40 seafarers have been killed in the region. Financial Times reports this, according to UNN.
Details
According to the publication, which cites analysts from maritime security company Ambrey and the International Maritime Organization (IMO), more than 570 vessels have been hit in the Black Sea since the beginning of 2026. During the third quarter alone, 387 vessels came under attack—more than five times the figure for the previous quarter.
As FT notes, around 90% of attacks on shipping in the region over the past 45 days have been linked to Russia’s actions. At the same time, attacks are increasingly occurring not only near Ukrainian ports but also in areas off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria, which are NATO members. In particular, drones attacked several merchant vessels near the Romanian and Bulgarian coasts in October. Some ships sank, and there were fatalities and crew members reported missing.
Experts estimate that Russian strikes are aimed, among other things, at disrupting the operation of Ukrainian seaports and limiting grain exports. Due to the constant attacks, shipowners are increasingly refusing to call at Ukrainian ports, while carriers are being forced to change their logistics routes.
The situation has also led to a sharp increase in the cost of maritime transport insurance. In some cases, war-risk coverage costs as much as 15% of the vessel’s insured value, making certain voyages economically unviable.
Against the backdrop of the worsening situation, NATO announced that it would step up surveillance of the Black Sea region using patrol aircraft, radar systems, and drones.
In addition, on October 22, the European Parliament adopted a resolution calling for consideration of a possible EU naval operation to ensure the safety of shipping in the Black Sea.
Analysts warn that a further increase in the number of attacks could deepen the maritime transport crisis, cause additional losses to Ukraine’s agricultural sector, and create risks to global food security.
Reminder
The European Parliament discussed the protection of shipping after six attacks allegedly carried out by Russian drones in ten days. The EU will strengthen monitoring and pressure on the aggressor state.

Anger and fear nudge voters toward different kinds of leader faces, study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
14:00:09 UTC
23:00:09 KST

The specific emotions that political issues stir up in voters may subtly shift the physical traits they look for in a leader. A new study published in Cognition and Emotion indicates that when people think about a policy problem that makes them angry, they lean slightly more toward dominant-looking leaders than when they think about one that makes them afraid. Fear, by contrast, appears to put more weight on whether a leader’s face looks trustworthy.
When people look at a stranger’s face, they form instantaneous impressions about that person’s character. As a 2008 behavioral and computer modeling study found, these rapid evaluations boil down to two main facial qualities: trustworthiness and dominance. Trustworthiness is an impression of a person’s intentions, signaling whether they appear warm, cooperative, and safe to approach. Dominance is an impression of physical strength and assertiveness, signaling a person’s capacity to impose their will or confront rivals.
These split-second facial judgments influence real-world voting decisions, and the traits voters prefer often depend on the surrounding political environment and their own personal beliefs. For instance, a 2025 study by members of the team behind the new research, covered by PsyPost, found that people who are generally distrustful of information from others tend to hold more rigid, dogmatic beliefs and more conservative views, which in turn predicts a preference for dominant, authoritarian-looking leaders. Broader contexts matter as well, with voters generally favoring dominant faces during wartime or conflict and trustworthy faces during peaceful periods.
Different emotional reactions to the same crisis can also pull people in different directions. Although anger and fear are both unpleasant, high-stress emotions, a 2001 study on emotion and risk showed that they trigger opposing mindsets: anger makes people feel certain and willing to take risks, whereas fear makes people feel vulnerable and cautious.
In the political arena, a 2025 panel study of Ukrainians conducted during the Russian invasion found that citizens who reacted to the war with aggressive, angry emotions showed stronger preferences for dominant leaders (and for the other leader traits measured, such as warmth and competence), while those who reacted with fear showed little change in their preferences.
Most research on these emotional dynamics has focused on wars, terrorist attacks, or major geopolitical crises. Far less is known about how anger and fear shape leader evaluations during everyday domestic politics, where citizens routinely react to policy debates over the economy, healthcare, or public safety. The research was led by Mariana von Mohr, a lecturer in social and affective neuroscience at the University of Kent, and conducted at the Centre for the Politics of Feelings at the School of Advanced Study, University of London, which is directed by co-author Manos Tsakiris, a professor at Royal Holloway, University of London.
“Political issues often evoke strong emotions, which can shape political behavior in different ways,” von Mohr told PsyPost. “For example, anger can increase support for tougher, more confrontational political action, whereas fear can lead people to seek reassurance and favor responses that promise greater safety and protection. Here we wanted to understand whether these emotions also shape who people would prefer to vote for when dealing with the issues that concern them most, simply based on how dominant or trustworthy a potential leader looks.”
To investigate this, the researchers recruited 201 American participants through the online platform Prolific, ensuring the group was evenly split between people who identified with or leaned toward the Democratic Party and those who identified with or leaned toward the Republican Party. After removing four individuals who did not pass attention checks during the tasks, the final sample consisted of 197 participants.
The experiment used a within-subjects design, meaning every participant went through both the anger condition and the fear condition in a randomized order. In the anger section, participants viewed a list of 16 major national problems taken from a Pew Research Center survey, such as inflation, gun violence, illegal immigration, and climate change. They were asked to select the single issue that made them feel the most angry, defined as an issue that upsets or annoys them and brings up hostility, and to rate the intensity of their anger on a scale from 0 to 100.
Immediately after reflecting on that issue, participants completed a leader choice task consisting of 36 rapid rounds. In each round, two computer-generated faces appeared side by side on the screen for up to three seconds, and participants had to click on the leader they believed would be most capable of handling their chosen political issue. These nine digital faces were drawn from a standardized scientific database and had been systematically altered to represent different combinations of facial dominance and facial trustworthiness.
In the fear section, the same participants went through an identical process, but this time they selected the political issue from the list that made them feel the most afraid, defined as an issue that worries them a lot and feels like a frightening threat. After rating their fear on the 0 to 100 scale, they completed the 36-round face selection task again to pick the best leader to address that frightening issue.
Across the sample, both emotions were felt intensely, with average intensity ratings of 86.51 out of 100 for anger and 81.95 for fear. The issues most frequently selected for anger were illegal immigration (19.3 percent), gun violence (17.8 percent), and inflation (15.2 percent). For fear, participants most commonly selected climate change (15.2 percent), illegal immigration (14.2 percent), and domestic terrorism (11.2 percent).
The researchers first combined each participant’s choices into an overall index measuring the probability of picking a more dominant and less trustworthy-looking leader. Statistical analyses accounting for emotional intensity and specific policy issues showed that participants had a 49.5 percent probability of choosing a dominant-looking leader when angry, compared to a 46.5 percent probability when fearful, meaning participants on average leaned slightly toward the more trustworthy-looking face in both conditions. How intensely participants felt the emotion was unrelated to their choices. While this 3 percentage point absolute shift between anger and fear is modest, the authors note that even small emotional shifts could matter across an entire population during elections, when campaigns frequently amplify fear- and anger-inducing issues.
To see what drove this shift, the authors broke down the choices round by round to look at how participants weighed dominance cues and trustworthiness cues separately. When participants were in the fear condition, a face’s level of trustworthiness increased the likelihood that it would be chosen, whereas a face’s level of dominance had no statistically significant effect on their choices. When participants were in the anger condition, the positive pull of facial trustworthiness dropped, while facial dominance gained a stronger positive influence on their selections.
“Our findings suggest that how we feel about political issues can influence the kinds of leaders we find appealing, even based on something as simple as their facial appearance,” von Mohr explained. “When angry, people placed greater importance on facial cues of dominance (appearing strong and assertive) and less on trustworthiness. When afraid, they placed more importance on trustworthiness (appearing reliable and benevolent).”
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2022, which similarly found that anger increased participants’ preferences for dominant-looking leaders over trustworthy ones. However, that earlier study examined anger triggered by non-political frustrations, whereas the new study suggests that anger tied to real-world policy issues is linked to a similar shift while directly contrasting it against political fear.
The researchers also examined the role of political party affiliation. Consistent with previous studies, Republicans showed a higher overall preference for dominant-looking leaders (52.5 percent probability) than Democrats did (43.5 percent probability), representing a 9 percentage point partisan gap. That gap was about three times as large as the 3-point difference between anger and fear. Even though Democrats and Republicans tended to pick different policy issues as their top concerns, the difference between anger and fear did not vary significantly by party, suggesting the emotions influenced leader choices in similar ways for both groups.
The emotion effects did not vary by participants’ gender and held when accounting for the order in which participants completed the tasks. When the researchers statistically controlled for the exact political issue each participant selected in the round-by-round analysis, the distinct effects of anger and fear on how participants weighed dominance and trustworthiness cues remained stable. In the overall-preference analysis, entering each specific issue as a separate factor left the anger-versus-fear difference about the same size but made the estimate less precise.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these findings. Because participants were allowed to choose whichever political issue personally angered or frightened them the most, the study cannot completely separate the effect of the emotion from the nature of the policy issue itself. Although the researchers used statistical controls to account for the different issues selected, future experiments that induce anger or fear while keeping the policy topic identical for everyone would help isolate the pure effect of the emotion. The study also compared anger only with fear, without a neutral condition, so it cannot say whether anger made dominant faces more appealing, fear made them less appealing, or both.
Additionally, the faces used in the task were standardized, computer-generated avatars rather than photographs of real politicians. While digital faces allow scientists to precisely adjust facial structure without interference from a person’s hairstyle, age, race, or gender, real-world elections involve all of those visual factors alongside party labels and campaign rhetoric. Finally, the study only tested American voters, so it is not known whether the same patterns hold in other countries. Future research could also examine whether other political emotions, such as hope or disgust, shape leader preferences.
The study, “Political emotions shape preferences for leaders’ facial traits: anger favours dominance, fear favours trustworthiness,” was authored by Mariana Von Mohr and Manos Tsakiris.

All aboard the TrainTok trend: spotters and staff boost rail content online
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
14:00:05 UTC
23:00:05 KST

They are not just gathered at the end of your local train station platform any more. Now they are on your social media platforms too.
Trainspotters have played a part in more than doubling the number of videos about British trains on TikTok in the last three months. According to the platform, the rise in rail content is also down to more people seeking information on cheap tickets, facts about the London Underground and tales from train staff.
Posts tagged with #UKTrains have increased by 247% over recent months. The trend has even led to train staff moonlighting as content creators. Shamal Cain, who goes by the handle Tube Bellingham, is a Transport for London employee who shares advice for commuters across the capital.
According to Cain, scrollers are keen to learn more about topics they know little about but that affect their daily lives. “I realised how many people use London transport but don’t actually know a lot of information about it,” he said.
Cain said many commuters were not fully aware of the TfL journey planner or how to avoid penalty fares from not tapping in and out. After noticing the gap, he thought: “Why don’t I just record giving information on what I do?”
He said: “A majority of people commute through TfL. I think because a lot of people are doing that on a daily basis, they’re very engaged with information.”
When Cain joined TikTok, direct messages came in fast, with followers asking him about alternative routes when services were down or for advice on getting a job with TfL.
The popularity of train content has also risen thanks to enthusiast rail influencers such as Nathan Pinnock-James, who makes educational transport videos.
“Since I started posting on TikTok, there’s been a lot of people that have the context of what a train is, how to use a train, but may not have noticed certain aspects of it,” said Pinnock-James, AKA Network Nathan. “They’re like: ‘Oh, wow! That’s quite shocking!’”
He said obscure hobbies thrived on the app. “TikTok has really opened the door to really niche, specific topics coming on to your ‘for you’ page. It’s allowed people to find things that they didn’t know were interesting to them.”
The 24-year-old said he found an audience online by creating videos about the best trainspotting locations, station openings, and explainers on how the shape of train wheels make DLR carriages wobble.
Yazmin How, the head of emerging communities at TikTok UK, said: “It’s inspiring to see such a wide variety of creators, whether it’s professional train drivers, tube historians, young enthusiasts or comedy creators, using short-form video to make transport content entertaining and accessible to everyone.
“The growth we’re seeing in #traintok reflects a real appetite among our UK community for authentic, educational storytelling that connects people, turning everyday travel into a shared community interest.”
Short video content about trains, sometimes called TrainTok, has been a growing part of the social media app for years. The media personality Francis Bourgeois found popularity on TikTok in 2021 after his videos of him reacting to British locomotives went viral.
While human creators are jumping onboard, AI-generated videos – including clips that show high-speed trains and passengers falling out of tube carriages – are also contributing to the growth. In late 2025, TikTok revealed that more than 1bn videos that included AI were hosted on its application.
The company said its content operations team “works closely with creators and publishers to support the flow of high-quality content in the TikTok ecosystem”.
TikTok, which announced the increase in train content during an annual trend report at its UK headquarters, said there was a growing interest in niche topics across its platform.
It said searches about history in the UK had gone up by 50% in the last six months, and posts about the National Trust had doubled during the same period.
How said: “The rise of train content on TikTok shows that even a niche passion can build highly engaged communities.”

Storm Boelo disrupts UK rail services as winds of 129 km/h forecast
The UK’s national weather service, the Met Office, issued amber warnings for Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and northern England. Gusts of 97–113 km/h are expected across affected areas, potentially reaching 129 km/h in exposed coastal locations.
Forecasters warned that strong winds and heavy rain could damage buildings, uproot trees, disrupt electricity supplies and force road and bridge closures. Air, rail and ferry services could also face cancellations and delays.
According to National Rail, several train operators have reduced services or advised passengers to avoid non-essential journeys.
London North Eastern Railway (LNER) has cancelled most services between Edinburgh and Aberdeen on Sunday. Avanti West Coast has advised passengers to avoid travelling north of Preston, while TransPennine Express has urged people to travel only if essential.
Greater Anglia also reported major disruption after a fallen tree damaged overhead wires. The operator advised passengers not to travel between Ipswich and Colchester amid severely limited services.
Rail disruption could continue into Monday, October 26, even after weather warnings expire, National Rail said.
Storm Boelo follows Storm Austen, which struck parts of Britain on Friday. The Met Office recorded gusts of 122 km/h at St Mary’s Airport in the Isles of Scilly during the earlier storm.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Storm Goretti swept across Britain and other parts of northern Europe in January, disrupting transport services and leaving thousands of households without electricity.

Kremlin says preparations for Putin-Xi-Trump trilateral summit have begun
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:51:59 UTC
22:51:59 KST

Elena Teslova
25 October 2026•Update: 25 October 2026
Preparations for a trilateral summit involving Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump have begun, a Kremlin official said Sunday.
In an interview with Russian broadcaster VGTRK published Sunday, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov said the administrations of all three presidents were ready to hold the meeting.
"I can say for certain now that Moscow, Beijing and Washington are in principle ready to hold it, and preparations have already begun," he said.
Ushakov said Russia and the US have not yet agreed on a bilateral meeting between Putin and Trump on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit scheduled for Nov. 18-19 in Shenzhen, China.
However, he said such a meeting was possible, as a trilateral meeting involving Xi was being planned.
"We have not agreed on this meeting yet, because so far we have been talking about this trilateral contact," he said.
"If two presidents are in the same place, they will at least greet each other, talk while sitting at a table, talk during protocol events. Such large international summits open up great opportunities for communication," he added.
Ushakov said Russia was currently focused on the November summit in Shenzhen and would consider the G20 summit in Miami later.
Asked whether the success of the November summit in Shenzhen would influence Russia's participation in the G20 summit in Miami in December, Ushakov said: "Naturally. But I am saying that November comes first, and then December."
Ushakov also said the Trump administration understood that Russia could not be ignored and that engagement with Moscow was preferable.
"In the US, you know, the general political backdrop is extremely unfavorable to Russia. But there is the Trump administration, which is trying to take into account its national interests, which boil down to the fact that Russia cannot be ignored and it is better to interact with Russia," he said.
Russia 'ready' to resume trilateral talks on Ukraine
Turning to Ukraine, Ushakov said Russia was ready to resume negotiations in the Russia-US-Ukraine format after Nov. 4, Russia's National Unity Day.
"Now the next deadline is Nov. 4, our big holiday. After that, we will be ready to resume negotiations," he said.
Ushakov cautioned against high expectations for the planned expert-level trilateral meeting, describing it as preliminary.
"One cannot resolve much at the first meeting. It will probably be of an exploratory nature," he said, adding that the sides still needed to work on a peace agreement.
He also said the Kremlin had believed after the Anchorage summit that Washington could pressure Kyiv into compliance, but that the effect had proved minimal.
On Europe's role, Ushakov said dialogue with the EU remained necessary because European countries were inclined to prolong the conflict.
"It is not enough to talk only to Kyiv, we must talk to the whole of Europe, which fully supports Kyiv," he said.
Separately, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov commented on reports that Finnish President Alexander Stubb could be proposed as Europe's negotiator with Russia on Ukraine.
Peskov said Moscow would support such an appointment if the envoy sincerely sought a peaceful settlement.
"If there is a negotiator, that is good. If it is a negotiator who sincerely strives to facilitate a peaceful settlement, that will be even better," he said.

Over 50 air defence towers reportedly built around Putin's Valdai residence
Another 16 air defence towers have been built around Russian leader Vladimir Putin's Valdai residence. The total number of air defence positions in the area has now exceeded 50.
Source: Radio Liberty's Russian Service, citing an analysis of satellite imagery conducted jointly with OSINT analyst jembobineuse
Details: The new towers were built mainly south of the residence, within a 50 km radius. They form an outer air defence ring facing Ukraine.
The journalists assume that Pantsir or Tor anti-aircraft missile systems may be placed on the towers.
Some of the new positions are located near the Hotilovo military airbase, which is used by Putin, and the Vyshny Volochyok Reservoir, where the Russian military built a secret laboratory complex.
The journalists estimate that there are now more than 50 air defence positions around Valdai. This is roughly half the number built in Moscow and Moscow Oblast since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Background: In mid-April, it became known that seven new towers armed with Pantsir air defence systems had been built around Putin's Valdai residence during March, bringing the total to 27.

Saudi air defences intercept Houthi barrage near Mecca

Saudi air defences intercept Houthi barrage near Mecca
Yemen’s Houthi rebels launch a barrage of missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia, triggering widespread civil defence alerts and international condemnation.
The Saudi-led coalition has intercepted a barrage of projectiles from Yemen that targeted cities across the kingdom.
Saudi Civil Defence said that shrapnel from two intercepted ballistic missiles, suspected to have been fired by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, fell in Jeddah, Taif, Rabigh, and Wadi Al-Mughammas in Mecca province.
A drone and ballistic missile were also intercepted over the Saudi capital Riyadh during the barrage, which began Saturday evening.
By midday Sunday, coalition forces had intercepted a cruise missile targeting Khamis Mushait, with warning sirens blaring out across Taif and Jazan. In total, 10 ballistic missiles directed at the southern region were intercepted.
Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed AlBudaiwi said the strikes represented “a grave violation of the sanctity of the Holy Sites and a provocation to the sentiments of Muslims worldwide”, referring to the interceptions in Mecca, home of the Kaaba and Masjid al-Haram. The Houthis, a Zaydi Shia group, have denied targeting Muslim holy sites in Saudi Arabia.
The kingdom has faced waves of Houthi missile and drone strikes in recent weeks, targeting civilian and military infrastructure.
Riyadh announced late Saturday that international flights from King Khalid International Airport would resume from Terminal 2 on Sunday, while Terminal 1 would be designated for domestic flights.
This follows the suspension of flights from the Riyadh airport after waves of Houthi strikes, including one on October 10 that killed 13 people and wounded hundreds.
Early Sunday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned civilians away from the Saudi capital’s airport.
“King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh is not safe because it is a military target, and we renew our warning to airlines, employees, and travelers,” Saree stated. He also announced seven operations targeting Saudi oil facilities and military bases.
Yemen has been in a state of war since Houthi forces captured the capital Sanaa in September 2014, forcing the government to flee south.
After a brief ceasefire, fighting in Yemen has intensified after government forces attacked Sanaa International Airport to prevent a Houthi delegation arriving from Tehran.
The Houthis then launched a surprise offensive in September, capturing Yemen’s western coast, including the city of Mocha.
Forces aligned with the internationally recognised government launched “Operation Dawn of Yemen” on October 5, aimed at retaking territories lost to the Houthis.
On Sunday, Yemen’s armed forces said the military had carried out 736 strikes on Houthi positions over the past 24 hours, leading to 307 people being “neutralised” and the destruction of 68 military vehicles.
Amid the military escalation, the Rasd Organization for Rights and Freedoms has warned of the dire humanitarian situation in the city of Taiz, which is under a Houthi siege.
“About 1,110 kidney failure patients face the risks of a shortage of dialysis supplies, given the need for about 120 dialysis sessions daily along with 192 patients in intensive care units and 154 children in incubators, due to the Houthi siege imposed on the city of Taiz since October 4,” the group said.

Previous winner of Mustafa Prize donates $160,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:49:13 UTC
22:49:13 KST

Mehmet Toner, a 2025 Mustafa(pbuh) Prize laureate, endowed his prize money to contribute to the advancement of the Rasul(pbuh) Medal.
MSTF Media reports:
Toner, one of the three laureates of 2025 Mustafa Prize, has requested that his cash prize be devoted to supporting young scientists through the Rasul Medal. Under the statutes of the Mustafa Prize, the cash prize of 500,000 dollars was shared among Toner and the two other laureates.
 
In previous years, Ugur Sahin (2019), Omid Farrokhzad (2023), and Vahab Mirrokni (2025) have donated their cash prize to help establish and advance the Rasul Medal.
Born in 1958 in Turkey, Mehmet Toner is a professor of biomedical engineering at Harvard Medical School. He won the 2025 Mustafa Prize for the development of nano/microfluidic devices with clinical applications. His technology enables the isolation of cancer cells from blood, supporting early diagnosis, monitoring, and designing precise treatments for patients.
The Rasul Medal
 
Previously known as the Young Scientist Medal, the Rasul Medal was founded based on the endowments made by Mustafa Prize laureates, Ugur Sahin, Omid Farrokhzad, and Vahab Mirrokni. It is awarded to scientists under the age of 40 residing in Islamic countries. The inaugural edition of the Medal was held alongside the 6th Mustafa Prize in 2025.  
The Medal is awarded to impactful works in the fields of Life and Medical Science and Technology, Basic and Engineering Sciences, and Computer Science by young scientists from Islamic countries. The candidates must be nominated by a third-party scientific or technological body, such as universities and research centers, reputable scientific and technological associations and institutions, academies of sciences, or science and technology parks.
 
The candidates for the Rasul Medal must be under 40 years old at the end of the year in which the medal is awarded. This means that candidates for the 2026 Rasul Medal must be born in 1987 or later.
The winners are bestowed a medal, a certificate, and a $10,000 cash prize in each category.
Established as a symbol of excellence and scientific merit of the young generation of scientific talent, the Rasul Medal promotes scientific and technological breakthroughs by young scientists in the Islamic world and recognizes their influential achievements.

Gaza’s visually and hearing-impaired children miss school due to Israel war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:46:51 UTC
22:46:51 KST

Gaza’s visually and hearing-impaired children miss school due to Israel war
Children in Gaza with auditory and visual challenges often have no access to specialist education.
Gaza City – With the help of his father, 13-year-old Kenan al-Sabaa attempts to adjust his hearing aid, which has malfunctioned. The plastic tubing and rubber ear mould on the device need fixing, but these parts and the depleted batteries are no longer available due to Israel’s siege on the Gaza Strip.
Before Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza started in October 2023, Kenan attended the Atfaluna Society for Deaf Children, which provided specialist teaching and opportunities to communicate with other hearing-impaired children.
But Atfaluna’s building in Gaza City was partially levelled during the war and quickly turned into an overcrowded shelter for displaced people, an example of the widespread destruction of infrastructure in Gaza. This includes the educational institutions disabled children rely upon.
Israeli attacks also forced Kenan’s family to flee to Gaza City’s Jalaa Street. Atfaluna has since set up temporary learning spaces, and Kenan has access to one near where his family now lives. But his father, Tamer al-Sabaa, said the interruptions to his learning during the war have left his son far behind in his studies.
He did not attend school at all during the first year of the war, and now attends classes only for a few hours a week, which Tamer says is not enough given the time he has lost at school during the war.
But Tamer fears that if Israel resumes large-scale attacks – an October 2025 “ceasefire” reduced the number of attacks but did not stop them – he will be forced to stop Kenan from attending.
“These few hours do not cover or repair the massive educational gap and academic decline my son experienced during the war,” Tamer said. “He is in dire need of restoring his equipped educational environment and the specialised care that was stripped away from him.”
“The school operates only three days a week, and for limited hours not exceeding two hours a day,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Being deaf makes Kenan’s movements fraught with danger, as he cannot hear the sounds of explosions, warning signals, or communicate with those around him.”
As a result, Tamer and his wife had to guide Kenan through unfamiliar neighbourhoods to help him learn about his surroundings.
Kenan can now reach school independently, but his safety is always a concern for his parents.
Little help available
The difficulties facing Kenan highlight the effect of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, on disabled children in the enclave.
Fadel Kuraz, a sign language interpreter and disability rights advocate with Atfaluna, said the war has increased hearing-related injuries and severely weakened the services available to children who need support.
“What we are experiencing today in the Gaza Strip represents an unprecedented health and humanitarian setback, and a real catastrophe unlike anything we have seen before,” Kuraz told Al Jazeera.
“To grasp the scale of the tragedy, the baseline number of persons with hearing disabilities registered before October 2023 was around 20,000 people. Today, according to field assessments, approximately 35,000 new individuals … have been added, having suffered total or partial hearing loss due to … explosions.”
Kuraz describes shortages of hearing aids, batteries, ear moulds, and spare parts, alongside major obstacles to specialist hearing tests and treatments. Children also face difficulties accessing visual learning materials because of electricity and communications outages, he said.
“The suffering does not stop at material needs. A deaf child suffers high levels of fear, stress and complex trauma without the ability to verbally express what is on their mind,” Kuraz told Al Jazeera.
Hearing-impaired children in Gaza are more often than not living in overcrowded tents or shelters which lack privacy or a proper space to do homework and study.
“I emphasise that responding to the needs of persons with hearing disabilities is no longer a secondary choice or a luxury; it is an urgent humanitarian necessity,” Kuraz adds. “It requires immediate intervention to break the siege, allow the entry of hearing aids, batteries, and spare parts, and establish safe, temporary alternative educational spaces to replace destroyed centres.”
Generation at risk
Children with visual impairments face issues similar to those faced by hearing-impaired children in Gaza, with the few educational facilities once available to them now closed or difficult to access. The materials and items they need to study, such as Braille, are also difficult to procure due to Israel’s siege on Gaza.
Al-Noor school was originally located in Tal al-Hawa, southwest of Gaza City, but was badly damaged in the genocidal war.
Duaa Omar Basheer worked as an educational counsellor at the al-Noor school for blind students in northern Gaza before the war. She said it was the only public school in Gaza designated for middle and high school students with visual impairments, but was forced to close during the war. Some primary education is available to children through educational centres run by the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA.
Previously, the school served about 80 pupils from across Gaza, many of whom arrived on dedicated buses, but damaged roads and a lack of suitable transport created further barriers.
Without regular instruction, Basheer fears students could lose their Braille and independent-learning skills, which they have taken years to learn.
“We are facing an entire generation of visually-impaired individuals at risk of illiteracy and academic loss,” Basheer said.
Broken glasses
In the Shati refugee camp in Gaza City, Jana Shreim’s mother, Wafaa Shreim, says her 12-year-old daughter, who is legally blind, relies on prescription glasses with high magnification and very strong lenses. But she could still only perceive light, shapes and nearby objects.
Her glasses broke amid the harrowing mass exodus from the Shati camp during Israel’s offensive on the neighbourhood in November 2023. The family tried to fix them with wire, but the lenses were damaged beyond use, and replacement glasses were too expensive.
Since the glasses broke – and with no possibility of replacing them due to the blockade – her vision has deteriorated to the point that she can barely see.
Now, when Jana goes to unfamiliar places, she stumbles and falls. Her mother says she is bullied by other children, and that she experiences pain in her eyes when she tries to focus.
“My daughter now has to identify people by their voices,” Wafaa told Al Jazeera. “Her sister and I now act as her ‘eyes’ at every step and everywhere she goes.”
Before the war, Jana attended the al-Noor centre, travelling there on a dedicated bus service. Her school closed when it was badly damaged in Israeli bombing, leaving Jana without any access to education.
“I am currently trying to teach her at home myself using a Braille writing machine we have, so she doesn’t lose her limited educational skills,” Jana’s mother said. She also cares for another daughter with a visual impairment, making it even more difficult to provide the specialist support they both need.
“I searched extensively and knocked on the doors of many institutions and organisations concerned with visual impairment, but the bitter truth is that … we have been left entirely alone,” she said.
“My only message and wish to all responsible parties is to look at our visually impaired children with mercy: provide them with glasses and medical supplies, and open safe educational and recreational spaces that restore their basic right to life and learning.”

What is spina bifida, and are there ways to prevent it? A doctor explains
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:46:42 EET
22:46:42 KST

What is spina bifida, and are there ways to prevent it? A doctor explains
Kyiv • UNN
Every year, up to 300,000 children are born with spina bifida. Doctors advise starting to take folic acid even before conception.
October 25 is World Spina Bifida and Hydrocephalus Awareness Day. Obstetrician-gynecologist, Candidate of Medical Sciences, and head of the postpartum department at the capital’s Perinatal Center Vladyslav Yavir told UNN in a comment about what these developmental defects are and what prevention of their occurrence exists.
Every year, up to 300,000 children worldwide are born with a diagnosis of spina bifida. In fact, this figure may be higher, as not all countries record information about this fetal developmental defect as a separate item in medical statistics.
Spina bifida — what it is and how this developmental defect is linked to hydrocephalus
Spina bifida (split spine) is a congenital neural tube defect (an embryonic structure from which the child’s central nervous system develops), in which the formation and closure of the structures of the spinal canal are disrupted. In severe forms, particularly myelomeningocele, the membranes and neural structures of the spinal cord may protrude through the spinal defect.
As Vladyslav Yavir explains, severe forms of spina bifida are associated with impaired normal circulation of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
"As a result, CSF may accumulate in the ventricles of the brain, causing hydrocephalus to develop. At the same time, hydrocephalus does not occur in all children with spina bifida," the doctor says.
Prevention with folic acid
Taking folic acid can help prevent the development of spina bifida.
"Timely intake of folic acid can significantly reduce the risk of neural tube defects. According to research, a substantial proportion of such defects can be prevented by ensuring an adequate supply of folates to the body even before pregnancy begins. However, even proper prevention does not guarantee the complete elimination of the risk," Yavir explains.
According to the doctor, the neural tube forms and closes very early — approximately by the 28th day after fertilization.
"That is why folic acid supplementation should begin before pregnancy, preferably 1–3 months before conception," the doctor says.
According to him, there is a standard preventive dose of folic acid. However, there are high-risk groups for whom significantly higher doses may be recommended.
"First of all, these include women with a previous pregnancy complicated by a neural tube defect, patients with pregestational diabetes mellitus, and women taking certain medications (antiepileptic drugs)," Yavir explains.
High-dose supplementation is usually started before conception and continued until the end of the 12th week of pregnancy.
"It is important to emphasize that a high dose of folic acid should not be prescribed independently. It must be determined by a doctor after assessing individual risk factors.
That is why I always emphasize the importance of preconception care: the best time to prevent many congenital developmental defects is before pregnancy begins," the doctor says.
Folates can be obtained from foods such as green leafy vegetables, legumes, and citrus fruits. However, as the obstetrician-gynecologist explains, even a balanced diet does not always provide a sufficient amount of folates to prevent neural tube defects. Natural folates have lower bioavailability compared with synthetic folic acid, and some of them are destroyed during heat treatment.
"That is why the WHO and CDC recommend that women planning a pregnancy or capable of becoming pregnant take 400 mcg (0.4 mg) of folic acid daily in the absence of indications for a higher dose. Proper nutrition is important, but it does not replace the recommended prevention with folic acid," the doctor says.
Detecting developmental defects during pregnancy
Modern prenatal diagnostics makes it possible to detect spina bifida during the child’s intrauterine development. The primary diagnostic method is an ultrasound examination (ultrasound scan).
-  First-trimester ultrasound (11–13 weeks + 6 days): an experienced specialist may already suspect open spina bifida based on characteristic ultrasound signs, including changes in the fetal intracranial structures. 
-  Second-trimester ultrasound (18–22 weeks): the main stage for a detailed assessment of fetal anatomy. It makes it possible to detect a spinal defect, possible protrusion of the spinal cord membranes and neural structures, as well as characteristic changes in the brain.  
-  Biochemical screening: an elevated level of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) in the mother’s blood during the second trimester may indicate an open neural tube defect, but in itself does not confirm the diagnosis. 
Timely detection of the defect makes it possible to conduct an in-depth examination, assess the prognosis, and determine the further management plan for the pregnancy.
"Today, a diagnosis of spina bifida does not mean that treatment options are unavailable. In specialized centers, fetal surgical closure of myelomeningocele may be possible when clearly indicated. Studies have shown that, in carefully selected cases, such an intervention may reduce the need for cerebrospinal fluid shunting and improve the child’s motor function. Surgical treatment after birth is also available. In such cases, the defect is usually closed during the first days of the child’s life. If hydrocephalus is present, additional neurosurgical treatment may be required," explains Vladyslav Yavir.
At the same time, the doctor emphasizes that none of these methods guarantees the complete elimination of neurological impairments. In addition, surgery carries serious risks, so the decision is made by a multidisciplinary team after detailed counseling of the parents.
That is why preventive folic acid supplementation before pregnancy remains the most optimal approach. It should be started at least one month before planned conception, and, as the doctor clarifies, preferably three months beforehand.
"This is a simple, accessible, and scientifically proven way to significantly reduce the risk of severe congenital neural tube defects. As an obstetrician-gynecologist, I always emphasize: a healthy pregnancy begins not with two lines on a test, but with a conscious attitude toward one’s own health even at the stage of planning it!
After all, the best treatment is the one whose need we were able to prevent through timely prevention," Yavir concluded.
Attention!
This material is for informational purposes only and is not medical advice or a treatment recommendation. It does not replace consultation, diagnosis, or treatment by a specialist and may not serve as a basis for self-prescribing medications. If you are planning a pregnancy or are already pregnant, consult an obstetrician-gynecologist or family doctor.

Educator, lecturer, and writer Zalman Eisentstock brings stories from the Talmud to life by providing them to readers in a “newspaper” format accompanied by cartoon drawings.
The Talmud Chronicles: Bringing Talmudic Events to Life covers significant historical events from around 100-200 CE and breathes life into characters from the Talmud. The “editions” included in this publication trace the history of the Jewish people through Ancient Rome, the Parthian Revolt, and the Bar Kochba rebellion as the sages of the time lay the foundations for the creation of the Mishnah.
An entertaining journey through topics ranging from astronomy to the Olympics

Talmud Chronicles is an ideal coffee table book. Picking it up provides an opening for learning, whether directly from its stories or through the questions that arise from reading it, which can lead to further study and/or fascinating discussions.
It appears to be aimed at both adults and children, and there is something for everyone in its varied sections, inspired by real newspapers.

Israel needs unity: Why Herzog must bring Netanyahu, Eisenkot together - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:44:53 UTC
22:44:53 KST

I am a right-wing religious Zionist, an Ethiopian-born Israeli-American, and a father raising four children in Jerusalem, and I am frightened.
Not because Israelis disagree, disagreement is part of democracy, but because our politics increasingly teaches us to hate one another more passionately than we love the country we share, while our enemies watch, our international standing collapses, and the wounds of October 7 remain open.
I know where I stand politically. I believe in secure borders, Jewish sovereignty, and Israel’s unquestionable right to defend its citizens. Hamas must never again govern Gaza. Iran and its terrorist proxies must be deterred. The Jewish people cannot subcontract their survival.
Right-wing and left-wing are equal owners of the same country
But being right-wing does not require me to treat left-wing Israelis as enemies. Their children serve beside ours. They run into shelters when the sirens sound. They bury loved ones, pay taxes, and worry about the future of the same country. They are equal owners of it. The same is true in reverse.
Supporting a change in government does not justify dismissing millions of traditional, religious, or conservative Israelis as primitive, dangerous, or morally inferior. Netanyahu’s voters will not disappear if he loses an election, just as his opponents will not disappear if he wins. Israel belongs to all of us.
That truth should guide President Isaac Herzog after the election. Current polls show Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party competing for leadership, while neither bloc appears certain to command the 61 Knesset seats needed to govern. Israel may awaken to another divided parliament and another invitation to paralysis. We cannot afford it.
October 7 was not only a military and intelligence catastrophe. It was a warning about what happens when leaders become distracted by internal warfare, institutions lose public trust, and citizens begin viewing one another as threats. Hamas crossed a physical border after we had already allowed hatred to cross every political and social border within Israel.
Our enemies study us. They hear our leaders call one another traitors, fascists, and enemies of democracy. They see clashes among secular, religious, right-wing, left-wing, Jewish and Arab citizens.
They do not interpret our division as healthy democratic debate. They interpret it as weakness and wait for the next fracture.
Israel’s diplomatic position is also in danger. The Jewish state is increasingly portrayed not as a democracy defending itself, but as the source of every regional crisis. Antisemitism and propaganda drive much of this campaign, but our poisonous politics makes it easier. A country that cannot speak respectfully to itself will struggle to speak persuasively to the world.
This is why Herzog must become more than a ceremonial observer after the election. He cannot dictate a coalition, overturn the voters’ decision, or force rivals to trust one another. But he possesses something rare in Israeli public life: an office intended to represent the entire nation.
Herzog should invite Netanyahu and Eisenkot to the president’s residence and keep bringing them back until they seriously consider a broad Zionist unity government.
Not a government without disagreement. Not a government designed to rescue political careers. A government of limited national repair.
Such a coalition should begin with a clear program: restore security and border readiness; establish an independent state commission to investigate the failures surrounding October 7; confront Iran and its proxies; rebuild Israel’s international diplomacy; reduce the cost of living; require meaningful military or national service across society while respecting genuine Torah scholarship; and protect every law-abiding citizen from terrorism, organized crime and political violence.
It must also address Israel’s excluded communities. Ethiopian Israelis should not be remembered only during elections or cultural ceremonies. Arab citizens who reject terrorism and accept the laws of the state should not be treated as a permanent fifth column. Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) citizens should not be spoken about as if they are strangers to the Jewish future.
Rights bring responsibilities, but responsibilities must also bring belonging. Unity does not mean moral confusion. Israel must distinguish democratic disagreement from support for its destruction.
Leaders who excuse terrorism cannot be trusted with national security. But disagreement over courts, settlements, religion, or Gaza does not make an Israeli disloyal.
Becoming protectors
Rabbi Jonathan Sacks, of blessed memory, taught that society is the home we build together. A home cannot survive when family members would rather burn it down than allow a rival to sit at the head of the table.
Netanyahu has devoted much of his life to Israel’s security and international standing. Eisenkot served the country as a soldier, commander, and chief of staff, and he paid the unbearable price of losing family members in war.
Each man represents citizens who love Israel. Each also carries responsibilities greater than his personal grievances. They do not have to admire one another. They do not have to erase their disagreements. They must decide whether their hatred and mistrust are more important than the country they both claim to serve.
I made aliyah with my wife and four children shortly before October 7 because I believe in Israel, not merely as a refuge, but as the shared moral project of the Jewish people. I did not bring my children home so they could inherit a nation divided into tribes that no longer recognize one another.
The next October 7 must never happen. Preventing it will require weapons, intelligence, and secure borders. It will also require Israelis to become protectors of one another again.
Herzog, bring Netanyahu and Eisenkot to the same table. Ask them to place Israel above ego, party, and personal history. The election will determine who wins seats. Leadership will be measured by whether they can save the house we all share.
The writer is a former New York City Supreme Court detective, an investigator and educator in conflict resolution and restorative peace, and a moral diplomacy expert. His upcoming book, Moral Diplomacy for a Broken World, is inspired by the late Rabbi Jonathan Sacks.

UAE’s Lana Nusseibeh receives more support in bid to become next UN secretary-general
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:44:44 UTC
22:44:44 KST

Cypriot Foreign Affairs Minister Constantinos Kombos said on Friday that he supports UAE Ambassador Lana Nusseibeh as the next United Nations secretary-general.
Kombos wrote on X/Twitter that he has known Nusseibeh for years, noting that she "is an experienced, highly effective and well-respected diplomat, with an approach focusing on dialogue, compromise and tangible outcomes, while also having a strong track record in supporting multilateralism and the United Nations."
He also noted that it was time for a woman to become the next secretary-general, saying, "it is becoming time-sensitive to ensure that the selection process proceeds."
On Thursday, Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi said member states unanimously endorsed the United Arab Emirates' nomination of the ambassador for the position, according to the Saudi Gazette.
This is important as support for Nusseibeh grows, with Albudaiwi attributing the unanimous support to the GCC countries' commitment to strengthening multilateral cooperation and reinforcing the UN's role in maintaining international peace and security in accordance with the principles and objectives of its Charter, the Saudi Gazette reported.
The Maldives, BoP's Nikolay Mladenov support Nusseibeh's nomination
The Maldives said on Sunday that it welcomed Nusseibeh's nomination. In addition, Nikolay Mladenov, who is a key official with the Gaza Board of Peace and formerly served as Bulgaria's defense minister and Foreign affairs minister, wrote on X that "Lana Nusseibeh has always understood that the #UN works when someone is willing to systematically build the bridges nobody else wants to build."
"In the Security Council she did that quietly and consistently and with great professionalism," said Mladenov. "She now has the chance to take that same spirit and ethos to the UN Secretariat. Wishing you courage and strength for the journey ahead and much success!"
Nusseibeh has served as the UAE’s foreign affairs minister and as the UAE’s permanent representative to the UN in New York from 2013 to 2024. She also served for four years as foreign affairs assistant minister for political affairs.
Since the organization was founded in 1945, the UN has had ten secretaries-general, including an acting leader from 1945 to 1946, though some have been more memorable than others. Sweden’s Dag Hammarskjöld, who served from 1953 to 1961, was an energetic leader who sought to achieve a ceasefire in the Congo. He died in a plane crash while on his way to Zambia.
U Thant, who served in the 1960s, was the first non-Western secretary-general. He was followed by Kurt Waldheim in the 1970s. Waldheim was an intelligence officer under Nazi Germany, which made his appointment strange, considering the UN was founded after the defeat of the Nazis. In the 1990s, former Egyptian diplomat Boutros Boutros-Ghali became the head of the UN. He was largely seen to have failed at key moments, such as during the Rwandan genocide.
In the last decades, the UN has seen secretaries-general who appeared relatively ineffectual, such as Kofi Annan, Ban Ki-moon, and current UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.
As part of a complex election process, an informal straw poll of officials in the deciding UN Security Council last week gave [former Costa Rican vice president Rebeca] Grynspan a narrow lead over her closest competitors: Guyana’s former Foreign Minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett and Argentina’s International Atomic Energy Agency Director-General Rafael Grossi, Euro News reported.
The report notes that the winner needs at least nine votes from the 15-member UN Security Council without a veto from any of the five permanent members - the US, the UK, France, China and Russia - and they have until the end of December to choose the successor to Gutteres, before the UN General Assembly confirms the appointment.
Euro News also noted other candidates, including former Ecuadorian foreign minister Maria Fernanda Espinosa, former Senegalese president Macky Sall, former UN under-secretary-general Olara Otunnu of Uganda, and Ecuadorian diplomat Ivonne A-Baki.
Nusseibeh currently serving as UN Women Executive Board president
According to a UN biography of Nusseibeh, the ambassador currently serves as UN Women Executive Board president and was recently appointed co-facilitator of the Ad Hoc Working Group on the Revitalization of the UN General Assembly by the General Assembly president.
A website that appears to have been created for her candidacy notes that Nusseibeh is currently on leave from government responsibilities to focus on her UN secretary-general candidacy.
The website also includes a statement attributed to Nusseibeh, in which the ambassador says she is "stubbornly optimistic about the future of our world and the important role multilateralism will play in it."
"I am offering active, hands-on leadership on peace and security: acting earlier, bridging divides and pursuing practical first agreements that save lives now and create space for broader peace," she said, adding that she "will bring that same urgency and focus on results to development and human rights – building a more focused, responsive UN that delivers for the people it serves."
Nusseibeh was born in 1978, is married, and has two children. She has a BA and MA from Queens’ College at the University of Cambridge. She also has an MA in Israeli and Jewish Diaspora Studies from the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS), University of London.
Prior to her UN role, she established the UAE Foreign Affairs Ministry's Policy Planning Department in 2009 and served as its first director for three years. She also served as the UAE’s Co-Special Envoy to Afghanistan and Pakistan. She also headed the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) task force at the ministry.
French-language media platform and digital news outlet IsraJ noted Nusseibeh’s important family background, saying her family originally lived in Jerusalem and that her Emirati citizenship came from her father, Emirati President Cultural Advisor Zaki Nusseibeh.
It added details about the family's rich academic and intellectual background and its long roots in Jerusalem and the region, with relative Anwar Nusseibeh having been a prominent figure in Palestinian and Jordanian politics.
Wounded in 1948, Anwar Nusseibeh served as Jordanian Defense Minister and later as Jerusalem Governor under Jordanian rule. After 1967, he conducted discreet contacts between Israel and Jordan regarding the future of the West Bank.
IsraJ further noted that the ambassador's uncle, Sari Nusseibeh, is a former president of Al-Quds University in the West Bank. He wrote several important books, including Once Upon a Country about his family and Palestinian issues.

Why Netanyahu's supporters remain loyal to him despite his failures - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:44:33 UTC
22:44:33 KST

For over a decade, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has demonstrated an extraordinary ability to retain the loyalty of his supporters despite profound failures under his leadership. He has been described as Israel’s most successful politician, the greatest political survivor, and the leader of a personality cult.
Millions of Israelis vote for Netanyahu because they genuinely share his political worldview that Israel must be exceptionally strong, distrust the Palestinians, fear Iran, oppose territorial concessions, and regard the Israeli Left as naïve, all legitimate political positions.
The more puzzling question is why personal loyalty to Netanyahu remains so resilient even when events appear to contradict the image of him as Israel’s indispensable protector.
What does Netanyahu offer his followers beyond policy? Perhaps the answer lies in something deeper than politics. He offers psychological security through powerful rewards: security, identity, certainty, conviction, and collective struggle. To reinforce these bonds, he has also used the divisions within Israeli society with remarkable effectiveness, creating a powerful distinction between “us” and “them.”
Understanding these psychological dynamics may help explain Netanyahu’s extraordinary political resilience, and why his most devoted followers remain loyal even when the facts appear increasingly difficult to reconcile with his image.
Netanyahu’s most powerful political appeal
Netanyahu’s most powerful political appeal has long been security, not merely security as policy but as an emotional promise. Israelis live with a profound awareness of vulnerability shaped by the Holocaust, wars, terrorism, Iran, Hamas, and Hezbollah.
Netanyahu has built his political persona around the image of an experienced leader who recognizes dangers and can protect Israelis. During Operation Protective Edge in 2014, he said, “The ultimate responsibility for your security and peace is mine, as prime minister.”
The message is not only about trusting his security policies but more about trusting him with their security. Security is identified not with a government or policy but with Netanyahu himself. The question is no longer whether Netanyahu made mistakes, but who can protect us if not Bibi.
Netanyahu also offers identity. His rhetoric often blurs the distinction between himself, his supporters, and the nation. In October 2025, he told the Knesset: “We are Jews, we are Israelis, we are strong.”
This framing makes opposition to Netanyahu appear to some supporters not just as political disagreement but as opposition to the country and its security. It also taps into longstanding resentment toward Israel’s traditional elites.
Netanyahu has been remarkably effective at turning that resentment into solidarity with himself. Politics shifts from a contest between competing ideas toward an “us versus them” struggle. Once politics becomes an identity conflict, evidence is less powerful.
Another characteristic is Netanyahu’s projection of certainty. In July 2026, describing a change in Israel’s security doctrine following October 7, he said: “I am taking the reins, and I am changing it.” Netanyahu consistently presents himself as someone who sees what others cannot see and possesses the experience to provide the solution. His implicit message is reassuring.
Since people dislike uncertainty, particularly when it feels existential, they want someone who appears to understand what’s happening, knows what must be done, and is confident to act.
Another mechanism sustaining Netanyahu’s following is his ability to turn criticism into conviction. In 2021, he said: “The test of leadership requires that the right decisions be made even when they are not understood at any given moment and their justification becomes clear later on.”
Netanyahu has created a protective shield around him. If events prove him right, he was right. If they prove him wrong, it means history has not caught up with him. Therefore, he is never wrong, as it may simply be too early to know. This creates a remarkably resilient form of loyalty.
The fifth element is the sense of permanent external collective threat. Iran has occupied a central place in Netanyahu’s political narrative for decades, while Hamas, Hezbollah, and other enemies reinforce the perception that Israel is surrounded by hostile forces. The threats are real and Netanyahu’s uncompromising strength is presented as the only reliable means of protection.
In January 2024, Netanyahu declared: “No one will stop us, not The Hague, not the axis of evil, and not anyone else.” Such language positions him as the leader standing between his people and a hostile world. And his followers feel they cannot afford to weaken the person protecting them. As long as the threat remains, the protector is indispensable.
The phenomenon of cognitive dissonance
Netanyahu’s political success cannot be separated from his ability to turn political disagreement into questions of identity and belonging. Israeli society has long contained profound ideological, religious, ethnic, and social divisions. The crucial question is what political leaders do with those divisions.
When opponents are portrayed as dangerous rather than simply mistaken, compromise becomes harder. Disagreement can become disloyalty, and defending the leader can become a way of defending one’s own side.
This helps explain the phenomenon of cognitive dissonance. When reality conflicts with a deeply held belief, people may reinterpret reality, so the belief can survive. Political attachment can become intertwined with identity, fear, and belonging. After years of defending a leader, acknowledging that he failed can mean reconsidering one’s own judgment.
That may be the deepest source of Netanyahu’s resilience. For some devoted supporters, letting go of Netanyahu may feel like letting go of a part of their identity, security, and certainty that he has come to represent.
The writer is an Israeli Canadian, formerly an economist and senior policy adviser in the Ontario Public Service, Canada. She is active in Jewish community life in Toronto and Miami, and writes about Israel, Zionism, and the relationship between Israel and the Diaspora.

Settler violence is a political blind spot in Israel’s election campaign - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:44:25 UTC
22:44:25 KST

Even as settler violence grows increasingly prominent abroad, Israelis seem somewhat ambivalent. According to a recent survey, 78% of the public call Judea and Samaria and a Palestinian state important or very important. But asked to prioritize, they rank it dead last: cost of living at 35%, haredi (ultra-Orthodox) conscription at 18%, the Iran war at 17%, judicial reform at 16%, and the future of Judea and Samaria at just 7%.
Before accusing Israelis of monstrous disregard, remember that in the Israeli political system they have only one vote to decide the prime minister, judicial reform, and security policy all at once. If you had only one dollar to invest, where would you place it?
Israelis will faithfully recite the cost of living – but as Naftali Bennett has discovered, to his dismay, they are not being honest. His comprehensive economic plan, released in early July, landed somewhere between negligible and nil. By contrast, the cost of living barely features in Gadi Eisenkot’s campaign, yet that hasn’t stopped the exodus from the one party to the other. The real number-one concern for Israeli voters has always been, and continues to be, security.
To an outsider, the correlation between settler violence and security looks weak, if not negative. The vigilantism rampant in the West Bank doesn’t make Israelis safer – but for a certain sector, cracking down on it represents the opposite. That is why the opposition hasn’t capitalized on the seeming "wild west" created, largely by government incompetence, 20 minutes from the capital. They will mention the issue when a particularly egregious event occurs, but don’t expect a poster reading “If he can’t secure Judea and Samaria, can he secure Tel Aviv.”
Such an ad would collide with two associations of settler violence, both of which the movement itself reinforces. In the Israeli political dictionary, the antonym of the settlements is the Palestinian state: Speak harshly of the movement’s excesses, and you are heard as lending a hand to the people trying to bring one about.
Settler violence tied to claims to Palestinian statehood
Meir Deutsch, director-general of the prominent settlement NGO Regavim, drew that connection explicitly not long ago, arguing that the “settler violence” narrative is a foreign-funded campaign engineered “to create the tool that will force the State of Israel to establish a Palestinian state.”
The second association is folded into that same charge: foreign. Regavim’s report casts the campaign as EU-financed and amplified by hostile voices abroad, and Deutsch points to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s own acknowledgment that settler violence helped justify a partial American arms embargo in the middle of the war. To make settler violence a headline issue, then, is to risk sounding at once obtuse about the real threat and faintly foreign in one’s preoccupations.
All of this is built on a fundamental truth: Israeli elections run in only one direction – rightward.
That’s why the self-styled “right-wing defense minister,” Israel Katz, fired the head of IDF Central Command on live TV for continuing to hold a violent settler, Tal Yinon Dardik, in custody and why even now he flatly rejects reinstating administrative detention for what he insists are a “handful of Jewish rioters.” The stunt ended in a swift and humiliating walk-back, but it captures a broader perception on the Right: Taking on the campaign against settler violence is a winning cause.
If there is internal polling on the issue, it has not been leaked. The truth is no one knows how many votes such actions secure, but it certainly secures a flank.
Right-wing politicians rarely hesitate when red lines are clearly crossed: A direct assault on IDF troops, like the violence seen last April, triggers immediate outrage across the political spectrum, while an indefensible action against Palestinian civilians, such as the Jit rampage, forces even figures like Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich to disavow perpetrators as rogue “criminals” divorced from mainstream Zionism.
But when the focus turns to the daily friction, political calculus changes. Leaders find it far safer to dance around the problem than to risk getting launched leftward for stepping on a partisan landmine.
Settler violence won’t be the wedge issue of the election. It won’t even be a widely discussed one – it’ll feature in attacks on the government as second fiddle at best. Not because people think settlers are right, but because attacking them makes one sound left-wing.
The writer serves as the English director of the Ribo Center and the editor of Amit Segal’s newsletter, It’s Noon in Israel.

Audi has said it will spend $4bn (£3bn) to build its first factory in the US, as its parent company, Volkswagen, struggles with the impact of steep tariffs imposed by Donald Trump.
The German brand’s chief executive, Gernot Döllner, joined Trump on stage at a campaign rally on Saturday night to announce the factory in Macon, Georgia, in an unusual move by a big European brand just days before the US midterm elections.
The Republican party under Trump is trying to retain control of both houses of Congress, but it is polling poorly as it struggles with higher fuel prices caused by Trump’s war on Iran, as well as his trade war against some of the US’s biggest trading partners.
Trump has long tried to convince voters that his tariffs are helping to increase the number of manufacturing jobs in the US, and has seized on any new factory investments. However, US vehicle and parts employment has fallen since Trump took office last year.
Audi, Volkswagen’s most important premium brand, has suffered from Trump’s 15% tariffs on imports from the EU as well as the president’s efforts to cut sales of battery electric vehicles in favour of petrol cars.
It said it aims to build 200,000 SUVs at the new US factory, creating 4,500 jobs. The factory will build the Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs, shifting some production from Bratislava in Slovakia.
Volkswagen has said Trump’s tariffs cost it up to €5bn(£4.2bn)a year, before the impact of lower sales. The German manufacturer this month said it was still struggling with “continued high pressure from import tariffs”. The carmaker was also forced to shift some production of its cheapest cars, such as the Jetta saloon and Taos SUV, from Mexico to the US.
The new factory may add to tensions in Germany, where Volkswagen has started to cut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories. It has blamed the job losses on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as the tariffs and a need to invest heavily in the shift to EVs for markets other than the US.
Döllner said he accepted the invitation to speak at Trump’s rally out of respect for the US.
“We are planning to bring our biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” he said at the event. “This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market.”
Volkswagen’s chief executive, Oliver Blume, told investors in July that “US tariffs create a significant burden and restrict international trade”.
However, the group has said there is still demand in the US for Audi’s large petrol SUVs, and it is planning its largest-ever SUV, the Q9, with the American market in mind. Large petrol-powered SUVs have played a big role in global carbon emissions.
