Up to two billion pounds to replace the SA80 rifle
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
10:20:52 GMT
19:20:52 KST

The programme to replace the SA80 family of weapons carries an estimated value of £2 billion including VAT, and the contract is expected to run from July 2029 until the end of March 2045, according to a contract notice published by the Ministry of Defence.
The notice, issued by the National Armaments Director Group on 23 October, announces an industry day for Project GRAYBURN, which is considering the future replacement of the SA80 and the provision of associated small-arms capability for defence as a whole. The estimated value excluding VAT is given as £1,666,666,666.67, and the tender notice itself is not expected until 2 July 2027.
The notice states that the authority “is at an early stage of developing the requirement and is using this engagement to inform its understanding of the market and potential delivery approaches”, and that “the scope and approach to any future procurement remain subject to further development and approval.”
It adds: “This notice does not constitute a call for competition, an invitation to tender or a commitment by the Authority to commence a procurement. The Authority has not selected a preferred procurement route, delivery model, supplier, product or contractual structure.”
Maria Eagle, then Minister of State for Defence, told Parliament in April 2025 that “due to the current phase of the project, we are unable to provide a formal cost estimation yet”, and said a figure would follow once the scope, timeline and complexity were confirmed. A senior defence official told reporters in July this year that the programme “is funded” while adding “I don’t think we’ve got the specific line in the document”, referring to the Defence Investment Plan, as this publication reported at the time. The notice now puts a number on it.
The dates have moved as well, and a procurement pipeline notice issued by Defence Equipment and Support in January gave indicative contract dates of 2028 to 2045 and carried no value, and this publication reported then that those dates were notional and should not be taken as a commitment to enter production at that point. The start has moved to July 2029, and a date has been attached to the tender notice for the first time.
The life of the weapon being replaced has stretched over the same period. Ministers gave the L85A3’s projected out of service date as 2030 through 2025 and into this year, including when Eagle told Rebecca Paul, the Conservative member for Reigate, that “the L85 rifle (‘SA80’) will be replaced over the coming decade through Project GRAYBURN”. By July officials were saying the rifle is expected to remain in service into the early 2030s. A contract starting in July 2029 and running to 2045 leaves the existing weapon carrying the load into the period the replacement is being delivered.
The January notice set out five planned variants, likely built on a common lower receiver: a standard dismounted close combat rifle to replace the SA80A3, a short dismounted close combat variant, a personal defence weapon to replace the L22 carbine, a generalist rifle to replace the SA80A2 and a cadet rifle to replace the L98. Requirements listed in that notice included United Kingdom manufacture to strengthen sovereign supply chains, a possible long-term strategic supplier relationship covering delivery, support and spiral development, the ability to defeat current and emerging adversary body armour, day optics as standard with rapid acceptance of in-line night vision systems, signature reduction on selected variants and reliability across all climatic and environmental conditions.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, confirmed in January that the programme covers the whole dismounted close combat weapons portfolio, from pistols to machine guns, and said it is “desirable for the project to create skilled employment in the UK” in line with the Defence Industrial Strategy. Answering Ben Obese-Jecty in February he said the department has “set clear expectations that Project Grayburn will be manufactured in the UK to enhance sovereign industry”, while “there is currently no specific definition for the future export potential of Project Grayburn.”
The industry day will be held as a hybrid event, with organisations attending in person or over Microsoft Teams, and each will be offered a single one-to-one session of no more than fifteen minutes. Attendance is by invitation only, organisations must register by five o’clock on 30 October, and the department intends to confirm attendance by 6 November. The engagement deadline is 27 November. The notice flags the opportunity as particularly suitable for small and medium-sized enterprises, and the one-to-one sessions will not be used to evaluate or down-select suppliers or solutions.
The SA80 entered service in the 1980s and has been through two major upgrades, the A2 rebuild carried out by Heckler & Koch and the A3 configuration that brought a new upper receiver and mounting arrangements. The calibre of the new weapon remains open, with performance, interoperability with allies and technological complexity among the factors under consideration, and approvals will run through the Combined Operational Effectiveness and Investment Appraisal process.
The project takes its name from Lieutenant John Grayburn of the 2nd Parachute Battalion, who was awarded a posthumous Victoria Cross for his actions at the Arnhem road bridge in September 1944.

Fresh clashes rock France as protesters march on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
10:17:13 UTC
19:17:13 KST

Getty Images
Clashes erupted across France on Oct. 24 as protesters took to the streets, a week after marches that degenerated into violence and prompted a firm security backlash from President Emmanuel Macron, who is scrambling to restore order.
Police arrested nearly 1,000 people as officers faced "an extremely elevated level of violence" from black-clad "ultra-left" extremists, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said.
Riot police squads fired tear gas at protesters in the capital as well as in Marseille, Lyon, Bordeaux, Lille, Toulouse, Montpellier and Nantes.
Two people were "seriously" injured, Nunez said: One man in Toulouse, who reportedly had fingers blown off, and another person in Clermont-Ferrand. He did not give details of either case.
Authorities had deployed 70,000 security personnel across the country for the new marches, called to protest the cost of living.
The violence came a week after rioting that saw public buildings vandalised, hundreds of shops looted and 2,700 people arrested, casting a pall over the country six months before an election to choose Macron's successor.
Nunez said Saturday's outcome was more "positive" than a week ago, with more police on the streets acting more rapidly, conducting more pre-demonstration checks and better protecting businesses.
But there was widespread anger at the government over a protest crackdown viewed as an assault on the right to protest.
Saturday's demonstrations drew between 410,000 and 800,000 people across the country, according to different estimates by authorities and the organizing CGT union.
The main Paris march had between 110,000 and 250,000 attendees, according to those sources.
Macron's government has ordered police to prevent protesters reaching city centers, where shops are concentrated, and in Paris and some other cities, partial curfews were imposed in certain urban zones.
The French president had ordered non-union demonstrations be banned as "illegitimate."
In Paris, where many shops had boarded up windows to prevent looting, and the Louvre and the Musee d'Orsay museums shut for the day, the main demonstration passed off largely peacefully.
The march had been pushed to the capital's southeast rim under a last-minute order by authorities.
Afterwards, though, clashes broke out as the crowd was dispersing, with Nunez blaming "500 rioters" at the back of the march.
Thousands of protesters in the western city of Nantes broke through lines of police firing tear gas and a water cannon to reach the city centre, an AFP journalist witnessed.
In the southern cities of Cannes and Montpellier, far-right activists clashed with "ultra-left militants," in what authorities said was an unprecedented development.
There was looting on the sidelines of the marches in Marseille and Grenoble, police said.
The Yellow Vests, who staged disruptive protests against Macron eight years ago, called for more demonstrations on Oct. 31 for "the freedom to protest."
Far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon, who marched in Paris, said the movement "is going to repeat itself every week."
Tensions were heightened by a rally in the city of Orleans by far-right leader Marine Le Pen's National Rally party to kick off her campaign for the presidential election.
Thousands of counter-protesters chanting anti-fascist slogans marched in the city.
The unrest across France highlighted the febrile political atmosphere ahead of the vote, in which Le Pen leads in surveys.
Inflation in France, particularly affecting the cost of fuel, has surged since the start of the Middle East war in February.
Protests have also broken out in Italy, Belgium, Spain and Portugal over different issues, yet with some overlap on inflation and education problems.

China Focus: China brings archaeological sites closer to the public
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
18:17:11 CST
19:17:11 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- At the Dahecun National Archaeological Site Park in Zhengzhou, central China's Henan Province, reeds sway in the autumn breeze and deer can be heard calling across the nearly 2,400-mu (160-hectare) landscape. The new Dahecun Site Museum within the park is built largely underground, with a sloping entrance leading visitors into the history of a Neolithic settlement dating back about 7,000 years.
"This is the country's first thematic museum to present the Yangshao Culture in a panoramic form," said Wang Xiaoya, a guide at the museum. "Its rectangular roof is level with the ground, allowing the building to blend into the landscape like an archaeological site emerging from the soil."
Inside, more than 1,500 cultural relics illustrate the Yangshao Culture and shed light on the history of the Dahecun site. Outside, the core protection zone displays the remains of a large Yangshao-period settlement. Offering an important window into a Neolithic culture that lasted about 2,000 years, Dahecun is one of China's major archaeological sites, where protection and public presentation are making the traces of ancient life more accessible to the public.
Known in Chinese as "dayizhi," these archaeological sites include the remains of major ancient settlements, cities, palaces and tombs, as well as related groups of sites and cultural landscapes. They carry historical and cultural information across different stages of ancient Chinese history, and are distinguished by their scale, historical and cultural significance, and far-reaching influence.
The category includes sites such as Liangzhu in east China's Zhejiang Province, the Yin Ruins in Henan, Sanxingdui in the southwestern province of Sichuan, the Old Summer Palace ruins in Beijing, the Xixia Imperial Tombs and the Great Wall. These sites attest to China's million-year human history, 10,000-year cultural history and more than 5,000-year-old civilization.
China now has 150 such archaeological sites. A total of 65 national archaeological site parks have been established based on some of these sites, incorporating the surrounding areas.
Luoyang, a city in Henan with 4,000 years of urban history and more than 1,500 years as a capital, is home to several major archaeological sites that are closely woven into the modern cityscape.
"Several major archaeological sites lie within an east-west stretch of less than 50 kilometers along the Luo River, including Erlitou, the Yanshi Shang Dynasty Capital Ruins, the Han-Wei Luoyang Ancient City site, the Sui-Tang Luoyang City site and the Mangshan tombs," said Zhao Xiaojun, head of the Luoyang municipal cultural heritage bureau. "The density, scale, time span and richness of historical content are rare in the world."
As early as the 1950s, Luoyang developed a new urban area away from the old city and required archaeological excavations before construction began. Authorities have adopted site-specific regulations to protect these archaeological sites. The Sui-Tang Luoyang City site, the Han-Wei Luoyang Ancient City site and Erlitou have all become national archaeological site parks and cultural landmarks woven into city life.
Nationwide, more people are visiting such places. According to statistics, visits to China's national archaeological site parks rose from 20.97 million in 2021 to 97.74 million in 2025, bringing the five-year total to 303 million.
Their benefits also extend beyond archaeological research and museum exhibitions. In Zhejiang, efforts to link Liangzhu Culture with rural revitalization have supported local economic development. The operating income of village collectives in 14 villages within the site area rose 19 percent year on year in 2025. At the Liulihe site in Beijing, a China-U.S. international field archaeology summer school offers young people from around the world a platform to learn about Chinese civilization.
China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) for the development of national cultural heritage calls for systematic protection and utilization of such sites.
A recent national conference on work related to major archaeological sites stressed the need for high-level archaeological research, sustainable protection and efficient management, while also calling for high-quality presentation.
For sites in city centers, small-scale exhibition spaces will be integrated into the urban fabric, while sites in suburban and rural areas can explore models that combine rural revitalization with educational field trips and study programs. Efforts will also be made to improve the cultural services provided by these sites, better realize the value of cultural heritage and meet public needs.
For visitors, these sites offer a more direct encounter with the past. Standing among the reeds at Dahecun, they may wonder whether the people who lived here 7,000 years ago saw the same landscape. ■

Apple CarPlay and Android Auto Make Your Phone Hot. Here’s How to Keep It Cool
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

Android Auto and CarPlay have transformed the way people drive.
Rather than putting up with whatever infotainment systems car manufacturers have put together, we're now able to interact with our phones from our car dashboards—with our contacts, our music, our podcasts, and our mapping apps all available. And the list of supported vehicles just keeps growing.
Both the Google and Apple solutions for this are really simple to use too. Most of the time they'll connect up automatically once you've done the initial setup. What you might not realize, though, are the demands that Android Auto and CarPlay put on your phone. Your handset is essentially doing all the regular phone stuff and then powering a large tablet-like display at the same time. That typically includes constantly updating a map in real time.
With that in mind, your Android phone or iPhone can quickly start to lose battery life and heat up when it's connected to your vehicle, which you've perhaps already noticed. To keep your handset cool and your battery in good shape, here's what you need to do.
Go Wired if You Can (but Watch the Charging)
Wireless Android Auto and CarPlay are convenient, just like wireless charging is convenient, but it puts more stress on your phone. If you've got the option of a wired connection, that's preferable—but that introduces a new potential heat problem, which is that your phone will always be charging up.
To counter that, you can set charge limits (Battery and charging from Android Settings, Battery > Charging from iOS Settings), or simply make sure your phone is kept in a cool, dark spot of the car.
This wired option has the added bonus of letting you switch to airplane mode on your phone, which will go a long way to limiting heat. Again there's a trade-off though: No one will be able to reach you, and you'll need to have your maps, music, podcasts, and whatever else you need downloaded to your device in advance.
If you do stick with wireless Android Auto or CarPlay, try to avoid charging your phone at the same time, especially on the wireless pad built into the car’s dash (which generates more heat). You don't want to end up with a dead phone half way through the journey, so you may have to compromise at certain times.
Think About Where Your Phone Is Placed
As mentioned above, where your phone is in the car makes a real difference to how hot it's going to be. If you have your phone's interface up on your car dashboard, then you don't necessarily need to have it fixed to the dashboard, too, possibly under direct sunlight. The glove compartment will do just fine.
If you have a mount for your phone, think about attaching it in front of one of your car's air vents. Blasts of air conditioned air will significantly reduce how hot your handset gets, working like a DIY cooling system.
You might also want to think about taking the case off of your phone for the length of the trip, if your phone is fitted with one. Your handset is less likely to be dropped or knocked while you're driving anyway, and a case can trap the heat in.
The rules aren't too different to keeping your phone cool generally, though with the added wrinkle of needing to keep it connected to your car somehow. Make sure the cabin in general is at a comfortable temperature, though you're probably already doing that for your own sake. The bigger thing to remember is to avoid leaving your phone behind in a vehicle that's going to heat up in the sun if you're stopping off somewhere.
Limit the Work Your Phone Has to Do
If your phone is hooked up to Android Auto or CarPlay, then it's probably got some work to do—whether it's getting you to a destination or streaming music. However, you can still reduce heat by keeping phone tasks down to a minimum. If your calls and (voice-activated) messages can wait, leave them until the end of the journey.
We mentioned offline syncing above, but it doesn't have to go along with airplane mode. If you sync your tunes, podcasts, and maps to your phone ahead of time, your handset has less work to do while you’re driving since it doesn’t need to pull data from the cloud while also constantly searching for a wireless signal as you travel. Less stress on the modem means less heat overall.
Both Apple Maps and Google Maps let you download maps ahead of a trip. In Apple Maps, tap your profile picture, then Offline Maps, then Add Offline Map and find your location. With Google Maps, tap your profile picture, then choose Offline maps > Select your own map to choose the coverage.
There may be times when your phone has to be charging, wirelessly connected, making calls, in direct sunlight, and streaming music over a cellular connection, but try to keep these times to a minimum. Check regularly on how hot your phone is getting while connected to Android Auto or CarPlay, so you can take action if needed.

Data security breaches rise in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
10:13:43 UTC
19:13:43 KST

Data security breaches rise in 2026
Data security breaches in Switzerland have surged in 2026, with the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC), Adrian Lobsiger, reporting 455 incidents so far this year.
There were 343 such incidents throughout 2025. However, the actual number of incidents is likely to be significantly higher, as there are a large number of unreported cases, he said in an interview with the Swiss German weekly Sonntagsblick.
Following the cyberattack on a software provider used by several Swiss pension funds, the IFPDT launched a formal investigation last week. The investigation is currently focused on the external IT provider. In the interview, however, Lobsiger did not rule out extending the proceedings to federal bodies and pension funds at a later stage. For reasons relating to the confidentiality of the investigation, he was unable to provide further details on the specific case.
The IFPDT did, however, emphasise that the interconnection of data and the elimination of data silos increase the risk of security breaches. Furthermore, it must be ensured that only data that is strictly necessary is transmitted and that work is carried out preferably using anonymised test data.
In the interview, Lobsiger went on to describe the threat posed by artificial intelligence as “real”. However, an analysis of the causes of reported attacks reveals that, in the vast majority of cases, the weak point is not the technology itself, but human error.

Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia continued Sunday, rocking capital Riyadh as it prepared to reopen its international airport.
Saudi Arabia, which leads a military coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis, has faced a barrage of strikes from the group in recent weeks.
The fighting erupted after a yearslong truce between the Houthis and Yemen's Riyadh-backed government fell apart.
Riyadh's international airport said flights would resume Sunday after a two-week closure following the Houthi strikes. However, it remained unclear to what extent the airport was operational.
The Houthi fighters have carried out waves of strikes on the airport, including an attack this month that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.
The group has also targeted oil infrastructure and other sites, with the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen announcing Sunday it had intercepted 10 Houthi missiles fired at southern Saudi Arabia.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned that Riyadh airport was still "unsafe" and a "military target."
"The Yemeni Armed Forces warn all international, regional and local airlines – as well as staff and travelers – against using King Khalid Airport in Riyadh, as it is unsafe and serves as a military target for our forces," he said.
"The Saudi regime shall bear the consequences of any operations at the airport."
An AFP journalist in the city heard three explosions in the early hours of Sunday, with residents receiving alert messages for a "hostile aerial threat" urging them to stay in a safe place.
The warning came as the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had downed a ballistic missile launched by the group towards Riyadh, as well as two drones in the capital area.
"Air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh," the coalition posted on X.
Later Sunday morning, the coalition said its forces intercepted a cruise missile fired by the Houthis at the kingdom's southern city of Khamis Mushait.
Attacks appeared to target areas across the south, with warnings also issued for Abha city and Namas Governorate.
"The bombardment has been very heavy since this morning – may God keep us safe. Everything is shaking because of the explosions," one resident in Khamis Mushait said Sunday on condition of anonymity.
The attacks came after the Houthi fighters said that – in the space of 24 hours – they targeted three Saudi airports, including in Riyadh, energy installations, a pipeline and an air base.
The Saudi civil defense agency said it had also responded to falling debris in the Mecca and Medina regions on Saturday after intercepting two Houthi missiles.
The Houthis denied targeting the cities, the two holiest in Islam, calling the Saudi claim a "huge lie."
The Houthis also fired at the southern Yemeni city of Aden, the interim seat of the Saudi-backed government, saying they targeted a naval base and military camp overseen by Saudi forces.
The flare-up in Yemen, with the Houthis taking control of the entire Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive last month, has further destabilized the region and disrupted oil markets.
The Houthi attacks have dealt a blow to Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest exporter of crude, disrupting businesses, airlines and residents, and rattling its drive to shift its international image.

Beirut's $13 chicken sandwich becomes symbol of Lebanon divide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
10:10:33 UTC
19:10:33 KST

Beirut's $13 chicken sandwich becomes symbol of Lebanon divide
BEIRUT, Oct 25 - Seven years after Lebanon’s devastating financial meltdown, a debate over a chicken sandwich has exposed an increasingly stark divide between those who can still spend freely and those struggling to get by.
A trendy health restaurant wanted to offer its calorie-conscious customers a healthier take on the beloved Levantine wrap known as the shish taouk. So, The Glow Paradise launched the “Chic Taouk”, pricing it at around $13 — nearly double what an un-chic chicken sandwich typically goes for in Beirut.
The pricy pun proved hard to swallow, with outraged critics accusing the restaurant of overcharging in a country where many households struggle to afford basic necessities.
Yet while the debate raged on social media, customers kept buying. The Glow Paradise sold more than 20,000 Chic Taouk sandwiches in just 11 days, according to managing partner Hrag Jeghalian, who described the online exchanges as "natural marketing".
The contrasting reactions touched a nerve in Lebanon, where years of financial turmoil, political dysfunction and conflict have reshaped the country's social landscape, hollowing out much of the middle class while leaving a smaller group of consumers able to sustain an affluent lifestyle.
DEBATE PULLS FOCUS AWAY FROM URGENT CRISES
Sami Nader, an economist at the Saint Joseph University of Beirut, said the throngs at The Glow Paradise belied another reality.
“So you see people in the restaurant, but what you don't see is that 22 restaurants closed last month,” Nader told Reuters.
Lebanon’s Instagram-active community was split between those accusing the restaurant of theft and others saying the sandwich was intended for those who could afford it.
Some questioned whether the dispute itself reflected misplaced priorities in a country grappling with urgent crises, from Israel’s occupation of large swaths of the country’s south to the endemic electricity and water crises.
Lebanon’s 2019 financial collapse was prompted by decades of corruption and profligate spending by the ruling elite, and several rounds of conflict since then have worsened the country’s economic outlook.
GDP has declined by nearly 40% since 2019 and inflation is expected to rise to 17.5% due to rising global energy and shipping prices eating away at people’s purchasing power, according to the World Bank. The figure is more than quadruple the global headline inflation rate flagged by the International Monetary Fund in July.
Four in five households in Lebanon struggle to afford basic necessities, the UN children’s agency said in September.
'PEOPLE CAN'T KEEP UP'
The country’s middle class has “disappeared,” Nader said, dismantled by a series of crises including the collapse of the financial system in 2019, the 2020 Beirut Port explosion and two wars in under two years.
Monthly bills from private generator operators, which provide electricity to many homes and businesses during outages on Lebanon's failing national grid, jumped by nearly 20% in August 2026 alone, bringing rates nearly 60% higher than they were in February of this year, according to the kilowatt-hour prices set by Lebanon’s energy ministry.
For many, that means paying for 24/7 electricity now costs several hundred dollars a month, in a country where the minimum wage is set at $400.
“Everything has become expensive, and people can’t keep up,” said Fouad Fakhreddine, a 53-year-old restaurant worker from nearby Hamra. “We are now getting paid, then getting in debt over that just to get by.”
The years of economic instability, he said, have produced “a class that is living, and a class that is not dead and waiting to die from the unbearable situation it is in.” REUTERS

Serbia Votes as Student Movement Mounts Major Challenge to Vučić
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
10:07:00 UTC
19:07:00 KST

Serbia is voting on Sunday as a mass student protest movement seeks to unseat long-time populist leader Aleksandar Vučić in the biggest challenge to his rule for more than a decade.
The snap parliamentary elections, called by Vučić in September, come after almost two years of student-led demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism triggered by the deaths of 16 people when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad in 2024. The students have since gained widespread support.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Unusually long lines formed at polling stations in Belgrade and Novi Sad before the start of voting at 7 a.m. local time. Voting ends at 8 p.m. with first indications of results expected around two hours later.
A student victory would be a profound political shift in the Balkan country of some 6 million people, reminiscent of the defeat of Hungary’s Viktor Orban in April. It also potentially offers a blueprint for other student movements across Europe, which have taken to the streets in recent weeks to protest, in some cases violently, against poor education standards and a lack of prospects.
But Vučić, who resigned from his second term as president to run again for prime minister, is a strong incumbent. Many voters thank him for pulling Serbia from economic obscurity and orchestrating a period of sustained modernisation including new highways, railways, schools and hospitals.
US Senators Threaten Nomination Block Over Ukraine Starlink Curbs
“I came out early today because the students called us,” said Ana, 30, at a polling station in Belgrade.
Opinion polls predict tight race
Domestically, Vučić has pledged higher pensions and public sector salaries, investment in state healthcare and subsidies for young couples. On the international stage, he has balanced closer ties with China, a major investor, and Russia, Serbia’s traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas, while leaving the door open to joining the European Union.
The students’ domestic agenda aims to root out graft and improve schooling, but they have been quieter on their international ambitions. Their list of 250 largely unknown candidates includes university professors, actors and farmers, and is led by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic.
Opinion polls predict a tight race. In an Ipsos poll published on Thursday, Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) is seen leading with 47% of votes versus 40% for the students. But other polls have put the students in the lead.
Student protests increase pressure on Vučić
The student-led street protests sparked by the station disaster quickly became the biggest in a generation, calling for Vucic to step down. Rights groups and activists say repression has worsened in the period since.
Bogdan Pavkovic was one of thousands in central Belgrade for a final student rally on Thursday. He said he wants to change “this awful, horrendous system which cheats on us, which spies on us, which beats us.”
Vučić’s office and the Interior Ministry did not respond to requests for comment. Vučić and the SNS have repeatedly denied accusations of repression, corruption and spying on their opponents. He says the students are funded by foreign agents in Croatia and Montenegro, a charge the students dismiss.
“This has been one of the most difficult but the most emotional campaigns,” Vučić told his supporters on Thursday. “We stood against those who wanted to destroy Serbia.”
Relations sour with EU
Relations with the EU have frayed as the bloc has become increasingly frustrated with Serbia’s lack of reforms over the judiciary, rule of law and corruption.
In a report this month after a visit to Serbia, a delegation from rights body the Council of Europe noted the “hostile and aggressive rhetoric” against opponents.
And in September, EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned the huge public funeral of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic held in Belgrade, saying it contradicted “the values underpinning Serbia’s path towards the European Union.”

WASHINGTON, Oct 25 - Relations between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy took a sharp downward turn in recent weeks, with each leader openly criticizing the other. Here's how the relationship soured:
WHAT IS THE HISTORY OF TRUMP-ZELENSKIY TENSIONS?
Trump has been skeptical of US involvement in Ukraine ever since his first term when, shortly after taking office in early 2017, he was asked to provide lethal aid to Ukraine and approved the sale of Javelin missiles to Kyiv.

Trump's current frustration centers on Kyiv's attacks on Russian diesel infrastructure.

“We don't have to pressure Zelenskiy. If he wants to make a deal he'll make a deal. I think Putin is putting a ton of pressure on him and he (Zelenskiy) is putting some pressure on Russia but Russia doesn't seem to be minding it as much even though they are getting hit."
On Thursday, Trump said he had asked SpaceX CEO Elon Musk to restore Ukraine’s access to the company's Starlink satellite system. Starlink's disruption temporarily hampered Kyiv's military drone operations and spurred fears that Kyiv would be left defenseless against Russia's attacks going into the winter.
WHAT IS THE STATUS OF MOSCOW-KYIV PEACE TALKS?
Peace efforts have continued but so far have not yielded tangible results.
At talks in Oslo on October 20, Ukraine presented new proposals, and Trump’s son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner repeated Trump's demand that Ukraine stop attacking Russian diesel refineries.
The next day, envoy Witkoff – a close friend of Trump's - met Putin in St. Petersburg. Putin agreed to release detained American Stephen Hubbard in what the two countries called a goodwill gesture.

Explainer-Four ways US foreign policy could change if Democrats win in November
WASHINGTON, Oct 25 - Nonpartisan analysts say Democrats stand a good chance of winning the US House of Representatives and possibly the Senate in the November 3 midterm elections, which would give them a slice of power in Washington after two years of Republican control.
Democrats argue that Republicans have allowed President Donald Trump's administration to declare war and control spending, even though the US Constitution reserves those powers for lawmakers.
Here are some ways a Democratic Congress could hem in Trump's foreign policy.
CURB THE IRAN WAR
Trump did not secure approval from Congress before he launched the war with Iran on February 28, and Democrats have voted repeatedly to end the fighting unless he does so. One of these resolutions passed with support from a handful of Republicans, but Trump's administration ignored it.
With control of the House or the Senate, Democrats could cut defense spending to pressure Trump to obtain permission from Congress to continue the war. They could also require administration officials to testify publicly about their plans.
FRESH SUPPORT FOR UKRAINE
Trump has largely halted direct US financial and military aid to Ukraine, despite broad support from Democratic and Republican lawmakers as it fights a Russian invasion.
Most recently, he has angered members of Congress, including many Republicans, by lifting sanctions on Russian diesel and waiving sanctions on Russian energy only weeks after signing them into law.
With a victory in both chambers in November, Democrats would be able to decide what gets voted on and when.
That could allow them to approve new aid to Ukraine, which likely would pass with the two-thirds majorities needed to overcome a Trump veto.
They could also target other Trump activities. For example, Representative Gregory Meeks of New York, who could head the House Foreign Affairs Committee if Democrats win control, has introduced bipartisan legislation to block Trump's plan to bring Russian diesel back into the global market.
END MILITARY AID TO ISRAEL
Support for Israel has plummeted among Democrats over its conduct in the Gaza war, which has killed tens of thousands of Palestinian civilians. The ongoing violence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's close alliance with Republicans have also been factors.
Democrats could limit or end military aid to Israel, which amounted to $3.8 billion in the most recent fiscal year. That is more than was provided to any other country.
Nearly half of House Democrats voted this summer to cut off aid to Israel. Some of those who voted against that effort, such as Meeks, have backed limits on providing weapons like heavy bombs to Israel.
LIMIT MILITARY SPENDING AND RESTORE FOREIGN AID
Democrats are far more likely than Trump's Republicans to limit military spending. Trump asked for an unprecedented 67% increase in the military budget this year, to $1.5 trillion, but Democrats blocked it in the Senate, citing his refusal to consult Congress about the Iran war and his steep cuts to social programs.
Trump has also withheld or canceled billions of dollars in foreign aid approved by Congress. Many Democrats have been angered by the cuts and say they will try to restore funding. REUTERS

Storm Boelo: warnings in place in Scotland, Northern Ireland and north of England as high winds batter UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
10:03:31 UTC
19:03:31 KST

A 60-year-old man has been killed by a falling tree and more than 82,000 properties have been left without power as Storm Boelo continues to batter Scotland, Northern Ireland and the north of England.
The adverse weather hitting northern parts of the UK on Saturday evening was the second named storm in as many days, after Storm Austen brought strong winds to south-west England on Friday.
The Met Office said wind speeds widely reached 60-70mph, affecting areas in an amber warning zone that came into force at 9pm on Saturday.
The warning covered Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, with gusts reaching more than 80mph in exposed coastal spots. The island of Tiree in the Inner Hebrides was hit by 82mph winds, according to the forecaster, while wind speeds reached 84mph in Argyll and Bute and 83mph in Snowdonia (Eryri).
Approximately 53,000 homes in Scotland were still without power by 5pm on Sunday, according to updates from SP Energy Networks and Scottish and Southern Electricity Networks (SSEN).
The Scottish government’s Resilience Room met to discuss the impact of the storm on Sunday afternoon, ministers focusing on the outages and how they were being restored.
The storm has led to at least one fatality as Police Scotland revealed that a man had died on Sunday morning.
A spokesperson for the force said: “We were made aware of a 60-year-old man having been struck by a falling tree on a minor road at Mid Kelton about 10.30am on Sunday, 25 October 2026.
“The man was pronounced dead at the scene. There are no suspicious circumstances and a report will be submitted to the procurator fiscal in due course.”
Engineers had restored power to 344,900 customers but 82,6000 remained disconnected, the Energy Networks Association (ENA) said on Sunday morning. The figure included more than 30,000 homes across Scotland.
The ENA said: “The networks have been focused on reconnecting customers this morning, though the continuing severe weather in some regions is limiting network engineers’ opportunities to safely start the work of restoring customers’ power today and access to certain areas remains difficult. Engineers are working around the clock to identify and fix faults.”
Train travel was disrupted on Sunday. Network Rail Scotland shared an image of flooding from the tracks to the platform at one Glasgow station, and fallen trees above the lines near another. Speed restrictions were in place across Scotland and several sections of its railways were closed, the operator added.
Network Rail shared images of a trampoline beneath a train and a shed by the tracks, and it reminded people living near rail lines to firmly secure objects in their gardens.
Some flights were diverted from landing at Leeds Bradford airport and others were cancelled.
The Met Office advised people in affected areas to secure loose items in gardens and to stay indoors as the storm posed a danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves.
The Met Office chief forecaster, Jason Kelly, said: “Storm Boelo will be felt across the UK this weekend, with the strongest winds and greatest potential for disruption in the north. Amber warnings are in place across mainland Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, where gusts of 60-70mph are expected widely, with the potential for 80mph in exposed coastal locations.
“Strong winds will also affect other parts of the UK, with gusts of 50-60mph possible in places. Heavy rain will provide an additional hazard, particularly in the north, bringing the potential for further impacts. People should prepare for the potential for disruption, particularly to travel and power supplies.”
Several events have been cancelled this weekend due to the inclement weather. Visit Liverpool said the River of Light event, featuring illuminated artworks, had been cancelled “in the interests of safety”, while London’s annual Diwali on the Square celebrations on Sunday were cancelled on the advice of independent health and safety experts.
Edinburgh Castle was closed on Sunday because of the high winds and adverse weather, while the Fountains Abbey estate in North Yorkshire was also closed for the day, after its Fountains by Floodlight event on Saturday evening was cancelled.
The Environment Agency had issued six warnings as of 1.45pm that flooding was expected for spots in northern parts of England, as well as 50 alerts stating flooding was possible. The Scottish Environment Protection Agency said 17 flood warnings and 11 flooding alerts were active as of the same time.
Cumbria police said they had received a number of calls overnight to localised flooding and fallen trees blocking roads across the county, and urged motorists to drive with care while emergency services worked to clear the obstructions.
The amber warning sits within wider yellow wind warnings, which cover parts of England farther south, as well as north Wales and the whole of Northern Ireland.
Hundreds of homes were still without power in south-west England after Storm Austen hit the region on Friday, bringing 76mph winds to St Mary’s airport in the Isles of Scilly, with 74mph recorded at Aberporth in south Wales and 71mph at Culdrose in Cornwall.

Hyve Smart Package Locker Review: Protecting Your Holiday Deliveries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
10:01:00 UTC
19:01:00 KST

The onslaught of tech gear being delivered for WIRED Reviews, combined with the samples I receive constantly for my side hustle at Drinkhacker, means that delivery trucks are a constant occurrence on my suburban street. UPS and FedEx both make drops at my house nearly every day, and that’s not to mention occasional deliveries from the likes of DHL and, of course, Amazon and its ilk. But it’s usually not a problem. I work from home, so picking up packages left on the doorstep is just part of the scenery.
What is a problem is that I can’t be home 24 hours a day, and even though I have a very kind neighbor across the way who keeps an eye out for boxes on my front steps when I’m traveling, he isn’t always at home either. Package hold requests aren’t consistently honored by either of the major carriers—and earlier this year, FedEx seemingly discontinued its vacation hold option without bothering to tell anyone, the modern epidemic of porch piracy be damned. (A rep has since confirmed this with me, though no formal announcement has ever been made.)
Having packages held at shipping centers or access points usually costs money, typically about $5 per package and often more depending on the length of the hold, and that involves a trip after I get home to collect what’s arrived. If I’m gone for a week, that can mean fetching a dozen boxes or more.
All of that is a time-consuming pain, for which a startup called Hyve has come along to offer an assuagement: A smart lockbox that lets delivery drivers drop off packages in a secure location, notifying the homeowner whenever it’s been accessed. While the growing pains were significant, after weeks of testing, I found it a useful device that—just maybe—may earn a permanent home on my front porch.
Locking and Loading
Parcel lockboxes aren’t exactly a new concept. They operate basically like a standard post office mailbox, with a cantilevered hatch up top that allows deliveries to drop into a secure storage area below, where they can only be accessed through a keyed door. Delivery folks can put packages in through the hatch, but only you can get them out.
The Hyve Smart Package Locker is a play on this idea, forgoing the two-chamber design in favor of an electronic hatch accessed via 4-digit PINs. The box itself measures 32 inches high, 20 inches wide, and 20 inches deep, with interior dimensions about 4 inches shorter in each direction. That makes for a total of 7.4 cubic feet, which Hyve says will fit 80 percent of Amazon package sizes (though obviously this depends on the specifics of your ordering habits). For me, that math worked out: Deliveries of three-pack bottles of wine fit fine, but anything larger was typically left out by the courier.
It’s built from a combination of plastic and steel, and while the side panels seem a little flimsy, there’s enough reinforcement behind them that I never worried that the unit would be easily damaged by a would-be package thief without power tools. Units are available in gray or white; I requested the latter to match my home’s color, but alas received a gray one.

Your body makes its own cannabis-like chemicals as you run, and neuroscience research finds they keep rising all the way to the marathon finish line, a possible clue to the runner’s high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
10:00:48 UTC
19:00:48 KST

A long run appears to keep the body’s own cannabis-like chemical messengers active for hours. New research published in BMC Medicine indicates that one of these compounds, anandamide, climbs steadily during a marathon and stays elevated 45 minutes after the finish, and that levels are also higher after ultramarathons of up to 230 kilometers. These chemical changes occurred alongside shifts in mood, such as reduced anxiety after running, although the study did not test whether one caused the other.
The runner’s high is a state some people report during or after endurance exercise, marked by euphoria, reduced anxiety, less pain, and a sense of calm afterward. Early explanations credited endorphins, the body’s natural opioid painkillers, but endorphins are large, water-soluble molecules, and there is no convincing evidence that they cross the blood-brain barrier, the protective filter between the bloodstream and the brain, in meaningful amounts.
Endocannabinoids offer an alternative: they are small, fat-soluble molecules made on demand from cell membranes, they can cross that barrier, and they act on the same cannabinoid receptors targeted by THC, the main psychoactive compound in cannabis. The two best studied are anandamide and 2-arachidonoylglycerol, often shortened to 2-AG.
Laboratory experiments began supporting this shift in thinking when a 2015 animal experiment led by Johannes Fuss, the senior author of the new study, showed that wheel-running mice relied on cannabinoid receptors, rather than opioid receptors, to experience reduced anxiety and lower pain sensitivity. Human research soon followed, including a 2021 clinical trial by the same group where researchers gave participants a medication that blocked opioid receptors. The runners still reported the typical calm and euphoric sensations of a runner’s high, suggesting that endorphins were not required for those effects.
In a 2022 systematic review, the same group found that 14 of 17 studies detected a rise in endocannabinoids after a single bout of exercise. But as the authors of the new study note, nearly all of that human research involved workouts lasting under an hour, leaving open what happens during true long-distance events.
“Humans are capable of running for many hours, sometimes even days, and we wanted to understand what happens to the endocannabinoid system during such extraordinary endurance efforts,” lead author Michael Siebers, a psychiatrist at LVR University Hospital Essen, told PsyPost.
“I believe that our ability to run long distances cannot be explained by anatomy alone,” Siebers explained. “We probably also need an entire orchestra of neuromodulators that reward us for sustained physical activity and help us continue running despite fatigue and discomfort. Thanks to a wonderful collaboration with researchers from Ulm and the German Sport University Cologne, we were able to investigate these processes during marathon and ultramarathon running, including distances of up to 230 kilometers.”
To investigate these biochemical and emotional shifts under real-world conditions, Siebers and his colleagues, including senior author Johannes Fuss of the University of Duisburg-Essen and collaborators at University Hospital Ulm and the German Sport University Cologne, designed two field studies of trained endurance athletes.
The first investigation examined 19 experienced runners, including seven women and 12 men, who completed a marathon course consisting of three 14-kilometer loops around Lake Baldeney in Essen, Germany. To establish a realistic comparison, each runner returned one to two months later to complete an identical-duration walking session along the same route at their preferred pace. Blood samples were drawn at the start, at the 14-kilometer and 28-kilometer marks, immediately after the full course (about 43 kilometers), and after a 45-minute rest period. Alongside blood draws, participants completed visual rating scales to score their current levels of euphoria, anxiety, and physical pain.
The second investigation followed 36 athletes (16 ran 100 kilometers, 7 ran 160, and 13 ran 230) taking part in the TorTour de Ruhr, a non-stop ultramarathon in central Germany. These athletes, comprising 13 women and 23 men, provided blood samples and mood ratings before the race and shortly after crossing the finish line. In both studies, laboratory technicians measured several key lipids, including anandamide and 2-AG.
In the marathon study, levels of anandamide rose progressively across the entire run. By the mid-race mark, anandamide was higher during running than during walking, which produced only modest changes, and it remained higher 45 minutes after the marathon ended. Running was also far more intense, with runners averaging about 83 percent of their estimated maximum heart rate, compared with about 58 percent while walking. The compound 2-AG displayed a different trajectory, showing lower levels early in the run compared to walking, but climbing during the final kilometers and staying elevated during early recovery.
The ultramarathon runners exhibited similar biochemical patterns upon completing their races. Anandamide and 2-AG concentrations were both higher after the race across all three ultramarathon distances compared to pre-race baselines. In an exploratory comparison, post-race anandamide levels after the marathon were nearly double those seen after the ultramarathons (32.4 versus 17.1 in the study’s measurements), which the authors suggest may reflect the higher running intensity of the shorter race.
Mood ratings also shifted during running. Marathon participants reported higher euphoria while running than while walking at several points, although at the 28-kilometer mark, a stage where runners often describe “hitting the wall,” euphoria was no longer different from walking. Anxiety ratings started slightly higher before the marathon than before the walk, then fell toward the end of the run, and pain ratings showed little change after 14 kilometers but rose markedly from 28 kilometers on. In the ultramarathon group, anxiety decreased after the race, more so at 100 and 160 kilometers than at 230, while pain rose and euphoria did not change in a statistically significant way.
When asked afterward, only 3 of the 19 marathoners said they had experienced a runner’s high during the marathon, while 8 said they had not and 8 were unsure; among the ultramarathoners, 12 said they had and 19 said they had not.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2022, which found that acute exercise consistently increased endocannabinoid levels, especially anandamide, with moderate intensity yielding stronger boosts than low intensity.
“This is an interesting study, particularly because it’s not easy to investigate physiological responses to exercise over marathon and ultramarathon distances,” said Danielle McCartney, a research affiliate at the University of Sydney who was not involved in the study. “The key finding is that circulating concentrations of anandamide (AEA), an endocannabinoid, increased progressively throughout the marathon and were also elevated following ultramarathons of 100, 160 and 230 km.”
“Previous studies have consistently shown that moderate-intensity running increases blood concentrations of AEA,” McCartney told PsyPost. “However, most of this research has focused on relatively short bouts of exercise (less than 60 minutes). This study fills an important gap by examining much longer running distances, and shows that increases in AEA also occur during marathon and ultramarathon running.”
The researchers see the sustained activity as a possible clue to how humans manage hours of running.
“One of our most important findings is that the body’s own cannabinoid system remains active even during extremely prolonged exercise,” Siebers noted. “We observed substantial increases in endocannabinoids, particularly anandamide, not only during marathon running but also after ultramarathons lasting many hours.”
“These molecules are sometimes described as the body’s own cannabis-like substances because they act on the same cannabinoid receptor system targeted by THC,” he said. “They may contribute to the rewarding, calming, and potentially pain-modulating effects of running. From an evolutionary perspective, I find this particularly fascinating. Humans have an extraordinary capacity for endurance running, and the endocannabinoid system may be one of the biological mechanisms that make prolonged running not only physically possible but also psychologically rewarding.”
Siebers described the shift many runners report over the course of a run.
“At the beginning of a run, everything may feel uncomfortable,” he observed. “Your calves are aching, your back feels stiff, and every step requires some effort.”
“But after a while, something can change,” he noted. “Your movements become smoother, running feels increasingly effortless, and you may enter a state of flow. Sometimes this develops into euphoria, while everyday worries and stress seem to fade into the background.”
Siebers also sees potential relevance for mental health.
“As a psychiatrist, I find this especially interesting because running can become a valuable tool for coping with stress, improving mood, and supporting mental well-being,” he added. “Of course, exercise is not a replacement for professional treatment when it is needed, but for some people, it can be an important part of their recovery and everyday life.”
The study did not test whether runners whose anandamide rose the most felt the most euphoric or calm.
McCartney cautioned, however, against assuming that these chemical increases directly generate the emotional sensations reported by participants. “It’s important to recognize that this study doesn’t establish that increases in AEA are responsible for the ‘runner’s high,'” she explained. “It shows that prolonged running increases blood AEA concentrations and is associated with changes in mood, including increased euphoria and reduced anxiety. While these findings are consistent with the idea that AEA contributes to the runner’s high, they don’t establish a causal relationship.”
The TorTour de Ruhr presented extreme physical demands, requiring runners to navigate unfamiliar routes for up to 230 kilometers, often through the night and in isolation.
“What impressed me most was witnessing what humans are capable of achieving,” Siebers recounted. “Some of our participants ran distances of up to 230 kilometers, maintaining their effort for many hours, sometimes running alone through the night on unfamiliar trails. Equally fascinating was the atmosphere among the ultramarathon runners. Despite the enormous physical demands, there was a remarkable sense of community and positivity.”
“I was particularly struck by participants who reported very little anxiety after these extraordinary distances, even after spending hours alone in unfamiliar surroundings,” he said. “Some runners also reported surprisingly little pain despite covering distances that would seem almost unimaginable to most people. These observations make me wonder how strongly our internal neuromodulatory systems can influence the way we experience physical effort, pain, and fear.”
Pain was still common: 29 of the 36 ultramarathoners reported pain during the race, only five reported none, and eight said they used pain medication, particularly in the longest race.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The marathon study used walking as a comparison rather than having participants sit quietly, meaning the control condition still involved mild physical exertion. Participants also selected their own running and walking speeds, which preserved a realistic race environment but introduced variation in how hard each individual was working.
“I have reasonable confidence in the main findings, particularly because the increases in AEA were consistent across the marathon and ultramarathon studies and align with previous research,” McCartney told PsyPost. “However, there are some limitations worth considering. Measuring endocannabinoids in blood can be technically challenging, and although the authors used established analytical methods, they don’t explicitly report whether these methods were validated.”
“I’d also have liked more information about what participants ate during and after exercise,” McCartney added. “We know that nutrient intake can influence blood AEA concentrations, so it’s possible that dietary behavior affected the measures.”
The authors describe their laboratory analysis as following established, standardized protocols, including adding chemically labeled reference versions of each compound to every sample to allow exact measurement. They also acknowledge that participants’ nutrition, rest, and time of day were not fully controlled.
Every participant also ran the marathon before doing the walking session, which the authors note may have raised anxiety at the start of the running day. The samples were also small, with 19 marathoners and between 7 and 16 runners at each ultramarathon distance, and no blood was drawn during the ultramarathons themselves.
The emotional measures relied on brief, single-item rating scales, which capture only a snapshot of complex mental states like flow or emotional relief. Logistics during the ultramarathon also meant that pre-race samples for the 230-kilometer group had to be collected the previous evening rather than right at the starting line.
“One important distinction is that we measured endocannabinoids in the blood, not directly in the brain,” Siebers pointed out. “Although our findings show substantial changes in circulating endocannabinoid concentrations, we cannot yet determine precisely what happens in the brain during prolonged running.”
“Another important point is that the runner’s high is not simply caused by one molecule,” he added. “Endocannabinoids are probably part of a much larger and highly complex orchestra of neuromodulators, including dopamine, serotonin, endogenous opioids, and other signaling systems. Furthermore, not everyone experiences a runner’s high, and running does not necessarily become more enjoyable the longer someone continues.”
When considering future research, McCartney highlighted both pharmacological and nutritional avenues for follow-up testing. “Ideally, I’d like to see whether blocking cannabinoid receptors prevents the runner’s high,” she said. “Unfortunately, the safety concerns associated with drugs like rimonabant make that a difficult experiment to conduct in humans!”
Rimonabant, a drug that blocks the main cannabinoid receptor, was pulled from the European market in 2008 after it was linked to depression and suicidal thoughts.
“More realistically, I’d be interested in seeing whether nutrition influences the endocannabinoid response to prolonged exercise,” McCartney told PsyPost, “particularly given that runners typically consume substantial amounts of carbohydrate during marathon and ultramarathon events.”
Looking ahead, the authors hope to examine how these chemical messengers operate directly within the central nervous system during physical exertion.
“One of my main interests is understanding how running influences mood changes and the brain itself,” Siebers said. “So far, our research has primarily focused on measuring endocannabinoids in peripheral blood. However, the runner’s high ultimately involves processes within the central nervous system, and we still know surprisingly little about what actually happens in the human brain during running. I would therefore like to investigate these central mechanisms more directly, potentially through neuroimaging and other methods that allow us to study neuromodulation in the brain.”
“In addition, I am particularly interested in how the endocannabinoid system interacts with pain regulation during prolonged exercise,” he continued. “Why can some individuals continue running for hours despite considerable physical stress, while others experience increasing discomfort? Understanding these mechanisms could provide valuable insights not only into endurance exercise but also into pain regulation and mental health.”
Beyond laboratory measurements, the researchers also reflected on the broader personal and evolutionary dimensions of sustained running.
Siebers emphasized that the effect requires no outside substance. “What fascinates me is that our bodies can produce their own cannabis-like substances simply through physical activity,” he told PsyPost. “Under the right circumstances, this can contribute to a completely natural high, without consuming any external substance.”
“For me, the most exciting message is that running is much more than moving our legs,” Siebers said. “It is a fascinating interaction between our body and brain, and understanding this interaction may help us discover why humans have developed such an extraordinary relationship with endurance running.”
The study, “Endocannabinoid dynamics across marathon and ultramarathon running: evidence from two field studies,” was authored by Michael Siebers, Dana Huvermann, Christoph Siebers, Deborah Canales-Romero, Alexandra Florea-Ghile, Lina Keite, Lucas John, Moritz Munk, Roman Bizjak, Jens Witzel, Sebastian Schulz, Johannes Kirsten, Laura Bindila, Anke Hinney, Marijke Grau, Daniel A. Bizjak, Harald Engler, and Johannes Fuss.

How China’s regional leadership changes offer clues to the future of the Communist Party
The coming months will see a series of provincial congresses as part of a process that will determine the membership of key party bodies

China’s five-year leadership cycle is getting under way at a provincial level, with new teams being installed in a process that offers important clues to the future of the Communist Party at a national level.
Last week, four provinces – Anhui, Henan, Shanxi and Xinjiang – wrapped up their respective party congresses and appointed new standing committees for the next five years.
The meetings were held a week before a key party gathering in Beijing – known as the fifth plenum – that runs from Monday to Thursday, where the Central Committee will discuss measures to strengthen party governance and discipline.
The plenum will also offer an opportunity to prepare for a major overhaul of the national leadership, which will take place at the party congress next year and will be key to the country’s goals of becoming an economic and military superpower by the middle of the century.

How ancient Chinese night watchmen patrolled streets, used ‘dripping buckets’ to tell time

Fran Luin Beijing
In ancient China, before the advent of mechanical clocks and digital devices, people relied mainly on night watchmen to keep time, prevent fires and maintain their daily routines. But how did the watchmen tell the time?
Chinese night watchmen mainly used two methods: clepsydras and incense sticks.
A clepsydra, also known as a water clock, measures time through the regulated flow of water from a vessel.

Retail leads the way on paternity leave as government urged to improve offer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

“Being able to take six weeks’ paid paternity leave, flexibly, made a huge difference to me and my family, giving me the time to support my partner and settle into being a new parent,” said Marks & Spencer employee Joe Erskine.
The food and clothing retailer increased its paternity leave offering from two to six weeks at full pay in 2024, meaning Erskine benefited from the new policy when his second child was born 17 months ago.
M&S and Tesco are among the retailers leading the way in offering enhanced paternity leave to their staff, new research has shown, highlighting the widening gap between the more family-friendly policies offered to new fathers working in the retail sector compared with those in construction, manufacturing and agriculture.
Both companies offer six weeks at full pay to employees, far outstripping the statutory two-week minimum paternity leave offer and making them among the most generous of UK blue-chip companies listed on the FTSE 100, according to figures compiled by campaign group The Dad Shift and Ian Dinwiddy of Inspiring Dads.
Privately owned companies Ikea, Lego and Virgin Media O2 now also offer more weeks of fully paid leave to new fathers.
The enhanced paternity leave offered by retailers including Asda, Waitrose and Lidl in recent years means that just five employers are responsible for upgrading parental leave for nearly 650,000 workers.
Retail businesses and the shop workers’ union Usdaw held a roundtable discussion in parliament, hosted by Labour MP Connor Rand, to discuss the transformation in working parents’ lives brought in by changes to parental leave.
Rand, who was a researcher for Usdaw prior to his election to parliament in 2024, said the entitlement was crucial for his family: “Through the ups and downs, I could bond with my son and support my partner because of paternity leave. Too many dads in our country can’t do this. That’s bad for them, bad for their partner and bad for their children. It must change.”
Campaigners have long argued that the UK has one of the least generous paternity leave offers in the world, ranked 40th out of 43 Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development countries. Over two decades after paternity leave rights were introduced in Britain, they argue the country has fallen behind and now has the least generous entitlement in Europe.
Employed fathers in the UK are entitled to two weeks’ statutory paternity leave paid at £194.32 a week, or 90% of their average weekly earnings, whichever amount is lower, totalling less than half the national living wage.
Many companies offer enhanced paternity leave by topping up the statutory offer to full salary, in some cases for a longer period of time.
However, there is a growing disparity between different sectors of the economy. Analysis by The Dad Shift found that the construction sector employs around one in 10 working men, but only accounts for about one in 15 recipients of statutory paternity pay.
This could partly be because some construction workers are self-employed and currently have no entitlement to paid paternity leave, as is also the case for many of Britain’s agricultural workers, the majority of whom are self-employed.
Construction company JCB only offers two weeks’ full pay in paternity leave, although this has been increased from the three days it previously offered.
Engineering firm Rolls-Royce, which makes jet engines for planes, turbines for ships and small nuclear power plants, has a workforce that is more than 80% male but currently only offers two weeks’ fully paid leave.
More than 100 Labour MPs have called on Andy Burnham in recent weeks to commit to improving the UK’s paternity leave in the upcoming budget, warning that lowest-paid fathers are the hardest hit by inadequate paternity leave provision.
They are calling for the introduction of six weeks of paternity leave paid at 90% of earnings, capped at £1,200 a week, with the offer extended to self-employed fathers. An 18-month government review of the UK’s parental leave system is expected to report later this year.

Five uncanny venues where guests are treated to frightfully unique interiors

This is the latest in our lookbooks series, which provides visual inspiration from Dezeen’s archive. For more inspiration, see previous lookbooks featuring billiard tables, wooden staircases and bookmaxxed interiors.
J Boroski, China, by Atelier XY
The owner of this Shanghai bar is interested in insects – local studio Atelier XY honoured this through the addition of over 1,000 preserved specimens.
A wooden grid covering the back wall and ceiling of the bar area features thousands of beetles housed in individual recesses, while a glass-brick wall containing 42 preserved Thai Black tarantulas acts as a partition. The atmosphere of being inside an oven was recreated in this Valencia nightclub by Spanish firm Clap Studio.

Bar Far, Italy, by Clementine Keith-Roach and Christopher Page
Human legs support tables, disembodied hands hold candlesticks and torsos emerge from walls in this unsettlingly cave-like bar by artists Clementine Keith-Roach and Christopher Page.
The space, which was open on a temporary basis during early 2026, was described as being “at once church and tomb, prophecy and ruin, heaven and hell” by installation curator Vittoria Bonifati.
Dark wood panelling and chairs upholstered in tartan set the mood for The Scottish Room, which inhabits the third floor of The Audley, a pub in London’s Mayfair neighbourhood.
Designed by architecture studio Laplace, this room belies the rest of the comparatively playful interior, being dominated by a sprawling chandelier made from deer antlers hanging above a nine-metre-long oaken table.
ÅBEN, Denmark, by Pihlmann Architects
A former butchery in Copenhagen’s Meatpacking District has been converted into a lofty brewery by local studio Pihlmann Architects, with an interior partitioned using translucent curtains.
The studio elected to retain the original system of hanging rails, which the abattoir would have once used to suspend up to 980 animal carcasses.
