TAIYUAN, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- As the starting gun went off, the Tianjin Marathon 2026 got underway on Sunday. Among the runners was Japanese running enthusiast Himiko Izumi, who once again embarked on a marathon tourism journey in a new Chinese city.
"Running is just an excuse. Traveling is actually more important," Izumi said.
Based in Beijing, Izumi enjoys taking part in marathons in different parts of China in her spare time. During her trip to the Taiyuan Marathon late September, she visited the Shanxi Museum to see an exhibition she had long wanted to explore. This time, she traveled to Tianjin to combine the marathon with sightseeing.
"Every time I compete in a different city, I get to see different scenery," she said. In Baotou, she explored the vast grasslands and local museums. During the Marathon around Chagan Lake, she also cycled along the lakeshore.
In recent months, mass-participation sporting events, including marathons and trail-running races, have been held across China. An increasing number of foreign participants are combining competition with travel, discovering the vitality of Chinese cities and their cultural appeal along the way.
According to data provided by the organizing committee of the Taiyuan Marathon 2026, nearly 100 foreign runners from 12 countries and regions took part in this year's event, with the number increasing year by year.
At the Shanghai Marathon 2025, foreign runners accounted for more than 13 percent of participants. The number of international participants rose from 32 in 2024 to 585 in 2025, covering 26 countries and regions.
In Shanxi, marathons have also become a way for international students to venture beyond campus and gain a deeper understanding of local customs and culture.
In September, 18 students from Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan, Yemen and Vietnam participated in a 10km running event in Shanxi's Anze County.
"Taking part in a marathon is more like a group trip for us. Before the race, we also visited other places to explore new cultures and heritage sites and meet new people. These experiences are just as important as the competition itself," said Pakistani student Bilal Ahmad.
The experience extended well beyond the racecourse. During their visit, the students explored the Xunzi Cultural Park, attended a Mid-Autumn Festival concert, watched performances of Puzhou Opera and visited many historical scenic spots.
Cheng Minduo, a professor at the School of Physical Education at Shanxi University, said the growing variety of mass-participation sporting events and improvements in their organization were making them important gateways for foreigners to understand and experience China.
Unlike professional athletes, amateur runners often participate not only to challenge themselves and improve their fitness, but also to explore their host cities and experience local culture.
Zhang Xinda, executive chairman of the Linfen Athletics Association, attributed the growing enthusiasm among foreigners for participating in sporting events in China to improvements in event services, efforts by local governments to integrate sports, culture and tourism, and increasingly convenient arrangements for foreign visitors to China.

Istanbul air pollution rises: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
08:28:00 UTC
17:28:00 KST

Air pollution in Istanbul rose by 3 percent this September compared to the same period last year, driven by industrial activity, transportation, and residential heating, according to a report from Istanbul Technical University (İTU).
The study noted that the Kağıthane 1 and Sultangazi 2 monitoring stations were among the locations with the highest pollution levels.
Prominent meteorologist Professor Dr. Orhan Şen stated that while air pollution in Istanbul is currently at a moderate level, meteorological conditions can significantly amplify the impact of pollutants. Explaining that the temperature inversion associated with high pressure can trap pollutants near the ground, Şen said, “Vehicle-related nitrogen dioxide emissions and ground dust in Istanbul are trapped in the lower atmosphere due to the low-level inversion layer, thereby increasing air pollution.”
Şen emphasized that urban sprawl increases air pollution, saying, “The high-rise architecture in Istanbul’s Levent, Maslak, and Ayazağa districts blocks the north winds. Unable to find a wind corridor due to urban sprawl, these winds collide with skyscrapers, forcing air pollution down toward ground level.”
Şen pointed out that unlike New York’s Manhattan district, where street design creates wind flow, Istanbul lacks the structural layout necessary to create urban air corridors.
Warning individuals with chronic conditions about the heightened air pollution, Şen urged citizens to monitor real-time data from the Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Ministry’s National Air Quality Monitoring Center. He added that pollution levels peak during morning and evening hours, making it vital for those with asthma or bronchitis to wear an N95 or surgical mask outdoors.

U.S. Navy begins upgrading 22-year-old destroyer with new radar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
08:11:17 UTC
17:11:17 KST

- USS Pinckney (DDG 91) began a depot modernization period at General Dynamics NASSCO to become the first U.S. Navy ship with the SPY-6(V)4 radar.
- The $149.6 million availability, part of DDG MOD 2.0, also adds new high-capacity air conditioning plants and runs through September 2028.
The U.S. Navy destroyer USS Pinckney (DDG 91) has entered General Dynamics NASSCO’s shipyard in San Diego for a second depot modernization period that will make it the first warship to receive the Raytheon AN/SPY-6(V)4 radar, the Navy’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Maritime said.
The availability will also make Pinckney the first ship fitted with the Navy’s new High Efficiency Super-Capacity air conditioning plants, which are needed to handle the heavier electrical and cooling demands of the upgraded combat systems. The work is part of Destroyer Modernization 2.0, or DDG MOD 2.0, the Navy’s program to upgrade its older Flight IIA Arleigh Burke-class destroyers with a new radar, electronic warfare suite and combat system software.
“The collective effort by all stakeholders has finally brought us to the point of execution. Upon Depot Modernization Period completion, USS Pinckney will rejoin the Fleet equipped with the most comprehensive multi-spectral integrated sensor suite designed to maintain maritime superiority for decades to come,” said Capt. Tim Moore, program manager for DDG MOD 2.0.
The SPY-6(V)4 replaces the ship’s legacy AN/SPY-1D(V) radar. It uses four fixed array faces, each with 24 radar modular assemblies, for 360-degree coverage, and is a scaled-down version of the SPY-6(V)1 radar built into the Navy’s new Flight III destroyers, which use 37 assemblies per face. The radar will be fully integrated with Aegis Combat System Baseline 10 and is designed to detect and track ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, aircraft and surface threats at longer ranges than the older system.
The Navy is splitting the upgrade into two phases so that shipyards and contractors can learn from each installation. Pinckney completed the first phase in 2024, becoming the first warship to receive the AN/SLQ-32(V)7 Surface Electronic Warfare Improvement Program Block 3 suite, along with structural sponson modifications to carry the new equipment. It then deployed to the Pacific and Middle East, returning to San Diego in August after nine months at sea. Janes has reported that Pinckney became the first DDG MOD 2.0 ship to see combat, during operations against Iran in March.
The Navy awarded NASSCO $149.6 million on Sept. 5 for the current depot period, which is scheduled to run through September 2028. Raytheon installed the first SPY-6(V)4 array at the Navy’s land-based test site at Wallops Island, Virginia, in August, so engineers can integrate the radar with its power system before it goes aboard the ship and reduce testing time in the shipyard.
Pinckney leads a four-ship group of Flight IIA destroyers chosen to pioneer the DDG MOD 2.0 upgrades, along with USS Chung-Hoon (DDG 93), USS James E. Williams (DDG 95) and USS Halsey (DDG 97). Commissioned in 2004 and built by Ingalls Shipbuilding, the San Diego-based destroyer is named for William Pinckney, a Navy Cross recipient who rescued a fellow sailor aboard the aircraft carrier USS Enterprise during the Battle of Santa Cruz in World War II.

Edirne unveils major library and restored Ottoman-era lodge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
08:10:00 UTC
17:10:00 KST

The northwestern province of Edirne, which served as the Ottoman Empire’s capital for 92 years, has gained a new center for knowledge and learning with the opening of a five-story public library offering 8,812 square meters of indoor space and capacity for more than 1,000 people at a time.
Speaking at the opening ceremony of the Edirne Provincial Public Library, Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said he was pleased to bring a new library to a city entrusted to the present by its ancestors.
Ersoy said the library would enrich the city not only through its books and information resources but also through the voices of children, the energy of young people and the curiosity of readers.
Ersoy said the ministry continues to modernize libraries in line with society’s changing needs. Edirne currently has 10 public libraries affiliated with the ministry: one provincial library, eight district libraries and one neighborhood library.
Built on a 3,530-square-meter plot owned by the ministry, the new library has a total indoor area of 8,812 square meters and can accommodate 160,000 books. Construction and furnishing work has been completed.
The facility offers a study environment for students, research areas for young people and spaces where residents can read and pursue personal development. Its seating capacity allows more than 1,000 people to use the library simultaneously.
Designed to serve people of all ages, the library includes dedicated areas for babies and children, a 24-hour study hall, adult reading spaces and group study rooms.
Workshops, a conference hall, a mini cinema and accessible facilities for people with disabilities have also been incorporated into the building.
“This is not merely a place where books are kept; it will be a meeting point where people of all ages can learn, create and prepare for the future,” Ersoy said.
He added that the new generation of public libraries offers a broad range of services, from information and digital resources to educational programs, workshops and cultural and arts events.
The Edirne Provincial Public Library also houses a service area for the Selimiye Manuscript Library, which operates under the Türkiye Manuscripts Institution.
Its existing collection includes more than 3,500 manuscripts and over 9,000 rare printed works, according to Ersoy.
The new facility features six exhibition units and a storage area with a capacity of 30,000 works. Researchers will be able to consult facsimile and translated editions, access manuscript databases and obtain high-resolution digital copies.
The space will also host academic meetings, manuscript seminars, thematic workshops, panels and introductory programs for students, supporting scholarly research and the sharing of cultural heritage.
Addressing children and young people, Ersoy encouraged them to use the library to study, read, research, discover, create and dream.
HH Nearly 500-year-old Muradiye Mevlevi Lodge restored
Following the library opening, Ersoy attended the inauguration of the Muradiye Mevlevi Lodge, a historic structure with a history of nearly five centuries that was demolished in 1935.
The lodge was restored on its original site following archaeological research excavations carried out in 2024 and has now reopened as a cultural and arts center, Ersoy said.
The center comprises a library, workshops for calligraphy, Edirnekâri decorative arts, illumination and marbling, as well as a gathering space known as the Assembly of Conversation and Wisdom and a semahane, a hall used for Mevlevi whirling ceremonies.
Ersoy said the restored complex would contribute to Edirne’s cultural and artistic life.

- DARPA tested four autonomous unmanned ground vehicles at Fort Knox on Oct. 15, linking satellite imagery to a simulated strike with human approval required.
- U.S. European Command requested the demonstration, and DARPA plans a soldier-feedback test in December.
DARPA, a central research and development organization within the United States Department of War, put four autonomous unmanned ground vehicles through their first end-to-end test at Fort Knox, Kentucky, on Oct. 15, sending them as a team from a satellite-imagery tip all the way to a simulated strike on an enemy position, with a human operator approving every engagement.
About two dozen visitors from military and government organizations watched the demonstration at the post’s St. Vith Range. The vehicles run autonomy software developed under DARPA’s Robotic Autonomy in Complex Environments with Resiliency program, known as RACER, which wrapped up its main development work earlier this year.
“We can drop a ten-digit grid on a traversable mobility corridor that the ground vehicles use with their onboard sensors to understand the terrain and then drive to it comparable to a human,” said Dr. Jason Gregory, technical advisor at DARPA.
The scenario began with an operator receiving a tip about a simulated threat from satellite imagery and tasking the team. The lead vehicle, carrying a closed box that housed a drone, drove down a road searching for targets while the other three waited. Halfway up a hill it spotted a possible target and stopped to wait for a command. Two more vehicles moved up the road to provide cover, a simulated rocket struck the target on an adjacent hill about 275 m (300 yards) away, and the fourth vehicle advanced as the lead vehicle crested the hill.
In a real operation, the drone in the box could be launched to take a closer look at a target or, armed with a munition, attack it from the air.
The vehicles search for targets on their own, but they do not decide what to do once they find one. Each detection is sent to an operator as an image of what the vehicle has seen, and nothing is engaged without human approval.
“It’s controlled engagement. All the mobility, all the movement, all the detections, all of that is autonomous. But they don’t pull the trigger until a human says pull the trigger,” said Gregory.
Gregory said the test was the first time the team had connected the whole chain, from satellite imagery down to vehicles on the tactical ground, after earlier component and integration testing at the performers’ own sites. DARPA is now adding kinetic and non-kinetic payloads to the vehicles and working on human-in-the-loop detection of both close and deep targets.
The demonstration was organized at the request of U.S. European Command, which asked DARPA how robotic assets could be sent beyond the forward line of troops to give soldiers early warning of enemy forces. Stakeholders recommended Fort Knox as terrain representative of the European theater.
RACER launched in 2021 to develop software that lets off-road military vehicles drive themselves at speeds comparable to a human driver. DARPA said in January that the program had completed its final tests and was ready to transition to military use after eight major field experiments. In October 2025, the U.S. Army’s 36th Engineer Brigade paired a RACER Heavy Platform with an M58 mine-clearing line charge in a breaching demonstration at Fort Hood, Texas, and in November 2025 soldiers from the 11th Armored Cavalry Regiment used RACER Fleet Vehicles, based on the Polaris RZR, for autonomous long-range reconnaissance at the National Training Center.
“We’ve completed about a five-year program on software development for autonomous mobility to go highspeed off-road in complex environments,” said Gregory. “So, now we can take a vehicle that has a sensor suite and drive-by-wire and equip it with autonomy software so it can be tasked by a Soldier as opposed to manually driven.”
DARPA plans the next test for December, when it will bring in a group of soldiers to suggest how the vehicles should be employed.

From luxury hotels to gastronomic tourism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
08:03:56 UTC
17:03:56 KST

AA Photo
North Cyprus is one of the Mediterranean’s most distinctive destinations, yet much of its tourism potential remains untapped. Girne’s (Kyrenia) historic harbour, the coastline where the Girne Mountains meet the sea, its cultural heritage and culinary traditions all offer the ingredients for a far stronger story in international luxury travel.
But natural beauty alone does not establish a destination in the luxury market. It takes investment, high standards of service and, above all, a sustainable tourism culture.
From Zephyros Bay to Today
The tourism story of Zephyros Bay, in Girne’s Alsancak area, dates back to the 1970s. The property now known as Merit Crystal Cove was then a hotel with around 120 beds. Damaged during the conflict in 1974, the building served other purposes in the following years before returning to tourism.
It reopened in 2001 following investment by Net Holding, marking an important turning point in North Cyprus’ hospitality industry. Merit Royal, Royal Premium and Royal Diamond followed, creating a collection of luxury hotels along the same coastline, each catering to different expectations.
HH Reha Arar’s contribution to Cyprus
One name deserves particular attention in Merit’s story: Reha Arar.
A longstanding figure in the group’s management, Arar’s approach to hospitality goes well beyond running hotels. He represents a philosophy that recognises that adding more rooms is not enough to develop a destination. Its cultural identity must also become part of the visitor experience.
His particular interest in gastronomy and his work in the field have played an important role in bringing North Cyprus’ local cuisine back into focus.
Today, gastronomy is no longer simply another service offered by a hotel. It has become a reason to travel in its own right. People increasingly travel not just to stay in a fine hotel, but to discover a destination through its cuisine, local producers and food culture. Cyprus has a remarkably rich heritage to draw on.
HH Could Cypriot cuisine tell a new tourism story?
Halloumi, şeftali kebabı, molohiya, kolokas, pirohu and kleftiko are more than local dishes. They reflect the different cultures that have shaped the island over centuries.
From the tasting menu prepared by Executive Chef Vural Bayar at Zephyros Restaurant in Merit Crystal Cove to the various dining concepts at Merit Park, the programme demonstrates how traditional Cypriot cuisine can be presented through a contemporary gastronomic approach without losing its character.
For me, the real opportunity is not simply to serve local dishes to hotel guests, but to make this cuisine part of Northern Cyprus’s international tourism identity. After all, the Mediterranean has no shortage of beautiful bays, five-star hotels or luxury resorts. Yet not every destination can offer the same depth of culinary heritage.
HH Girne’s (Kyrenia) future is about more than new hotels
Girne has a significant opportunity ahead. But building more hotels, adding rooms or making larger investments will not be enough on their own. Authenticity, cultural experiences, gastronomy and personalised service are becoming increasingly important in international luxury tourism.
Of course, North Cyprus still faces structural challenges, including international access, direct flights and restrictions linked to its political status. These remain obstacles to tourism growth. Yet much can already be achieved by offering existing visitors more meaningful experiences, strengthening the island’s culinary appeal and extending tourism beyond the summer season.
Because a destination’s future is shaped not only by the hotels it builds, but by the culture it brings to life. Perhaps Girne’s next chapter is not about another five-star hotel, but about becoming a distinctive Mediterranean destination that travellers from around the world will want to experience.

Türkiye’s active R&D centers exceed 1,300 amid innovation drive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
08:02:23 UTC
17:02:23 KST

AA Photo
Türkiye’s innovation ecosystem grew significantly over the years, driven by state support, with the number of active research and development (R&D) centers reaching 1,365 and design centers totaling 348 by the end of September.
Industry and Technology Ministry data showed that R&D hubs provide employment to nearly 94,000 workers nationwide, made up of a highly educated workforce that includes nearly 57,700 employees with bachelor’s degrees, over 18,500 with master’s, and over 2,100 with a doctorate or higher.
R&D workforce has completed more than 80,400 projects to date, with nearly 16,000 still underway.
The robust innovation hubs have generated almost 49,000 patents so far, over 17,500 of which have been registered, while some 31,300 await examination results.
Türkiye’s R&D network spans the country and many sectors, from energy, agriculture, and healthcare to transportation, logistics and aviation.
The machinery and equipment manufacturing sector led with 160 centers, followed by the auto supply industry with 136 and the software sector with 128, the data showed.
The main drivers of R&D innovation were the computer and communications technology sector with 86 centers, followed by chemicals with 82. The textiles and electrical sectors each accounted for 77 facilities, while food and defense (excluding weapons and ammunition) followed with 65 each and general manufacturing with 43.
While R&D facilities are spread nationwide, Istanbul has the highest concentration with 428 centers. Ankara follows with 168, Kocaeli with 137, Bursa with 134, İzmir with 105, Tekirdağ with 54, Manisa with 34, Konya with 26, Sakarya with 25 and Antalya with 21.

North Korea's Kim Jong Un touts ties, opens bridge with China on first trip in a year
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited China on Saturday, inaugurating a new bridge that connects the two countries and vowing to expand cooperation with his powerful neighbor.
Kim's visit to China, the first in a year, is his latest move in an increasingly assertive foreign policy as he seeks to align Pyongyang with Beijing and Moscow in a united front against the United States under what he portrays as a "new Cold War."
Kim arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong Saturday after crossing the newly opened bridge, according to South Korea's Unification Ministry and China's official Xinhua News Agency.
In Dandong, Kim visited a memorial marking China's support of North Korea during the 1950-53 Korean War and met with Wang Huning, a member of the Standing Committee of China's Communist Party.
At the memorial, Kim said that the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) will "firmly carry forward the invincible DPRK-China friendship forged at the cost of blood all the time," according to the North's official Korean Central News Agency.
During their meeting, Kim reaffirmed a resolve to develop bilateral cooperation, while Wang conveyed Chinese President Xi Jinping's greetings and said Kim's visit to the memorial was "of great significance" in carrying forward the friendship between the two countries, KCNA said.
The two toured a car factory as well, before Wang accompanied Kim to the bridge to send him off, according to KCNA and Xinhua.
While returning home via the bridge, Kim said "the bridge would undoubtedly and correctly fulfill its historic mission of linking the two countries and firmly joining the minds of the peoples of the two countries," KCNA reported.
Kim has recently taken steps to bolster ties with China, the North's traditional main ally and economic lifeline, after years of prioritizing ties with Russia. China, for its part, has sought to restore its unique influence over North Korea.
North Korea has sent thousands of troops and conventional weapons to support Russian President Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine, possibly in exchange for military and economic assistance.
Kim last visited Beijing in September 2025, when he met with Xi and watched a military parade alongside Putin and other foreign leaders.

Russia launches new stealth corvette Grozny
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
07:54:40 UTC
16:54:40 KST

- Russia’s Amur Shipbuilding Plant launched the Project 20380 corvette Grozny for the Pacific Fleet on Oct. 23 in Komsomolsk-on-Amur.
- It is the fifth ship of the class built at the plant, laid down in August 2021, with commissioning expected within the next few years.
Russia’s Amur Shipbuilding Plant has launched the multipurpose corvette Grozny, the fifth Project 20380 warship it has built for the Russian Navy’s Pacific Fleet, the fleet’s press service said. The ceremony took place on Oct. 23 in Komsomolsk-on-Amur, in Russia’s Far East, more than five years after the ship was laid down on Aug. 23, 2021.
The corvette was rolled out of the construction hall and floated with the help of the Amurets launch pontoon dock, then moved to a pier where workers will finish outfitting it. Russian officials did not give a date for its commissioning, saying only that the ship is expected to join the fleet within the next few years.
“The crew for the corvette Grozny has been formed and began training on October 5, after which it will arrive at the plant to complete the ship together with you and bring it into the fleet in the coming years,” said Adm. Viktor Liina, commander of the Pacific Fleet, RIA Novosti reported.
Project 20380, known in the West as the Steregushchiy class, was designed by the Almaz Central Marine Design Bureau and was the first major surface combatant class developed in Russia after the collapse of the Soviet Union. The ships use stealth shaping to reduce their radar signature. The standard design displaces about 2,200 tonnes fully loaded, is about 104 m (341 feet) long and is armed with a 100 mm gun, Redut surface-to-air missiles, Uran anti-ship missiles, close-in weapon systems and anti-submarine torpedoes, and carries a helicopter. Officials did not detail Grozny’s specific equipment.
Four ships of the class already serve with the Pacific Fleet, all built at the Amur plant: Sovershenny, Gromky, Geroy Rossiyskoy Federatsii Aldar Tsydenzhapov and Rezky. Officers have said the corvettes have proven able to operate as far as the Indian Ocean.
The plant, part of the state-owned United Shipbuilding Corporation, is the Pacific Fleet’s main source of new warships in the Far East. It is currently building 10 ships of various projects, and its order book is fully covered by state defense contracts, according to Khabarovsk Krai Governor Dmitry Demeshin, who said the yard has delivered 99 submarines and more than 100 surface ships to the Pacific Fleet over its history.

China hosts forum to pool wisdom for better future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
07:53:12 UTC
16:53:12 KST

The 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiongan) opened on Friday in Xiongan New Area, north China's Hebei Province. Hosted by the Chinese People's Institute of Foreign Affairs, it is themed "Rebuilding Confidence and Cooperation: Reforming and Improving Global Governance in a Transforming World."
In a message to the forum, Chinese President Xi Jinping noted the world is undergoing accelerated transformation unseen in a century, and the deficits in peace, development, security and governance are growing rather than diminishing.
"I have put forward the GGI to promote the building of a more just and equitable global governance system and a better world," he said.
China stands ready to work with all parties to uphold the vision of global governance featuring extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits, pool strength through confidence-building and tackle challenges through cooperation, Xi said.
He called for efforts to promote the implementation of the GGI to inject more certainty and positive energy into a world of turbulence and transformation, and jointly move toward a community with a shared future for humanity.
"The forum offers a window for the world to follow the developments of China's vision for global governance. One of the key points is to invite all countries to communicate together and build a world together and share the outcomes together," said Selcuk Colakoglu, director of the Ankara-based Turkish Center for Asia-Pacific Studies.
Nearly 400 representatives from strategic, political, academic, business, media, and youth sectors from more than 90 countries and international and regional organizations, including the UN, attended the event.
The GGI emphasizes sovereign equality, international rule of law, multilateralism, a people-centered approach, and practical outcomes, providing an opportunity for all parties to further engage in the global governance system, international cooperation and dialogue, former Nepali President Bidya Devi Bhandari said.
The world today faces severe challenges such as economic inequality, poverty, geopolitical tensions, armed conflicts, climate change, and food security, while rising protectionism and unilateralism further complicate international cooperation. No single country can address these shared challenges alone; they require dialogue, enhanced cooperation, and joint efforts among all countries, Bhandari said.
Former Kyrgyz Prime Minister Djoomart Otorbaev said countries of the Global South support the GGI and want a world of growth, cooperation and progress instead of hegemony or interference.
"Our system is still designed without giving developing countries sufficient weight. So we see the need in the United Nations to make reforms to our governance systems," UN under-secretary-general Guy Ryder said.
It is important to enhance the representation and voice of the Global South in international affairs, advance reform of the international financial system in accordance with the timetable and roadmap agreed by all parties, increase the representation of developing countries in the Security Council, and give full play to the important role of emerging multilateral cooperation mechanisms such as BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi said.
Wang also called for improving governance rules in emerging fields, turning new frontiers such as the deep sea, the polar regions and outer space into areas for international cooperation, and evolving an artificial intelligence (AI) governance structure based on general consensus soon.
China and the United States have both the capability and the responsibility to jointly develop and govern AI well, ensuring that its development remains under human control and benefits the people, Wang said when meeting with co-chair of the Board of Trustees of the Asia Society John L. Thornton and The New York Times columnist Thomas L. Friedman on the sidelines of the forum.
Thornton and Friedman said that the international community is paying close attention to the upcoming APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting hosted by China, and expects that China will take this opportunity to play a unique and positive role in tackling global challenges.
Source: Xinhua

Türkiye remains Europe’s 6th largest car market despite sharp sales decline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
07:51:01 UTC
16:51:01 KST

Türkiye remained Europe’s sixth-largest passenger car market in the January-September period of 2026 despite a sharp contraction in sales, according to data from the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA) and the Automotive Distributors and Mobility Association (ODMD).
Passenger car sales in Türkiye fell 15.45 percent year-on-year to 627,977 units in the first nine months of the year, placing the country behind Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy, France and Spain in Europe’s market rankings.
Türkiye also ranked sixth in Europe for battery electric vehicle sales, with 120,329 units sold during the period. However, unlike most major European markets, both passenger car and electric vehicle sales declined.
The European car market, including the EU, EFTA countries and the United Kingdom, expanded 6.3 percent year-on-year to 10.56 million units in the first nine months of 2026 despite high energy prices and economic uncertainty.
Germany remained Europe’s largest car market, with sales rising 5.3 percent to 2.22 million units. The United Kingdom followed with 1.74 million units, ahead of Italy with 1.27 million, France with 1.23 million and Spain with 912,059 units.
While all of the five largest European markets recorded growth, Türkiye posted the steepest decline among Europe’s 10 largest passenger car markets.
In the battery electric vehicle segment, Türkiye retained its sixth-place ranking, selling 120,329 units between January and September and outperforming markets such as Norway, the Netherlands, Italy and Spain.
Germany led electric vehicle sales with 604,144 units, followed by the United Kingdom with 454,947 and France with 387,342. Belgium ranked ahead of Türkiye with 125,220 units, while Denmark recorded 124,049 units.
However, sales trends diverged sharply from those in other major markets. Battery electric vehicle sales increased 58.1 percent in Germany, 79.1 percent in France and 30.2 percent in the United Kingdom, while Türkiye recorded a 9.1 percent decline.
As a result, Türkiye was the only market among Europe’s top 10 electric vehicle markets to post a contraction in sales.
Europe’s shift toward electrification also accelerated during the period. In EU countries, the market share of battery electric vehicles rose to 22.7 percent from 16.1 percent a year earlier. Hybrid vehicles became the most preferred powertrain with a 36.3 percent share, while plug-in hybrids reached 10.1 percent.
By contrast, the combined market share of gasoline and diesel cars declined to 28.2 percent from 36.9% percent in the same period of the previous year.
Despite remaining Europe’s sixth-largest market for both passenger cars and electric vehicles, Türkiye faces the risk of being excluded from the EU’s proposed “Made in EU” plan.
The initiative, backed by Germany and France, has continued to draw criticism from manufacturers. Most recently, Ola Källenius, chief executive of Mercedes-Benz, warned that local production requirements could increase costs across the automotive industry.
“A modern automobile consists of thousands of parts sourced from different regions of the world,” Källenius said. “You are creating resilience, which is a good thing, but you are also pushing costs higher. It is a matter of balance.”

France sends patrol planes to Black Sea after ship attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
07:47:16 UTC
16:47:16 KST

- A French Navy Atlantique 2 deployed to Constanța and is supporting rescue efforts after drone attacks on merchant ships off Romania and Bulgaria.
- A U.S. Navy P-8A Poseidon from Sigonella was also observed over the Black Sea, as NATO pledged more patrol aircraft for the region.
A French Navy Atlantique 2 maritime patrol aircraft has deployed to Romania and is supporting search and rescue efforts after a wave of drone attacks on merchant ships off the Romanian and Bulgarian coasts, while a U.S. Navy P-8A Poseidon has begun patrolling the Black Sea at Bulgaria’s request.
The Atlantique 2 arrived in Constanța on the evening of Oct. 18, Romanian outlet Curs de Guvernare reported, citing flight-tracking data. France has confirmed that the aircraft, operating under NATO arrangements, has supported rescue efforts near Bulgaria and Romania.
The same evening, the P-8A flew in from Naval Air Station Sigonella in Sicily to the Bulgarian port city of Varna and began circling off the Bulgarian coast. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Oct. 20 that the U.S. aircraft started patrolling after Sofia asked allies for help following the attacks on ships in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, adding that some allies had responded very quickly.
Both aircraft are built to find things at sea. The Atlantique 2 was designed for anti-submarine warfare and has been upgraded to carry out surveillance, detection and electronic intelligence missions using onboard radar and sonar, and it can fly very low over the water to track ships and submarines. The P-8A, based on the Boeing 737, is the U.S. Navy’s main maritime patrol aircraft and is used for surveillance, reconnaissance and anti-submarine warfare.
The deployments follow drone attacks on at least seven merchant vessels in the Black Sea this month in the exclusive economic zones of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria. On Oct. 13, drones struck two cargo ships off Bulgaria, sinking one and leaving 11 sailors missing. Two tankers anchored near the Sulina Canal, which links the Danube to the Black Sea and serves as an export route for Ukraine, were hit days later, and seven crew members went missing when the chemical tanker Wine Trader caught fire on Oct. 15. A NATO military source told Reuters the two tankers were struck by Russian drones.
On Oct. 17, Romanian F-16s shot down two Russian jet-powered Geran drones over the Black Sea that, according to Romanian authorities, were heading to attack merchant ships.
The latest attack came on Oct. 23, when the Comoros-flagged cargo ship Khoryv capsized about 13 nautical miles (24 km) east of Constanța after a drone strike that Romanian President Nicușor Dan blamed on Russia. Of its 13 crew members, 10 Ukrainians and three Azerbaijanis, nine were rescued and one was found dead, while three remained missing. Romania’s naval authority said bad weather and poor visibility prevented a rescue helicopter from flying.
At Romania’s request, NATO’s North Atlantic Council met in Brussels on Oct. 20 to discuss Black Sea defense and deterrence. Afterward, the alliance said it would send additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems and drones to the region. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte had said a week earlier, after meeting Dan and Radev, that the alliance would adjust its deterrence and defense posture in the Black Sea and was ready to help Romania and Bulgaria strengthen counter-drone defenses and maritime monitoring.
“Our armed forces have prepared for an intensification of hybrid interference and will continue to prioritize air defense and maritime security,” said acting Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Țoiu.
French Atlantique 2 aircraft regularly fly over Romanian waters as part of NATO surveillance missions and took part in the alliance’s Neptune Strike exercise in the region in May.

Xi's remarks on upholding authority, role of UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
07:46:07 UTC
16:46:07 KST

On multiple occasions in recent years, Chinese President Xi Jinping has reiterated China's support for the international system with the United Nations at its core, and called for upholding the authority of the United Nations, practicing true multilateralism, and observing the purposes and principles of the UN Charter.
The following are some highlights of his remarks.
Sept. 13, 2026
At the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India, Xi said all countries, regardless of their size, strength or wealth, are equal members of the international community.
"Global South countries should hold high the banner of multilateralism, uphold the authority and role of the United Nations, support multilateral institutions in advancing reform and increasing efficiency, and ensure the equal participation of all countries in international affairs," he said.
July 17, 2026
At the opening ceremony of the 2026 World AI Conference and High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance held in Shanghai, Xi said that AI is an invaluable asset that encapsulates humanity's collective wisdom.
"We should practice true multilateralism and recognize the important role of the United Nations," he said. "We should enhance alignment and coordination on AI development strategies, governance rules and technical standards, so as to form a consensus-based global governance framework at an early date to make this frontier technology better benefit humanity."
Sept. 1, 2025
At the "Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Plus" Meeting in north China's port city of Tianjin, Xi said the purposes and principles of the UN Charter and other universally recognized basic norms of international relations must be observed comprehensively, fully and in their entirety.
"We should firmly safeguard the status and authority of the United Nations, and ensure its irreplaceable, key role in global governance," he said.
Aug. 30, 2025
When meeting with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on the sidelines of the SCO Summit 2025, Xi said that China will always be a trustworthy partner of the United Nations.

07:44:20 UTC
16:44:20 KST

Turkish scholars, students and political figures say the military odyssey offers insights into China's revolutionary history and development path, while calling for deeper cultural and people-to-people exchanges between the two countries.
The Red Army, led by the Communist Party of China (CPC), was mainly made up of soldiers from peasants' and workers' families during the Chinese revolution. Between 1934 and 1936, the army trekked roughly 12,500 kilometers to break through the encirclement of the Kuomintang forces, a journey later known as the Long March.
Murat Tamer, a Turkish scholar specializing in cultural exchanges between China and Türkiye, said the Long March deserved greater recognition in Türkiye. More than a historic march, it demonstrated the CPC's determination, organizational strength and strategic thinking in the face of formidable challenges, he said.
The great spirit of the Long March, Tamer added, could help Turkish people better understand how China overcame difficulties and forged its own path of development.
For Turkish students in China, the Long March also offers lessons that resonate with their own experiences.
Berfin Adiyaman, a master's student in applied economics at Northwestern Polytechnical University, said learning about the Long March had deepened her understanding of the importance of perseverance.
While studying in China, she has faced challenges including language barriers and homesickness. Her involvement in exchanges between Chinese and Turkish businesses, as well as her work at a logistics company in Xi'an, northwest China, enabled her to gain a closer look at Chinese society, she said.
"Whether it is a country or an individual, courage and perseverance are essential in the face of adversity," Adiyaman said, adding that she hoped to contribute to China-Türkiye economic cooperation and youth exchanges.
Yuksel Mansur Kilinc, a member of the Türkiye-China Interparliamentary Friendship Group of the Grand National Assembly of Türkiye, said China's development path has attracted attention in Türkiye, particularly its focus on common prosperity, harmony between humanity and nature, and the coordinated development of material and spiritual civilization.
Kilinc said China and Türkiye have new opportunities to deepen bilateral ties. Events marking the 55th anniversary of diplomatic relations have been held across Türkiye this year, reflecting interest in expanding exchanges between the two countries.
Describing cultural exchanges as an important foundation for bilateral relations, he called for closer cooperation in the media and cultural sectors alongside economic and technological collaboration, saying such efforts could promote mutual understanding and support the long-term development of China-Türkiye relations.

Philadelphia startup’s unmanned vehicle makes U.S. Army shortlist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
07:37:53 UTC
16:37:53 KST

- Raptor Defense Company’s PIT VIPER advanced to Phase II of the U.S. Army’s GroundBreaker 1 unmanned ground vehicle demonstration at Camp Grafton, North Dakota.
- The company was also named one of nine finalists in the U.S. Army xTech G-TEAD USARPAC autonomous sustainment competition.
Philadelphia-based Raptor Defense Company is advancing in two U.S. Army programs with PIT VIPER, a small modular wheeled unmanned ground vehicle the company calls a “Personal Combat Vehicle” and designs to be fielded at the level of the individual soldier, the company announced.
Raptor was selected for Phase II of GroundBreaker 1, a joint unmanned ground vehicle demonstration, after a government technical evaluation of its Phase I solution brief. The company said the Army’s selection notice found its proposed solution showed strong potential to meet critical mission requirements.
The company was also named one of nine finalists in the G-TEAD USARPAC ACE 27-01: Autonomous Sustainment competition, run through the Army’s xTech program, in the category of autonomous ground delivery systems for logistics and resupply. Raptor said it will demonstrate PIT VIPER on Oahu, Hawaii, showing how the vehicle can carry out autonomous resupply, reduce risk to personnel and sustain dispersed forces across contested terrain in the Indo-Pacific.
“Being selected to advance in both GroundBreaker 1 and Army xTech is a major milestone for Raptor and the PIT VIPER program,” said Andrew DeLuca, founder and CEO of Raptor Defense Company. “More importantly, these programs give us the opportunity to put the platform directly in front of Soldiers, receive real operational feedback, and continue developing the system around the needs of the warfighter.”
Raptor developed PIT VIPER as an alternative to traditional unmanned ground vehicles, which tend to be larger, more expensive and built around a narrow set of missions. The company instead set out to build a smaller, rugged vehicle cheap enough to issue widely and flexible enough to take on many jobs. Its modular design accepts mission-specific payloads for resupply, casualty evacuation, reconnaissance, breaching and communications.
“We built PIT VIPER to be affordable enough to deploy at scale, rugged enough to operate across demanding terrain, and adaptable enough to support virtually any mission,” said DeLuca. “Our vision is to make robotic capability an everyday asset for the warfighter rather than a specialized capability available only when the mission or budget allows.”
The company began as a dorm-room startup building robotic vehicles to detect landmines. It later worked with Ukrainian units during the war, gaining direct experience of how ground robots hold up in active combat, and gathered feedback from the U.S. Army before shifting its focus to the personal combat vehicle concept. Ben Franklin Technology Partners of Southeastern Pennsylvania was its first institutional investor.
GroundBreaker 1 is a Department of War event organized through the Drone OTA Consortium, which issued its call for unmanned ground vehicles on Aug. 21. Platforms at Camp Grafton were to be operated in realistic field conditions, including by service members who give feedback on usability and mission effectiveness. Other companies selected for Phase II include BLADE, with its Hunter WOLF vehicle, and GaardTech.
A successful Phase II evaluation may lead to an invitation to Phase III, where Raptor could submit a full proposal for a prototype Other Transaction Authority award, a fast-track contracting route the Pentagon uses to buy prototypes from nontraditional suppliers. The xTech competition offers a similar path to an Other Transaction Authority opportunity for selected participants.

China plays important role in advancing traditional medicine globally, WHO official says
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:36:14 CST
16:36:14 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- China has an important role to play in advancing traditional medicine globally, drawing on its experience in integrating traditional medicine into the broader health system, said Saia Ma'u Piukala, the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Director for the Western Pacific.
In an interview with Xinhua on the occasion of the World Conference on Traditional Medicine 2026, Piukala said traditional, complementary and integrative medicine is an important and growing part of global health care, contributing to people's health and well-being, people-centered care and universal health coverage.
When appropriately integrated into health systems, traditional medicine can improve health outcomes by expanding access to services, especially in primary health care. Yet, such integration must be grounded in the latest scientific evidence and ensure safety and effectiveness, he said. Even long-used practices require rigorous validation of their efficacy and safety, he added.
The WHO's Western Pacific regional framework for traditional and complementary medicine sets out four strategic actions: promoting the role of traditional and complementary medicine in national policies; strengthening context-specific mechanisms to ensure the safety, quality and effectiveness of services; improving service coverage and equitable access to safe and effective care; and supporting the documentation, research and innovation needed to inform policy and practice.
The World Conference on Traditional Medicine 2026 was held in Beijing on Oct. 17 and 18.
The conference provided a valuable opportunity to build on countries' knowledge and experience, including China's longstanding contributions, and strengthen international cooperation, Piukala said.
He expressed hope that the conference would advance scientific research, promote the harmonization of international standards and strengthen regulatory cooperation, while supporting the appropriate integration of traditional medicine into health systems based on scientific evidence, with safeguards for safety and effectiveness and in accordance with national regulatory arrangements and country contexts.
China's experience offers valuable lessons as countries respond to population aging, the growing burden of noncommunicable diseases and rising demand for people-centered, integrated health services, Piukala said.
China has established a well-developed traditional medicine system supported by a strong policy framework and sustained investment in education and training, research, service delivery and regulatory capacity, said Piukala.
China's experience in integrating traditional medicine into primary health care and other health services, while applying risk-based regulation to products and practitioners, is particularly relevant to other countries in the Western Pacific region, he noted.
China's efforts to strengthen professional training, quality assurance and scientific research also offer valuable lessons for improving the safety and quality of traditional medicine and helping people make informed choices about its use. Other countries can draw on these experiences while adapting them to their own health systems and populations' needs, guided by scientific evidence and appropriate regulation, Piukala said.
Turning to technological innovation, Piukala said modern technologies, including artificial intelligence, can further support the development of traditional medicine by helping researchers analyze complex biological data, investigate potential mechanisms of action, identify promising compounds, develop new research approaches and evaluate the safety and effectiveness of traditional medicine products and practices.
Such innovation must be guided by scientific rigor, ethics and responsible data governance, while respecting traditional knowledge and associated rights, he stressed.
Piukala also emphasized the importance of sustained international cooperation. Multilateral collaboration enables countries to learn from one another and make progress together, he said, calling for practical partnerships, stronger networks and greater solidarity to build on the momentum of the conference.
"Ultimately, international cooperation on traditional medicine will maintain its momentum and deliver tangible benefits to people when we turn our shared commitments into sustained, collective action," he said. ■

The leader of the pro-Russian far-right Vazrazhdane party, Kostadin Kostadinov, is in third place on 10-13 percent.
Polling stations opened at 7:00 am local time (0500 GMT) and close at 8:00 pm.
Iotova took over this year as president of Bulgaria, a European Union and NATO member state, when Rumen Radev stepped down to run in parliamentary elections, eventually becoming prime minister.
If successful in a runoff set for November 1, she would become the first woman ever elected president in the country of 6.4 million people.
A win for Iotova would be a boost for Radev, who has also called for dialogue with Moscow.
A former journalist and member of the European Parliament, Iotova was elected vice-president alongside Radev in 2016 and 2021.
'President of peace'
Appealing to patriotic sentiment, she launched her campaign by the Golden Church in Veliki Preslav, the former capital of the First Bulgarian Empire.
Calling for national unity and action against poverty in the EU's poorest member state, she has also made peace in Ukraine a central theme of her campaign, promising to be a "president of peace".
Without questioning Bulgaria's membership of the EU or NATO, she opposes military aid to Ukraine and advocates negotiations.
"We do not need a Coalition of the Willing for Ukraine, but a Coalition for Peace in Ukraine," she said at a rally in Varna, arguing that military support would prolong Russia's invasion.
At another rally for Iotova in the southern town of Dimitrovgrad, retired teacher Irina Ilieva, 85, said the Ukraine war was her main concern.
"Whoever is elected... will have to do everything possible to ensure that the problems are resolved peacefully," she said.
Four vessels were struck off Bulgaria's coast this month, leaving 21 people missing, in suspected spillover from the Russia-Ukraine war.
While Radev said the attacks appeared to serve Russian interests and summoned the Russian ambassador, his government insists there is so far no evidence directly linking Moscow to them.
An American P-8 Poseidon reconnaissance plane has started to patrol the Black Sea following Sofia's call for help after the attacks.

Ukraine accuses Musk of false claims over Starlink
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
07:26:37 UTC
16:26:37 KST

- Ukraine rejected Elon Musk’s claim that its military used civilian Starlink for offensive drone strikes in breach of SpaceX’s terms of service.
- Presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said Starlink terminals in Ukraine have been capped at 70-90 km/h since February 2026 and do not work over Russia.
Ukraine has rejected Elon Musk’s claim that its military broke Starlink’s terms of service by using the civilian satellite network for offensive drone strikes, with a presidential adviser saying that restrictions SpaceX placed on the service in February make such use physically impossible.
Musk made the accusation on X on Oct. 24, the same day Ukraine said its satellite access had been restored after more than a week of speed restrictions that disrupted front-line operations.
“Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be,” wrote SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week.”
In the same post, Musk said Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade version of the network, “is controlled by the US government,” and that Starlink remains critical to Ukraine’s defense because it is “the only system that cannot be jammed or blown up, at least for now.” He wrote that Ukraine’s front line “would collapse immediately” if Starlink were turned off, said SpaceX has done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth, and closed by telling people he called warmongers, “May you burn in hell.”
Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky on defense technology, responded that Musk’s claim ignores how Starlink actually works in Ukraine. Since February 2026, he said, every Starlink terminal over Ukrainian territory, including occupied areas, has been capped at movement speeds of 70 to 90 km/h (43 to 56 mph), and Starlink does not work over Russia at all.
“It is very strange that Elon Musk does not know about the restrictions on Starlink’s operation in Ukraine,” said Beskrestnov. “Thus, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and middle strikes.”
A terminal capped at road speeds cannot stay connected aboard an attack drone, and the long-range strikes Musk referred to take place over Russian territory, where the service is switched off.
Serhii Sternenko, who worked on the issue at Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense as an adviser to Mykhailo Fedorov, said the system Ukraine built in February left no room for the misuse Musk described. Stationary terminals could be registered by both military personnel and civilians, but any terminal used on the move had to be placed on a special list and connected to Starshield.
“In other words, using civilian Starlink for drone missions was technically impossible. All drone missions that required satellite communication could only be carried out using Starshield,” wrote Sternenko.
“We are very grateful to the United States and SpaceX for access to critically important satellite communications. Ukraine did not violate the terms of use,” wrote Sternenko.
Musk’s Oct. 24 post differs from what he said 10 days earlier. On Oct. 14, as speed limits disrupted Ukrainian drone operations, Mykhailo Fedorov wrote on X that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h (99 mph) was being restored and that removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely had become critical for Ukraine’s defense. Musk replied the same day that the limits were not SpaceX’s decision.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” wrote Musk on Oct. 14. “Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
President Donald Trump has said he did not order the restrictions. CBS News and The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this week that Musk was behind the slowdown, and his Oct. 24 post was the first time he said SpaceX had closed what he called a loophole.
Ukrainian commanders said the restrictions cost them drones and disrupted missions. Starshield has become the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and battlefield communications, including the interceptor drones used against Russian attack drones. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said on Oct. 24 that full use had been restored, with its monitoring systems recording stable connections on objects moving faster than 400 km/h (250 mph).

Collapse and outbreak of civil war waiting for Israeli regime
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
07:22:38 UTC
16:22:38 KST

The continuation of the consequences of the Gaza war, military confrontation with Iran, insecurity on the northern front, disputes over the performance of Benjamin Netanyahu's cabinet, and the increase in military costs have raised serious questions about Zionist regime's ability to simultaneously manage internal and external crises.
The Daily Telegraph newspaper, also referring to the social and political fissures in occupied Palestine, has raised the possibility of intensified internal instability.
Political Fissure; A Crisis Beyond the Dispute Over Netanyahu
One of Israel's most important challenges is the deep disagreements among political and social currents over the nature of governance, security policies, and the manner of running the occupied territories. The dispute between religious and secular parties, the controversy over judicial reforms, the issue of military service for Orthodox Jews, and criticisms of the cabinet's performance regarding the attack of October 7, 2023, are among the factors that have made political cohesion difficult.
According to a report by the Israeli Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) in June 2026, only 25 percent of respondents had high trust in the cabinet; in contrast, 73 percent rated their level of trust as low. Also, high trust in Benjamin Netanyahu was reported at 31 percent and low trust in him at 67 percent. These figures indicate a considerable gap between the cabinet and parts of Israeli society; although they alone cannot be considered a definitive sign of political collapse.
Under such circumstances, the election result and the manner of forming parliamentary coalitions can affect the intensity of disputes. Netanyahu's competition with opponents, including the political current associated with Gadi Eisenkot, is not merely a competition over seats of power; rather, it also includes disagreement over political accountability, the future of the governance structure, and security priorities.
The Costs of War; Pressure on Israel's Economy
The economic consequences of the war are another important axis of this crisis. According to the annual report of the Bank of Israel, the financial cost of the war that began in October 2023 has been estimated at about 350 billion shekels for the years 2023 to 2026; a figure that does not include the decisions and costs related to military operations against Iran from late February 2026.
Also, Israel's public debt-to-GDP ratio rose from about 60.5 percent at the beginning of 2023 to 68.5 percent at the end of 2025. The Bank of Israel has identified military costs, civilian expenditures related to the war, and their financing through debt as important factors of pressure on the regime's financial situation.
These figures show that even if economic growth is maintained, the continuation of conflicts can restrict the regime's financial resources and increase the opportunity cost of investment in construction, education, and social sectors. However, Israel's economy still has capacities for adaptation, and one cannot speak of economic collapse merely on the basis of rising debt.
The Gaza War and the Northern Front; The Issue of Realizing Strategic Objectives
One of the fundamental questions about Israel's military performance is the possible gap between operational achievements and the realization of the political objectives of the war. Extensive military attacks and the destruction of Gaza's infrastructure have imposed a heavy human cost on the Palestinians; but assessing the strategic success of such operations is not possible merely by the extent of destruction or the number of attacks.
The continuation of the security issue, the future of Gaza's administration, and the dispute over the fate of prisoners and captives are among the issues that are important in evaluating the performance of the Israeli cabinet. The International Institute for Strategic Studies, in an analysis in August 2025, had also referred to the difficulty of the Netanyahu cabinet in converting military achievements into a sustainable political result. At the same time, this institute has also spoken of Israel's military achievements against Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran.
On the northern front as well, the return of residents of evacuated areas and the rebuilding of economic activities have become an important issue. Reports published in October 2026 about Kiryat Shmona indicate continued security concerns, damaged economic activities, and the dissatisfaction of part of the residents. This situation shows that military operations alone do not necessarily lead to the sustainable return of security and normal life.
Confrontation with Iran; A Test of the Cost and Benefit of the Military Strategy
Direct war with Iran has been one of the Zionist regime's most important security challenges in 2026. American and Israeli attacks on Iran from February 28 were accompanied by Iran's retaliatory attacks and the expansion of the scope of war in the region. A report by the US Congressional Research Service in September 2026 shows that this war, in addition to the Israeli regime and Iran, has also affected American military bases, regional infrastructure, and commercial shipping.
According to the same report, the April ceasefire and the June 2026 memorandum of understanding could not lead to a sustainable agreement, and the conflicts resumed afterward. This process indicates the difficulty of converting military pressure into sustainable political and security arrangements.
From a strategic perspective, the main issue for Israel is not only the extent of damage inflicted on the opposing side; rather, the ability to achieve the declared objectives, maintain deterrence, manage reciprocal attacks, and prevent the expansion of war is also important. In contrast, Iran has also faced heavy human, economic, and infrastructural costs; therefore, assessing this confrontation without taking into account the costs of both sides provides an incomplete picture.
Overall, economic pressures, political disputes, the consequences of the Gaza war, insecurity on the northern front, and the costs of confrontation with Iran have placed a set of interconnected challenges before Israel. The simultaneous intensification of these pressures can reduce the Israeli regime's room for maneuver, deepen social fissures, and provide the ground for new political crises.

Chinese Communist Party's fifth plenum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
07:20:00 UTC
16:20:00 KST

AP Photo
President Xi Jinping and other top members of China's ruling Communist Party will meet in Beijing today for a crucial gathering that could hint at the country's next generation of leaders.
The fifth plenary session of the party's Central Committee precedes the five-yearly party congress next year, where Xi will likely secure a fourth term.
Plenums are closed-door gatherings of the party's Central Committee -- the top 300 or so members -- where major national and party decisions are debated.
Today’s meeting is the fifth since this cohort was selected in 2022 and will focus on party governance.
The plenum comes ahead of an expected leadership reshuffle at the 21st Party Congress in autumn 2027, where Xi, 73, is likely to secure another term as leader.
A 2016 plenum enshrined him as the Party's "core", while the 2021 edition elevated Xi's doctrines and adopted a new resolution on party history.
This time, analysts speculate that Xi could bolster his authority by assuming the title "party chairman," a position Mao Zedong held.
The meeting, which concludes on Thursday, will debate and adopt a decision on "full and rigorous party self-governance," with Xi keen to institutionalise discipline measures.
Xi remains frustrated with cadres not implementing his orders, despite a 14-year anti-corruption drive that has snared thousands of officials -- including dozens of Central Committee members.

India’s proposed 11,200-MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project, planned across three districts of Arunachal, is being pitched as a strategic counter to China’s mega dam upstream. But the plan has faced resistance from indigenous tribes, who fear the reservoir could submerge villages and sever their deep-rooted ties with the river.Known as the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet, the Siang enters Arunachal Pradesh near Gelling and flows for 294km before meeting the Dibang and Lohit rivers at Sadiya in Assam to form the Brahmaputra.

Brazil votes in tight runoff between leftist Lula and Bolsonaro Jr
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
07:11:03 UTC
16:11:03 KST

Brazil votes in tight runoff between Lula and Bolsonaro
SAO PAULO/RIO DE JANEIRO, Oct 25 - Brazilians voted on Sunday in a tight runoff vote that could move Latin America's largest nation sharply rightward, bringing it closer to the United States as part of a broader conservative shift across the region.
The runoff pits leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro. Flavio scored a major upset at the start of the month by defying pollsters to lead voting in the first round.
A victory for Bolsonaro, 45, would extend a wave of right-wing victories for Latin American candidates friendly to US President Donald Trump, while a fourth mandate for Lula would be a disappointment in Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security.
WASHINGTON DENIES ACCUSATIONS OF MEDDLING
Reuters on Saturday revealed a campaign within Trump's State Department to help get the Bolsonaros back in power.
Trump has so far declined to endorse a candidate. Asked on Sunday who he hoped would win, Trump declined to say.
"I don’t want to get into that, but we are watching," he told reporters in Washington.
Brazil's election race has been dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of US meddling, which Washington denies. It has also been colored by fallout from Jair Bolsonaro's 2025 conviction for plotting a 2022 coup, with Flavio pledging to free his father if elected.
Trump has called the case a "witch hunt" and imposed a 50% tariff on Brazil in 2025, in a decision explicitly linked to Jair Bolsonaro’s trial. While this was later watered down, Trump unleashed new levies against Brazil this year, citing unfair trade practices.
Lula has cast the Trump administration’s proximity to the Bolsonaro clan as part of an attempt to sway the election, while labeling tariffs and other punitive measures as bullying.
“We can’t just hand Brazil over,” said Elenildes dos Reis, a 60-year-old lawyer in Sao Paulo who voted for Lula and said his victory would be a way of standing up to Trump and what she described as a rising wave of fascism.
“It won’t just be our victory, it will be the world’s,” she said.
On economic issues, despite falling inequality and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over an electorate grappling with high living costs and heavy household debt. Endemic gang violence also weighs on voters’ minds.
Bolsonaro has sought to capitalize on cost-of-living concerns and has promised a heavy-handed approach to fighting crime, pledging maximum-security jails and chemical castration for serious sexual offenses.
“We need change,” said Jose Carlos Jarra, a 61-year-old retiree in Sao Paulo who worked in healthcare and voted for Bolsonaro. He hoped the senator would tackle public security and do more for retirees, calling Brazil’s minimum wage “a disgrace.”
In Rio de Janeiro, 75-year-old retiree Alba Marques said her vote for Bolsonaro was a vote against Lula's Workers' Party, not for Bolsonaro.
"I can’t stand 40 years of a guy saying he’s going to fix Brazil anymore. The same promise," she said.
CANDIDATES ARE NECK AND NECK
Casting his ballot in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday, Bolsonaro urged people to come out to vote "come rain or shine."
Lula voted in Sao Bernardo do Campo, near Sao Paulo, and thanked his supporters. "What the people did for me these past few days is something I can never repay," he told reporters.
Polls show the candidates practically tied going into the runoff.
Historical precedent favors Bolsonaro, however, as no candidate has ever won the presidency after coming second in the first-round vote.
Bolsonaro picked up 47% of ballots cast in the first round, while Lula trailed with 45%.
The senator's first-round win sent Brazil's markets and currency soaring on expectations of pro-business reforms.
His first-round success was mirrored in congressional elections for his Liberal Party and other right-wing politicians, which could pave a legislative path for him, or complicate governance for Lula. REUTERS

Disenchanted Netanyahu supporters are prize of Israel election campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
07:10:43 UTC
16:10:43 KST

Disenchanted Netanyahu supporters are prize of Israel election campaign
DIMONA, Oct 25 - In the remote Negev Desert town of Dimona, long a bastion of Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party, disenchanted voters are going door-to-door campaigning for his top rival, hoping to bring down the veteran prime minister in Israel's election on Tuesday.
The ballot is Israel's first since Hamas' October 7, 2023, surprise attack that shook the country and plunged the region into turmoil, as Israel went to war on the militant group in Gaza and its allies in Lebanon and Iran.
The October 7 security breach saw Likud's popularity plummet. Opinion polls for months have predicted Netanyahu's coalition of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties losing its majority. But his top rival, centrist Gadi Eisenkot, has no clear path to power either, and the race has become tighter as the election nears.
Dimona, where an Iranian missile wounded dozens in March, has become a political battleground.
"We must have change. Bibi has to go," said Yossi Assayag, 74, who says he has supported Likud most his life. "Bibi has brought disaster to Israel."
LIKUD LOYALISTS
Assayag is part of a cohort of town residents trying to convince their community to vote for Eisenkot's party Yashar, which is neck-and-neck with Likud in the polls.
It's a tough task in Dimona, where half the voters in the previous 2022 election cast a ballot for Likud.
"I will never betray Likud," said Ruti Ohana, a pensioner, who says she has voted Likud ever since immigrating to Israel from North Africa more than 60 years ago. She said Netanyahu was a cut above his rivals, and the blame he receives from detractors for October 7 was unfair.
Right-wing Likud long ago formed a core voter base among Jews of Middle Eastern and North African descent, known as Mizrahis, who felt neglected by the European-influenced centre-left Labor Party that dominated Israel for generations.
Labor has since dwindled to a rump as Israeli politics have shifted rightwards, and there are now around half a dozen other parties courting Likud voters, from the centre to the far right. But the link to the party among its past supporters remains strong.
"Most people here vote for Likud just because that's how they were raised," said Oria Asaf, 25, a past Likud voter now backing Yashar. "The change will come when people start to think about their children's future rather than their parents' past."
BATTLE FOR WAVERING LIKUDNIKS
While Netanyahu has a hard core of supporters that can't be won over, the prize is undecided voters who "understand that we are in a state of crisis" and are open to persuasion, said Michal Elmalem Abu, elected as a member of the city council from Likud and now leading Eisenkot's Dimona campaign.
Some 13% of Israeli voters have yet to decide how they will vote, according to data collected by the Viterbi Family Center for Public Opinion and Policy Research at the Israel Democracy Institute.
Of those who voted for Likud in 2022, just 55% now say they will vote for the party again on Tuesday. Fifteen percent will support parties aligned against Netanyahu, including 8% for Yashar. Another 14% will vote for alternative right-wing parties, and 9% are undecided.
It is in places just like Dimona where Eisenkot stands a chance to bite a chunk out of Likud's base, said Amotz Asa-El, a political scientist at the Hartman Institute.
A child of Moroccan immigrants who rose through the ranks to become military chief of staff, Eisenkot, 66, has a personal story of humble origins from the Mizrahi community that "appeals to a big swath of the Israeli electorate, particularly Likud's traditional electorate", said Asa-El.
In an electoral field crowded with ex-soldiers, his peerless security credentials are an asset. The loss of his son, killed in combat in Gaza in December 2023, resonates with voters.
At a town hall during a visit to Dimona in July, residents said they were excited about the prospect of a leader of Mizrahi descent. Others approached him with hugs and tearful condolences for the loss of his son.
But a week later Netanyahu held his own event, demonstrating his powerful appeal in the hardscrabble Negev, where Likud governments have long boasted of bringing development funds.
"Look around you, look at your community, look at what was here then and what is here now, and ask yourselves which governments invested in this monumental effort. And I do this out of immense love," he said.
Lior Katzav, a Likud former mayor of Kiryat Malachi, another small-town stronghold, said party surveys show voters who had abandoned Likud are returning as the election nears.
But even some who are sympathetic to Netanyahu say it may be time for a change. Israel's youngest prime minister when he was first elected 30 years ago, he has since become its longest-serving, now 77, having governed for 18 years over six terms.
"It's time for him to go," said Dimona software engineer David Iskali. "He's done a lot for Israel but it can't go on. I won't give my vote to someone almost 80 years old." REUTERS

The key question is not whether multilateralism can survive, but how it must evolve to meet today's challenges, the prime minister said. ■
