Abuse survivors approve $800 million settlement with Archdiocese of New York
WASHINGTON, Oct 24 - Survivors of clergy sexual abuse have agreed to an $800 million settlement with the Archdiocese of New York, lawyers said on Saturday, to resolve claims brought by approximately 1,300 people.
• The Catholic Archdiocese of New York agreed to the payment in May, one of the largest payouts in a wave of lawsuits over clergy sex abuse in the US.
• Jeff Anderson & Associates, which represents 300 abuse survivors, called it "a powerful moment in the pursuit of justice."
• The settlement is second only to an $880 million deal reached by the Archdiocese of Los Angeles in 2024.
• The Catholic Church has paid billions of dollars in settlements across the US in the past several years, after New York and other states enacted laws that temporarily enabled victims of child sexual abuse to file lawsuits over decades-old crimes.
• In addition to the $800 million settlement, the archdiocese agreed to release documents pertaining to sexual offenders in the Church.
• The settlement also allows survivors to litigate against the Church's insurers for additional payouts, but avoids a bankruptcy by the archdiocese. REUTERS

Bodies of ambushed Salvadoran soldiers found in Haiti, New York Times reports

Bodies of ambushed Salvadoran soldiers found in Haiti, New York Times reports
PORT-AU-PRINCE, Oct 24 - Bodies believed to be those of four Salvadoran soldiers missing since an ambush by armed gangs in Haiti have been found outside the capital, Port-au-Prince, the New York Times reported on Saturday, citing two people close to the security mission.
The newspaper said the remains were recovered on Saturday and were badly burned, meaning autopsies would be needed to confirm their identities. It said the bodies were handed over at the international airport to a Salvadoran military team that had flown into Haiti on Friday.
The international security mission declined to comment. Reuters could not immediately confirm the report.
The four Salvadorans went missing on Sunday after they jumped from a burning armored vehicle that came under attack on the outskirts of Port-au-Prince while they were returning from a market to their base, Salvadoran officials said earlier this week. The ambush was the first major attack on the Gang Suppression Force, a United Nations-authorized multinational mission, since it began operations in Haiti this year.
President Nayib Bukele said on Wednesday that gangs were holding the four men and that El Salvador had launched a military operation to bring them back unharmed. Additional Salvadoran troops were later deployed to support search and security operations.
No group has publicly claimed responsibility for the attack. Local media have linked the ambush to gangs operating in the area, including powerful armed groups Chen Mechan and 400 Mawozo.
A year into its mandate, the GSF has about 2,000 troops on the ground, well below its authorized ceiling of 5,500. An earlier Kenyan-led security effort struggled with chronic shortages of money, equipment and personnel.
Haiti's gangs have expanded sharply since the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moise, taking control of large parts of Port-au-Prince and displacing 1.4 million to 1.5 million people. REUTERS

Before ballot, a message from street

Konstas crunches another ton for NSW, pushing case for Test recall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
22:58:18 UTC
07:58:18 KST

Sam Konstas has continued his run-making campaign to impress Test selectors, with a big one-day century for NSW.
Konstas smashed an unbeaten 149 off 131 in a 78-run One-Day Cup win over the Warriors at the WACA.
It came days after the former Test opener's 71 and 151 not out against Western Australia in the Sheffield Shield.
Sam Konstas has struck his second century in the space of a week to send national selectors yet another reminder he is ready for a Test recall.
Just days after posting scores of 71 and 151 not out in New South Wales' Sheffield Shield draw with Western Australia, Konstas cracked 149 off 131 balls on Saturday to lead his side to a 78-run victory over the Warriors in the One-Day Cup at the WACA Ground.
NSW posted 8-371 on the back of the monster knock from Konstas combined with handy contributions from Josh Philippe (51), Jack Edwards (45) and Lachlan Shaw (44).
Loading Twitter content
In reply, Sam Whiteman plundered 116 from 113 balls to give WA a faint hope of chasing down the mammoth victory target.
But with spinner Ashton Agar (43) and Ashton Turner (41) the only other WA batters to pass 40, the home side fell well short of what was required, bowled out for 293 in 46.3 overs.
The result left WA with a 0-3 record, all but ending its title hopes just three games into the season.
NSW moved into second spot with a 3-1 record.
But it remains to be seen how much longer its will have Konstas in its Shield and one-day ranks given his rich vein of form.
The 21-year-old burst onto the international scene in December 2024 when he made a memorable Boxing Day Test debut against India, scoring 60 in his maiden knock.
Konstas failed to pass 25 in his next nine Test innings, with his most recent appearance in the baggy green coming in July last year against the West Indies.
The talented opener has worked hard on his game over the past 15 months, and it was on full display on Saturday as he cracked 15 fours and four sixes in a masterful display.
And with Australia still crying out for an opener to make his mark ahead of a busy Test schedule, it seems just a matter of time before Konstas is donning the baggy green again.
Whiteman was brave in WA's run chase, but he simply lacked the support needed.
Jack Nisbet snared 3-47 for NSW, including the key scalp of Whiteman in the 46th over, while Bryce Jackson chipped in with 2-58.
One rare highlight for WA came earlier in the day when Agar leapt high into the air to pull off a stunning one-handed catch at backward point to remove Ben Dwarshuis for 20.

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Oct 25, 2026

Unknown Publisher

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Oct 25, 2026
Violence flares in Paris after largely peaceful protests
Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators marched in France on Oct 24, with largely peaceful rallies giving way to clashes in Paris and Marseille as night fell despite a huge security operation aimed at preventing a repeat of last week’s unrest.
The Interior Ministry said 410,000 people took part in protests nationwide, though unions said the true figure was twice as high.
The main demonstration took place in Paris, where around 110,000 people marched on the south-eastern fringes of the capital, denouncing rising living costs and growing inequality.
The atmosphere deteriorated sharply after the rally ended. Riot police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse a group of around 500 hooded youths who hurled stones at officers, a security official said.
Trump votes early in Florida for US midterm elections
US President Donald Trump on Oct 24 voted early in his home state of Florida for the Nov 3 midterm elections, in which his Republican Party is battling to maintain control of Congress.
Trump and his wife, Melania, cast their ballots ahead of an appearance by the president at a campaign rally in the southern US state of Georgia.
Trump said he voted party line, or exclusively for members of his Republican Party.
Obama blasts Trump’s ‘chaos and cruelty’ at Ohio rally
Former US president Barack Obama delivered a scathing critique of his successor, Donald Trump, at a rally on Oct 24 in Ohio to support Democratic candidates ahead of the Nov 3 midterm elections.
“After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, ‘Enough is enough’,” Obama declared in Cleveland. “We are voting for change right here in Ohio.”
The 65-year-old Democrat blamed the Trump administration for the rising cost of living, a top voter concern amid soaring fuel prices.
Man dies after being buried alive while digging in Johor
A man died after being buried under soil while digging near the Taman Kedidi water tank in Pasir Gudang on the morning of Oct 24.
The Johor Fire and Rescue Department Operations Centre said in a statement on Oct 24 that it received an emergency call at 10am about the incident involving the 48-year-old victim.
“The operation team conducted a search and rescue using specialised equipment, hoes and spades to facilitate excavation. The victim was successfully extricated and pronounced dead by Ministry of Health personnel at 12.33pm,” the statement read.
Kimi Antonelli storms to pole for US Grand Prix
Kimi Antonelli took another step towards securing his maiden Formula 1 world title by beating Max Verstappen to pole position for the United States Grand Prix on Oct 24.
The 20-year-old Italian will wrap up the drivers’ championship on Oct 25 if he wins the race, his Mercedes teammate George Russell finishes outside the top eight and Lewis Hamilton finishes outside the top four.
Verstappen’s Red Bull teammate Isack Hadjar qualified in third place, and Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc fourth.

BARCELONA – A total of 100 people were arrested in Barcelona on the evening of Oct 24 after hooded demonstrators who participated in an anti-establishment rally looted shops and set fire to street furniture around the city's central Plaza de Catalunya.
Nuria Parlon, the interior minister for the Spanish region of Catalonia, said around 25% of those arrested were minors. More than 30 fires were reported and 14 stores vandalised or looted in a part of town popular with tourists and weekend shoppers, she added.
Demonstrators were called in social media posts to a movement “against the system”. In English, the phrases translate as “Indignant High School Student”.

DAR ES SALAAM, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- The 36th Chinese medical team to Zanzibar conducted a free medical outreach on Saturday at Chaani Health Center, bringing healthcare services to local communities, with nearly 100 patients treated during the event.
At the outreach venue, the team set up dedicated service areas for surgery, internal medicine, ophthalmology, otolaryngology, and dentistry, according to team leader Wang Wei.
With portable medical equipment, the medics delivered integrated one-stop care for local residents,applying characteristic traditional Chinese medicine techniques, including acupuncture, to treat prevalent musculoskeletal complaints such as neck, shoulder, lower-back, and joint pain, Wang noted.
Beyond clinical consultations, the team also held health education sessions focusing on the prevention of Ebola, schistosomiasis and malaria, raising local residents' awareness and enhancing their self care capabilities.
Annia Ibrahim Ndossa, an official with Zanzibar's Ministry of Health, noted that such grassroots initiatives bring healthcare closer to communities and improve residents' access to professional medical advice.
Wang said the team will keep collaborating with local health institutions to address community medical needs. It will boost medical exchanges, support the improvement of local health services and further advance China-Tanzania health cooperation. ■

Feature: Taste of China's Wuyi Mountain at Switzerland's Grindelwald-First
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
06:06:38 CST
07:06:38 KST

Participants attend an unveiling ceremony marking the sister-peaks partnership between Yunv Peak, a landmark of China's Wuyi Mountain, and Switzerland's Grindelwald-First mountain in the canton of Bern, Switzerland, Oct. 23, 2026. (Xinhua/Lian Yi)
GENEVA, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- A display board showcasing China's Wuyi Mountain was unveiled at Switzerland's Grindelwald-First mountain on Friday in simultaneous ceremonies linked by video, marking the destinations' sister-peaks partnership between Yunv Peak, a landmark of Wuyi Mountain, and the Swiss Alpine destination.
At an altitude of more than 2,100 meters, Grindelwald-First mountain was dusted with drifting snow as Alpine peaks emerged from the mist before fading from view. On the newly unveiled board, Yunv Peak was reflected in a clear stream, with bamboo rafts gliding below. The display brought together the landscapes of China and Switzerland, as guests in both countries witnessed the ceremonies via video link.
Oliver Hammel, chief executive of Jungfrau Railways, which operates Grindelwald-First mountain's tourism facilities, said he hoped the display would inspire more international visitors to explore Wuyi Mountain.
"We receive guests from all over the world," he told Xinhua. He expressed hope that visitors would scan the board's QR code to learn more about Wuyi Mountain and eventually travel there themselves.
Presented in Chinese and English, the board highlights cooperation in sustainable tourism and cultural exchange. It also showcases Wuyi Mountain's UNESCO World Heritage status, which recognizes its cultural and natural significance, as well as activities such as hiking, bamboo rafting and visits to tea plantations.
Yunv Peak, also known as Jade Maiden Peak, and Grindelwald-First form the fourth pair of sister peaks linking China and Switzerland. Previous partnerships have linked Yulong Snow Mountain with the Matterhorn, Mount Huangshan with the Jungfrau, and Mount Emei with Mount Rigi.
Fujian Wuyishan Culture and Tourism Group and Jungfrau Railways signed the agreement in November 2025 to promote tourism and cultural exchanges between the destinations.
Located in Switzerland's Jungfrau Region, Grindelwald-First attracts visitors with its spectacular Alpine scenery and diverse outdoor activities. Wuyi Mountain, meanwhile, is renowned for its Danxia landforms, characterized by striking red sandstone cliffs and peaks, as well as its tea culture, rich biodiversity and cultural heritage.
Hammel noted that two of the Swiss peaks involved in the partnerships -- the Jungfrau and Grindelwald-First -- are in the Jungfrau Region.
"The Chinese market, Chinese guests, and exchange with China are important for us," Hammel said, adding that he looked forward to welcoming more Chinese tourists.
In his ceremony address, Hammel also said the two destinations could share experience in sustainable tourism and conservation, helping preserve their landscapes for future generations.
Cui Ke, counselor at the Chinese Embassy and director of the China Cultural Center in Bern, addressed the ceremony on behalf of Chinese Ambassador Qian Minjian. He described the unveiling as another example of cooperation between the two countries in culture and tourism.
Cui expressed hope that the display would serve as more than a photo opportunity, encouraging visitors to discover both destinations and fostering closer ties between the two countries.
Speaking at the outdoor ceremony in Wuyi Mountain, Li Yan, deputy mayor of Wuyishan City, called for closer cooperation in mountain tourism. She said she hoped more Swiss visitors would discover Wuyi Mountain and more Chinese travelers would experience the Swiss Alps.
For Swiss participant Roger Strahm, Wuyi Mountain is already on his travel wish list.
"I am keen to visit Wuyi Mountain to explore its beautiful landscapes and experience China's rich tea culture and profound historical heritage," said Strahm. "I hope that there will be more opportunities for exchanges between the two destinations, allowing more Swiss friends to discover Wuyi Mountain, appreciate its beauty, and fall in love with all that it has to offer." ■

Protests sweep Italian cities, clashes reported
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
06:06:37 CST
07:06:37 KST

Police stand guard near Circo Massimo for an anti-war march in Rome, Italy, Oct. 24, 2026. Protests over rising living costs, military expansion and increased arms spending swept across several Italian cities on Saturday, with clashes between demonstrators and police reported in multiple locations. In Rome, demonstrators set off from Piazza della Repubblica, according to the ANSA news agency. Clashes erupted between protesters and police in the city center later in the evening, prompting police to use water cannons and tear gas in an attempt to disperse the crowds. (Xinhua/Wang Kaiyan)
ROME, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Protests over rising living costs, military expansion and increased arms spending swept across several Italian cities on Saturday, with clashes between demonstrators and police reported in multiple locations, according to Italian media.
In Bologna, clashes broke out between some demonstrators and police on Saturday evening, the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera reported. Emergency medical services received 17 calls for assistance, and six people were taken to hospital by ambulance.
In Rome, demonstrators set off from Piazza della Repubblica on Saturday afternoon for an anti-war march, according to the ANSA news agency. Clashes erupted between protesters and police in the city center later in the evening, prompting police to use water cannons and tear gas in an attempt to disperse the crowds.
In Turin, demonstrators protesting mainly against increased military spending and rising fuel prices clashed with police on Saturday evening. Some protesters threw fireworks and bottles at officers, who responded by firing tear gas.
Following demonstrations that escalated into riots and looting last weekend, particularly in Milan, Italian Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi ordered additional police forces to be deployed across the country. The reinforcement was focused particularly on major cities where the largest rallies were expected.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni condemned the violence in a social media post on Saturday evening, stressing the need to protect both peaceful demonstrators and the wider public.
"Everyone's safety must be guaranteed: those who wish to demonstrate peacefully, those who work, and those who want to live in their cities without fear," she said. "We must leave no room for those who seek nothing but confrontation and violence." ■

Iran's supreme leader meets judiciary chief, urges compensation for U.S.-Israeli "crimes": statement

TEHRAN, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has stressed the need for "serious" efforts to pursue the Iranian people's rights and ensure the payment of compensation for the damages inflicted on the country during the U.S.-Israeli attacks.
The issues were highlighted in a meeting between the supreme leader and the country's Judiciary Chief Gholamhossein Mohseni-Ejei, according to a statement published on the leader's website on Saturday.
Among the issues underlined during the meeting were promoting justice, safeguarding public rights, fighting corruption and its root causes effectively, handling judicial cases promptly, precisely and decisively, enforcing judicial rulings in a timely and deterrent manner, and bringing about a "comprehensive and tangible" transformation in the country's judicial apparatus.
The other matters included the necessity to draw up plans and make efforts to decisively fight crimes as well as to seriously pursue the restoration of the Iranian people's rights and compensation for the material and non-material damages resulting from the "crimes perpetrated by the U.S.-Israeli criminals."
On Feb. 28, Israel and the United States launched joint attacks on Tehran and other Iranian cities. Iran responded with waves of missile and drone attacks targeting Israel and U.S. bases and assets in the region, and tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz. ■

In a social media post, Lantratova said she had held an online meeting with Lubinets, who heads the Ukrainian negotiating team, with the humanitarian mission in Oleshky as the main topic.
She told Lubinets that a ceasefire in the area would take effect at 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (0100 GMT) on Oct. 27. Lubinets, in turn, said the Ukrainian side would begin its ceasefire at 3:00 a.m. Kiev time, meaning the two sides would halt fire simultaneously.

Oleshky is located on the left bank of the Dnieper River, opposite the Ukrainian-controlled city of Kherson. The town has been facing a severe humanitarian situation, with residents reportedly experiencing worsening shortages of food and other essential supplies amid continuous fighting.
On Friday, Russia and Ukraine agreed to a temporary ceasefire in the area to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations. ■

====================================================================================================

Explainer: Why Serbia's parliamentary elections attracting attention
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
06:06:19 CST
07:06:19 KST

BELGRADE, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Serbia is scheduled to hold parliamentary elections on Oct. 25, marking another major political event following Aleksandar Vucic's resignation as president on Sept. 27.
Why are the elections attracting widespread attention? How will the vote proceed with the presidency vacant? And can Vucic become prime minister through the parliamentary election?
WHY IT MATTERS
Before formally resigning as president, Vucic accepted the Serbian Progressive Party's (SNS) nomination on Sept. 5 to head its electoral list and serve as its candidate for prime minister. On Sept. 9, he signed a decree dissolving the National Assembly and calling snap parliamentary elections for Oct. 25.
Under Serbia's Constitution, the election of a new National Assembly will set in motion the process of forming a new government. After lawmakers elect a new parliamentary speaker, the speaker, acting as president, will nominate a candidate for prime minister. The nominee must present a government program and a proposed list of cabinet members and secure the support of a majority of National Assembly deputies to form a new government.
The parliamentary election therefore marks the beginning of a new political cycle in Serbia and has attracted considerable international attention.
Vucic has long prioritized economic development, infrastructure construction and improvements in people's livelihoods, helping him build a base of political support. In recent years, however, his government has also faced sustained challenges from opposition forces and disruption from some protests.
Analysts say that the election will be a test of the governing performance of Vucic and his political allies while directly affecting the power structure in the new parliament and the formation of the next government. The outcome will also influence Serbia's domestic and foreign policy direction to some extent in the coming years.
HOW IT PROCEEDS
Under Serbia's Constitution, when the president resigns, the speaker of the National Assembly assumes the duties of acting president and is responsible for setting the date of a presidential election. Although the National Assembly has been dissolved, Speaker Ana Brnabic continues to serve as acting president until a new parliament is elected.
Serbia uses a proportional representation system for parliamentary elections. Voters cast their ballots for electoral lists submitted by political parties, coalitions and other eligible political groupings. The 250 seats in the National Assembly are allocated proportionally according to the votes received by each list.
The competing lists encompass Serbia's main political forces. They include "Aleksandar Vucic - United Serbia" led by the SNS; "Student List - Students Win" backed by student groups; and "Ivica Dacic-Stability Factor!" formed by the Socialist Party of Serbia and its allies.
A total of 8,392 polling stations have been established for the election, with approximately 6.45 million registered voters. Polling stations will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. local time (0600 to 1900 GMT) on Oct. 25. The Republic Electoral Commission is required to announce the nationwide election results within 96 hours of the close of polling.
CAN VUCIC BE ELECTED?
Whether Vucic can become prime minister and continue his political career will have implications for Serbia's domestic politics and foreign policies.
Vucic was elected president in April 2017 and re-elected in May 2022. Under Serbia's Constitution, the president serves a five-year term and may serve a maximum of two terms. Before becoming president, Vucic served as Serbia's first deputy prime minister in 2012 and became prime minister in 2014.
According to official Serbian statistics, the unemployment rate fell from about 24 percent in 2012 to around 9 percent in 2025, while nominal gross domestic product measured in euros more than doubled over the same period. In 2024, Serbia attracted approximately 5.2 billion euros (about 5.84 billion U.S. dollars) in foreign direct investment, a record high.
An Ipsos poll conducted from Oct. 20 to 22 put the "Aleksandar Vucic - United Serbia" list, led by Vucic, at 47.4 percent, compared with 40 percent for "Student List - Students Win".
Unlike traditional electoral lists associated with established political parties, the one of "Student List - Students Win" brings together figures from a range of professional backgrounds, including doctors, university professors, actors, athletes and financial professionals.
Jan Nowinowski, a researcher at the Centre for Eastern Studies in Poland, wrote in an analysis that the student-backed electoral list was one of the main challengers to the electoral list headed by Vucic and its supporting political forces.
He noted, however, that while the student groups' calls for anti-corruption measures and other demands had broad mobilizing appeal, their policy positions remained relatively general, lacking a systematic reform blueprint, clear implementation pathways, and detailed plans for carrying reforms forward. ■

Houthis claim 7 attacks on Saudi targets as heavy airstrikes hit Yemen
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
06:06:12 CST
07:06:12 KST

SANAA, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Saturday that it had launched seven missile and drone attacks on airports, oil facilities and a military base across Saudi Arabia, as heavy Saudi-led airstrikes hit various Houthi-held areas of Yemen.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a statement broadcast by Houthi-run al-Masirah TV that the group had used ballistic missiles and drones in the attacks targeting airports, oil facilities and a military base in the Saudi cities of Riyadh, Yanbu, Rabigh, Dammam, Najran and Khamis Mushait.
Sarea said King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was targeted in two stages. Other attacks struck targets including Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu and King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.
There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the claimed strikes.
Sarea said the attacks were launched after what he described as 100 Saudi airstrikes on Houthi-held areas of Yemen over the previous 24 hours. He claimed Saudi Arabia had carried out a total of 3,123 air and missile strikes on Yemen since the latest escalation began.
Meanwhile, al-Masirah TV reported on Saturday casualties from heavy Saudi-led airstrikes across Houthi-held areas. It said four people were killed and several others wounded when a house was hit in the Asr neighborhood of the capital Sanaa, citing a preliminary toll.
In the western province of Hodeidah, five members of one family were killed when an airstrike hit their home in the At Tuhayta district, while another child was wounded, according to al-Masirah.
The broadcaster also reported that eight people were killed and more than 10 others wounded in airstrikes on housing for cement factory workers in Hamdan district of Sanaa province.
Separately, Sarea said in a statement posted on social media platform X that Houthi forces had targeted what he called Saudi-backed "mobilizations" at Al-Nasr camp and a naval military base in the southern port city of Aden, where Yemen's internationally recognized government is based.
The strikes came amid an intensifying confrontation between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces backed by the Saudi-led coalition, with missile, drone and air attacks escalating across several parts of the country in recent days.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of the country's north. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. ■

PARIS, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Around 410,000 people took part in a new round of protests across France on Saturday, French news channel BFM TV reported, citing the Interior Ministry.
In Paris, the police prefecture estimated that 110,000 people had taken part in the demonstrations. Meanwhile, more than 500 rioters attacked law enforcement officers on Cours de Vincennes.
However, the General Confederation of Labour (CGT) put the nationwide turnout at nearly 800,000, including 250,000 in Paris, according to BFM TV.
Several French cities had authorized demonstrations for Saturday, including Lille, Strasbourg, Mulhouse, Grenoble, Marseille, Toulouse, Amiens and Paris.
French police had made 135 arrests during demonstrations across the country by 1 p.m. local time (1100 GMT) on Saturday, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said at a press briefing.

Feature: Returning farmers in Syria's Afrin struggle to restore livelihoods through olive farming
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
06:06:07 CST
07:06:07 KST

A woman sorts freshly harvested olives in the Afrin countryside of Aleppo province, Syria, Oct. 21, 2026. (Str/Xinhua)
by Hummam Sheikh Ali
ALEPPO, Syria, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Across the hills of Syria's northern Afrin region, farmers climb wooden ladders to pick olives from trees, while others sort the freshly harvested fruit on sheets spread beneath the branches.
Among them is Orai Aref Naso. For Naso, the harvest is part of his struggle to rebuild a livelihood disrupted by years of displacement.
Returning from the northeastern province of Hasakah about 10 months ago, Naso found his family's olive trees still standing, but weakened by years of inadequate care.
"The people of Afrin are very happy to return to their land and olive trees," he told Xinhua. "Olives are very important to the people here. Their livelihoods depend on them."
Afrin, a predominantly Kurdish region in northern Aleppo province, saw widespread displacement during Syria's prolonged conflict, particularly after fighting intensified in 2018. Many farming families were separated from their land for years, leaving their groves without regular maintenance or in the care of others.
Since returning, Naso has been trying to restore his family's trees, but the rising cost of diesel, fertilizer and other agricultural supplies has limited what he can do.
"We have been caring for the trees since we returned, but we cannot give them the same attention as before," he said.
His experience reflects the challenges facing returning farmers in Afrin.
Abdulrahman Aibo, an agricultural engineer and olive farmer, said many displaced landowners had relied on relatives to maintain their groves, while others lost access to their properties during the conflict.
Aibo said many growers cannot afford sufficient fertilizer, while labor shortages during the harvest season have forced some to bring in workers from outside Afrin.
Despite the difficulties, olive production in Aleppo province has shown signs of recovery.
Elias Samaan, head of the olive division at the agriculture and agrarian reform directorate in Aleppo, said preliminary estimates put the province's olive fruit production at about 225,000 tonnes this season, compared with 198,000 tonnes last year.
He attributed the improvement largely to better rainfall, although the effects of last year's drought continue to limit productivity.
Afrin accounts for about 48 percent of Aleppo's olive production, Samaan said.
He added that the return of landowners was helping revive cultivation and olive press operations, but shortages of irrigation water and expensive agricultural supplies remained significant challenges.
For farmers, improved production has not necessarily translated into better returns.
Naso said a tin of olive oil was selling for around 50 to 60 U.S. dollars this season, compared with nearly 100 dollars or more in previous years.
With fuel, fertilizer and labor costs remaining high, the decline in prices has squeezed farmers' earnings.
"Even paying the daily wages of workers has become difficult," Naso said.
Aibo expressed hope that improved economic conditions and greater support for farmers would help restore the region's agricultural productivity.
Naso, meanwhile, hopes to bring his family's olive trees back to their former condition before his displacement.
"Our wish is for our trees to grow again and return to how they were before," he said. "We know how to care for our land. What we need is support to keep doing it." ■

====================================================================================================

Roundup: Türkiye opens new museum district showcasing major Chinese porcelain collection
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
06:05:58 CST
07:05:58 KST

Visitors view Chinese porcelain exhibits at the newly opened Porcelain Museum within the Topkapi Palace in Istanbul, Türkiye, Oct. 25, 2026. Türkiye on Saturday inaugurated a new museum district within Istanbul's historic Topkapi Palace, where thousands of Chinese porcelain pieces are on display, reflecting centuries of cultural exchanges between China and Türkiye. Restored into a historical neighborhood complete with its own streets and squares, the palace's former mint now houses the Porcelain Museum, which displays 5,300 pieces -- including 3,500 Chinese porcelains -- across 19 halls. Dating back to the 13th century, Chinese porcelains -- particularly those from Jingdezhen -- traveled along the ancient Silk Road to the Ottoman court. (Xinhua/Liu Lei)
ISTANBUL, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Türkiye on Saturday inaugurated a new museum district within Istanbul's historic Topkapi Palace, where thousands of Chinese porcelain pieces are on display, reflecting centuries of cultural exchanges between China and Türkiye.
Speaking at the opening ceremony, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan emphasized the nation's exceptional heritage in history, culture, architecture, and art, noting that these artifacts reflect an understanding of civilization shaped over centuries.
Ahead of the opening, Yasin Yildiz, president of the National Palaces, highlighted the significance of Topkapi Palace's Chinese porcelain at a press briefing.
Restored into a historical neighborhood complete with its own streets and squares, the palace's former mint now houses the Porcelain Museum, which displays 5,300 pieces -- including 3,500 Chinese porcelains -- across 19 halls.
Yildiz emphasized that Topkapi Palace holds one of the world's most prominent collections of Chinese ceramics, noting that their prolonged absence from display had created a long-standing public expectation. "We are finally meeting this expectation," he said.
The opening has drawn considerable interest from academic and archaeological circles.
"There is no doubt that this is one of the most important porcelain collections in the world, where we will perhaps have the chance to see the rarest examples of Chinese porcelain," Turan Takaoglu, a researcher at the Archaeology Department of Canakkale Onsekiz Mart University, told Xinhua.
Dating back to the 13th century, Chinese porcelains -- particularly those from Jingdezhen -- traveled along the ancient Silk Road to the Ottoman court. The sultans' deep admiration for these exquisite pieces not only made them a symbol of prestige but also inspired the flourishing of traditional Ottoman ceramic arts, creating a unique cultural synthesis.
For Ke Guoxing, general manager of the Jingdezhen porcelain official flagship store in Istanbul, the exhibition marks a milestone in cultural exchange.
"For a long time, these collections were mostly kept in storerooms, with very limited access," Ke said. "Now, the centralized display of 3,500 Chinese porcelains gives more people their first chance to appreciate this history closely."
He emphasized the collection's immense academic value, particularly regarding the blue-and-white porcelains from the Yuan and Ming dynasties.
Many Yuan-era pieces from Jingdezhen were custom-made for the Islamic world, featuring large forms and dense patterns that are rarely seen within China itself, Ke noted.
"These collections provide irreplaceable physical evidence for studying the export of Chinese porcelain and the fusion of aesthetics," he added, expressing hope that the public display would facilitate joint research between Chinese and international scholars.
Beyond porcelain, the sprawling mint complex features four other distinct museums dedicated to Calligraphy, Weapons, Maps, and Minting History. ■

Restored into a historical neighborhood complete with its own streets and squares, the palace's former mint now houses the Porcelain Museum, which displays 5,300 pieces -- including 3,500 Chinese porcelains -- across 19 halls.

WINDHOEK, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Wildfires have affected 3,513 square kilometers, or about 16 percent, of Namibia's Etosha National Park during the current fire season, as extreme heat and strong winds threaten to complicate firefighting efforts, the Ministry of Environment, Forestry and Tourism said Saturday.
No human or wildlife casualties had been reported as of Saturday, the ministry said.
According to preliminary figures released by the ministry, fires affected 926 square kilometers of the park in October, compared with 2,587 square kilometers in September, bringing the cumulative area affected to 3,513 square kilometers.
Nearly 80 personnel, including members of the Namibian Defence Force, neighboring conservancies and farm workers, have been battling fires in various parts of the park since Oct. 20, the ministry added.
The ministry warned that temperatures reaching 45 degrees Celsius and winds of 20 km per hour on Saturday could cause the fires to flare up again, hampering containment efforts.
Meanwhile, the Namibia Meteorological Service has warned that a heatwave, with temperatures ranging from 36 to 42 degrees Celsius, would persist across much of the country through the weekend.
The weather service attributed the extreme heat to a strong high-pressure system over northern Namibia that is gradually shifting toward central parts of the country, causing sinking air to warm rapidly.
Last year, wildfires affected 37 percent of Etosha National Park, one of Africa's largest and most renowned wildlife sanctuaries, and a cornerstone of Namibia's conservation and tourism sectors. ■

Houthi-run al-Masirah TV reported multiple casualties from the strikes, including eight killed and more than 10 others wounded when airstrikes hit housing for cement factory workers in the Hamdan district of Sanaa province.
The strikes came as Yemen's internationally recognized government forces, backed by the Saudi-led coalition, intensified their "Dawn of Yemen" offensive against the Houthis, while the group has responded with missile and drone attacks.
In a separate statement, Sarea said Houthi forces had targeted what he called Saudi-backed "mobilizations" at Al-Nasr camp and a naval military base in the southern port city of Aden, where Yemen's government is based.

Amid the escalation, the U.S. Department of State said Saturday that it had updated its travel advisories for Middle East countries, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Iraq, Lebanon and Israel, citing threats from the Houthis.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of the country's north. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. ■

====================================================================================================

Australia has an Asian history, too, you just have to look for it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
22:00:00 UTC
07:00:00 KST

analysis
Boyer Lecture: Australia has an Asian history, too, you just have to look for it
This year's Boyer Lecture series explores the opportunities and challenges of Australia's engagement with Asia in the 21st century. Dr Louisa Lim, Associate Professor at the University of Melbourne, reported from China for a decade for NPR and the BBC. This is an edited extract of her lecture, Tell it Slant.
When I was asked to reflect on Australia's role as part of Asia, I sat on a flat, white beach under a grey winter sky and thought about what that meant.
I suspected I was meant to address the logic of political realignment; potential economic markets; durable bridges between Australia and Asia. Tidy bullet points, bolstered by neat statistics, tessellating into a clear argument. (Preferably one that would fit on an Instagram tile.) Instead, I'm going to talk about a dancing white lion… but not quite yet.
As the sky darkened over that beach, I felt the weight of being the first Asian Boyer lecturer. I'm a new Australian, one of just three years standing. I have a Singapore Chinese father, a white British mother. I've written two books about the Chinese Communist Party's erasure and rewriting of its own history. What do I know of Asia and Australia?
The topic needed research. My first stop was Readings in Carlton, in Melbourne's north, with its stock of tens of thousands of books. At the counter, a harried man was punching at the till.
When I asked if they had any books on Australia's Asian history, he seemed surprised. He said they used to have one.
We went over to the Australian Studies section together. Eighteen shelves, maybe 400 books. He ran his hand over the spines.
"It's not there, I'm afraid," he said, crestfallen.
"What was it?" I asked.
"A biography," he said. "Someone in Bendigo. I can't remember who."
After that, I asked the same question at every bookshop I went to. Each time, it was a no. Though my writing explores forgotten and hidden histories, I was surprised to glimpse that invisibility here in Australia.
To be fair, these books do exist; more than 40 titles on the history of Chinese in Australia have been published in the past decade, but none were on the shelves of the shops I visited. They're not mainstream. You would only find the canon of work if you know where to look (in work done by scholars like Mei-fen Kuo and Juanita Kwok).
But there isn't even a single university course on the subject, let alone an Asian Australian studies centre at an Australian university.
History is story is identity. And that continuing invisibility has deep consequences for Australia's Chinese population.
The costs we pay
"When I was six years old, one of the kids at school called me 'Ching Chong Chinaman, born in a jar, christened in a teapot'. Ha, ha, ha."
That's Photographer William Yang. He was born in Dimbulah in Queensland in 1943.
"I had no idea what he was talking about, although I knew from his expression he was being horrible to me. So I went home to my mother and I said to her, 'Mum, I'm not Chinese, am I?' And she said, 'Yes, you are.' Her tone was hard, and it shocked me. And I knew in that moment, that being Chinese was like a terrible curse."
I heard this story last year at William's show, named Milestone. It took me straight back to 2016. I was sitting in the principal's office of a state primary school. We'd just arrived in Melbourne.
My eight-year-old had complained they'd been teased by a boy, backed up by his mates. He'd been taunting them with "ching chang chong", pulling back his eyes. Yes, this was in 2016. The same old story as William's, but almost 70 years later.
I wanted to know what action the school would take. But the principal was a busy woman, with a school to run. She looked at me as if I were a naughty child.
"The boys were only joking," she said wearily. "They've been told not to do it. It won't happen again."
That day I discovered there were no teachers of colour at that school. There was no one who even recognised racism. And it's still common.
According to the 2023 recent Lowy Institute report on being Chinese in Australia, one in five Chinese Australians reported being called offensive names in the past 12 months. For younger people aged 18 to 29 the reported rates of racism were even higher.
After that, I moved my child to another school. One with an excellent Chinese immersion program, diverse students and teachers. Every day for three years, we drove there and back. Half an hour each way, twice a day. Twelve hundred hours over three years. That was just one cost we paid. Five months' worth of workdays.
I was at work earlier this year, when the same child rang me. They're 19 years old now. But that day, they were sobbing so hard I couldn't understand what they were trying to say.
It turns out, they'd been walking down the street, holding hands with their boyfriend, just round the corner from his house in inner north Melbourne. Suddenly, a complete stranger began screaming at the pair of them; she was shouting "Find yourself an Australian girl!"
I dropped everything and I drove to pick them up. When I got there, the pair were sitting by the side of the road, heads bowed into each other, dazed. How can I talk about Australia's role in Asia when I'm crouched in the gutter, hugging my child?
Words and names matter
"Growing up in Australia, I've always felt very disconnected from my heritage."
That's comedian Noah Szto. He's a doctor who also writes very funny stand-up. He has a white Australian mother, and a Chinese Australian father.
"If you'd asked me when I was a kid how I felt racially, I probably would have told you that as far as I was concerned, I was 100 per cent white but there just happened to be a Chinese man in my house sometimes."
I've thought about those words a lot. For Noah, they're personal. But they also sum up the mindset left behind by the White Australia policy. Deep down, I suspect many Australians feel like Noah felt about his family: Australia is a white country that just happens to have Chinese people living in it.
That feeling is grounded in history. One reason for Federation, back in 1901, was to pass unified legislation limiting Chinese immigration. The modern Australian nation is rooted in anti-Chinese sentiment and in fear. When MPs debated the Federation bill, they were deciding not just who would be let into Australia, but who would be allowed to become Australian.
Being Chinese often precluded becoming Australian. The underlying fear, the anti-Chinese sentiment, they're still visible.
One school holidays, I took my family to Bright, in Victoria's High Country. It was bitterly cold. We went sledding, whooping as we skidded down the white hills, our cheeks chapped by snow. The next day I got up early to visit the Chinese bridge at Wandiligong. It marks the contributions of the Chinese miners who transformed a small village into the largest town in the region in the 1850s.
Nowadays the Chinese bridge is handsome, painted red, crowned at either end with a corrugated iron pagoda. I was pleased to see Chinese contributions so publicly remembered. Then I read the signboards. They quoted books of the time. This was how they described Chinese miners: "To us they were just chows or chinks to be ridiculed and baited or given a wide berth."
Those words felt like a slap in the face.
Another year, our holiday trip was to Metung, in East Gippsland. My morning run skirted the beautiful bayside, taking me through a place called Chinaman's Creek. That word stopped me short. Chinaman. According to the Macquarie dictionary, it's "widely considered to be an offensive term". Yet there are still 235 places in Australia with 'Chinaman' or 'Chinamen' in their names. It's just one indication of how normalised anti-Chinese racism still is in Australian life.
Names matter. As the author Richard Flanagan said, "We become the words we speak." This repetition and incantation of racism, it replicates and amplifies it.
A scattered history
After that, I began seeking out Australian Chinese history. I needed other narratives, ones that were more useful to me.
That was why I was tramping up a hill in Vaughan, south of the central Victorian town of Castlemaine, with my friend Natasha. Our feet rustled through the copper-coloured gum leaves. We knew we were in the right place when we found stones arrayed in a perfect circle on the ground.
This was the Chinese cemetery from the mid-1850s, at the peak of the gold rush, when there were 49,000 Chinese immigrants on the Victorian goldfields. They had to pay entry taxes of 10 pounds a head, about $15,000 today; they also paid residence taxes not imposed on any other group.
"Daylesford Cemetery: on the Daylesford-Trentham road, 1.5km east of the Farmers Arms Hotel, across the street from the Daylesford Dharma school, one Chinese headstone: severe damage."
This is the poetry of Grace Yee, from her collection Joss: A History. Grace spent two years in the State Library of Victoria. She read the archives, then she turned them into poetry. Even the Bulletin's Anti-Chinaman Special Number of 1888.
By then, anti-Chinese sentiment had led to organised attacks on Chinese in Buckland, in Lambing Flats, mob violence in Bendigo, Ballarat, Maryborough and elsewhere.
Natasha and I used Grace's poetry as our guidebook; we couldn't find any other.
"Maryborough Cemetery: on the outskirts of town, a 17 minute walk south-east from the Maryborough Wattle Reserve Netball complex, eighteen Chinese headstones: gardeners, labourers, storekeepers: humble lane. From 2.8km west of Ballarat Bird world."
The poetry provided unexpected compass points, orienting us differently to landscape and history. Headstones whose Chinese calligraphy was worn smooth by wind and rain. A brick tower for burning paper offerings.
The sights we were seeing felt strangely archaeological. Holes in the ground that had once been Chinese baths. A Mad Max moonscape. Once, a Chinese mine, now dotted with burned-out cars.
"Chiltern cemetery, 1.3km northeast… near the Chiltern bushland reserve. Four Chinese graves, friends meeting)."
But this is recent history, just 170 years old. The visible traces of Chinese migrants on the landscape are so clear, yet so much of Australia's Chinese heritage is now lost. Forgotten, abandoned. Victim to the 20th-century racism of white Australia.
What remains of our Chinese history lies scattered, but the connective tissue is missing.
These gaps are being filled by the poets and artists, the photographers and novelists. Maybe the artists are less governed by institutions, less governable. Those institutions have gate-kept the past, deciding what research to fund, what to teach, what Australian students should learn. The Roman empire, oh yes. Australia's Asian history, less so.
The poets and artists, the photographers and novelists; they're freer agents. Their work is freighted, weighted, fuelled by white hot anger, burning curiosity, the need to explore the gaps in their own histories.
They have family trees that go back a single generation. Grandfathers who changed their names, wiping clean their Asian pasts, internalising that racism into the silence that became a family legacy.
Again, I think of a poet's words — Emily Dickinson this time: "Tell all the truth but tell it slant."
That word "slant" is so tainted by racism and the taunts of the playground… but it's time to reclaim it.
Emily Dickinson writes, "Success in circuit lies", and maybe the circuitous route journeys through photographers' eyes, poets' words, to reach a different set of truths about Australia's past. Both about the extent of Chinese influence in Australia, and the ugliness of the persecution.
"Let's languish on Little Bourke street; the longest continuous/Chinese settlement in the western world."
Back in 1968, in his Boyer lectures, the anthropologist WEH Stanner coined the term The Great Australian Silence. The cult of forgetfulness, as he put it, practised on a national scale towards Indigenous people and history.
The lie of the tabula rasa wipes out 65,000 years of First Nations history. That Great Australian Silence has over time swallowed up Australia's Chinese history too; we need to fill it with voices, lives, stories.
"I am learning to/Prioritise my heritage in this shiny-buckled civilisation, /Where yellow-perilled white men brass the city's walls."
History is story is identity
When I moved here, I felt more Chinese than I ever have. Maybe because that was the way I was treated.
It came as a surprise that so many Australians seemed to view the country as part of Europe, just displaced to the other side of the world. As historian David Walker writes, Australia has seen itself as "a nation in the region but not of it".
That mental geography needs to change. Our future is here as part of Asia.
And so too is our past. History is story is identity.
It is an indisputable fact that some of Australia's cities were also Chinese cities. For four decades, Darwin had more Chinese residents than white ones. Broome's population was majority Asian for much of the first half of the 20th century. Bendigo's population was 20 per cent Chinese. Many Indigenous people also have Chinese heritage.
Australia has never been a monoculture. Its history is not a singular narrative. It is polyphonous, multilingual, plural. Yet the country keeps looping back into the same stale old arguments, driven by domestic politics.
That disregard for Australia's Asian history has dire consequences in the present, most urgently a lack of Asia capacity.
My child was very lucky to go to a Chinese immersion school. Only seven government schools offer Chinese immersion programmes in the whole of Australia. Just four secondary schools. (Only three per cent of our high school students learn Chinese, Japanese or Indonesian.)
Fewer than five students a year graduate from honours programmes in Chinese studies with language skills. We can barely talk to our neighbours, let alone understand them.
We need different role models, new points of reference.
I found one a few years ago when I was invited to the Bendigo Writers festival. I was speaking at the Golden Dragon Museum. When I walked inside, I was astonished to find myself face to face with a gigantic dragon. His head alone, fringed with blue gills, was bigger than my whole body. This is Dai Gum Loong, the longest processional dragon in the world.
He's the highlight of Bendigo's Easter parade. After I saw him, I went back the next year with my family.
It was a true community event. Stilt walkers led the parade, followed by BMX bikers, firefighters, religious puppets.
And dragons of literally every stripe. From all over Australia. There was a Falun gong dragon carried by members of a sect banned in China. There was a LGBTQIA+ dragon in trans colours.
And, of course, there was Dai Gum Loong.
Longer than a soccer pitch, carried by more than sixty Bendigonians, of all ethnicities, all genders.
The thing is: dragon dances at Easter aren't a Chinese tradition at all. It's one that began in Bendigo in 1892. In the Golden Dragon museum, I saw sepia pictures of the people responsible. Chinese men with white wives and Wasian kids. Families like mine, but a century and a half earlier. They stayed on through the White Australia era, and they used their traditions to raise money for Bendigo's hospital.
This dragon, and the museum itself, they were both the brainchild of Russell Goldfield Jack. An Australian born in 1935, he's also known as Louey Yeung Man. He was the subject of the book I couldn't find at Readings, a biography by Dianne Dempsey.
Sadly, he has just passed away, aged 91.
In September I went to his funeral. He was accompanied on his last journey by a silver-white funeral lion, the Chinese colour of mourning. It shimmered as it danced slowly through Bendigo's streets.
In the theatre where his funeral was held, the lion bowed to his coffin, which was covered with an Australian flag. This was the first ever state funeral for a Chinese Australian.
"He was a great man, a great Australian," said former state premier Jacinta Allan.
At the grave side, people bowed with incense. His family burned paper money. The funeral lion went up in flames too, as firecrackers exploded around us.
I never met Russell Jack, but I benefited from his legacy. He made visible a different version of Australia's history. One that foregrounds Australia's Asian history, its Asian story, its Asian identity.
The white lion is the symbol of a society where citizens do not need to choose between being Australian and being Asian. To truly integrate into the region, Australia first needs to reckon with its own Asian past, and its continuing legacy of racism.
Story is history is identity. But this time, let's tell it slant.
This lecture and other Boyer Lectures will air on consecutive Sundays from October 18 on ABC Radio National's Sunday Extra program. They can also be found on ABC listen.

Inside the Trump-administration campaign to return Brazil’s Bolsonaro clan to power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
21:50:22 UTC
06:50:22 KST

Inside the Trump-administration campaign to return Brazil’s Bolsonaro clan to power
SAO PAULO, Oct 24 - Two US State Department officials led a campaign to restore the right-wing Bolsonaro clan to power in Brazil and successfully pushed for sanctions aimed at tilting the election in their favor, according to 10 current and former US officials with direct knowledge of the matter.
Their plan faces a reckoning on Sunday, when Senator Flavio Bolsonaro faces leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a tight run-off. Lula has warned Washington against encroaching on Brazil's sovereignty and accused his opponent of plotting with the Trump administration.
The two officials were Darren Beattie, a Senior Advisor for Western Hemisphere Affairs who oversees Brazil policy, and Ricardo Pita, another senior advisor promoted this year to Deputy Assistant Secretary for North America. The details of their campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power haven't been previously reported.
Beattie and Pita, both political appointees, operated with wide latitude to manage Washington's relationship with the second most-populous country in the Americas, the people said.
In the months before election campaigning began, they instructed US diplomats in Brazil that it was US policy to restore former President Jair Bolsonaro as Brazil’s leader – even though he had been disqualified from office for plotting a coup in 2022, when he lost the presidential election to Lula, three of the people said.
After Bolsonaro received a 27-year sentence in September 2025, the two men pivoted to supporting the candidacy of his son, right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the three sources said. Beattie and Pita told embassy staff not to interact with other conservative presidential contenders who could challenge the younger Bolsonaro, they said.
Since last year, the two men have successfully advocated for punitive US government measures on Brazil designed to weaken Lula and boost the Bolsonaros, the 10 people told Reuters. The policies included designating Brazilian gangs as terrorist groups and imposing US sanctions against the Brazilian Supreme Court Justice who was spearheading the investigation into Jair Bolsonaro.
Reuters could not determine the extent to which the two men were acting on orders from the White House or Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Trump, a vocal defender of Bolsonaro since his election defeat in 2022, hasn’t publicly endorsed any candidate.
The White House declined to comment and referred questions to the State Department.
State Department Spokesman Tommy Pigott didn't answer questions about specific measures and directives involving Beattie and Pita but said in a statement: "All actions taken by the United States against narco-traffickers and to protect free speech are to defend the rights and lives of the American people. The Brazilian people have the right to choose their leaders through free and fair elections."
Lula’s office did not respond to comment requests.
Orna Blum, one of the officials who spoke to Reuters about Beattie and Pita’s efforts, led the State Department's Brazil and Southern Cone office until retiring last year over her opposition to the Trump administration.
Washington "has every right to pursue its economic and strategic interests," she said. "But when American foreign policy instruments are used to pressure another democracy over the legal fate of a political ally, the line between diplomacy and political intervention has been crossed."
SANCTIONS ON A SUPREME COURT JUSTICE
Beattie is a former White House speechwriter fired in 2018 after addressing an event frequented by white nationalists. He’s also the architect of "free speech diplomacy," a policy advocated by Trump allies that seeks to punish nations they accuse of censoring right-wing speech by US citizens, companies and global right-wing allies.
The United States has accused Brazil Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes of violating free speech rights by jailing Brazilians for political social-media posts and by censoring content of US social-media companies. Moraes has argued he was ridding social media of fake news that undermined public faith in Brazil's democratic institutions.
Moraes did not respond to a comment request.
Pita, a conservative Venezuelan-American, is among many in Rubio's orbit who view Lula as a threat to US interests in Latin America. Rubio has been a key leader in the administration’s aggressive policy in the region, which has included an invasion of Venezuela to oust its president, an oil blockade of Cuba, and military attacks on suspected drug boats from Latin America.
Beattie and Pita were drawn to the Bolsonaro family’s right-wing politics, their antipathy towards Lula, and the idea that Jair Bolsonaro was a victim of abuses by Brazil's Supreme Court.
Like Trump in the 2020 US election, Bolsonaro refused to concede he lost Brazil’s 2022 presidential vote, triggering riots by supporters who stormed government buildings. The Supreme Court convicted him in September 2025 of plotting a coup to remain in power.
Before the conviction, in early 2025, the Bolsonaros were aggressively lobbying Washington for sanctions under the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act against Moraes, who had led criminal investigations into Jair Bolsonaro. The act is a 2016 federal law allowing US sanctions against foreign individuals responsible for human-rights abuses or severe corruption.
Around April 2025, Jair Bolsonaro’s younger son, Eduardo, visited Beattie in his State Department office in Washington DC, according to two former US officials. Eduardo Bolsonaro had been making the public case for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes since at least 2024, and in March 2025 he said in a livestream that it was "practically certain" the Trump administration would do so.
Eduardo Bolsonaro did not respond to requests for comment.
Beattie made calls to the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control to appeal for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes, said a former US official with direct knowledge of the matter.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, whose department administers Magnitsky sanctions through OFAC, offered no opposition, the former official said.
The US announced Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes in July 2025, citing his alleged violations of free-speech rights by censoring anti-government social-media posts.
A Treasury official said Bessent and Rubio are "fully aligned on the administration’s foreign policy."
TERRORIST DESIGNATIONS
The Bolsonaro family was also pushing for Washington to designate Brazil's top gangs – the Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Comando Vermelho (CV) – as terrorist organizations. They believed such a designation would hurt Lula, who some opponents have criticized for failing to control crime.
Eduardo Bolsonaro had become friends with Pita through US conservative circles, and both supported the effort to designate the gangs as terrorist groups.
In May 2025, Pita joined a US delegation that visited Jair Bolsonaro at his residence in Brasilia as he awaited his trial, according to public announcements at the time. Also in the group: David Gamble, the State Department’s top sanctions official at the time.
Back in Washington, Pita asked State sanctions officials to explore how terrorist designations like those announced against Mexican cartels in February 2025 could be used in Brazil, one former official said.
Nearly a year later, in May 2026 – after Pita was promoted to a new job that pulled him out of Brazil affairs – presidential contender Flavio Bolsonaro met with Beattie and Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau in Washington to discuss "the urgency of designating the PCC and the Comando Vermelho as foreign terrorist organizations," according to an X post by right-wing influencer Paulo Figueiredo that included photos of the attendees.
The State Department announced the designation the following day.
Reuters could not determine the extent of Pita or Beattie’s influence in securing the final decision.
BACKFIRES AND SETBACKS
In July 2025, Washington also announced a series of other measures against Brazil, including the revocations of eight Supreme Court justices' visas and 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, citing the "persecution" of Jair Bolsonaro.
Reuters could not determine what, if any, role Beattie or Pita played in the additional measures. But if they were intended to undermine Lula, many of them backfired, according to political analysts in Brazil.
Measures targeting the court did nothing to stop it from proceeding with Bolsonaro's trial, while the tariffs boosted the Lula government's poll numbers, the analysts said.
Major US and Brazilian firms reliant on bilateral trade – including meatpacking giant JBS - controlled by Brazilian billionaires Wesley and Joesley Batista – also pushed back on the tariffs, which Washington eventually watered down.
Beattie and Pita’s campaign also hit setbacks. Without an official explanation from the Treasury Department, the US removed Justice Moraes from the Magnitsky sanctions list in December, and in March Brazil barred Beattie from entering the country to visit Bolsonaro in prison.
Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at risk intelligence firm RANE, said Trump may have decided to withhold a public endorsement of Bolsonaro to avoid being seen as meddling in Brazil's election – a perception that could boost Lula’s popularity.
Still, after Flavio Bolsonaro narrowly outperformed Lula in the first-round election earlier this month, Trump called it a big victory.
"Close, but a very, very big victory," he told reporters. "Amazing, actually." REUTERS
