Dennis called. She did not answer.
Mark Dennis: I pay you $300 watch one hour 😂😂
No thanks
The chat ended with Akara sending a dog-barking emoji — one final effort to make him stop.
The ABC has reviewed the metadata to verify the text messages were sent from the same number Dennis used for his legal work.
Akara said she had no idea why Dennis sent the messages and did not report them to Sunrise or police.
"I feel horrible," she told the ABC. "I'm still thinking 'why, why, why'. It's disgusting."
In January, Dennis was charged with possessing and transmitting child abuse material, but he was found dead in his home before facing trial.
The ABC has revealed Australian and Cambodian national police are still jointly investigating Dennis's network, including his links to Sunrise, in a cross-border investigation codenamed Operation Queenstown.
Dennis sponsored a handful of children at Sunrise over many years, regularly visited these and other children in the orphanage, and maintained close relationships with some children he met through Sunrise once they left as adults.
Former Sunrise employees have alleged inappropriate behaviour by Dennis, including sexual harassment of an employee, excessive touching of teenage girls and entering children's dormitories.
None of these allegations were reported to Sunrise. A spokesperson for Sunrise said police had informed the charity that no current or former Sunrise child had been identified as one of Dennis's victims.
"We take child protection extremely seriously. Sunrise operates under Cambodian, Australian and international child protection standards, is independently audited, and any concern raised by a child or graduate is followed up thoroughly."
Now, documents obtained by Background Briefing and ABC Investigations reveal that Sunrise was made aware of allegations of misconduct, including against two former Sunrise employees and one current employee.
The claims include one historical allegation of rape by a former employee against a Sunrise girl, after being given a "final warning" for sexual misconduct years earlier.
Sunrise declined to comment on what action was taken in response to this for privacy reasons but added that some allegations that had been made to the ABC did not align with its records.
The revelations have prompted former Sunrise staff to come forward with historical concerns about the celebrated charity's policies and culture, and wider reflection across the industry about how all charities balance fundraising with child safety.
Maggie Eno, a co-founder of Cambodian children's charity M'Lop Tapang, speaking generally, said the ABC's investigation raised awareness across all charities about unsafe practices, which "goes on a lot sadly", and questioned the future of orphanages in Cambodia.
"We're not post-Khmer Rouge anymore, where there really genuinely was so many orphans. The need is not there. The need is for family-based care, community-based care," she said.
Social worker Rob Madsen, who worked as Sunrise's operations manager from 2008-2012, said there needed to be an independent investigation run by Cambodian experts into Dennis's role at Sunrise.
"There's been a significant intrusion by an alleged offender," he said. "There needs to be an arms-length investigation. If there are potential victims, those victims must be identified and provided support."
A 'revolving door' of visitors
Madsen was excited to join Sunrise Cambodia in 2008, a high-profile Australian charity celebrated for helping disadvantaged children.
He had spent the previous 15 years working with government agencies and non-government organisations in child protection, and his skills were embraced by the charity's founder Geraldine Cox.
"You have strengths to bring to Sunrise that have never been offered before, and I know the children will benefit from what you have to give," Cox wrote to Madsen.
However, upon starting as operations manager, Madsen was quickly disturbed by some of what he saw.
He said a busload of tourists came to see the children, who performed dance shows, in what he described as a "revolving door" of visitors and sponsors who felt entitled to take children outside the orphanage.
"I was shocked," Madsen said. "Australians have come to Cambodia for the sole purpose of harming children, sexually abusing a child."
Madsen introduced new rules for visitors, staff and sponsors — designed to limit and supervise adult interactions with children, and record and investigate any allegations of wrongdoing.
Sunrise said it used standard guidelines provided by the Cambodian government prior to Madsen's arrival but acknowledged "more extensive" policies were developed at that time.
Madsen's framework was tested in December 2008, when an Australian sponsor emailed Cox about an interaction with a young girl who told her a Sunrise employee was a "bad man" because of something that happened in the bedroom.
"I am very concerned that he may be a paedophile or at least acting improperly … I will leave the matter in your capable hands," the sponsor wrote.
"As a primary teacher with 20 years' experience, I feel I know when children are telling the truth."
The following day, Cox responded that she was having "this looked into privately".
"But find it difficult to believe that [staff member] is guilty of anything along the lines of your message. He is a dedicated father [Sunrise term for employee] of 43 girls and has been with us for over 10 years."
In response, Madsen initially wrote to Cox saying that he thought the sponsor was "clearly overstepping her perceived role as sponsor".
He suggested the staff member not be left alone with children "so as he is not placed in a position of further accusation".
Then, Madsen said he did eventually put the staff member on watch, and when the same person was accused of sending pornographic material to a young teacher the following year, he was sacked.
Asked about this account in a series of questions, Sunrise did not respond.
Bus driver accused of rape
Not long after, Sunrise faced a bigger crisis when a 16-year-old girl alleged she had been raped by the charity's long-term bus driver.
According to reports compiled two months after the alleged incident, the bus driver dropped the children at school but asked one girl to stay behind, then drove to a quiet plot of land, and allegedly raped her.
The girl fell pregnant and underwent an abortion. She reported what happened to Sunrise and the police. The bus driver was terminated by Sunrise but disappeared to evade police arrest, according to the documents.
This same bus driver had a history of multiple allegations of sexual misconduct towards children at Sunrise, detailed in the documents.
An incident report, written by Madsen, said the bus driver was given a "final warning" in 2004 for "abnormal sexualised behaviour" towards children, including "flirting and watching girls undress in the toilet".
"I cannot hide my feeling of anger and frustration over this, and the fact that such behaviour was not taken more seriously at the time."
Madsen wrote the staff member should have been "instantly dismissed", and he was worried the "mild action … may very well come back to bite".
He also warned Sunrise was at risk of "being exposed in the media" and said there had been "clearly a number of serious gaps" with previous management of this staff member.
"I am confident though, that we are now doing all we can to ensure the best possible protection of our children."
Sunrise said historical allegations the ABC asked it to comment on did not reflect the "substantial safeguarding measures, oversight mechanisms, and continuous improvements that Sunrise has implemented to protect children and promote their wellbeing".
Boy 'rewarded' despite abuse
Sunrise reported another case — of sexual assault by a child — to authorities, but a subsequent decision raised questions about its attitude towards offenders.
For decades, Sunrise sent Cambodian students on exchanges to private schools in Australia.
The opportunities were highly sought-after among the children, and only a handful of students were selected through a competitive process.
In 2010, a teenager was chosen to study at a prestigious boys' college in Australia despite the boy admitting to "penetrative, forced sex with a female child" in Cambodia two years earlier.
"The police were informed of the abuse," Madsen wrote to the board. "A brief record kept in the file at [Sunrise]."
However, Madsen said the boy did not undergo a psychological assessment before being selected and warned that choosing the boy sent the wrong signal to other children.
"We, by our actions, also give other children a clear message that in life, we can indeed do wrong — break rules of life and law, and in fact be rewarded without consequence."
Sunrise did not respond to specific questions about Madsen's email or the case.
Employee accused of lacking professional boundaries
Sunrise staff members have not just raised historical concerns.
The ABC has obtained a resignation letter written by a senior employee in 2020 raising concerns about another Sunrise employee, who remains employed by Sunrise at the time of publication.
In the letter, the resigning employee told Cox and other managers that this employee should not stay in his current position because "his behaviour is against child protection policy".
"He takes children to his house and he sleep in the same bed," the senior employee wrote. "And he likes to bring the children that he likes outside."
The allegation was that this man had unprofessional boundaries with children.
The ABC has spoken with two additional sources who also made claims against the same employee but did not report these to management.
Sunrise said an investigation into the 2020 letter found the bed-sharing claim was unsubstantiated but confirmed the employee had taken children to his home on multiple occasions with other people and had "shown favouritism in taking children on outings".
"[The employee] was warned about this behaviour by Sunrise management at the time," a spokesperson said. "Sunrise therefore does not accept any suggestion that the concerns about [employee] were simply disregarded."
Sunrise also released a statement on behalf of the employee, saying he "strongly rejects any suggestion of inappropriate conduct".
'He misses his mother'
Sunrise was founded by Cox in the 1990s on land gifted to her by then-Cambodian prime minister Hun Sen as an orphanage for children with nowhere to go.
Cox has spoken publicly about how her infertility morphed into a maternal instinct for the children under her care.
"I feel about these children as though they are my own," she said in the documentary My Khmer Heart. "It's very difficult for me to make people understand that these are my children."
However, many of the children living at Sunrise — like other orphanages in Cambodia — have living biological families.
Madsen said he was surprised by the number of children in Sunrise who were not orphans, but had living parents or relatives.
This became apparent during his first Khmer New Year on the job, when the orphanage cleared out as children returned to stay with their families.
"That was the first light globe moment to me," he said. "And the question that came to me is, 'What's going on? They've got family?'"
Madsen hired case workers to track down family members.
The team discovered a "harrowing" case of a young girl who was incorrectly classified as an orphan. Her mother was found, but died suddenly before they could be reconnected.
"She didn't get the chance to be reunited in any sense with her mum. She went to [her] mum's funeral," Madsen said.
UNICEF has long warned about how institutional care could harm child development. Madsen said it was also cheaper to support families to send children to school while living at home, and pushed for more families to be reunited.
Sunrise acknowledged paperwork was often incomplete or missing, but said this was often out of their control, and they did their best to reunite families.
"This is the reality of life in Cambodia," Cox said.
Sunrise said helping children return to live with family, known as reintegration, has always been a priority, and that many children live in the centre due to abandonment, family violence or other factors that make it unsafe to return home.
Reports obtained by the ABC show poverty alone has also been a reason that children lived in Sunrise in the 2010s, with reports detailing parents struggling with harsh living conditions or low-paid jobs in garment factories and food markets.
"She [mother] wants to live together with the child, but she is afraid that the child cannot have a bright future if the child lives with her," one stated.
The reports also detail experiences of some Sunrise children who suffered emotionally from family separation.
"She sometimes misses her mother until she cries at night," one report stated. "He misses his mother and wants to visit his mother," another said.
Yi Soksan, who worked at Sunrise in management roles from 2010 to 2018, said Cox accepted reintegration was necessary but felt this was sometimes difficult because she had formed emotional bonds with the children.
"We don't want to hurt her [Cox], but sometimes we have no choice," he said. "She doesn't want kids back to the family."
In an email sent shortly before he left in a management restructure in 2012, Madsen said some children were made to "jump through hoops" to leave Sunrise.
"Unless there is a serious risk of abuse or neglect, I see no reason why Sunrise Children's Villages should deny the rights of this family to live together.
"To deny such rights will certainly open Sunrise to some serious criticism."
Cox said families had always been reconnected when it was safe.
"What you describe as the feelings of former staff members may well come down to nothing more than a difference of opinion as to approach and emphasis, as can happen in any workplace."
Sunrise said residential care was no longer its core program and children who continued to live there were referred by the Cambodian government or facing "imminent danger".
It said it complied with all Cambodian government regulations and had passed its last three audits with 100 per cent compliance.
"Reintegration must be carried out with great care, as once custody is handed over, we can no longer intervene," it said.
Children wrote letters to sponsors
Sunrise said its child protection policies "have evolved significantly … as have international standards and practices across the NGO sector" and has sought to draw a distinction between current and prior leadership.
But in the past, Sunrise, like many other charities, promoted connections between sponsors and children to drive donations.
Meeting minutes from 2018, sent to directors including Dennis, show efforts to raise funds by increasing communication from children to donors through emails, photos and drawings.
Around Christmas and birthdays, children were asked to write letters "thanking them" for presents and asking for more money.
Sponsors also received annual reports with photographs of individual children, along with personal details, such as their weight, age, height and the "best thing you did last year".
"He always behaves like girls," one sponsor report stated about a child in 2019. "He always makes up his body very similar to the girls in girl dressing."
Other reports included a 10-year-old girl's history of sexual abuse, and another child's experience of domestic violence.
Responding to questions about whether this breached the children's privacy and created an unhealthy dynamic between sponsors and children, a Sunrise spokesperson said this practice was "immediately stopped and new child privacy policies were applied" under current leadership.
"Child histories are now strictly confidential, even among staff and children. However, children are of [course] free to speak about their own background."
M'Lop Tapang co-founder Maggie Eno said fundraising was difficult, but there should be "zero contact" between children and sponsors.
"They're not friends. They're not uncles or aunties. They are strangers to that child," she said. "They have a power dynamic over that child, and they don't have the right to be playing with that child."
She said the charity sector in Cambodia had come a long way in the past two decades, but she was surprised that child sponsorship was still being used.
"It's just inconceivable that a sponsor and a child would even know each other," she said. "In 2026, I just can't really fathom the idea that that still goes on, to be honest."
Former Sunrise director Peter Winkler, who said he had not been involved since 2015, said children "should never be used as attractions for fundraising or tourism".
"My understanding is that SCV [Sunrise] has not kept up with the times."
Winkler, who now advocates to end residential care in Cambodia, said the Dennis case should be handled transparently and had broader lessons for all donors.
"Australian-funded charities working overseas are, in many ways, a reflection of Australian values, and we have an obligation to undertake due diligence."
*Name has been changed.

Athens stage performance honors Minab school victims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
19:03:30 UTC
04:03:30 KST

Athens stage performance honors Minab school victims
TEHRAN- A theatrical performance commemorating the schoolchildren killed in the US-Israeli attack on Shajareh Tayyebeh School in Minab has been staged in Athens, Greece, as part of a cultural program highlighting the human consequences of the tragedy.
“Reading Sara’s Memories from Minab,” written and directed by Greek theater artist Andreas Zafeiris, was presented at the Brecht Stage of the 2510 Cultural Center in cooperation with Iran’s Cultural Attaché Office and Embassy in Greece on Thursday.
The play draws on the memories of Sara, a girl who survived the attack on the school in southern Iran. Through the perspective of a child, it portrays everyday life, fear, loss and the lasting consequences of the assault, bringing the experiences of those affected into focus.
The program also featured documentaries about the attack on the Minab school, as well as a screening of the short film “MINAB 168.”
Following the theatrical performance and film screenings, writers and media activists took part in a discussion titled “The Role of Art in Resistance and the Fight against Oppression and Injustice.”
Mohammadreza Bahmani, Iran’s cultural attaché in Greece, referred to the killing of thousands of children in Gaza, Palestine, Yemen, Lebanon and Iran over the past three years. He described protecting children and defending human dignity as responsibilities that transcend political and geographical boundaries.
Bahmani also emphasized the role of art in exposing injustice, conveying the voices of victims and preventing such tragedies from fading from collective memory. He expressed appreciation for the Greek artistic group’s efforts to commemorate the children martyred in Minab.
Palestinian writer and translator Nawzat Hadid spoke about the role of art in preserving collective memory and the historical identity of the Palestinian people. She described artistic expression as a means of documenting displacement, conveying experiences of resistance and representing the suffering of individuals whose lives can otherwise disappear behind statistics and reports.
Greek journalist, writer and director Thomas Sideris highlighted the responsibility of the media in covering wars and humanitarian crises. Drawing on his professional experience, he said journalists should go beyond reducing victims to numbers and communicate their actual lives and experiences to audiences.
Konstantina Karouti, a representative of the “Until Victory / MINAB 168” campaign, stressed the importance of preserving the memory of the 168 children who lost their lives and turning public sympathy into social action. She described art and cultural activities as ways to challenge indifference, racism and the normalization of violence.
Zafeiris said theater could bring audiences closer to victims’ experiences and encourage them to listen to their stories. He emphasized that taking time to hear about other people’s lives could help transform passive spectators into responsible participants.
The program also included video messages from Minab artist and eyewitness Jafar Qassemi, Lebanese journalist Marwa Othman and Australian researcher Tim Anderson.
An art exhibition titled “MINAB 168” was another feature of the event, paying tribute to the children killed in the attack.
According to the organizers, proceeds from the program will go toward rebuilding Shajareh Tayyebeh School. The play is scheduled to return to the stage on October 29 at the Brecht Stage in Athens.

Majid Entezami to perform his memorable pieces in Tehran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
19:02:57 UTC

Majid Entezami to perform his memorable pieces in Tehran
TEHRAN – Maestro Majid Entezami will conduct a 150-piece orchestra on October 29 at the Espinas Palace Hotel in Tehran, at a concert featuring the memorable works he has made for Iranian films and TV series.
The works to be performed in the concert include “Kolah Pahlavi,” “From Karkheh to Rhein,” “The Glass Agency,” “The Scent of Joseph’s Shirt,” “The Insane Flew Away,” “Kani Manga,” “Men of Anjelos,” “Duel,” “Once Upon a Time, Cinema,” “The Eagles,” “Zaal and Simorgh,” “The Train,” “The Wolves,” and “The Symphony of the Epic of Khorramshahr,” Honaronline reported.
In 2023, the veteran composer and conductor Entezami staged the concert “Along with Memories,” in which he presented a selection of his works accompanied by Iran’s National Orchestra at Tehran’s Vahdat Hall. His presence on the stage, which happened after an 11-year hiatus, was met with remarkable audience reception, and the concert was extended for multiple runs.
Also an oboist, Entezami, 78, has composed music for over 80 movies, 10 television series, and 10 suite symphonies. He holds the record for winning the most Crystal Simorgh awards in the Best Original Score category at the Fajr International Film Festival.
He studied at State University of West Berlin under the supervision of Karl Steins and Lothar Koch in 1968. He performed successful concerts with the Berlin University Symphony Orchestra in Lyon, Nancy, and Marseille from 1969 to 1972.
In 1973, Entezami came to Iran by the invitation of the Tehran Symphony Orchestra and performed a successful Mozart concert as oboe soloist, conducted by Helge Dorsch. Then he returned to Germany as a member of the Berlin Symphony Orchestra and the West Deutsche Philharmonie.
In 1974, he became a member of the Tehran Symphony Orchestra as well as a teacher at the Tehran Conservatory and the music department of the University of Tehran. He performed two oboe recitals with Lucette Martirossian on piano and harpsichord and Ivan Pristas on bassoon in 1976 and a concert with the Les Jeunesses Musicales de l’Iran orchestra conducted by Ali Rahbari and Valodia Tarkhanian as viola d’amore soloist.
Despite being the son of famous Iranian actor Ezzatollah Entezami, Majid's entrance into the cinema industry was his own.
He has a profound understanding of the picture and has always tried to tell the untold essence of the story. He also has experience with a variety of styles, which has given his portfolio variety, from comedies to epic war movies.
The music of Entezami is orchestral and based on Western classical music, but with Iranian instruments and unusual rhythms which give his works an eastern feel.
Every theme and musical color heard in Entezami's work has a rational explanation in the story. He believes that music tells a part of the story that is not already told in the picture. Some of his works seem to be narrative, almost like part of the script, but he maintains that no director has ever asked him for such characteristics.

Iran slams US-Israeli attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities, condemns double standards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
19:01:24 UTC
04:01:24 KST

Iran slams US-Israeli attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities, condemns double standards
TEHRAN– Iran’s ambassador to the United Nations has condemned US and Israeli attacks on Iran’s peaceful nuclear facilities, accusing Western countries and international nuclear authorities of applying double standards and politicizing global non-proliferation efforts.
Addressing the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York on Friday, Gholamhossein Darzi, Iran’s ambassador and deputy permanent representative to the United Nations, reaffirmed Iran’s inalienable right under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) to develop nuclear energy for peaceful purposes, including uranium enrichment.
Darzi said the United States was challenging the rights of NPT member states by questioning their entitlement to pursue the full nuclear fuel cycle. He argued that denying countries access to uranium enrichment technology while claiming to support peaceful nuclear energy was incompatible with Article IV of the treaty.
“No State can unilaterally rewrite the Treaty or impose its own political veto on the legitimate rights of other States Parties,” he said, warning against the use of non-proliferation concerns as a means of exerting political pressure on sovereign nations.
The Iranian envoy said the United States and Israel had launched two wars of aggression against Iran in 2025 and 2026, targeting its peaceful nuclear facilities under International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) safeguards. He described the attacks as violations of international law, the UN Charter, the IAEA Statute, relevant IAEA General Conference resolutions and UN Security Council Resolution 487 (1981).
According to Darzi, the attacks caused extensive destruction and claimed thousands of lives, including that of Iran’s Leader, whose religious decree, or fatwa, rejects nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction.
Iran criticizes international response
Darzi strongly criticized the IAEA’s governing bodies, its director general and the UN Security Council for failing to condemn the attacks on safeguarded nuclear facilities. He said the absence of a clear response had exposed the selective application of international non-proliferation standards.
“Instead, pressure is directed against the victim while the aggressors escape accountability,” he said.
The envoy contrasted the treatment of Iran, an NPT member since 1970, with that of Israel, which he described as the only nuclear-armed state in the region and whose nuclear facilities are not subject to comprehensive IAEA safeguards.
He argued that continued political and military pressure on Iran, alongside 'impunity for Israel,' undermined the credibility of the international non-proliferation regime. He also criticized the withholding of technical cooperation that, in his view, deprived Iran of the benefits of peaceful nuclear development that the IAEA is mandated to promote.
Safety conditions remain central to inspections
Addressing calls for the resumption of inspections, Darzi said Iran had neither abandoned nor formally suspended its safeguards obligations. However, he stressed that the military attacks had fundamentally changed the physical and security conditions under which verification activities could take place.
He noted that the IAEA’s own reports acknowledged that verification activities had ceased and inspectors had been withdrawn for safety reasons. Such concerns, he said, could not be disregarded when demands were made for their return.
“No country can reasonably be expected to provide access amid military operations and persistent threats without adequate safety guarantees,” Darzi said, adding that responsibility for creating these conditions rested with the countries that carried out the attacks.
He concluded that Iran remained prepared to cooperate with the IAEA to the extent permitted by prevailing circumstances, but emphasized that such cooperation must not compromise the safety of the Iranian people, nuclear facilities or agency inspectors.
Darzi also insisted that the IAEA’s reporting must remain professional, objective and free from political influence, arguing that the agency’s credibility depended on technical integrity and impartiality.

Reuters: US sought to activate Starlink in Iran after strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
19:00:50 UTC
04:00:50 KST

Reuters: US sought to activate Starlink in Iran after strikes
TEHRAN – Successive US administrations have repeatedly asked SpaceX to activate or disable its Starlink satellite internet service in different countries to advance Washington’s foreign policy objectives, including requests to provide internet access inside Iran following US-Israeli strikes, Reuters reported on Saturday, citing six former senior US officials familiar with the matter.
According to the report, the administration of former US President Joe Biden asked SpaceX to activate Starlink in Iran during protests in September 2022 following the death of Mahsa Amini. A former senior official in President Donald Trump’s administration and another person familiar with the matter told Reuters that the administration also discussed activating Starlink in Iran following US-Israeli strikes in June 2025 and February 2026, with the stated aim of expanding internet access and communications for anti-government protesters.
The report said neither the Trump administration nor SpaceX had publicly confirmed whether the terminals involved in the latest discussions were activated. It also cited a February report by The Wall Street Journal that the US government had sent thousands of Starlink terminals into Iran.
The revelations come as Iran has formally protested the unauthorized operation of Starlink terminals on its territory, accusing Norway of failing to take effective action and raising concerns about the use of foreign satellite communications infrastructure by the United States and Israel.
Iran protests Norway’s inaction over Starlink
On October 4, Iran’s Foreign Ministry summoned Norwegian Ambassador to Tehran Paul Bjornstad to convey Tehran’s formal protest over the continued operation of unauthorized Starlink terminals inside Iran.
According to Iran’s Foreign Ministry, Mohammad Hassan-Nejad Pirkoohi, the ministry’s director general for international peace and security, told the Norwegian envoy that the United States and Israel were exploiting Starlink’s satellite communications infrastructure to pursue interventionist activities against Iran.
The Iranian official criticized Norway for failing to fulfill its responsibilities as one of the administrations involved in registering the Starlink network with the International Telecommunication Union (ITU). He called on Oslo to take immediate and effective measures to halt unauthorized transmissions within Iranian territory and handed the ambassador a formal note of protest.
According to Tehran Times, the dispute had been under consideration by the ITU’s Radio Regulations Board since 2023. According to documents published by the international telecommunications body, Iran has repeatedly reported unauthorized Starlink operations within its territory.
The board has repeatedly called on Norway and the United States to take appropriate action to stop unauthorized transmissions, including by having the satellite operator remotely disable terminals operating without permission where necessary.
At its 98th meeting, the board concluded that there was evidence of unauthorized Starlink transmissions inside Iran and urged Norway to take measures within its capacity to stop them. It also asked Norway and the United States to explain why terminals operating without authorization in Iran could not be disabled in the same way as terminals in several other countries.
At its 101st meeting, the board concluded that Norway’s actions did not comply with relevant ITU resolutions and Article 18 of the Radio Regulations. However, it said it lacked the authority to suspend frequency assignments to satellite systems on the grounds that the administration responsible for notifying the network had failed to comply with the rules.
Tehran has maintained that the continued operation of Starlink terminals without authorization violates Iran’s sovereignty and national security. The dispute also highlights questions over the responsibilities of governments involved in registering satellite networks and the ability of operators to prevent services from being provided in countries where they are not authorized.
Starlink and US foreign policy
Reuters reported that the Biden administration also asked SpaceX to disable terminals allegedly used by Yemen’s Houthi movement and Hezbollah in Lebanon. Former US officials said the administration shared intelligence with the company concerning the possible use of diverted Starlink terminals by the two groups and requested that the devices be identified and deactivated. At least some terminals were subsequently switched off, according to two of the officials.
The disclosures have renewed questions about the extent to which US administrations rely on Elon Musk’s privately owned company to implement foreign policy and security objectives. SpaceX did not respond to Reuters’ requests for comment on the reported requests concerning Iran.
For Tehran, the issue extends beyond internet access to the regulation of satellite communications and the use of foreign technology inside Iranian territory without authorization. Iranian officials have repeatedly called on the countries responsible for the Starlink network’s registration, as well as its operator, to ensure that the service complies with international telecommunications regulations and Iran’s requirement for authorization.

Daughter’s inheritance rights can’t be defeated by limitation: J&amp;K and Ladakh high court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
19:00:49 UTC
04:00:49 KST

JAMMU: The high court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh has restored a woman’s right to inherit her father’s property after a 44-year-long legal battle, holding that an adverse revenue entry recorded during when she was a minor cannot automatically defeat a legitimate inheritance claim on limitation grounds.The dispute dates back to Sept 14, 1982, when Themu, daughter of late Sonu, filed a civil suit claiming half share in land measuring 58 kanals and 11 marlas left behind by her father.She challenged mutation no. 43 dated Oct 15, 1966, which had been entered exclusively in favour of one Shib Devi and sought declaration of her inheritance rights along with consequential possession.
On March 9, 2004, the sub-judge court in Kishtwar passed a decree recognising her entitlement. However, the district judge reversed the decree on Nov 7, 2012, primarily on the grounds of limitation and failure to establish paternity.Justice Shahzad Azeem of the HC, while allowing the appeal filed by Themu, set aside the judgment of the district judge, Kishtwar, observing that limitation cannot be determined on presumptions and conjectures, particularly where the claimant was a minor when her rights were initially disputed and the defendants failed to establish when the cause of action actually arose.

Russian embassy denies reports of staff leaving Iran’s Bushehr nuclear power plant

Russian embassy denies reports of staff leaving Iran’s Bushehr nuclear power plant
TEHRAN – The Russian Embassy in Tehran has dismissed reports that Russian diplomatic staff and specialists working at Iran’s Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant are leaving the country, stressing that activities are continuing as usual.
In a statement, the embassy said it was aware of reports published by certain hostile media outlets alleging that an evacuation of Russian embassy personnel and specialists at the Bushehr facility was underway.
“We would like to clarify that neither embassy staff nor Russian specialists at the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant are leaving Iran,” the statement said.
The embassy emphasized that operations were proceeding as normal, describing contrary reports as false information and saying their origins were entirely clear.
Located on Iran’s southern coast along the Persian Gulf, the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant is Iran’s first commercial nuclear power facility. Although construction at the site was initially undertaken by the German company Siemens in the 1970s, Russia took responsibility for completing the plant’s first reactor unit under an agreement signed with Iran in the 1990s. The first unit was connected to Iran’s national electricity grid in 2011 and reached full capacity in 2013.
Russia has continued to cooperate with Iran on the development of the facility, including the construction of additional reactor units. The project forms part of broader cooperation between Tehran and Moscow in the peaceful use of nuclear energy.

Twelve countries condemn any attack or threat against nuclear facilities
Unknown

Twelve countries condemn any attack or threat against nuclear facilities
TEHRAN – Twelve countries, including Iran, Russia, China and Pakistan, have issued a joint statement declaring that nuclear facilities must never, under any circumstances, be subjected to attack or the threat of attack.
On Friday, the 12 countries — Belarus, Burkina Faso, China, Cuba, Eritrea, Iran, Nicaragua, Niger, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan and Zimbabwe — issued the joint statement during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly’s First Committee. The statement addressed the prohibition of any attack or threat of attack against nuclear sites and facilities that are under the safeguards of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and dedicated to peaceful purposes.
According to IRNA, the statement was read out by Gholamhossein Darzi, Iran’s ambassador and chargé d’affaires to the United Nations. It contained eight points, as follows:
1. We reaffirm the importance of the full and effective fulfilment of the objectives of the International Atomic Energy Agency, particularly its statutory mission to accelerate and enlarge the contribution of atomic energy to peace, health and prosperity throughout the world. We also reaffirm the inalienable right of all states to develop research into, produce and use nuclear energy for peaceful purposes without discrimination.
2. We recall United Nations Security Council Resolution 487 (1981), which strongly condemned a military attack against nuclear facilities. We also recall the relevant decisions and resolutions of the IAEA General Conference — documents GC(53)/DEC/13, GC(XXIX)/RES/443, GC(XXIX)/RES/444 and GC(XXXIV)/RES/533 — which clearly reflect the longstanding position of the international community opposing any attack or threat of attack against nuclear facilities under IAEA safeguards and dedicated to peaceful purposes.
3. We reaffirm that an attack or threat of attack against nuclear facilities violates the principles of the United Nations Charter, international law and the Statute of the International Atomic Energy Agency, and is fundamentally incompatible with the objectives and purposes of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT).
4. We emphasize that attacks against nuclear facilities have serious implications for nuclear safety and security and pose a grave threat to the integrity, effectiveness and credibility of the IAEA safeguards system, as well as to the broader global non-proliferation framework.
5. We emphasize that attacks against nuclear facilities would adversely affect the peaceful uses of nuclear energy and international cooperation, and could result in the release of radioactive materials, with severe consequences both within and beyond the affected country, including serious impacts on civilian populations and long-term environmental damage.
6. We emphasize that silence in the face of attacks against protected nuclear facilities undermines established international norms, erodes confidence in the international legal order and increases the risk of such attacks becoming normalised.
7. We therefore reaffirm that nuclear facilities must never, under any circumstances, be subjected to attack or the threat of attack.
8. We call on all member states to stand united in preserving the integrity and credibility of the IAEA safeguards system, strengthening nuclear safety and security, and protecting the peaceful uses of nuclear energy and international cooperation by expressing their clear and unequivocal opposition to any attack or threat of attack against nuclear facilities.

Tarrawingee tries to make sense of attack on local member Helen Haines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
18:48:05 UTC
03:48:05 KST

Tarrawingee tries to make sense of attack on local member Helen Haines
In a dark, overgrown home on the edge of a long, dirt driveway lived a man who nearby residents had grown to fear.
Empty beer bottles and slab cartons are strewn around the verandah and sheds, and the flyscreen door hangs perilously from its hinges, threatening to clatter from its fixings among broken glass.
Grass and weeds have grown tall around the property.
Through the windows, inside is dank and abandoned.
Brendan Nugent has been absent from the home since police arrested the 43-year-old on Monday afternoon, charging him with attacking federal MP Helen Haines, a long-time friend of the Nugent family.
Until then, few outside Tarrawingee had heard of the north-east Victorian hamlet.
By Tuesday, the media had arrived in force, and residents who say they had called for help with the man in the dark house had a new audience.
Bulldog country
About 400 people call Tarrawingee home.
It's a spread-out township, a short drive from Wangaratta with flat, flood-prone paddocks split down the middle by the Great Alpine Road.
A slightly faded sign at the edge of town welcomes you to "Bulldog Country".
It's big enough for a football and netball club, a town hall, and a picturesque pub. The town noticeboard has just one flyer, a faded invite to social pickleball: $5 a player.
The population skews older. "People love it so much they don't leave," one resident said.
Mr Nugent's home, understood to be owned by his family, stands in stark contrast to the enviable homes and well-kept gardens surrounding it.
Neighbours told the ABC of the barrage of heavy metal that emerged from the property at all hours.
One person said that the night after his arrest was their first good sleep in seven years.
By most accounts, Mr Nugent wasn't a part of the Tarrawingee community.
Peta Donaldson, who runs the Plough Inn, the town's 165-year-old pub, said she didn't know him.
She didn't even want to say his name.
"The man involved is not someone we recognise, nor is he familiar to the locals who regularly gather at The Plough Inn," she said.
"He certainly didn't involved himself within the community."
The ABC spoke to residents who were clearly rattled.
One property put a sign on the front gate pleading with media for some space.
It was handmade, laminated, with a pink background and bolded mauve font.
"We understand you want to hear our story, but we kindly ask you respect our privacy at this time," it read.
Tea at the Plough
On Friday, the Plough Inn opened for morning tea, giving locals somewhere to gather.
Police have been taking statements from residents, though few will speak on the record.
Several say they worry Mr Nugent could come home to "Tarra".
One resident said she feared for her life. Another was cynical about how long Mr Nugent would remain in custody and said he feared he could come "smash my windows".
Many say they had no idea he existed. Some who knew him did so through his father, Rod Nugent, and Rod's partner, Christine Cunningham.
Authorities are probing a reported rift between the family.
Asked whether the alleged attack on Haines was being investigated as possibly being, in effect, an attack on that family "by proxy", Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush said: "Yes it is."
Every line of inquiry, he said, remained open.
Police say nothing suggests Nugent belongs to the sovereign citizen movement, a fear some residents raised, but they are looking into his friends and associates.
A quiet strength
It's been hot in Tarrawingee this week, but a storm is forecast in the town for today.
The cameras have thinned out but police remain in the region in numbers.
Ms Donaldson and her husband have run the pub for only six months, so she's still getting to know the place. But she's confident the town will close ranks.
"The locals [here] are fiercely protective of their own," Ms Donaldson said.
"There's a quiet strength and loyalty here, and a genuine sense of belonging."
That loyalty is extended to Helen Haines.
Ms Haines wasn't born here. She was raised on the opposite side of the state on a dairy farm near Colac.
Moving to the north-east was her husband's idea.
But she has long since earned her place, and her constituents are protective of her. For now they wait on the twice-daily updates from The Alfred in Melbourne.
Brendan Nugent's next court appearance is not until February. Unless his lawyers apply for bail before then, he will remain on remand in Melbourne.
In Tarrawingee, life will eventually drift back into something like normal. Pub meals. Preseason training for football and netball. Perhaps even a game of pickleball.
"In the past few days we've seen people reaching out, offering help and finding ways to come together," Ms Donaldson said.
"People might live kilometres apart, but when something happens, that distance disappears.
"That's simply what neighbours do."

More than 14,000 Ethiopians have fled deadly fighting in southern Ethiopia into neighbouring Kenya, humanitarian officials said, amid fears that clashes between rival communities have killed more than a dozen people.
"We urgently need more well-wishers to support us with food and water. There is also a need for sanitary supplies and more toilets to avert diarrhoeal diseases," Malik Adan, Kenya Red Cross head of the Upper Eastern region, told reporters on Saturday.
The Kenya Red Cross said more than 10,900 displaced people were being accommodated at six temporary camps in the Kenyan border town of Moyale, while another 4,000 were staying with relatives and host families.
The figures mark a sharp increase from Friday, when Marsabit County Commissioner Stanley Kamande said more than 2,000 Ethiopians had crossed into Kenya following the outbreak of violence on Wednesday.
Residents reported on social media that heavy gunfire and shelling continued from both sides of the conflict, leaving Kenya as the only refuge for many civilians fleeing the violence.
The fighting involves Oromo and Somali communities in Ethiopia's southern border region, where a dispute over the display of the Somali Regional State flag in an area administered by Oromia has fuelled tensions. Both are federal regions of Ethiopia.
At least nine deaths were reported on Friday, but there are fears that more than a dozen people may have been killed as heavy fighting continues, according to humanitarian officials.
The Kenya Red Cross has distributed tents, blankets, sleeping mats and other essential supplies while providing nutritional assistance to children and breastfeeding mothers.
Local authorities have pledged additional food supplies, including rice and beans, but humanitarian officials warn that available resources may not meet the needs of the growing displaced population.
Moyale, a major crossing between the two East African countries, lies approximately 780 kilometres north of Nairobi, Kenya's capital, and 775 kilometres south of Addis Ababa, Ethiopia's capital, by road.
The continued fighting has disrupted cross-border trade and raised concerns about further displacement.

Violence flares in Paris after largely peaceful protests across France over living costs, inequality

- Most marches were peaceful, but clashes broke out in Paris, Marseille and other cities after dark, with tear gas, water cannon and raids on shops.
- The government deployed 70,000 police and gendarmes, while critics accused it of overreacting and warned the unrest could continue each week.
AI generated
PARIS – Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators marched in France on Oct 24, with largely peaceful rallies giving way to clashes in Paris and Marseille as night fell despite a huge security operation aimed at preventing a repeat of last week’s unrest.
The Interior Ministry said 410,000 people took part in protests nationwide, though unions said the true figure was twice as high.
The main demonstration took place in Paris, where around 110,000 people marched on the south-eastern fringes of the capital, denouncing rising living costs and growing inequality.
The atmosphere deteriorated sharply after the rally ended. Riot police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse a group of around 500 hooded youths who hurled stones at officers, a security official said.
In France’s second city, Marseille, youths dragged large metal sheets to block a street, set fire to rubbish bins, and hurled rocks and bottles at riot police.
The confrontations continued after sunset and police said two jewellery shops were raided.
Clashes also flared in Lyon, Bordeaux and Grenoble, while police fired volleys of tear gas at demonstrators in Clermont-Ferrand, Lille, Nantes and Nice.
However, the violence was still less intense than a week ago, when looters and vandals went on the rampage in a number of French cities.
Police carry out pre-emptive searches
The authorities deployed 70,000 police officers and gendarmes, 10,000 more than a week earlier, after conceding they had underestimated the scale of the unrest on Oct 17.
“We have to be ultra, ultra responsive,” Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told reporters on Oct 24, accusing far-left activists and criminal gangs of seeking to foment violence.
Much of central Paris took on the appearance of a city under lockdown, with shopkeepers boarding up storefronts, museums closing their doors and more than 20 metro stations shut.
Business groups urged retailers to remain closed after thousands of shops and businesses were damaged or looted across France last weekend.
“There are hardly any customers, so it’s not really worth staying open,” said Oskar, manager of a Kiton boutique in Paris.
Several of the capital’s best-known cultural institutions, including the Louvre, the Musee d’Orsay and the Paris Opera, closed for the day as a precaution, leaving tourists frustrated.
“Everything’s boarded up and we’re not quite sure where we should be,” said Xavier Dolliole, a tourist from the US city of New Orleans.
Protests ripple across Europe
The nationwide unrest began with small student demonstrations in suburban Paris in September to denounce school conditions.
After it spread into a broader protest against the state of the economy in France, it also prompted demonstrators to take to the streets in neighbouring countries.
On Oct 24, Belgian police used tear gas and pepper spray as they clashed in Brussels with anti-government demonstrators, while protests took place in a number of Italian cities for a second weekend.
Leftist leaders in France denounced a government move to limit the number of authorised marches in many cities, as well as a last-minute decision to shift the Paris event to the south-eastern fringes of the capital.
Hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon, who joined the Paris rally, hailed what he called a “magnificent mass display of collective discipline and self-restraint”.
He predicted the protests would continue until President Emmanuel Macron, whose mandate expires in 2027, addressed the social malaise in France, one of the world’s richest nations but with a growing debt mountain that has alarmed investors.
“Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week. There is still time for (Macron) to give in. After that, the only thing left to him will be the exit door,” Melenchon told reporters.
Far-right party holds congress
Many demonstrators have accused the government of overreacting, as soldiers were dispatched to patrol the Champs-Elysees, a grand boulevard lined with luxury shops and restaurants.
“We shed tears for shops, not for the people who are being impoverished all year round,” said Clara Lebbadi, a 22-year-old arts student.
“My friend and I almost didn’t come because we were scared, but we came precisely because it’s important not to let repression win,” she added.
The first authorised march on Oct 24 went peacefully in Orleans, around 120km south of Paris, where demonstrators rallied against Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally, which is holding a party congress in the city.
A shooting west of Paris on Oct 23 heightened tensions. A gunman suspected of acting out of Islamophobic hatred killed one person and wounded four others, including a 12-year-old girl.
“We have come to tell the far right, face-to-face, that we are not afraid,” said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis and a member of Melenchon’s France Unbowed party. REUTERS

Trump Thinks Alaskans Could Vote for the Wrong Sullivan. What Can the DOJ Do?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
18:26:54 UTC
03:26:54 KST

The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Thursday filed a lawsuit that intends to weigh in on the results of the Senate race in Alaska. It seeks to block certification of the election results under certain conditions if Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses.
Experts question whether it has the legal basis to do so—and if this intervention is a preview of how the Trump Administration might respond to unfavorable midterm results across the U.S.
The DOJ, in its filing, expressed concern that there might be “voter confusion” stemming from the fact that two candidates on the ballot are named Dan Sullivan. Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan is currently seeking re-election, and one of his challengers is Daniel J. Sullivan (who also registered as a Republican, but will no longer be listed as such, to better discern the candidates).
The GOP first raised concerns in May, prompting a proposal to add “incumbent” beside the sitting senator’s name on the ballot. But the party continued to warn that voters could split their votes between the two Sullivans, opening the door for Democrat Mary Peltola.
Alaska has traditionally been a state that leans Republican: Trump won the state by 13 points in 2024, and the state has not had a Democratic governor since 2002.
But the race is closer than analysts first expected. October polls from The New York Times/Siena, Alaska Survey Research, and Data for Progress show Peltola leading Dan S. Sullivan by between 2 and 7 points.
The DOJ lawsuit claims that the “sole purpose” of Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy is to benefit Peltola. Therefore, it seeks to block certification if the incumbent loses but would have won with all of Daniel J. Sullivan’s votes. To determine that, it proposes recalculating the ranked-choice count as though those votes had gone to the incumbent instead.
In a Wednesday Truth Social post, Trump said he was “very concerned” about the race and described the situation as “totally confusing.”
“Even 1, 2, or 3% could make the difference,” he wrote of the potential outcomes.
The DOJ said there would need to be an “investigation” to determine which vote was meant for which Sullivan. There is no indication of how they might distinguish voter intent. Neither the DOJ nor the candidates’ campaigns responded to TIME’s requests for comment.
On Friday, Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee asked to join the DOJ’s case as defendants, writing: “Alaskans, apparently, must elect Senator Dan S. Sullivan or the President will not let them elect anyone at all.”
Voting rights experts are calling it a “garbage lawsuit” and “an unprecedented intervention by the federal government.”
Lisa Murkowski, Alaska’s other senator and also a Republican, endorsed the incumbent Sullivan in January but on Friday condemned the DOJ’s efforts to intervene.
“Alaskans don’t need any help voting for their preferred candidates,” she wrote in a post on X. “The Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit.”
Asked to comment on the DOJ filing Friday, Trump told reporters: "I'm the one that said do it."
Why experts question the DOJ’s Alaska election lawsuit
Prior to the DOJ lawsuit, Republicans sought to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot in June.
When he decided to run, Republicans sent complaints to Carol Beecher, the director of Alaska’s Division of Elections. She wrote a letter to Sullivan in June saying that election officials had determined that he would be removed, claiming his candidacy was not filed “in good faith for the purpose of genuinely pursuing” leadership.
Sullivan challenged the decision and sued the state. Judge Thomas Matthews of Alaska’s Third District Superior Court ruled in June that he could remain on the ballot beside the other candidates. He wrote in a 32-page decision that elections officials were introducing a “new, previously unstated ‘good faith’ criteria” and said that this requirement is not present in state law or the Constitution.
That decision was upheld by the Alaska Supreme Court on June 29.
It was later determined that a “mitigating remedy” would be to present each candidate’s name with the middle initial and to add “incumbent” to the sitting senator’s name.
The Alaska Supreme Court ruling did not end scrutiny of Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy. In August, Reuters reported that the DOJ had issued grand jury subpoenas while investigating whether he entered the race to confuse voters.
The DOJ then filed its new lawsuit amid October polling that showed Peltola ahead.
The department justifies the move using language in the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) that says its purpose is to “protect the integrity of the electoral process.”
Experts, however, dispute whether that language authorizes the intervention.
Derek Muller, a professor of election law at the University of Notre Dame, wrote in a blog post after the filing that the proposed investigation is “essentially impossible.” But succeeding is not the point, he continues.
“The legal claim is so absurdly thin, there’s essentially no likelihood of success,” he wrote, adding that the real purpose of litigation is to signal to the press and public that the Trump Administration is “ready” if the result goes against the GOP’s interests in Alaska.
The Center for Election Innovation and Research (CEIR), a nonpartisan nonprofit working to inform voters, called the move “unprecedented” in a statement that also said the lawsuit “raises serious concerns about political interference.”
“I cannot recall an administration ever attempting to stop the certification of an election—and certainly not 11 days before polls close,” CEIR Executive Director David Becker said in the statement.
“Furthermore, this issue has already been fully litigated by Alaska’s courts,” he continued. “Alaska election officials are following state law, as the Constitution requires, and the courts will uphold that.”
Richard Hasen, a professor of law at UCLA, called the move a “desperate and unprofessional assault” on the American elections system.
Common Cause, a nonpartisan organization represented by the ACLU, filed a motion on Friday seeking to join the case to oppose the DOJ’s effort. Its president and CEO, Virginia Kase Solomon, said in a statement Saturday: “Politicians don’t dictate election outcomes; the people do.”
Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Dan S. Sullivan’s campaign, expressed confidence in his candidate’s re-election but told local media outlet KFSK on Friday: “We’ll let the DOJ complaint run its course.”
How has the federal government used the National Voter Registration Act?
The National Voter Registration Act was enacted in 1993 to address barriers to voter registration that depressed participation and disproportionately affected racial minorities. It was predicated upon the fundamental right of every eligible citizen to vote, as well as the duty of local and federal governments to protect that participation in the democratic process.
In the past 30-plus years, it has been used to sue states that fail to maintain their voter rolls or enforce registration requirements.
The Biden Administration also reckoned with Alaska in 2022, finding that the state wasn’t consistently letting residents register to vote—or update their voter registration—as part of their routine paperwork at the Department of Motor Vehicles. An agreement reached that June required Alaska to bring those procedures into compliance with the NVRA.
In 2012, the Obama Administration sued the state of Florida over a program intended to identify and remove suspected noncitizens from its voter-registration rolls too close to the elections. The parties agreed to dismiss the case in January 2013.
The George W. Bush Administration also sued several states under the NVRA to enforce requirements for offering voter registration and maintaining accurate voter rolls.
The DOJ’s Alaska lawsuit goes further than those earlier cases. Experts say the NVRA does not expressly authorize blocking election certification over suspected voter confusion.
If courts accept the DOJ’s argument, the consequences could extend beyond Alaska, warns Walter Olson, a senior fellow at the libertarian Cato Institute. It could give the federal government a new basis to challenge how states design ballots, determine which candidates qualify, and certify election results—all in the name of protecting election integrity.
“[The lawsuit] attempts to stretch a federal statute, the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA), beyond recognition by snipping language from the law’s preamble and treating it as if it creates vast and open-ended new duties that the federal government can enforce on states,” Olson said in a statement Friday. “If accepted, it would suddenly federalize many issues of local election administration.”

03:00:51 KST

Women who undergo breast reduction surgery often experience improvements in their sexual function, including enhanced desire, arousal, and satisfaction. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis published in The Journal of Sexual Medicine evaluated previous research to better understand how altering breast size influences sexual well-being. The combined data suggest that both physical relief and psychological shifts contribute to a better sexual experience after the procedure.
Breast reduction, medically known as reduction mammoplasty, is one of the most common aesthetic and therapeutic surgeries performed globally. The procedure involves removing excess skin, fat, and glandular tissue to create smaller, more proportionate breasts. Women often seek the surgery to alleviate the physical burdens of having very large breasts, a condition called macromastia. These physical burdens can include chronic back and shoulder pain, skin irritation, and difficulty exercising.
Beyond physical discomfort, excessively large breasts can impact a person’s mental health and body image. Breasts are closely associated with femininity and sexual identity in many cultures. Deviation from societal standards regarding breast size can sometimes lead to psychological distress, low self-esteem, and sexual health challenges. Women may feel self-conscious during intimacy, an internal distraction that can hinder sexual arousal and satisfaction.
While many patients pursue breast reduction hoping to improve their sexual life, previous research on the topic has produced conflicting results. Some studies have reported positive impacts on sexual desire and body image. Other studies found no measurable changes in sexual satisfaction compared to women who did not undergo the surgery.
To clarify these mixed results, a team of researchers based in Iran led the current investigation. The team included Mahdiye Taheri, Zahra Ghorbani, Fatemeh Alavi-Arjas, Maryam Firouzabadi, and Hamid Alavi Majd. They set out to systematically evaluate and synthesize the existing data on how breast reduction affects postoperative sexual function.
The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of medical databases to identify studies published up to April 2025. They specifically looked for original, English-language articles that quantitatively assessed sexual function in women after breast reduction surgery. They excluded studies focusing on breast surgeries performed for cancer treatment or gender affirmation. This exclusion kept the focus strictly on healthy women with symptomatic macromastia, avoiding the overlapping psychological effects of cancer or gender dysphoria.
Their search yielded 13 eligible studies containing data from 676 participants. The studies took place across several countries, including Brazil, Turkey, the United Kingdom, the United States, Italy, Iran, Poland, and Spain.
The review revealed that nine of the 13 studies documented an improvement in sexual function after surgery. Four of the studies reported no notable changes. Many of the included studies used the Female Sexual Function Index, a standardized questionnaire designed to measure domains such as sexual desire, physiological arousal, lubrication, orgasm, satisfaction, and pain. Across the research, women frequently reported enhancements in almost all of these categories following their operations.
For example, one study included in the review found that the percentage of women experiencing clinical sexual dysfunction dropped from 62.5 percent before the surgery to 21.4 percent afterward. Another prospective study conducted in the United States demonstrated an improvement in sexual function in over 68 percent of the women tracked.
Because eight of the studies used similar standardized instruments, the researchers were able to perform a meta-analysis. A meta-analysis combines the statistical data from multiple independent studies to identify overall trends. This combined analysis demonstrated that breast reduction was associated with a 13.27 percent increase in the mean score of sexual function among patients.
The researchers identified several physiological pathways that might explain these outcomes. On a physical level, reducing the volume of the breast can alleviate chronic pain and physical restrictions. This relief removes persistent physical discomfort that can act as a sensory distraction during sexual arousal.
Some evidence also suggests that removing excess tissue can normalize the distribution of sensory nerves in the breast. The nipple-areola complex is heavily innervated and plays a role in triggering the release of oxytocin, a hormone involved in arousal and emotional bonding. Modern surgical techniques aim to preserve these neural pathways, maintaining the physical triggers required for a full sexual response.
Psychologically, the surgery often leads to a reevaluation of body image. Women with large breasts frequently experience “spectatoring,” a cognitive process where attention is diverted from erotic sensation toward continuous self-monitoring of their appearance. This self-surveillance can induce performance anxiety and diminish sensory engagement.
By alleviating appearance-related anxiety, breast reduction allows individuals to engage more fully in sexual experiences. This psychological shift creates a positive feedback loop. Enhanced body image facilitates sexual satisfaction, and positive sexual experiences then reinforce a more cohesive self-concept and better global self-esteem.
The researchers noted that mental health benefits extend beyond the bedroom. One large database study cited by the researchers in their discussion reported that prescriptions for certain antidepressant and anti-anxiety medications dropped from 46.3 percent to 29.5 percent among patients following breast reduction. This alleviation of psychological distress likely establishes a stronger mental foundation for sexual desire.
Partner reactions also play a role in postoperative sexual well-being. Positive reactions from a partner regarding the physical changes can enhance the sexuality-promoting effects of the surgery. Conversely, criticism or neutral reactions can undermine the potential benefits. One study demonstrated that improvements in female sexual function after the operation were accompanied by an increase in their partners’ own sexual function scores.
While the combined data indicate a positive association between breast reduction and sexual function, the results rely primarily on observational studies. Observational research can identify links between variables but cannot definitively prove that the surgery directly caused the improvements in sexual function.
The individual studies included in the review often featured small sample sizes, typically involving fewer than 50 participants. Most of the research also relied on brief follow-up periods, usually checking in with patients just three to six months after their operations. This short timeframe limits the ability to determine if the sexual and psychological benefits persist over the long term or if delayed complications arise later.
The studies varied widely in their design and the surgical techniques used. The available data did not allow the researchers to measure how specific factors, such as the exact volume of tissue removed or the specific surgical methods employed, influenced the final sexual outcomes. Future research will need to record these surgical parameters to help doctors provide personalized advice to patients regarding nerve preservation and physical sensation.
Future studies would also benefit from evaluating more diverse populations. The current body of literature focuses almost entirely on cisgender, heterosexual women. Expanding this research to include LGBTQ+ individuals and women from a wider variety of cultural and socioeconomic contexts would provide a more comprehensive understanding of how breast reduction affects sexual well-being across different demographics.
The study, “Sexual function following reduction mammoplasty: a systematic review and meta-analysis,” was authored by Mahdiye Taheri, Zahra Ghorbani, Fatemeh Alavi-Arjas, Maryam Firouzabadi, and Hamid Alavi Majd.

Ghosts of past reports linger for NT child protection review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
Ghosts of past reports linger for Northern Territory child protection review
Poring over the 62 pages of the Independent Review into the Conduct of the Department of Children and Families report and its 45 recommendations, a multitude of systemic issues for the Northern Territory are made clear.
Underneath all of these complex challenges remains a key issue: accountability.
It's a question that threads through a growing mountain of reports and their hundreds of recommendations made over many decades, detailing failures in reducing harm for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians.
The NT government has committed to acting on all recommendations as a first step.
But the question remains: who has responsibility for making the changes to ensure children are kept safe?
Which leads to a further question.
What are the consequences if change does not happen?
Without an answer to these questions, communities are stuck with the status quo, or worse, having the wrong response applied without adequate means to correct course.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Social Justice Commissioner Katie Kiss has acknowledged the NT government's response, emphasising the need for "implementation that delivers lasting change".
Commissioner Kiss also remarked that "the NT government still has not implemented the recommendations of the 2017 Royal Commission into child protection".
Currently, the consequences of inaction and inappropriate responses are evident in the Closing the Gap measures that remain locked in place, or widening on many counts.
Youth crime, child removal, family and domestic violence patterns across Australia point to significant, systemic flaws in the way those with authority exercise their power.
This was made heartbreakingly clear in the alleged murder of Kumanjayi Little Baby.
WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the image of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of her family.
Tackling the problem at the root
The review's co-authors singled out the immediate need for an audit into current safety plans. This will ensure the appropriate people are given safety roles for the protection of children in the NT.
In the case of Kumanjayi Little Baby, the review found that one person in her family's safety network had a "long criminal history of violence, including five counts of threaten to kill".
Media reports and comments made in NT parliament have named this person as the man now charged with Kumanjayi Little Baby's murder.
Information such as this is of critical importance, so that all steps taken by authorised officers are based on relevant and appropriate processes.
But the co-authors were also determined to say that "the review does not suggest that a prior conviction, of itself, necessarily renders a person unsuitable" for a protective role.
Developing a clear mechanism for assessing the risk — the nature of which type of conviction represents a relevant threat — will be essential.
For a community with high rates of interaction with police, the justice system and incarceration, understanding the implications of this step is significant.
As is recognising the highly mobile and overcrowded nature of many households in communities across the NT.
These considerations sit within a broader landscape that presents myriad challenges for the most vulnerable.
We see children born into families facing significant disadvantage and dysfunction, where even the most basic needs, such as finding a home or shelter and having a means of getting there, are hard to access and becoming more so.
This month has seen the 400-bed YiSSA short-stay accommodation centre closed in Darwin, while the Bush Bus service, which operates between remote communities and Alice Springs, has had funding cut.
Dealing with this is hard enough.
But, as the review also revealed, "the current practice places significant responsibility on the non-offending parent to protect the child" — a burden the parent carries while their own safety is in jeopardy.
National Commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People, Sue-Anne Hunter, puts the onus on the Department of Children and Families.
"The question that needed answering was what the department did with what it knew. Responsibility for violence sits with the people who use it. Responsibility for the response sits with the department. It should never sit with a victim."
It's a view echoed by Muriel Bamblett, the chair of SNAICC, the peak body for community-controlled Indigenous children's services. She highlights the work of violence reduction programs in Victoria that tackle the problem at the root.
"You need behaviour change. You need to be able to work with those communities around preventing violence,"
she said.
"In Victoria, we've got violence reduction now […] It has to take a public health approach."
Rushed remedies
There is much to consider around community and child safety and, with lives in the balance, it is worth looking at the record set so far.
One case stands out: the Northern Territory Emergency Response, or NT Intervention.
When the Howard government suspended Australia's Racial Discrimination Act on June 21, 2007, military units were deployed to discrete Aboriginal communities.
The decision came after the release of the Ampe Akelyernemane Meke Mekarle "Little Children Are Sacred" report, led by Pat Anderson and Rex Wild QC.
Tasked with inquiring into the protection of Aboriginal children from sexual abuse, the co-chairs delivered a comprehensive 316-page report with 97 recommendations.
Clear guidance was provided: "In the first recommendation, we have specifically referred to the critical importance of governments committing to genuine consultation with Aboriginal people in designing initiatives for Aboriginal communities, whether these be remote, regional or urban settings."
That never happened. The legislation was rushed through in two months.
Ten years later, Anderson described the NT Intervention response as a "betrayal" that had led to "further abuse of Aboriginal people. That's what the intervention was".
The NT Intervention framework ended in July 2022 but stands as a stark reminder of the long-lasting impacts that can emerge when change is made without proper consideration of the recommendations.
This is something certainly worth remembering as the wheels turn once again on resolving this most enduring set of challenges.
